*Dīkṣādarśaḥ*. IFP T.N.O. 372.
Folios 1262–1670, copied from a manuscript belonging to Śundaradīkṣitar of Tirunelveli;
this is an important Siddhānta work by Vedajñāna, who lived in... [year].
*Vyāghrapuram* in Tamil Nadu. This work, titled *Dīkṣādarśaḥ*, treats the various types of initiation rites (*dīkṣā*) as described in the Āgamas, citing extensively from them.
I pay homage to Kalkaka Vighneśa, the Lord beloved by Yallamā, the bestower of boons upon all devotees, for the accomplishment of my desired aims.
I worship Śrīmadadabhrasabhānātha, who is honored by Vyāghrapāt and Śeṣa,
along with his power Ānandasarpinī, for the attainment of bliss.
He also honored the masters of the ritualistic tradition (*kriyākāṇḍa*) engaged in lineage succession,
as well as the sage Vedajñāna, who bestows the knowledge of liberation and is a virtuous and true teacher.
Because the scriptures are infinite and impossible to survey in their entirety, the Mirror of Initiation (*dīkṣādarśa*) is taught here for the sake of awakening.
Regarding the cause—
for this reason, I shall hereafter proclaim the sequential procedure for the initiation of Śiva (śivadīkṣā),
which is supreme, removes all sins, and is for the sake of achieving liberation for men.
It serves to destroy all diseases and bestows an abundance of wealth and grain.
Likewise, in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Henceforth, I shall explain [the state] of the unawakened embodied being."
But for one who is bound to all reality and consists of all phenomena, however...
For one who is liberated from the state of a beast and purified of the stains of beginningless impurity, hear these auspicious words concerning the supreme initiation that bestows union with Śiva.
In the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*:
"Through initiation one becomes fit for hearing [the teachings]; through initiation one is capable of worship;
and through initiation the duties of the spiritual stages proceed according to their true purpose."
Through initiation, knowledge is attained; through initiation, one becomes a possessor of supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
Just as initiation bestows liberation, it is the internal means for bestowing knowledge.
Those who have been thoroughly purified by the initiation of Śiva are qualified for everything;
there is no sacred site equal to initiation, and there is no austerity equal to initiation.
There is no dharma equal to initiation; there is no quality equal to initiation;
there is no knowledge equal to initiation; there is no mindfulness equal to initiation.
There is no greater auspiciousness than initiation; there is no lineage equal to initiation.
Even through hundreds of various statements, it is likewise the knowledge and ritual action of initiation.
The four [practices] beginning with *yogacaryā* certainly increase those [powers].
As stated in the *Pauṣkara*:
"Just as by the power of mantras and medicinal herbs, so too for one who is possessed by suppression (*saṃnirodha*), all [that is desired] occurs."
But the cessation of the five [elements] occurs through initiation.
As stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Just as one effects the removal of poison through the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and seed-syllables (*bīja*),
so too does the preceptor effect the excellence of speech in the sacrifice to Śiva."
Just as the eggs of the Dharmya-mantras are burned by those who act according to their strength, so too should the Noble One burn the fettered men through initiation.
In the Parākhyatantra:
"This initiation of the Supreme Lord brings about the destruction of merit and demerit; yet one is not liberated through knowledge alone, nor through yoga, nor through ritual conduct."
And here, liberation for all living beings occurs through initiation;
therefore, by the power of Śiva, liberation is accomplished everywhere.
From this extensive bondage, through its cessation and the establishment of the supreme state, initiation alone liberates one and leads [the soul] upward to the abode of Śiva.
Likewise, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the section concerning the curse of Bhṛgu, it is said: "In this [place],
there is no excellence for men that has not been achieved by others, except for the supreme initiation belonging to Śiva,
which liberates one from the three bonds."

Therefore, liberation comes through initiation alone, and not by means of his worldly actions or austerities. As stated in the Kauśika-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa: "And those men who desire liberation without the purification of the paths (adhva-śuddhi)..."
Though his hand was not holding a staff, he began to strike as he went along.
Just as those deprived of a boat desire to cross the ocean, so does one devoid of the purification of the path strive for liberation through mere benefit.
What is the use of speaking much more on this matter? I say it again and again: one whose self is purified through the purification of the six paths attains liberation, and not otherwise.
In the *Kāśī-khaṇḍa*:

"He who has performed [the pilgrimage] within the five *krośas* of Kāśī is indeed initiated into liberation (*nirvāṇa*). For those who even utter his name, there is always fearlessness; of this there is no doubt."
In the *Vāmana Purāṇa*, Upamanyu says to Vāsudeva: "I shall describe to you the supreme and meritorious sacrament (*saṃskāra*), which purifies all sins and was expounded by Śiva."
Because a person who has properly performed their duty in rites such as worship is thereby purified,
that purification is called the cleansing of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva-pariśodhana*).

In the Vāyupurāṇa, in the dialogue between Upamanyu and Kṛṣṇa: "That knowledge which is the meaning of the Śiva-āgama is called true knowledge; out of compassion for those who have taken refuge in Śiva, it is the means to the highest good and liberation."
Kṛṣṇa:
Now I wish to hear about the supreme Śiva-consecration; it was only briefly indicated during the collection of mantras, not in detail.
In the Varāha Purāṇa, Muktimatprati says to Īśvara:
"The divine initiation of the Pāśupatas and the Pāśupata yoga that arises here as something other than the Vedic path."
The nature of the "good" (sat) form of action is to be understood as that which is free from violent deeds;
for this very reason, it is heard in scripture that even Brahmā and all others were initiated.
As it says in the Raurava:
Their lords are said to be Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra;
the supreme sovereignty over them belongs to the high-souled Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras).
Those who are independent [of external means] recite up to the end of "vidyārājadhirājeśasteti."
Those who are skilled in severing the bonds of the cycle of birth, death,
and saṃsāra [attain it] through mudrās, maṇḍalas, initiations, sacrifices, offerings, and ritual observances.
And there is the concealment by knowledge, arising from the limbs of mantra and tantra,
as well as other divine favors that shine forth from the pure reality.
The Śivas, who are the lords of mantras, bestowed their grace upon them;
and Pitāmaha, having granted them great prosperity, did the same for them.
This supreme knowledge, the cause of the ultimate liberation of Śiva, was [taught] to the sages,
the gods, and the ancestors in due order.
At the command of the Grandfather, the sages, their doubts severed, bestowed this great tantra, the king of tantras, upon those of great soul.
Those who know the rules and procedures for initiation proclaim this to human beings;
it has issued forth from the mere thread [of light] originating from the moon-ray of Śiva.
O Lord, in the *Niśvāsa*, some say that the Goddess is the supreme illuminator of the eggs of the flood of nooses and darkness; who were the gods, demons, humans, Vidyādharas,
Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Sarpas initiated by her?
And the yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, piśācas, uragas, and kinnaras.
O Mahādeva, even the Guhyakas, who are cruel and destructive,
will certainly become [favorable] to this deity once one has been initiated by means of this mantra.
Therefore, O Blessed One, I wish to hear about that Lord; for it was told to me regarding Vijaya that Brahmā was initiated therein.
In the Niśvāsa, it is declared that where one is initiated by Na, Nda, Ra, or Ro, from him [proceed] Kubera,
Varuṇa, Yama, and even the two Aśvins.
O highly fortunate one, the Gaṇas and the Rudras were initiated there;
likewise, the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and those belonging to the Svāyambhuva [Manvantara] were present.
Two names have been proclaimed for him, wherein Dakṣa and the others were initiated,
as well as the lords of creatures and those who are the sons of Brahmā.
The initiated and those bound by vows, as well as the Asuras constantly, along with the Rākṣasas,
Gandharvas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Kiṃnaras.
The Garuḍas and other twice-born beings who reside in the worlds are divided into five classes, and they are indeed initiated in the Āgneya [tantra].
The Mothers, the houses, and those hosts of obstacles and the like are indeed proclaimed in the *Kiraṇa*,
where the Ādityas are consecrated.
Through the recitation of mantras, all those established as practitioners have attained accomplishment; this has also been fully declared in the *Makuṭa* by the proponents of the *Nidāna-kṣetra*.
It is always practiced by sages through mantra-rituals up to the very end of the throat.
Likewise, in the *Śaiva Purāṇa*, in the *Aumasaṃhitā*: "O son of Aditi, having received initiation into the Śaiva path from you, even Indra and the other gods [attained their status]."
The inhabitants of Tripura became solely devoted to the worship of the Śiva-liṅga.
For them, worship of Śiva has been performed, and their husbands are devoted to their wives as deities.
Regarding the method of initiation in the *Dīkṣottara*:
"The conjunction, the generation, the enjoyment of experiences, the severing of bonds, and likewise the extraction."
In the rite of initiation, it is fivefold.
Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*:
"The piercing of the bonds (*pāśas*) which possess the authority of binding occurs through the impossibility [of their persistence] once they have been heard [by the mantra].
Initiation is the supreme separation; it is the obstruction [of the soul] during the severing of bonds. It is the supreme purification, liberation, manifestation, and the ultimate atonement.
Having performed the expiation that restrains the power of the multitude of bonds, one should cause the Light to shine forth by means of the path that severs the ripening [of karma].
From such scriptural and Puranic statements, liberation is attained through initiation (*dīkṣā*) and not through Vedic sacraments (*saṃskāra*). Likewise, in the *Devīmata*:
"Where there is conduct and inquiry according to the Śiva-āgamas for those who have been initiated, the Vedic [rites] become redundant."
Likewise, there are mantras and other Vedic rites.
Wherever the Vedic mantras are the primary authority for a Brāhmaṇa, that which is spoken by the Ṛṣis is not a scripture superior to those [mantras].
Attached to that, deluded, and afflicted, those proponents of duality suffer;
for they are flawed purifiers, since they are stained by their state of being bound souls (paśus).
In this matter, since our Vedic mantras serve as the authority for the sacraments, no distinction can be perceived between the castes and those who have undergone the sacraments.
The primacy belongs to the knowledge of Śiva, and the essence is the reality of Śiva;
the knowledge that has entered the stage of Śiva—that is the scripture approved by Śiva.
Likewise, in the *Cintya-viśva*:
"The forty sacraments (*saṃskāras*) are to be performed even by Brahmins and the other [castes]; first for one's own wife, and immediately after that, the *garbhādhāna* (conception rite)."
The *puṃsavana*, the *sīmantonnayana*, and immediately after that the *viṣṇubali*; likewise the *jātakarman*, the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), and the rite of first going outside (*niṣkrāmaṇa*).

The first feeding of solid food, the departure on a journey, the tonsure ceremony, the initiation into Vedic study, the ritual release [of the student], and the funeral rites— these are the sacraments.
The final refuge, the gift of a cow, the ritual bath, and likewise the marriage—
these are proclaimed as the eighteen purificatory rites (saṃskāras) of the body.

The sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to the spirits, as well as the sacrifice to humans and the sacrifice to Brahman— these are proclaimed as the great sacrifices (mahāyajñas).
The Sthālīpāka, the Āgrayaṇa, the Caitra, the Āśvayuja,
as well as the Aṣṭakā and the Parvan— these seven are the Pākayajñas.
The Agnyādheya, the Darśa, and likewise the Paurṇamāsa;
the Āgrayaṇa and the Aṣṭakā, followed immediately by the Cāturmāsya.
The Nirūḍhapaśubandha, the Sautrāmaṇi, and the Rathāntaka, as well as these seven Haviḥ-yajñas, and likewise the Soma-saṃsthās.
The Agniṣṭoma, the Atyagniṣṭoma, the Ṣoḍaśin, the Vājapeya, the Atirātras, and beyond that, the Āptoryāma.
The seven sacrifices ending with the Soma-saṃsthā have been proclaimed by the wise; furthermore, there are forty Vedic purificatory rites (saṃskāras) to be performed in their proper sequence.
Indeed, for one who has performed [the rite] according to the stated method, liberation is attained through initiation alone.
As it is said in the *Sarvajñānottara*: "Just as copper attains the state of gold when the alchemical elixir (*rasa*) is perfected."
Likewise, through the connection with the ignorance of the Self, one attains the state of Śiva.
In Raurava:
"Having thus attained the Śaiva path, which arises from initiation and mantra, the initiated best of men does not undergo birth again."
When the body has dissolved, having become Śiva and being endowed with the nature of Śiva,
one attains the bliss of Śiva and becomes fit for non-duality.
Just as a river carrying its waters away becomes salty upon reaching the ocean,
it attains that state of saline water through the power of the great sea.
In this way, one whose body and self are dissolved indeed attains Śiva;
just as from the union of a river and the ocean, no separation ever arises.
Thus ends the introductory procedure in the *Dīkṣādarśa* composed by Vedajñāna, the son of Vāmadeva. Regarding the characteristics of a Śaiva here:
since initiation (*dīkṣā*) depends upon Śaiva conduct, the characteristics of a Śaiva are stated here.
Likewise, in the Vīratantra:
"The Śaivas are to be known as sevenfold; hear now their divisions:
the first is the Anādi-Śaiva, the second is the Ādi-Śaiva."
The third is Mahāśaiva, the fourth is Anuśaivaka;
the fifth is Vāntaraśaiva, and the sixth is called Pravara.
The seventh and the final division among the Śaivas is proclaimed as follows:
the Anādiśaiva (beginningless Śaiva), the Saśiva (Śaiva with Śiva), the Ādiśaiva (original Śaiva), and the Śivadvija (twice-born by Śiva).
The Brahmin who is a great Śaiva, as well as the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, are declared to be Anuśaivas;
the Śūdra is considered to be Antarasmṛta.
The Svarṇa, the Ṣaṣṭhamadhya, the Kulāla, and likewise the Pāraśava—these are declared to be the Pravaras; now the Antyaśaivas are described.
Those castes other than these are remembered as the Antya-Śaivas;
their nature, beginning with the Savarṇas, will be demonstrated later on.
In this regard, let it be understood from the Kāmika:
"The lineage-guru (sāntānika) is declared to be the benefactor of all;
those such as Śikha and others who were initiated at the time following the [initial] creation."
The twice-born who arise from that lineage and are devoted to Śiva are known as the Śaiva-santānika; they are to be understood as the Ādi-śaivas, remembered as the benefactors of all.
One born into an original Śaiva lineage is the most excellent for performing installations and other rites;
likewise, those initiated among all mortals are preeminent for consecrations and festivals.
In the rites of snapping the fingers, sprinkling, elsewhere, atonement, consecration, the exposition of a scripture, and so forth—
whether for one’s own sake or for the sake of others.
Regarding the cause:
those who have been initiated by Śiva are called Śiva-brāhmaṇas. Regarding the lineage—

The rites beginning with installation and ending with worship must be performed by one who is a primary Śaiva; for if anyone should cause them to be done otherwise, it will indeed lead to malevolent magic.
In the *Suprabheda*,
marriage is declared to be of eight kinds by Śiva, the Supreme Self; of these, the first...
But for a high-souled Brāhmaṇa, it is fourfold.
One should perform even the work of an Asura, but one should avoid three other things: a woman who is well-behaved, endowed with beauty, born of a noble family, and possessed of kinsmen.
For a wise man, having taken a virtuous bride who is not of the same lineage (*asagotrā*),
so it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"Having recognized that she is of the same lineage (*samānagotra*) and of the same ancestral line (*pravarā*), one should perform the union provided there is no blood relation."
One should always choose a maiden who shares the same lineage (gotra) and ancestral sages (pravara).
If she is married, he should protect her like a mother;
her protection must be ensured through food, clothing, and other necessities.
For the purpose of purifying the defects of marriage, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow,
provided that any [sexual] union has been committed with her through negligence.
The atonement for that is now declared here; upon a single occurrence, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
"A thousand [recitations] for a terrible mantra, but two thousand at a wedding," and so forth is demonstrated there in detail; let that suffice here. Likewise, in the *Vīratantra*:
One should never establish a matrimonial alliance with one who shares the same lineage (*sagotra*);
for even those born into such a union cause that family to be afflicted.
O best of Brahmins, one should never perform the initiation (*dīkṣā*) for those sages who have been born again and again as Śiva-Brahmins.

Having completed the presentation [of the offerings], one should worship Śiva within the mandala; one should then cause the twice-born devotees of Śiva to perform the ceremonial bathing for the sake of purifying the limbs.
In the *Dīpta*:
"I shall explain the divisions of the Tantras of the Śaivas and others in their proper order: namely, the Pāśupata, the Kāpāla, and likewise the Lākula."
Kāmika, Yogaja, Cintya, and likewise Ajita as the cause; Dīpta, Sūkṣma, Sahasra, Aṃśumat, and Suprabhedaka.
The Nārasiṃha, the Niśvāsa, the Svāyambhuva, and the Anala; the Raurava, the Vīrabhadra, the Makuṭa, and the Vijaya.
The Candrajñāna, the Bimba, the Prodyotālalita, as well as the Siddha,
the Santāna, the Sarvokta, and indeed the Vātula-tantra.
The Kirāṇa and the Pārameśvara, numbering twenty-eight, are declared to be the divisions of Śaivism;
now hear likewise of the Pāśupata.
The Prājāpatya, the Pāśupata, the expanded Padmasaṃhitā, the Vāsiṣṭha,
the Kāśyapa-kalpa, the Vārāha, and the Bhārgavāntara.
The Praphullavāsava, the one proclaimed by Vāyu, as well as the Vāruṇa,
the Bārhaspatya, and the Pārameśvara— these are the sixteen.

The Māyā system has been declared as the Pāśupata; now listen, O observer of good vows, to the Kāpāla, which was established in a former kalpa, consisting of five parts, and is the authoritative secret of Śiva.
*Sūham*, *Ādarśana*, *Padma*, *Kanakaśailaka*, *Nirukta*, *Suprāpa*, and *Siddhārtha*— these indeed are the fourteen [treatises].
The Kāpāla has indeed been explained; now hear, O Anala, about the Lākula, which is the Great Vidyā, superior in its ritual action, timing, and qualities.
The Varāha, the Kaumāra, the Viśvasārottara, and likewise the Saṃvartaliṅgakalpa— this is said to be the ninefold division.
Among these four divisions, by whichever [method] one has been initiated, by that very same [method] one should perform the installation and other rites according to the Tantra.
Likewise, regarding the cause:
"In these divisions of Śaivism, by whichever [division] they have been initiated, by that same tantra the rites such as installation (sthāpanā) and so forth must be performed."
In the *Vīratantra*: "Even among these various tantras, there is a mixing of each one. This is called the 'mixing of tantras' (*tantra-saṃkara*); one should not perform such a mixing of tantras."
Through the fault of mixing tantras, the kingdom and its king perish; the division of Śaivism is established as twenty-eightfold.
And the mixing of these [elements] does not result in any fault;
one should perform [the rite] according to that tantra by which the *prārabdha* (commenced action) was initiated. If it has not been stated [in that], [one should follow] another.
And one should perform all of that according to the Tantra.
That which is not stated [in one text] but is not contradictory should be accepted from another *saṃhitā*,
provided that the ritual action is being performed by one person and there is no other cause [for following a different version].
If that which was performed by another person should result in a confusion of teachers (*ācāryasaṃkara*),
it occurs where there is a contradiction regarding the very non-performance due to deficiency.
That ritual action must be performed by his disciple according to the scriptures;
if it is performed by anyone else, there is no doubt that the performer will perish.
In the *Suprabheda*: "The Siddhānta is indeed the essence of all; it is remembered as the pure and auspicious Tantra.
And these are threefold: Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, and Miśraka."
They are declared to be outsiders to Śaivism, yet they are honored by the Śaivas;
as stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*: "Of Kālakāpālaka and the others, in all the various enumerations."
A Śaiva indeed possesses authority over all, but a non-Śaiva never [possesses it] in any way.
The Śaiva root-āgama and especially the Śruti [declare this].
Likewise, in the Makuta:
"A Śaiva shall have authority over all, both in his own [tradition] and in others. Of others...
However, the qualification for one's own independent [tantras] does exist.
Thus ends the section on the rules for characteristics in the *Dīkṣādarśa*, composed by Vedajñānin, the son of Vāmadeva, a resident of the illustrious city of Vyāghrapura.
(p. 1276) Now, the rules for the characteristics of the preceptor (*ācārya*) are stated.
The characteristics of the teacher are stated in the Bhīmasaṃhitā:
"The characteristics of the teacher should be known as the primordial cause of all; the teacher is the root."
For everything, including the ritual placement and so forth, as well as the ritual action itself.

Therefore, that characteristic must first be examined with particular care; for when [an image] is installed by one of fierce intellect who is devoid of the [proper] characteristics, [it leads to misfortune].
If that [misfortune] is caused by karma, then there will be calamities such as those arising from the location;
therefore, one should perform worship and other rites with a person endowed with the appropriate characteristics.
By a teacher who is gracious, distinguished, and preeminent; and the auspicious characteristics of such a distinguished teacher.
In all the Āgamas, this is proclaimed for the sake of renown:
"The disciple who has been initiated into Nirvāṇa is a yogic master through his union with the Guru. (Cintyaviśve)
There is no entitlement to the worship of the linga for the sake of others.
Regarding the cause:
a maiden from the midst of the Himalayas [obtains] the pure [soma] produced from the black antelope; he who is born there as the primordial deity is called the best of teachers.
Likewise, in the Sarvajñānottara:
"In which [place] the black-colored deer upon whom the Lord moves...
One should know that region to be fit for sacrifice where it is presided over by Brahmins,
where there are Brahmins of virtuous conduct and ascetics whose wealth is their austerity.
Likewise, one should indicate the presence of Śāntideva and other deities, as well as regions of merit and so forth;
the teachers born in those regions and families are authorized by the scriptures.
Likewise, in the Kāmika:
"The illustrious [place] arising from Āyāvarta, endowed with all auspicious marks,
where there are Brahmins of virtuous conduct and ascetics whose wealth is their austerity."
The Vedas exist, and likewise the lands known as Āryāvarta are remembered [as their source].
In the *Sarvajñānottara* it is said:
"One should know that region to be fit for sacrifice which is inhabited by Brahmins."
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"The Gaṅgāravā, Mahītā, Gautamī, Sarasvatī, Yamunā, Kṛṣṇaveṇī, Kāverī,
and likewise the Gaṇḍakī."
The Gautamī, Sarayū, Sindhu, and Devikā— these fourteen are to be known as sacred rivers that bring welfare to all the world.
It was filled with great sages, ritualists, and those whose wealth is austerity;
it was crowded with self-manifested liṅgas and various other deities of the sages.
The lands arising on its banks are considered holy places by the wise.
As stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"Those born in the lineage of Ādiśaiva reside within the five spheres of perception."
One who knows the true meaning of all scriptures, is proficient in the knowledge of Śiva,
understands the reality of the Śiva-siddhānta, and worships Śiva, the sacred fire, and the Guru.
He is thoroughly certain of the single tantra, from ritual action up to gnosis.
One who is skilled in the *kriyāpāda*, engaged in the *caryāpāda*,
has practiced the *yogapāda*, and is devoted to the *jñānapāda*.
In the Mataṅga-tantra, those who know the ritual of their own seats, are intent upon what has been performed,
and have received permission and consecration, are remembered as the bestowers of grace.
Likewise, it is stated in the Parākhya: "The supreme Guru, endowed with the power of the action of crossing over [the ocean of existence], is one who possesses the highest complexion;
he is faithful, pure, skillful, initiated by the initiation of the three, and wise."
One who is authorized by the scriptures, a knower of reality, skilled in the subsequent procedures,
proficient in the rites of the six paths, and excellent in the ritual of the Caṇḍayāga;
One who knows the procedure for initiation, who understands worship and fire-rituals,
who is learned in the Śiva-āgamas regarding the lineage, who is wise, devoted to the worship of Śiva, and intent on meditation upon Śiva.
He is constantly proficient in the scriptures of Śiva.
In the fourth [quarter], he is one who has mastered the six limbs of the Veda, the Dharmaśāstras, and the Purāṇas;
he is a knower of the treatises on Logic (Nyāya) and Mīmāṃsā—the fourteen bases of knowledge.
The Bhāṣya consists of four [parts], and likewise eighteen are designated [as its branches];
all the Yoga-śāstras, as well as Vedānta and Jyotiṣa, are likewise included.
The sixty-four arts, as well as the six types of action, the science of archery,
the science of navigation, and the Soma-siddhānta.
Having understood the Lākula system alone, as well as the Pāñcarātra,
and this path of established doctrine (siddhānta), one becomes a knower of foreign lands.
In the Kāmika [Tantra]:
"The son of the Guru, whose soul is purified by the tradition (saṃpradāya), is praised;
he is one who knows the capacity for the liṅga and so forth, and is well-discriminating (*vibhakta*)."
One who is proficient in the *Kāmika* and other scriptures, endowed with the realization of Śiva-knowledge,
and is learned; one who, according to the *Mataṅga*, knows the truth regarding what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, is established in that purpose, and is skillful in ritual action.
He is free from passion and devoid of envy.
One who is fully engaged in the reality of the supreme boon, devoted to the teaching of Śiva,
skilled in the meaning of all the scriptures, and turned away from the scriptures of the bound souls (paśus).
With his mind solely devoted to the Śiva scriptures, intent on the welfare of all living beings,
he practiced the science of architecture (vāstu-vidyā) and was expert in the cultivation of rice fields.
Endowed with all proper conduct, compassionate toward ascetics,
a Brāhmaṇa from the Raurava region— a holy land— possessing complete limbs, pure, and proficient in the analysis of words and sentences.
The teacher is one who knows the means of valid cognition and has mastered the Saṃhitā.

The best of gurus is one who meditates on the *lakṣa* (the sacred syllable), bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation; the mediocre one knows its meaning; and the lowest would be one who merely knows its phonetic form.
Alternatively, one who has mastered the *Saṃhitā*, or is endowed with the instruction of a hundred thousand verses,
[should perform it]. This *Saṃhitā* consists of four quarters and is preceded by the *Kāmika*.
Likewise, it has been stated by Rāmakarṇācārya in his commentary, the *Kiraṇa*:
"That [work] in which the accomplishment [of the mantra] is demonstrated through the division of its four feet according to their names is called a *saṃhitā*."
In the *Cintyaviśva*:

"Because one should practice correctly knowledge (*jñāna*), yoga (*yoga*), ritual action (*kriyā*), and conduct (*caryā*), it is therefore called 'worship' (*ārcāya*) for the sake of the welfare of all beings."
Because he causes [others] to understand the meanings of the treatises and thereby establishes right conduct, and because he practices them himself,
he is therefore called an *ācārya*.
Likewise, in the *Niśvāsa*:
"Because he himself practices [it] and shows the conduct (*ācāra*), he is indeed called a teacher (*ācārya*); therefore, he is recited as such in the scriptures."
In the *Kālottara*:

"O Six-faced One, even a guru who is devoid of all auspicious marks is declared in the Śiva scriptures to be authorized for the installation of icons and other rites, provided he knows the meaning of the Śiva teachings."
One who is endowed with all auspicious marks but does not know the Śiva-weapon is neither a yogin,
nor one purified by vows, nor is he called an ācārya.
In the *Niśvāsa*:
"The preceptor should be one who knows the mantras and tantras, skilled in reasoning and refutation, conversant with the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*,
and one who has conquered anger and subdued the senses."
The steadfast one who endures all afflictions, possessing the great heart of the mantra-tantras, is a knower of the mantra rituals and is expert in the rites of expiation.
One who constantly awakens the ignorant through instruction on purity and right conduct is accepted as a guru, even if he is devoid of all auspicious physical marks, provided he possesses knowledge.
In the Devikālottara it is said:
"Even one devoid of all auspicious marks is accepted as a guru if he possesses knowledge; he who discriminates between the caste-qualified and the unqualified becomes a sinner."
With his mind and soul solely intent on the Śiva scriptures, turning away from the scriptures of the bound souls (paśu), he is single-mindedly devoted to bestowing grace,
humble in spirit, and free from envy.

One who is firm in his vow, learned in ritual action, wise, highly skilled in the rites of initiation, and a knower of the reality of Śiva’s true nature— he alone is traditionally recognized as the consecrator (sthāpaka).
In the Vīratantra:
"Because he is fit for the installation of the Liṅga, he is called the 'Installer' (sthāpaka). The Ācārya is indeed Śiva; Śiva is said to be the Ācārya."
He who understands non-difference is said to be distinct from the [lower] castes.
Likewise, in the Kāmika:
"The teacher should be Śiva himself; there is indeed no one other than Aghora. He who perceives..."
He who attains the realization of the distinction between these two shall reach the ultimate goal.
In the Niśvāsa:
"There is no difference between the two—the teacher and Śiva. Through the exhalation and inhalation accompanied by the syllable 'Sa', the partless (niṣkala) arises."
In him all sciences are contained, and he himself is the supreme Śiva; he is complete in all branches of knowledge and skilled in the meaning of every kind of science.
The Śivas beginning with Ananteśa do not at all create any distinction between the teacher, the mantra, the knowledge of Śiva, and Śiva himself.
All deities consist of mantra, and all auspicious ones consist of mantra; one should worship them in the Śiva-sacrifice with a mantra whose essence is Śiva.
Those who recite the Śiva-saṃhitā without having attained the state of Śiva, and who perform initiation without understanding it—
both the disciple and the preceptor go to a lower state.
The physician who performs a treatment without himself correctly understanding it causes the patient to suffer, and the doctor himself shall not obtain the fruit of his labor.
He who is skilled in both knowledge and discernment, even when passing through all states, liberates others from their bonds,
having shaken off all impurities by means of knowledge.
Likewise, regarding the ritual action in the Karma-kāṇḍa:
"A householder who is born in a good region, possesses an excellent form, is devoted to pure knowledge and action,
is patient, born of a noble family, pure-hearted, and a knower of the Siddhānta."

A Guru who knows the distinctions between the six types of disciples, who is likewise perfected in the rites of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), who is indifferent to worldly success, and whose meditation consists of the nature of Śiva—he alone is to be accepted as a teacher.
Here, the rule regarding the definition of the qualified candidate is stated: [it applies] to the ten classes beginning with the Brahmins.
The gravity [of the offense] has been stated. Likewise, in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"Among Brahmins and the other [castes], among those wearing the Yajurveda, and among the six [groups] beginning with the *anuloma*...
The status of teacher (ācārya) is prescribed for these ten types of persons.
Likewise, in the Kāmika:
"The four [castes] beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, and those who are considered to be born in the natural order (anuloma).
And in the Sarvajñānottara:
The Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are the most excellent; those born from the feet [the Śūdras] are to remain in the state of initiation (dīkṣā).
Mortals of other castes are inferior, following the sequence of the three [higher] varṇas.
Initiation must certainly not be performed; if a guru should do so out of greed, he goes to hell, and the initiate shall obtain no fruit.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"By whomsoever this distinction of castes was devised across all the nine divisions of Bhārata,
it does not exist in other countries."
Therefore, the distinction between castes is merely a matter of six conceptualizations; here, the distinction of castes is imagined according to the sequence of high and low.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"One should know that the *Savarṇa* is first, the *Ambaṣṭha* follows as second, and the *Pāraśava* is third; these are born from the Brāhmaṇa."

And those two are born as the *madgura* and the one with a fierce name for the king; for the Vaiśya, they are known as the *cūcūka*. Thus, there are exactly six [castes] born in the direct order (*anuloma*).

Having obtained a red-skinned maiden according to the prescribed rite and with the recitation of mantras, a Brahmin who begets a son of the same caste therein is honored among those born in the direct order of castes (anuloma).
He is to be known as a Brāhmaṇa, and he is remembered as a performer of the Atharvan rites. From the union of a yellow-complexioned woman and a Brāhmaṇa, one called an Ambaṣṭha is born.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:

"A twice-born man, devoted to his daily obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), should not perform [medical treatment] for one who has not been initiated; thereafter, a physician of the same caste may do so by appointment."
One born from a Brahmin father and a Śūdra mother is known as a Pāraśava;
he should worship Bhadrakālī according to the path taught in the Gulśāstra.
In every house, during the afternoon, he should call out, "Give alms! He should practice this daily until the end of his life.
Born from a king through a Vaiśya maiden, he is called a Madgura; his royal insignia do not exist, and his livelihood depends upon the Vaiśya.
Born from a Śūdra woman by a king, he is known as Ugra;
he should always cause the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras to perform service.
By the king's command, one should inflict punishment; indeed, one should punish without hesitation.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"One born from the union with a *kṛṣṇā* woman is indeed a *cūcuka*; [the others are] *śāka* and *kāṣṭha*."
They subsist on grass and other wild-growing plants.
Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras born of pure lineages—
these alone should be known as teachers, and never others.
In that very same work, the *Jātinirṇaya* (p.
1285), it is proclaimed: "The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are thus described."
And while they are performing these [rites], he should appoint them to the office of preceptor (ācārya).
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"O Six-faced One, Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are all pure as archers; according to their respective order, they may all serve as teachers."
In the Parākhyatantra it is said:
"A Brahmin who knows the purpose of the rite of self-identification (ahaṅkāra) may initiate all castes; a Kṣatriya, three [castes]; and a Vaiśya, two, including the Śūdra."
The Brāhmaṇa is traditionally remembered as the perpetual benefactor of all castes; among his own caste, the three [higher] teachers come first, followed by the others, such as the king and so forth.

Those among the three castes who are disciplined are considered to belong to that [highest] caste; initiation, however, should be performed for all those devotees of Śiva who are practitioners of yoga.
"The statement cited from Parāśara, 'for the three castes but not for Śūdras or those of the lowest birth,' is incorrect;
it refers exclusively to the subject of Śūdras."
Thus it is stated in the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā:
"For wicked Śūdras, those of the lowest castes, and especially for the fallen,
as well as for those born of mixed castes, purification by the path (adhva-śuddhi) is not prescribed."
If those [disciples] possess genuine devotion toward Śiva, the supreme cause, one should perform the purification of their bonds by means of offering water from his feet and other such rites.
In this regard, for those born in accordance with the natural order (*anuloma*) among the twice-born, or for those who are disciplined,
the mere performance of rites such as the purification of the path is appropriate for their own lineage.
In the *Suprabheda*:

"However, those Śūdras who do not drink liquor, who are devoted to the practices of a Śaiva teacher, and who are devotees of Śiva—for them the rite of initiation should be performed; otherwise, it is not."
Likewise, in the Parākhya:
"One who does not drink liquor, is of noble birth, and is constantly devoted to dharma should be known as equal to a Śūdra or a Kṣatriya; all others are far more blameworthy than him."
In the Vāyavīya Saṃhitā:
"Those belonging to the four castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, who are endowed with the Śiva-śāstras and are averse to the Paśu-śāstras, are proclaimed as Ācāryas."
In the Kālottara it is said:
"Initiation involving ritual action (kriyāvatī) is prescribed for the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa;
however, one should avoid the role of the *hautr* priest for artisans (*kāruka*) and others due to the risk of physical contact."
And thus, grace should be bestowed by all four teachers.
In the *Kāmika*:
"In this way, [the initiation] has been described and proclaimed as the liberator from all sins. There are four [levels of] knowledge (*vidyā*)."
And those which are considered to be in accordance with the natural order.
Those born of the Nyāya lineage or the Mūḍha caste are eligible for initiation;
however, for those of the lowest castes (antyaja), there shall be no officiation by the Hotṛ priest, but rather initiation through the gaze alone.
In the *Kiraṇa*, [regarding] Garuḍa (p.
"Tell me, who possesses the weightiness (*gurutva*) in the midst of the four syllables?"
Īśvara:
Here, the status of being a teacher for all four castes is declared. One who favors the fourfold group beginning with the Brāhmaṇas is considered a twice-born (dvija).
Among these three, the Kṣatriya [is superior] by two [stages], the Vaiśya by one, and the Śūdra by his own birth;
such is the favor toward one's own wife and others, according as one avoids [the lower].
And thus, the favor should be performed by all four teachers,
since the mantra is independent, as is its meditative cultivation.
Just as mantras bestow grace through their inherent nature, so too do they for even one born of the lowest caste; however, for such a person, initiation must be mental.
One should not, out of contact with artisans, imagine [the presence of] the Hotṛ priest;
for if one knows their supreme devotion, yet acts out of greed, one incurs fault.
In the Sūtasaṃhitā: "O bull among men, it is proclaimed that for all other men as well,
upon seeing a temple of the deity, a prostration should be performed."
In the Vātula:
"The class of those born blind should perform [the rite] for all [deceased] after having seen the stūpa.
In the Aṃśumatī:
The gross linga and the vimāna, the subtle linga which is Sadāśiva, and the auspicious linga at the base of the offering altar— these are said here to be the threefold linga.
In the subtle [level]:
"The body is called the palace; the embodied one is known as the liṅga. There is no difference between the two; therefore, one should meditate in this manner."

Pervading [the universe] in the form of both the pervaded and the pervader, the linga alone is the object of veneration; it is traditionally remembered as the very form of Śiva, extending from its golden base up to its pinnacle.
In the *Kiraṇa*: "For the destruction of all sins, one should resort to the temple of Śiva.
In the *Mataṅga*:
Furthermore, those Śūdra men who, out of devotion, worship the Māheśvara Liṅga with prostrations— they too become lords of the six classes.
Having reached the abode of the Lord of Umā, they rejoice in various enjoyments; those who desire Śiva should look upon the devotees of Śiva as being like Śiva himself.
Established by means of auspicious mantras by the Guru, who is the very embodiment of Śiva, they all possess identical qualities; nevertheless, this distinction is stated.
On this point, what is relevant is stated in the *Kāmika*:

"In the worship of all deities, a Brahmin who is a Śaiva from the very beginning is considered the Guru; [likewise] the three castes, beginning with the Brahmin, [are eligible] for initiation and for installation."
In the initiation ceremony, a Brāhmaṇa is desired for Kṣatriyas and others, a Kṣatriya for Śūdras and Vaiśyas, and a Vaiśya for Śūdras; this is also prescribed within their own respective castes.
Likewise, in the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*:
"The status of being a teacher here is declared for all four castes; however, among all castes, the twice-born is considered the benefactor."
A Kṣatriya may initiate three [disciples], a Vaiśya two, and a Śūdra one born of his own caste;
thus should the grace be bestowed by all four types of preceptors.
The three classes beginning with the Brahmin have the right to perform the installation of a mobile liṅga for their own sake—
If a Śūdra is a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika), he is qualified for the installation of a Bāṇaliṅga according to the Kāmika [Tantra];

likewise in the Svārtheṣṭi and in the installation of a mobile liṅga (calaliṅga). These three—[the aforementioned rites]—as well as the Śūdra-initiation (śūdradīkṣā) and the mobile liṅga for one's own sake, are permitted even for a Śūdra.
Or, even if the installer is not a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) regarding the vision of the Bāṇaliṅga,
provided he is well-versed in all mantras along with their traditional lineages, and especially in the knowledge of Śiva;
Even for a Śūdra householder, eligibility exists only for the Nityeṣṭi; here too, it is proclaimed that [the rites] are performed with mantras devoid of [specific] reverence.
Some say that the word *nāda* refers to the *praṇava*; that is incorrect, for it is heard in scripture that the letter *ha* is *nāda*. Likewise, in the *Kāraṇa*:
"It is said that *nāda* is the letter *ha*, while that which begins with *nāda* consists of the letter *sa* [and] the cruel syllable."
From the letter *kṣa* comes the digit-syllable, which is the letter *ma*.
By her, [the mantra] was spoken with many syllables:
"The sky, the crown, the sun, the illusion of space ending in Śiva, the *lakula* in the ether,
the fivefold hundred-thousand-fold resonance of the vital breath, and also the heart of Śiva."
They say that the seed-syllable (bīja) of the Heart is Śiva, and the Manu-bhuvaneśī-niṃbara is the Liṅga;

they call this the consecration (abhiṣeka) in the Kāmika [Tantra]. Yet, it is said that one who is unfit for this [consecration] is certainly unfit for installation and other rites. Herein lies the prohibition of the consecration for a Śūdra householder. In the context of the consecration of an Ācārya—
O Brahmin, one should then consecrate the twice-born in the north of the great city,
the Kṣatriyas in the east, and the Vaiśyas in the direction of Yama (the south).
But the Śūdra [should worship] in the western direction; all [the deities] are situated in the northeastern quarter.
Thus, O Brahmin, it has been declared in the *Pārameśvara* [treatise] concerning the *Pauṣkara*.
Likewise, in the Kālottara:
"One who has been thus consecrated— whether a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya,
or even a Śūdra— is qualified for the installation [of icons] and other rites."
Regarding these, the wise should not entertain such conceptual discrimination; rather, they should cause [the teaching] to be heard, meditate accordingly, and enter into the state of realization.

Thus, because the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of a householder Śūdra is established here, it should not be argued that this statement refers to a Śūdra who is a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika*); for [the text states]: "Of all four castes, whether they bear the marks of ascetics (*liṅgin*) or are householders (*gṛhin*)."

Because there is a contradiction with such statements as "the status of an *ācārya* does not exist in Śiva," which are established in the Siddhānta, and with those passages that establish the status of the preceptor (*guru*) for both the student (*brahmacārin*) and the householder (*gṛhastha*) among all social classes (*varṇas*). Therefore, it is thus:

In accordance with the plural number [of the word *vidhavā*], it must necessarily be admitted that the prohibition of the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of a householder Śūdra found in the *Kāmika*, which establishes the prohibition of installation (*sthāpanā*), serves as a proof by way of the *kaimutika-nyāya*. Now, regarding all four [castes]...
The claim regarding the superiority of castes is untenable, because of the censure [found] in the statement establishing that only a Brāhmaṇa may be a preceptor. As it says in the Merutantra:
"In this matter, there is a certain distinction: the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya [are superior] to the Śūdra; among these..."
One should never perform initiation even for one who has received all other teachings.
O Goddess of the Gods, some were initiated by a Kṣatriya, some by a Vaiśya, and some were initiated by a Śūdra, yet they went to the abode of Yama.
Having undergone hundreds of millions of births, one will certainly enter hell; therefore, one should cause a Brahmin who is opposed to the Vedas to undergo initiation.
In the *Mokṣakārikā*:
"Regarding the efficacy of initiation here, all four social classes (varṇas) possess the qualification;
however, regarding the status of a guru, it is proclaimed that only the Brāhmaṇa is qualified."
In the *Svāyambhuva*: "Then the excellent teacher, the illustrious and most handsome elder brother... In the *Mṛgendra*:

"An excellent twice-born man born in a holy land"—if it is argued that this establishes the status of the Guru for all four castes, we say: "Not so. These statements establish the preeminence of the Brāhmaṇa as the Guru;
they do not intend to prohibit the status of other castes as Gurus. Nor indeed...

It must be explained how the scriptural statement regarding the descent into hell for one who receives initiation from a Kṣatriya or similar person [is to be understood]. That statement also has the purpose of prohibiting initiation from anyone other than a Brāhmaṇa when a Brāhmaṇa is unavailable; it does not mean that [initiation] from a lower caste is superior to [that from] a higher caste.
Either the initiation [of a Śūdra] is intended to be a prohibition regarding caste,
or else the scriptural statements establishing that teachers may be obtained by all castes according to the sequence of their own respective castes would lack authority.

Therefore, by way of this incidental discussion, the authority of both [statements] is established; and conversely, the Brāhmaṇa possesses preeminence as a guru even among all his own castes. Furthermore, in the absence of a Brāhmaṇa, the status of teacher belongs even to Kṣatriyas and others according to the sequence of their own respective castes.
This established position is accepted by all; likewise, it has been determined and demonstrated by all the teachers who composed the manuals (*paddhati*).
In the *Kiraṇa*:
"Śiva, the supreme cause, is declared to be the benefactor of all; as for those castes beginning with the twice-born, they exist in states of relative deficiency or excellence."
If the result arises from the impression (saṃskāra) alone, why would it not be so? Or else, how could there be a variation in those impressions due to deficiency or excess?

O Blessed One, the consecration of a living being is not considered to apply to his birth or his body; if it were applied to the birth alone, then [the rite would be complete] in that single instance...
[dīkṣā].
Because he has attained the state beyond birth and death, he is not subject to rebirth;
thus, Śiva is declared to be the grace of pure consciousness, the benefactor of all.

Among the four stages of life (*āśrama*), the status of preeminence belongs to the student (*brahmacārin*) and the householder (*gṛhastha*), and not to the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) or the renunciant (*saṃnyāsin*). As it is stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Only two types of practitioners—the householder and the student—are the ones who perform grace for the world."
Neither a wandering mendicant nor an ascetic [is permitted].
Likewise, in the Kālottara:
"Among all castes, the householder is declared to be the best guru;
the lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) is to be known as inferior, and the materialist (bhautika) especially so."
However, the status of the *vānaprastha* and *vatī* [initiations] is never considered to be that of a guru.
As stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*: "Listen, O Six-faced One, to the reality of how enjoyment and liberation exist."
The celibate student, the householder, and the supreme teacher.
p.

1293) These two [types of practitioners] are also qualified for initiation (*dīkṣā*) and installation (*pratiṣṭhā*); however, supernatural power (*vibhūti*) belongs only to those whose minds are averse to liberation.
The celibate student (brahmacārī) is to be known as a guru, and the householder (gṛhastha) likewise is of two kinds here;
for those of the preceding castes and stages of life who remain steadfast in their respective duties.

Liberation is traditionally held to be common to all who possess knowledge of the reality of the means; however, that which pertains to ascetics is for the sake of those householders who have not yet attained [that knowledge].
It is the householder alone whom those seeking the fruits of ritual injunctions serve; for others besides the householder, there is no entitlement to enjoy such fruits.
Therefore, a householder should be treated as a guru by those seeking both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Likewise, in the *Santāna*:
"A householder is superior to one who has become a celibate student (*brahmacārī*)."
One who is firm and pure regarding everything from ritual action up to the knowledge [of reality] within a single tantra.
In the Kaśmīra-tantra:
"A body that is red in color is excellent; one that is dark is middling;
but a body that is entirely black leads to ruin in an instant."
In the *Suprabheda*, it is stated that even a householder should be known as supreme, as well as a material celibate (*bhautikabrahmacārin*). In the *Vīratantra*:
A householder should know that either the highest [guest] is one who is a student (*brahmacārin*), or the best of householders is one who seeks offspring;
for the householder is the source of those [other stages].
Whether he be a student of the elements (*bhautika*), a teacher of householders,
or a lifelong celibate (*naiṣṭhika*), he should abide among those who are lifelong celibates; this is considered the sequence for enjoyment and liberation.
In the *Kiraṇa*, the characteristic of the lineage (*santānika*) has been stated:
"But even one who was previously in another stage of life, having been purified by Śiva-initiation,
the qualified [initiation] bestows upon him both a lineage and a non-lineage."
One who brings an end to the fear of the existence of phenomena within the preceding and succeeding continuum is declared a lineage-guru;
such a householder is the supreme instructor.
One should know either the householder or the student to be supreme; the householder is the best of teachers for the attainment of both enjoyment and liberation.
In the *Kāmika*:

"Those such as Kauśika and others who were initiated at a time subsequent to the [first] creation, they shall belong to that lineage [of Śiva]; however, the *sāntānika* (one belonging to the lineage of the original progenitor) is one who is Śaiva by birth."
The best of gurus is one belonging to a spiritual lineage; in his absence, it may be a householder, a student of the elements (bhautika), or a celibate student who serves as a guide for householders.

The lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) should be among those who are lifelong celibates; he is considered [the teacher] through the sequence of enjoyment and liberation. For the sake of attaining both enjoyment and liberation, the householder is desired as the guru.
The lineage-guru (sāntānika-guru) is always declared to be one who bestows grace upon all; he may follow the direct order (anuloma), but the reverse order (pratiloma) is not desired.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:

"The Guru should initiate those who are lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika*) as well as householders (*gṛhastha*). But a householder who is merely a student (*bhautuka*) may not perform initiation for anyone else."
In the *Śaivasannyāsadīpikā*, p.
"When, by that [act], there is the true renunciation of the substance of one's internal dispositions (*bhāva-dravya*) by the ascetic..."
Therefore, those who are qualified for initiation (dīkṣā) and the establishment [of the lineage] (sthāpanā) are indeed by this alone.
Nevertheless, the gurus are to be known as the instructors for those who have renounced worldly life.
As stated in the *Kriyāsārapaddhati*:
"Then, the lifelong teacher [should initiate] those seeking liberation, preceded by their respective castes..."
But one should initiate a female ascetic (saṃnyāsinī) without delay.
Out of compassion, he bestows initiation for the sake of the enjoyment and liberation of living beings; such a guru is renowned, and one should always worship him as if he were Śiva himself.
Whatever pertains to initiation (dīkṣā) and consecration (pratiṣṭhā), that must be protected with great effort;
for it is by these that initiation and instruction are performed, and thus they are proclaimed as "gurus" by the teachers.
The teacher provides exposition for men, and by that he is sustained; exposition, ritual worship, consecration, and so forth, he performs constantly for those bound in existence.
An *ācārya* is so called because of his instruction of other disciples; thus, the nature of being an *ācārya* is here declared to be threefold in its essential meaning.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"A body consisting of red is excellent; one that is dark in the middle is mediocre; a body entirely black, the Guru should not lead [to liberation] even for a moment."
The specific distinction has been stated as follows:
"Among these ten castes— the four beginning with the Brahmin and the six born in the natural order (anuloma) and so forth— the status of being a preceptor (ācāryatva) is prescribed."
One should point out the various distinctions between castes according to the customs of the world; for others, [one should act] according to their caste and conduct,
and out of respect for their words.
One should not perform the consecration of other castes in that region;
having observed those who have fallen [from their status], the Śiva-fire is not established for them.
Therefore, it must be performed by ascetics, especially on the path of Śiva;
however, there is indeed some difference between the teachers and the ascetics.
For those who harm others and for those who have renounced through asceticism— fitness for these two to perform fire-rites is not prescribed.
Thus, for those two, consecration is prescribed even without the *homa* [fire sacrifice].

Thus ends the rule on the characteristics of the preceptor (*ācārya*) in the *Dīkṣādarśa*, composed by Vedajñāna, the son of Vāmadeva, a resident of Śrī Vyāghrapura. Now follows the characteristics of a guru to be avoided.
The procedure is now being stated.
Regarding the characteristics of the teacher to be avoided,
Śrī Nandikeśvara says in the Cintyaviśva:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, what are the characteristics of a teacher?"
Speak for the sake of protecting the world, and especially for our own.
In the Kāmika [Tantra], Īśvara says:
"One who, out of delusion, considers the Śiva-knowledge beginning with the Kāmikā and the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas to be equal— him one should avoid with effort."
Likewise, the sixth is the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*), which is free from deliberation and rejection; one should avoid those of the same lineage or kinship, as well as the *kusumākṣa*.
The elder brother who marries before his younger brother, the younger brother so superseded, one who has married a second wife while the first is still living,
the eating of forbidden food, as well as the son of a remarried woman, the son born of an adulterous union, and the son of a widow— these are likewise [excluded].
And likewise, one who has consumed [forbidden food], as well as the husband of a courtesan.
One who is devoid of learning, devoted to false scriptures, impotent, one who has recently given birth, one addicted to vices, an adulterer, or the husband of a low-caste woman.
One should avoid Citraka, Gāyaka, and likewise Kañca; as well as one who takes what belongs to Śiva through unjust means and is defiled by Hara.

One should avoid those of little learning, followers of the Māhiṣaka sect, and those who are deformed; likewise, one should avoid those who transgress the teacher’s command and those who are intent on finding fault in others.
One who is blind, one-eyed, or lame, as well as one with protruding teeth; one with a squint, a crow’s eye, or a distorted brow, beard, or hair.
One should avoid a guru who has a protruding belly, a large abdomen, and a foul-smelling mouth.
As stated in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"A guru who lacks the initiation of higher knowledge (*vijñāna-dīkṣā*), is devoid of devotion, and is full of envy and desire..."
Desiring all material things.
One who is devoid of service to the guru, one who is full of censure toward the guru, one who acts against the interests of the guru,
and one who treats the elder mantra as equal [to his own].
One who is agitated by the waves of anger and greed, empty of virtue yet wearing a deceptive guise; one who is harmful toward others, covetous, a thief, a fool, and a slanderer.
Fickle, a wielder of the water-pot, a performer of wicked and trivial deeds,
self-aggrandizing, ungrateful, and a defiler of the conduct of the covenant.
How can one who is devoid of the yoga of knowledge, afflicted by diseases such as consumption and leprosy, a performer of sacrifices,
attached to sense objects, and of evil character [attain liberation]?
A thief, one who lacks knowledge, one who follows an evil path, a glutton, one of foul mouth, as well as those who have themselves lost their vows— these are to be avoided, as it has been said.

One who possesses the scriptural knowledge regarding the procedure for Śiva-initiation and whose fire of austerity is intense, should daily worship Śiva and the others, as well as his own root-guru and the lineage of gurus.
Having abandoned the signs of others (*anyaliṅga*), one should take refuge in the *guru* alone; such a person is to be known as a *punarbhū*, and those born of her are considered *kaulikās*.

Gurus should be known by their conduct, just as forest fires are recognized by the way they protect [the land]; those who have fallen away from the teacher's discipline should be abandoned like a fire that has lost its fuel.

Those who have broken their vows, those who are unsteady, those who are remembered as being full of ashes, those born from the earth, those who are known as kings, and those born from that [lineage] are remembered as the Kauśikas.

These [inauspicious planetary positions] must be avoided by those desiring auspiciousness during initiation (dīkṣā) and installation (sthāpana). A Linga installed under these conditions is no means for attaining worldly enjoyment or liberation.
One who is endowed with such qualities as these is indeed not worthy of worship on the surface of the earth; one should not perform the consecration for him under the title of "Ācārya."
If the consecration is performed through negligence, one would incur fault. As stated in the *Suprabheda*:
Having avoided such persons, one is excluded from all ritual acts; if one should perform them out of delusion, the divine presence will never be attained.
In the *Vīratantra*:
"One who is devoid of these characteristics, even if possessing all limbs, is not a fit candidate for liberation.
Thus [ends the work] composed by Vedajñāna, son of Vāmadeva, a resident of Vyāghrapura.
The rule regarding the characteristics of a Guru to be avoided in the *Dīkṣādarśa*. Now, the characteristics of a disciple are stated.
Regarding the characteristics of a disciple,
likewise in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"Now I shall specifically describe the characteristics of disciples."
Non-violence, truthfulness, and non-stealing, while being free from anger and greed.
He is patient, powerful, and free from all those various afflictions.
Thus it is stated in the Pauṣkara:
"The non-arising of suffering in others, even through hundreds of acts of violence and malice—that indeed is non-violence."
For that violence, enjoined by the scriptures, is indeed to be understood [as such].
"Whether out of fear or even out of affection, that which is not true is not called truth.
Such [passages] are to be seen there. In the Śrīmad-Raurava:
A Brāhmaṇa endowed with vows, a Kṣatriya who has mastered the Dharma, a Vaiśya engaged in honoring [others], and a Śūdra possessed of service— [in these four, one should dwell].
One should perform the initiation of the Guru according to the ritual prescribed in the scriptures.
This has been stated in the *Pauṣkara*:
The service of men has been fully described.
Regarding the cause—
disciples born of the four castes as well as those born of the natural order (anuloma)—
and regarding the division of deities:

Six [castes] are declared to be born in the natural order (anuloma), and three are remembered as being born in the inverse order (pratiloma): namely, the Sūta, the Māgadha, and the Āyogava, produced through diligent effort.
In the *Cintyaviśva*: "Having diagnosed the diseases of the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, one should treat them;
they should be endowed with livelihoods such as the command of armies for the military classes. These five [occupations] belong to the family."

One born from a woman of the same caste (savarṇā) is considered the best for the rite of initiation (dīkṣā). Furthermore, those five who are born in the natural order (anuloma) are specifically regarded as mediocre in that context.
The fourteen are declared to be the anuloma mixed castes; the Kula-kumbhakāra is the lowest among those who have received initiation.
By way of livelihood, the sons are incapable; initiation is the lowest of the stations.
For the highest, the middling ones are five, and five follow the lowest mantra.
Furthermore, ten types of the lowest-of-the-low have been specifically mentioned; having considered these thirty-four, as well as those related to the family, within that collection.
Those who are low-born, engaged in base activities, or even involved in cruel deeds, as well as those whose livelihood is inferior—
the Guru should avoid initiating them.
For those born into [the lineages] beginning with the Dīkṣā, by means of ash without [specific] ritual procedure,
their bodies are marked with the Tripuṇḍra and they wear Rudrākṣa beads.

Furthermore, one should always, with devotion, perform prostrations and other such gestures from afar toward those who are without mantras, those who have received the Śiva-initiation themselves, and those who bear the *liṅga*.
Having constructed a temple of Śiva and other such works according to the requirements of one's own respective caste, one should perform them as is appropriate;
by that, one shall attain heaven.
Thereafter, having been born on this earth, they shall attain liberation through initiation;
especially so for one who has been initiated according to the rules, who wears the sectarian mark (liṅgin), and who is a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika).
O Nandikeśvara, once he is born, there is no connection at all for one who is material,
especially due to his conformity with worldly conduct.
"One must follow one's former birth"—this is the certainty of the scripture.
One should abide by trust toward one's kinsmen, freedom from malice, and the observance of the teacher’s command.
Faith, tranquility, patience, truthfulness, as well as purity, austerity, learning, and gratitude— if these ten qualities exist in a disciple, [he is fit].
He is the foremost among disciples, yet these others are not his primary ones;
for if a guru does not instruct a disciple who is endowed with devotion, [he fails in his duty].
It is certain that the sin committed by the disciple's ignorance falls upon the teacher;
therefore, one should examine all qualities with every effort.
Having examined the disciple in many ways through lowly tasks— whether he be lowly or excellent— and [having tested him] through high tasks, one should then perform the initiation.
When the defects are few and the qualities are abundant, or when they are equal, he should initiate him; at the end of a year of service, the supreme teacher should accept him as a disciple.
And in the *Suprabheda*:
"Having examined the disciples for a year regarding their virtues and faults,
those endowed with virtues should be accepted, while those devoid of virtues should be rejected."
The disciple, likewise, should accept [the teaching] only after having examined the teacher; otherwise, this [state] is not attained through the practice of sound alone.

"Even after a year, a disciple may resort to another teacher," and "Even a preeminent [disciple] may consider another as his predecessor," and so forth— such statements regarding the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*) apply generally; however, having divided the time for the [initiation of] the essential reality (*tattva*), the peak (*kṣora*), and the head (*śīrṣa*):
It is set forth in the *Sarvajñānottara*: "Namely—three, four, or five [villages] for a Brahmin; nine for a Kṣatriya;
eight or nine for a Vaiśya; and one should cause twenty to be given to a Śūdra."
At the time of initiation, one should deliberate upon the knowledge of Mīmāṃsā regarding the act of giving. As stated in the Pauṣkara:
"Since Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and even Śūdras [are eligible] in that manner..."
Those who are blind, deaf, or mute due to water [afflictions] are impelled by the power of initiation.
In the Mṛgendra-tantra: "And those who have dedicated their minds to Śiva [should receive] initiation...
They are devoted to good company, heroic, and take pleasure in avoiding bad company;
they are intent on listening [to the teachings], peaceful, and have been well-tested over time.
Those who are free from anger, not fickle, full of faith, and have conquered their senses—
such persons should always accept [the gift], for they are protected by conduct that is far removed from vice.
In the Kāśmīra-tantra:

"He who wears a shaven head or matted hair and remains established in the vow of celibacy— therein he may perform ritual action, even if uninitiated, provided it is consistent with the Vedas and Āgamas."
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"The exposition, the consecration, the mandala, and the gathering of disciples should be performed by the command of the Guru, even if [the journey] is only within a single village."
By the mere act of initiation, even a disciple becomes free from all defects; yet, subsequently, defects may arise through the actions of mind, speech, and body.
Having again informed the Guru of all this,
including his own misfortunes and every fault, he should salute the supreme teacher.
The preceptor shall subsequently proclaim the rules for expiation; however, in the absence of the preceptor, it must be performed in the presence of the eldest [brother].
Purification arises from expiation, and through purity one attains liberation.
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"One who is devoted to many arduous rites and intent on penance and acts of charity should examine the Guru."
The disciple [is bound] to him in many ways by his actions.
In that regard, concerning the initiation of a married couple, a specific rule is stated in the Devikālottara: "Thus, O Lord,
one initiated previously is the elder, while Amareśvara is the younger."
O Supreme Lord, if you have been initiated, [the rite] must be performed by you.

Listen, O Goddess: one who possesses the purificatory rites becomes superior even to the most superior. The initiation of Śiva should be performed by a single preceptor for both husband and wife together.

Because of the wife’s body being half of his own, because of musical instruments, and because of the words [of the scriptures] regarding the well-known coexistence of the two selves, one should initiate the couple together.
O lady of excellent hips, one should likewise show favor to one's father, mother, and brother,
as well as to one's wife and sister.
Those such as a son-in-law, a father, or a wife are suitable [as gurus] for those desiring liberation;
initiation must be performed by them, for Śiva is the object to be realized, not the status of being a son.
This innumerable statement has now been indicated for one who is established in the Śiva-samayī stage and was previously initiated by the eldest [guru].
According to the illustration of the scriptural teaching, he is said to be the son of the spiritual son, the practitioner of the practitioner, and even the teacher of the teacher.

In the teaching of Śiva, among those who have transcended [the world], the elder is he who is superior in spiritual refinement (saṃskāra); neither birth nor age constitutes seniority—mastery of knowledge is the cause of being the elder.
If two elder brothers are present, and the younger one has been consecrated first, some wait for the other elder brother or even for another preceptor before performing the rite.
p.
1305) And they should show mutual respect, except for the performance of formal salutation (*vandana*).
Thus it is stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
A younger brother must never perform a salutation to an elder, even if that elder is his preceptor in initiation or consecration, nor even to one who is superior in austerity or learning.
O Mataṅga,
those who are devotees of Śiva should be beheld by those desiring Śiva,
for they have been consecrated with Śiva-mantras by the Embodiment of Qualities (Guṇamūrti).
Born from the womb of Vāgīśī, all these men have obtained boons; their forms have been purified by the consecration of Śiva as prescribed.
Although all possess equal status, this rule is nevertheless prescribed:

even in the presence of their preceptor, they should perform service and salutations according to the proper sequence, with minds thus composed, while remaining within the range of sight of one another and filled with mutual joy.
Of the Guru.
Thus ends the rule for the characteristics of the disciple in the *Dīkṣādarśa*. Now, the characteristic of the descent of power (*śaktinipāta*) is described.

The characteristic of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*): Having recognized the respective signs in a disciple who possesses the aforementioned characteristics, according to the varying degrees of the descent of power that has reached him, one should perform initiation in accordance with those signs. Likewise:
In the Siddhāntaśekhara:
"The characteristics of the various types of the descent of power (śaktipāta) will now be described.
When equilibrium has been established between demerit and merit, that power descends."
When the supreme power (*parā-śakti*), whose essence is knowledge, is bestowed upon someone by Śambhu,
initiation is performed for that very person; he is liberated, of this there is no doubt.
I shall describe the characteristics of the fall of that [body] according to the degrees of embodied beings;
likewise, the falling away of the body, as well as karma, brings forth supreme bliss and joy.
Perspiration and horripilation—these are the characteristics of the *śamīpāta* [falling into tranquility].
For example:
just as the radiance of the sun is suddenly obstructed by masses of clouds, so too [is the mind].
The power whose nature is knowledge is bound by the nets of fetters.
When the bonds have ripened, she is clearly said to have "fallen" [into the world];
as stated in the Pauṣkara:
"In this regard, the equality of karmas is not the cause for her grace; rather, it is the ripening of that which is soft."
But rather, it is for the purpose of bestowing grace.
If the equilibrium of all karmas were the cause of grace, then how could there be grace for those who are liberated as pure consciousness (vijñānakevalins)?

Furthermore, the equality of karma in all cases everywhere is not the cause. In the *Kiraṇa*, Garuḍa says: "Initiation arises from the descent of power (*śaktipāta*); the descent does not occur through [the exhaustion of] karma.
The Lord says:
The application of words appears to occur through figurative usage, just as even a liberated person is called "eternal" or the Lord is called "without a master."
Just as the severing of the bonds is declared by the Lord Śiva, the King of Mantras,
so too is the descent of power (śaktinipāta) taught for the devotee in the Śiva-āgama.
Just as the sudden falling upon one of an object [causes harm],
so too is the "falling of power" (*śaktinipāta*) said to bestow the fear of worldly existence; therefore, it occurs elsewhere.
At that time, his very self was identical with the teacher.
In the Pauṣkara [Tantra] it is said:
"Detachment quickly arises from the ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra; and a desire to behold the two lotus feet of Śambhu also arises."
"When shall I behold the Lord of Gods? When shall I be liberated from bondage? Who indeed will show me Śambhu?"—such thoughts arise within him.
Thus, if the Lord favors those beings within saṃsāra,

even by this [fact], an inference of the cause for the learned is established for those of dull intellect as well; however, when [the cause] has ceased even slightly or partially— *mṛgendre*— [it is so stated].
O Lord of Darkness, you who are the obstructer!
These [defects] exist to some extent in embodied beings.
In the Pauṣkara it is said:
"In the teaching of Śiva, disciples must be examined for the sake of the descent of power (śaktipāta)."
One who is without devotion, devoid of the twice-born, cruel, fearless, or fallen from ritual action.

"In the *Ājñāpārameśvara*, it is stated that initiation (*dīkṣā*) destroys their [karmic] bonds; by initiation alone one may liberate [the soul] from bondage and bestow the state of Śiva upon the individual soul (*aṇu*)."
Likewise, in the Vidyāpurāṇa:

"One who is rich in virtues or has few defects is praised if he is a devotee of Śiva; one endowed with every virtue is not [praised] at all if he is not a devotee. Even a Mleccha, if he is a devotee of Śiva..."
His word is to be accepted without doubt.
1308) Even a Brahmin endowed with [auspicious] marks is not fit for initiation if he lacks devotion to Śiva.
He whose teacher is always firm in his ritual duties.

For one who is constantly engaged in the practice of the knowledge of Śiva and remains established in the expansion [of that realization], initiation is recommended; for no other person who is not devoted solely to this is it praised.
He who, as a teacher, can sustain the multitude of subtle elements— the body, substances, consciousness, speech, and actions— is worthy of refinement in this world.
In the Pauṣkara:
"Initiation should be performed for one person, or for two especially; beyond that it must not be performed, for [doing so] certainly leads to hell."
In the Niśvāsa:
"Those who recite the Śivasaṃhitā without having attained the true nature of Śiva, and who perform initiation without knowing it, fall to a lower state, both teacher and disciple."
In the *Svāyaṃbhuvatantra*:
"Those who, without knowing the true nature of Śiva, endeavor to perform initiation—their labor is in vain; thus, the Path (adhvan) is described here."
Likewise, in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā:
"One who desires purity without knowing the pervasion of reality is a deceiver; though pure, he is not capable of attaining the fruit."
His exertion is in vain and results only in misfortune.
As stated in the *Kālottara*:
"If a Guru performs initiation without knowing the two portions of the abode (*ālaya*)," [it is fruitless].
The teacher, together with his disciple, shall be cooked in the Raurava hell.

The teacher, however, having understood [the disciple] through diligent effort, should perform the initiation; for one who does not know the true essence of the scriptures and the collection of the principles of knowledge [is unfit].
If one performs initiation out of delusion and subsequently feels regret, one should mutter the formidable mantra five hundred thousand times, or if one desires auspiciousness.
Thus ends the procedure for the determination of the descent of power (*śaktinipāta*) in the *Dīkṣādarśa*. Now, the varieties of initiation (*dīkṣā*) are described.
In the *Mṛgendra*: "The initiation that brings about the attainment of one's desires, which has issued from the mouth of the Supreme Lord, is declared in brief;
because its purpose is twofold, it is of two kinds."

It is both material and ultimate, distinguished by its internal subdivisions; it is dependent and independent, pertaining respectively to those who follow the worldly path and those whose nature is Śiva.
