In the *Svāyaṃbhuva*, the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the word "initiation" (*dīkṣā*) is stated: it is the cause that grants success in liberation,
as far as the meaning of its syllables is explained.
The true essence of knowledge is bestowed, and the latent impressions of karma are destroyed;
through this conjunction of bestowing and destroying, initiation effects the purification of the self.
Likewise, in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"The true essence of knowledge is bestowed and the three impurities are destroyed;
thus initiation is described as that which bestows knowledge and removes impurity."
And by the Guru alone, for all [practitioners], initiation is considered the primary one;

the classification of initiation for those who are "devoid of mental constructs" (*vijñānākala*) is based on the distinction between having a support (*sādhāra*) and being without support (*nirādhāra*).
It is explained in the *Cintyaviśva* as follows:
"In the Kali age, three types of persons are to be favored by the teaching: those for whom consciousness has dissolved."
The third is indeed complete, while the first consists of mere impurity.
One who is conjoined with both impurity (mala) and karma is indeed a *pralayākala*, while one who is subject to the range of states beginning with *nivṛtti* and ending with *kalā* is a *sakala*.

Nandikeśvara says that for them, the ritual initiation (dīkṣā) involving action is of two kinds: with support (sādhārā) and without support (nirādhārā). The one with support, however, belongs to the Sakala [category].
The initiation consisting of grace (dīkṣā) called "without support" (nirādhārā) has been declared for others by Śambhu through His intense power, independent of a preceptor.
Whatever rite is performed correctly is proclaimed to be "without support" (nirādhāra), provided one remains established at the root of the Guru,
whether according to the [specific] system or the general division.
Through devotion, Śambhu performs those rites which are empowering; the fourfold initiation of action (kriyādīkṣā) consists of that with seed (sabījā) and that devoid of seed (bījavarjitā).
One who is endowed with authority is different from one who lacks authority; for men who are engaged in the practice of the observances (samaya), there exists that which possesses seeds.
In the *Varuṇapaddhati*:
"The first [initiation] is twofold and distinct according to whether it possesses a seed-syllable (*sabīja*) or not; the former is the nature of Śiva.
It is the existence of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the teacher (*ācārya*), distinguished by place, time, and other factors."
Where action, consisting of both dharma and adharma, which is manifold regarding the past and the future, is purified through deliberate reflection—
that indeed is said to possess the nature of Śiva.
The second [state] is pure, having unrighteousness as its mother and possessing worldly dharma;
because it constantly presides over the measures, it is equal-minded with its sons.

For the sake of the capable, there is indeed no fixed entitlement; rather, it is contingent upon the occasion for those who possess the qualification. This applies constantly to the practitioner and the teacher regarding both regular and occasional rites.

Because it effects the goal in every respect, and because it has been established for both [the bound soul and Śiva], the initiation into Nirvāṇa is twofold: the worldly and that characterized by Śiva-nature.

This is not the worldly initiation of the *grahas*; the initiation of those who possess the signs (*liṅgin*) and follow the way of Śiva is that which is conjoined with the topknot and the sectarian mark (*khaṇḍa*); that alone is the initiation of the way of Śiva.
This Śivadharmiṇī is twofold, distinguished as *bhautika* (worldly) and *naiṣṭhika* (ascetic), as stated in the Siddhāntaśekhara:
"That Śivadharmiṇī is of two kinds: the *bhautika* and the *naiṣṭhika*."
That which is conjoined with the release from vows is called *bhautika*.
The *naiṣṭhikī* [vow] is considered that of one who observes the vow until the fall of the body. Its intended meaning is:
having performed the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and the vow for some time according to what is taught in the scriptures...

The completion of his vow according to the prescribed rule is the *bhautikī* [vow]; the lifelong observance of celibacy until the fall of the body is the *naiṣṭhikī* initiation (*dīkṣā*). As stated in the *Varuṇapaddhati*:

Now, that initiation by means of seed-syllables (*bījadīkṣā*) is said to be divided into two types: the higher (*parā*), which bestows immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇadā*), and the lower (*apara*), which bestows liberation after death (*śirannirvāṇadā*).
In the *Kāmika*, it is stated that both the *prārabdha* (commenced) and *sañcita* (accumulated) [karmas] are purified at the time of [the initiation of] action;
for those who are utterly detached, she grants immediate liberation (*sadyonirvāṇa*). Just as she provides the experience of *prārabdha* karmas, so too does she grant imperishable liberation.
The powers and so forth proceed, and it becomes pure, bestowing nirvāṇa; just as there, the practice is preceded by the circle of earrings.
That which has objects consisting of mere mental activity is considered "possessing knowledge" (jñānavatī); it is said to be of many kinds, and its detailed exposition is as follows.

The initiation of sight, the initiation of touch, as well as the verbal and mental initiations, the scriptural initiation, the initiation of yoga, the initiation of the hotṛ-priest, and so forth, are manifold.

When, having opened one's eyes and meditated upon that reality, one gazes at the disciple for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the fetters, this is considered the ocular initiation (ākṣuṣī-dīkṣā).
Having placed Śambhu, together with the Brahmāṅga, in his right hand,
and having placed it upon the head of the disciple, this becomes the initiation by touch (sparśadīkṣā).
Having established the mind in reality and with inner splendor directed forward,
the Guru should recite the mantra gathered through the initiation of mantra.

Through yoga, there shall be the initiation of yoga; through the bestowal [of mantras], it becomes born of yoga. The Śaiva initiation is described as being accompanied by fire-rituals and the duties of the *hautra* priest.
One should utter the mantras with speech; that is the vocal initiation (vācikī-dīkṣā).
By the bestowing of the Śiva-scriptures, the initiation of the weapon (astra-dīkṣā) is likewise accomplished.
Then, having examined the disciple who is endowed with devotion and desires the meditation upon Śiva, and having observed his impurity with a stern gaze, the Guru—
One who has performed the daily obligatory rites should perform the work of initiation;
just as darkness perishes in the presence of the sun.
By the mere initiation from a guru, one is liberated from all sins; whoever the guru touches with his hand, and whomever he beholds with his eye— [he too is likewise purified].
All that becomes auspicious solely through the grace of Śiva; it is not stained by impurity, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
Therefore, the Guru is declared to be Śiva, and the power of the Guru is Manonmanī;
even though he has performed hundreds of thousands of initiations for those with sins, [he remains pure].
If you have not yet attained the knowledge of Śiva, you should resort to the journey of knowledge; having found a teacher devoid of knowledge, how will you attain liberation?
Just as one who relies on a broken ship does not reach the further shore of the ocean, therefore,
with every effort, one should take refuge in that which leads to the further shore of knowledge.
Just as a bee that has found honey moves from flower to flower in the forest,
so too a disciple greedy for knowledge should go from one teacher to another.
Even a disciple who has fallen low should give away what he has obtained as his own; Mataṅga says that she,
being humble and speaking kindly, was touched by the hands of Śiva’s power (Śivaśakti).
Free from anger and devoid of malice, he bears [the teachings] in his heart, having conquered his senses.
Those who are always free from cruelty and maintain their own proper conduct are to be accepted; otherwise, there is no qualification for either the one to be initiated or the initiator.
Likewise, in the Vāmadeva-śivāgama:
"In the Śivāgama, initiation is taught by Śiva, the Supreme Self, as threefold: namely, the Śāmbhavī, the Śākta, and the Māntrī."
O wise one, by the mere sight of the Guru, or even through touch or conversation, that [power] which causes the destruction of bonds arises immediately.
That initiation is declared to be Śāmbhavī; it is further divided into two types: intense (tīvra) and more intense (tīvratarā), according to the degree of destruction of the bonds (pāśa).
That [intensity] by which his liberation occurs immediately is considered the most intense; yet even more intense than that is the ultimate intensity, which purifies the fetters of the person.
The initiation pertaining to Śakti, which possesses knowledge, enters the body of the disciple and is performed by the Guru through the path of yoga with the eye of wisdom.
The initiation consisting of mantras and ritual action, preceded by the sacrificial pit and the mandala,
should be performed by the Guru outside [the inner circle] for those who are dull-witted or very dull-witted.
One ought to bestow grace upon disciples according to their capacity.
As stated in the Pauṣkara:
"By means of a gaze imbued with compassion, in accordance with their fitness, he purifies them."
Or whatever [he may do] with authority, even as the Supreme Lord.
p.

1315) Regarding the one to be favored and the discipline, as well as the one to be favored and compassion— Śiva must bring about the union of these two, for such a conjunction is very difficult to attain.
In this initiation, the fruit is precisely the attainment of Śiva-nature once impurity has ceased.
As it is said in that very same [text]:
"Initiation alone shall liberate one from bonds and bestow Śiva-nature upon the individual soul (aṇu)."
Likewise, in the Raurava:
"Having thus attained the Śaiva path arising from initiation and mantra, the initiated best of men does not undergo birth again."
When the body is dissolved, having become Śiva and endowed with the attributes of Śiva,
one attains the nature of Śiva and becomes fit for non-differentiation.
Just as a river flowing along after being purified reaches the ocean,
it attains the state of salty water through the power of that great sea.
Thus, one whose self is separated from the body attains Śiva alone;
through the very act of separation, it arises like the meeting of a river and the ocean.
Therefore, in the sacrifice to Śiva, there is a clarity of color in the conceptualization of forms.
For example:
"Just as fire remains hidden within wood, so too do they abide therein. Let it be so.
Just as fire is clearly [produced] by means of a flint-stone.
That which knows its own nature as luminous is stainless; here, indeed, Śiva himself is the blind one, the eternal Sadāśiva.
Having assumed the body of a teacher and remaining intent on favoring the virtuous,
he should be known as being like Mantramaṇḍana, and also like the araṇi wood for the sacrificial fire upon the path.
Vāgīśī is to be known as the womb (yoni), and Dhūmā is to be known by me as the creator of the letters and so forth. The self is indeed said to be like fire, while the practitioner is supreme Śiva.
Freed from impurity, karma, kalā, and the rest, and devoid of all duality, one is not afflicted even while remaining there,
because one is exceedingly pure.
Since copper is joined with mercury and fire,
it is purified by those who know the reality and thereby attains the state of gold.

Just as copper does not again attain its state of redness once it has been transformed, so too the Self, once realized, does not return to its former condition; therefore, O unmantra, delight in the power of mantra, for action is to be known as being like fire.
O Goddess, Śiva, the knower of reality, has the body of the Ācārya; the Self is to be known as gold, while impurity (mala) is to be known as Kālikā.
O Dear One, because he has been rendered stainless by a Guru who knows the [inner] reality through the application of mantra, substance, and ritual action upon the external support;
It no longer undergoes impurity; being stainless, it attains the state of Śiva.
As stated in the Vātula: "Just as copper pierced by mercury does not return to its state of copper."
Likewise, the embodied soul who has attained gnosis shall never again fall into the state of a bound beast.
The person presided over by that very [power] is liberated from the ordinary state;
he is the Guru, Brahmā, whose knowledge is this, and who stands beyond the world of mortals.
p.
1317) Behold, one is not defiled by sins such as the killing of a Brahmin or the horse sacrifice.
Thus ends the procedure for determining the divisions of initiation in the *Dīkṣādarśa*. Now...
The procedure for defining the location of initiation is now stated.
The procedure for the instruction on initiation— namely,
as it appears in the Svāyaṃbhuvatantra:
Now, for the successful accomplishment of the sacrifice, there should be a place such as Brahmāvarta,
inhabited by living beings and abounding in sacrificial fuel, flowers, and water.
It is composed of earth, kusha grass, and other medicinal herbs; it is not a work that reviles the nihilists.
Regarding the location:
on the Sahya, the Pāriyātra, Mahendra, or Malaya mountains; or on the bank of a sacred river or ocean, and especially at a confluence.
Near a milk-tree or, alternatively, in a flower garden;
likewise, in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"On Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Pāriyātra, Himālaya, Vindhya, and Mandara."
On Śrīgiri and on the Himālaya mountain.
On the banks of the Gaṅgā, the Kālindī, the Narmadā, the Tuṃbhadra, the Sarasvatī,
the Payasvinī, and on the banks of the Kāverī and the Kanyakā.
Furthermore, in meritorious fields and regions such as Vārāṇasī, or on the shore of the ocean, by a river, or at a pure great lake.
Or always in a flower garden, or near a milk-exuding tree,
or in a palace, or in a monastery, or in the house of one learned in the Vedas.
In a pure and delightful place, on a level surface with abundant soft earth— whether on one's own land,
or on Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śrīśaila, Himavat, or Pāriyātra mountains— the wise [should perform the rite].
Declare purification on the Vindhya mountain.
In the Gaṅgā, in the Yamunā, and in the space between them; in the Sarasvatī, the Dṛṣadvatī, the Godāvarī, and in the ocean.
On the Narmadā, the Kṛṣṇaveṇī, and the Sindhu, as well as at Pañcanada, on the banks of the Tuṅgabhadrā,
and on the banks of the Candrabhāgā.
In the sacred bathing-places of secret shrines, at the confluences of rivers, in dwellings, in forests, in cow-pens,
in Śrīpura, and in Kṣīra* * *.
In the Brahmakuṇḍa, at the Kadaṃba tree, and especially in the temple of the Guru, which is most beautiful,
or in a house facing the southern door.
One should designate the site for initiation at the foot of a *kuṇḍa* tree,
or in a temple of the deity, a monastery, or likewise in the house of the teacher or the disciple; such is the site for initiation.
A pavilion should be constructed according to the prescribed ritual rules.
In the *Kāśmīra-tantra*:
"Initiation is always praised in a field of merit and in a field of Śiva.
Thus it is stated in the *Kriyākaraṇamaṇḍanapaddhati*:
In gardens, in temples of Śiva, on the banks of rivers, in lotus-pools, in Kāñcī, in Vyāghrapura, on the shore of the ocean, at the mountain where [the mantra] has been recited, and in a cow-pen.
Furthermore, for embodied beings, initiation is praised at the abode of the Guru, in one’s own home, at Śrī Kālahastīśvara, or at the highly purifying Gokarṇa.
As stated by Mataṅga:
In the excellent forest, there are grounds situated within the abode of Śiva; there is the highly meritorious river Gaṅgā and also the irreproachable Kālindī.
The Sarasvatī, the Narmadā, and four other excellent rivers originating from Āryāvarta,
as well as the great ocean itself, have been cast away.
Between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā lies the unsurpassed field of initiation;
the confluence of rivers is auspicious, as is a delightful garden.
O best of rivers, [bring me] the stainless Sarasvatī, or where there is a beautiful lotus pond; from among these, bring that which is auspicious or pleasing to the mind.
A specific location for the Ālaya and other [structures] has been stated in the *Kāmika*:
"One should construct a pavilion in front of the temple, and the sacrificial hall on either side or in the north."
It should be fashioned so that it becomes perfectly square.

Regarding the house and other such locations, having set aside a space equal to the height of the door's elevation in front of it, one should construct a pavilion for the purpose of sacrifice in the area outside that, measuring ten cubits.
Thus, it is said in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
Having left a space equal to the height of the door, the wise man should have a pavilion constructed in front of the house-linga, measuring ten cubits in size.
This very [mandala] should be constructed as the pavilion for the installation of a *liṅga* intended for one's own benefit.
As stated in the Mataṅga: p.1320) mataṅge -

In the east, there should be auspicious water; in the south, a beautiful and excellent mountain; and the sacrificial ground (kṣatra) should be bound with dūrvā grass and the like, and enriched with kuśa grass and bilva fruits.
However, having thoroughly examined the objects of perception as impermanent in their proper sequence,
one should avoid the region mentioned in the Smṛti— the kingdom of Sindhu-Sauvīra and its inhabitants.
Having gone to Koṅkaṇa, Vaṅga, and Kaliṅga, one deserves consecration (*saṃskāra*). Now, the entry-offering (*praveśabali*) is prescribed for the purpose of seizing the ground (*bhūparigrahaṇa*).
In the Kāmika:
Regarding the appropriation of the ground:
having divided the earth into nine parts starting from the Brahma-position in due order, the one who knows the Vāstu-ritual should offer oblations at the nine and other locations with this mantra.
These bhūtas, piśācas, and rākṣasas who dwell here on this earth may go wherever they wish; let them come to this ground for those residing here.
One should cast their sacrificial pit (bila) with other offerings combined with curd, clarified butter, and cakes.
This specific detail has been elaborated by us in the *Śivanirmāṇasthāpanādipaddhati*; let it be observed there.
Hereafter, I shall explain the purification of the earth's surface,
as well as the knowledge for its examination and its formal acceptance.
One should examine a pure plot of ground situated near a body of water; having first dug it to the depth of one cubit, it is auspicious if it remains filled with soil even after being excavated.
The middle finger should be known as even; it is not filled by the little finger.
He whose complexion is dark from the application [of collyrium] is beautiful, and he is indeed found to possess such qualities.
Having performed the purification of the ground, effect the generation of the field; once the auspicious field has been generated, then indeed follows the formal acceptance of the site.
Likewise, in the Niśvāsa: "The examination of substances, as well as the formal acquisition of the ground,
[is prescribed] for the initiation of the practitioner (sādhaka) and likewise for the teachers (ācāryas)."
In the *Mṛgendra*:
"Having performed the demarcation of the ground according to the procedure to be described,
[one should act] at a sacred river site provided with fuel-sticks, flowers, *kuśa* grass, and water."

In a region, the Lord of the East should resort to ground that conforms to the [caste] colors; for whichever caste—such as the Brāhmaṇa and so forth—the ground has a certain nature as will be described, that very nature is what is meant by "conforming to the color. This is stated in that very same [text]:

It has the appearance of snow, blood, and dark blue; it is the supreme essence of honey and other liquids; it produces ghee and other substances according to the region; it is an intoxicant that causes the excellent growth of fragrant plants.
One should acquire land for the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes respectively—[lands] that are white, reddish, black, and green in color; that have astringent, sour, salty, and bitter tastes;
and that possess the scents of ghee, blood, cow-dung, and blood-vessels. And thus:
It is declared that all lands possessing the fragrance of the essence of Brahman should be accepted by Brāhmaṇas;
for a Kṣatriya, three types beginning with *ājya* are to be avoided; and for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, five types are prescribed, including land containing stone deposits.
Regarding the cause:
due to the power of that field, it is said to be the earth for those who follow the natural order (*anuloma*).
In the *Niśvāsakārikā*:
"Three [handfuls] for a Brahmin, two for a Kṣatriya, and one for a Vaiśya; for a Śūdra, the rule is that the ground should be made as firm as stone."
Having performed the sacrifice, O Goddess of the gods of gods, one should offer oblations eight hundred times in sequence;
therein, the bali offering must be presented by the high-souled preceptor.
O Goddess, this has indeed been declared to you as the acquisition of land;
when a woman of the aforementioned caste gives birth, she should cause her offspring to attain the caste of that [father].
Thus it has been said:

"In the absence of the [four] castes, such as Brahmins and the rest, one should perform the induction of the castes by means of their respective lords through a fire-oblation of more than a thousand [offerings]."
In the *Svāyaṃbhuvamanvantara*:
"There, the ground should be examined; it should be free from depressions and elevations, not saline, neither too moist nor too dry, and composed of soft clay and sand."
Free from husks, hair, and bones, devoid of ashes and charcoal,
released from wicked thorns, smooth, full of luster, and auspicious.
The earth, freed from the shapes of winnowing baskets and the like, sloping toward the northeast, purified by the hand and the conch,
and examined by digging with the hand;

The earth, complete with its various castes and non-castes, bestowing the fruits of desire, and preeminent for the gratification of the mind— this is indeed the accomplishment (siddhi) as it has been described.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"At that time, one should examine the signs of the auspicious and the inauspicious; if they are auspicious, one should set out, but if they are inauspicious, one should turn back."
Having spread the fire over an inauspicious [sign], one should offer a hundred oblations with the *Śiva-mantra*.
According to the *Niśvāsa*:
"One should know [the result] to be evil in the case of an inauspicious [sign], and one should predict auspiciousness in the case of an auspicious [sign]."
Disregarding his beds, he performs his work with pride.
The subjects of inquiry are obstructed, hindered, and overcome; therefore, one should honor the omen in all undertakings.
Now, the rule regarding the ground to be avoided is stated.
In the *Santāna*:
"The ground to be avoided—"
One should avoid [sites] with anthills, medicinal herbs, or those infested by crawling insects.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Avoiding pits, saline soil, and holes containing hair, bones, thorns, and the like..."
[One should avoid ground] from which snakes and venomous insects have been removed, and which is strewn with ashes, charcoal, and husks.
In the *Kāmika*:
"One should avoid ground infested by crabs, as well as anthills and the like, with both feet.
Now, the procedure for the installation of the *śaṅku* (sacrificial post) is described."
In the Pauṣkara:
"For the purpose of encompassing the earth, one should drive in stakes and lay out lines.
In the Aṃśumati:
Having determined the measurement, one should dig that depth first for its enclosure;
it should be three *tālas*, two *tālas*, or even a *kṛkatāla*.
Having taken up clay and purified it, one should contemplate it with other types of clay in a sacred field,
on a riverbank, or in a clean and delightful place.
Having gathered and taken the earth, one should fill that pit level;
as stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"One should sprinkle [the site] with the water from the five pits, with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and with the water of Śiva."
Having bathed, being pure and wearing washed garments, he should then rinse it once more.
Then, with water filtered through a cloth from jars belonging to families that have not yet reached their time of death,
one should have [the materials] ground by means of *palāśa*, *aśvattha*, and green gram.
Having obtained such a site as this— the earth, which is like the surface of a mirror and thoroughly examined in every respect— one should perform the most excellent maṇḍala sacrifice.
Thus concludes the procedure for the acquisition of the ground. Now, the time for initiation is declared.
Regarding the determination of the time:
Listen, O Goddess, to this supreme secret, the most excellent preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*).
I shall tell you in its entirety all that is common to every compendium: the auspicious lunar days, constellations, weekdays, and omens.
Having obtained [the auspicious moments] pertaining to the gods, the sages, the stars, and the earth, one should perform [the rite] correctly.
As stated in the *Makuṭa*:
"During the period of the sun's northern course (uttarāyaṇa), in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day, during the conjunction of the moon with the asterism Āditya, and likewise at the equinox."
The day of Rāhu (the eclipse) is auspicious on that very day.
In all months, on a day joined with [an auspicious] yoga, at a favorable moment and a favorable lunar mansion, the teacher should perform the rite of initiation.
In the *Svāyambhuva*:
"The ritual procedure for initiation is most excellent when performed during the conjunction of autumn and spring; even if those two are not available, it is praised as being obligatory."

In this regard—the pair of months beginning with Śarad is for those seeking liberation alone, while the pair of months beginning with Vasanta is intended here as the cause for both enjoyment and liberation; in this context, enjoyment is primary and liberation follows as a consequence. Thus, the ritual procedure for initiation during these four months is the most excellent.
In initiation and consecration, as well as in the formal adoption of mantras, in the seizing and releasing of spirits, and in rites for the acquisition of material wealth;

One should worship Jupiter on the full moon days of Kārttika and Vaiśākha, during an eclipse of the sun, at the solstices, at the equinoxes, and when it is situated at the commencement of a zodiacal sign.

The divisions of time according to the categories of *uttama* (best) and so forth are stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*: "Initiation during the autumn season or in the month of Vaiśākha bestows the most excellent fruit."
Initiation in the months of Phālguna and Mārgaśīrṣa is indeed middling;
that in Āṣāḍha and the month of Māgha is declared to be the lowest.
Initiation is prescribed for the months of Śrāvaṇa, Caitra, Puṣya, and Bhādrapada; it is likewise taught even during censured months, provided it coincides with an eclipse.
Initiation is prescribed even during months that are otherwise censured, provided it occurs at an eclipse, at the equinoxes,
at the solstices, or during the great festival at the end of Āṣāḍha.
Initiation (dīkṣā) should be performed at the proper times during the festivals of the Pavitra rite;
initiation in the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) is auspicious from the first day onwards, while in the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), it is auspicious from the fifth day onwards.
And regarding the cause:
the time for initiation has been stated by means of the primary [time] being avoided.
Namely:
in Pūrvabhādrapadā, Revatī, Āṣāḍhā, and Mārgaśīrṣā; the wise one should not perform initiation during these months, but may perform it in other months.
A specific rule is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"The installation, the sprinkling, initiation, Śivarātri, and the Śivotsava festival should be performed in the solar month;
however, the *vicitraka* [festival] should be performed in the lunar month."
Then, during the bright fortnight, under an auspicious constellation and favorable weekdays; specifically,
during the bright fortnight when the lion [the sun] is moving along the northern path on a propitious day.
This was stated by Aghoraśivācārya in the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*.
Without Caitra, without Pauṣa, and without Avarṇa, it is praised; in all other months, the rite of initiation brings happiness.
In the *Mohaśūrottara*:

"One who desires his own welfare should not perform initiation and the like, the installation [of deities], the purification rites (*pavitra*), or the hundred sacrifices (*śatakratu*) during an intercalary month."

In this regard, even the month of Vamrīka and others are prohibited, as has been demonstrated by us in the *Kālaviveka*; let that not be further scrutinized here. Now, the [proper] time is described in the *Suprabheda*:
On the seventh, the ninth, or even the eleventh lunar day,
as well as on the full moon or the new moon, the rite of initiation (dīkṣā) is destroyed.
In the *Vīra-tantra*: "The second, or the fifth, or especially the sixth [lunar day].
Either the twelfth day should be observed, or it may be on the thirteenth day.
These are declared to be the most auspicious for the rite of initiation; specifically,
for those seeking worldly enjoyment, the fourth or ninth lunar day, or any other day in the bright fortnight except for the full moon, are excellent.
Regarding that born of yoga— the eighth, ninth, and new moon days should be avoided.
(From) the *Svāyambhuva-sūtra-saṃgraha*:

The full moon, the eighth day of the bright fortnight, and likewise the fourteenth day are the lunar days for initiation when one intends to enjoy [the fruits of] worldly actions; however, for rites involving liberation, they are performed together with the dark fortnight.
Days joined with [inauspicious] gaps and so forth, as well as other lunar days (tithis) that have been mentioned;
or even on a Sunday, because it is conducive to the limbs of the sacrifice, it should be accepted for the sacrificial rite.
As stated in the Kālottara:
On the fourth, the eighth, and likewise on the fifteenth day,
as well as on the full moon, those desiring prosperity should always perform [the rite] during the bright fortnight.
They should be without flaws and not improperly joined, as prescribed by other authorities for the *atithi* [measure].
Now, the rule for the *vāra* [measure] is stated:
In the *Vīratantra*:
"Monday, Friday, Wednesday, and Thursday are the most excellent among the days.
In the *Suprabheda*: "Wednesday..."
They declare those [lunar mansions] to be auspicious on Sundays and Mondays; and on Wednesdays, Fridays, and Saturdays, they are excellent for the rite of initiation.
Now, the procedure for the lunar mansions (nakṣatra) is described.
Born under Yoga:
Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Śraviṣṭhā, and the three Uttarās.
Puṣya and Śatabhiṣaj are declared to be the lunar mansions for initiation (dīkṣā).
In the Svāyaṃbhuva [Manvantara]:
the three Uttaras, Rohiṇī, and Saumya (Mṛgaśiras) have Jupiter as their deity; Maitra (Anurādhā), Saura (Śravaṇa), and the final asterism (Revatī) are purifying.
The Nairṛta, Vaiṣṇava, Brāhma, and likewise the Puṇyādhidaivata;
these are the fourteen prasthas in the Śiva-sacrifice.
One should not abandon eleven sacrifices due to the failure of even one; being well-composed, one should begin the remaining sacrifices among those already commenced.
Regarding the causes: Puṣya, Rohiṇī, Āditya (Punarvasu), Śravaṇā, Aśvinī, Makhā (Pūrvaphalgunī),
Sāvitrī (Hasta), Tvāṣṭra (Citrā), Vāyavya (Svātī), Nairṛta (Mūlā), and Maitra (Anurādhā).
Tiṣya (Puṣya), the three Uttarās (Uttaraphālgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttara-bhādrapadā), and Ādya (Kṛttikā) grant the birth of a son without weapons.
The determination of the deities of the lunar mansions and so forth is not written here, as it has been explained in detail in the *Śaiva-kālaviveka*.
One should cause the auspicious constellations to be employed for the rite of initiation: Pūṣā, Revatī, Āditya, Punarvasu, Sāvitra, and Hasta.
Citra is for Tvaṣṭṛ, Svātī for Vāyu, Mūla for Nirṛti, Anurādhā for Mitra,
Uttaraphālgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and the three Uttaraproṣṭhapadās likewise. Thus it is stated in the Niśvāsa:
The three Uttarās, Rohiṇī, Puṣya, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Hasta, Svāti, Anurādhā, Aśleṣā, Mūla, and Revatī.
Abhijit and Śravaṇa, as well as the fourteenth [tithi] in a Śiva-sacrifice;
during an eclipse of the moon or sun, and at the beginnings of the sixteenth [lunar days].
During the conjunctions of planets and constellations, at the equinoxes and festivals, and during all solstices,
a sacrifice bestows the fulfillment of all aims.
In this regard, the characteristics of the sixty-eight openings are set forth in the Niśvāsa Tantra:
"The Gemini and Virgo, as well as Sagittarius and Pisces."
Thus, four [periods] are proclaimed as the "mouths of the sixty-four" (ṣaḍaśītimukha).
These two sets of four zodiacal signs are called the "mouths of the sixty-four.
Now, the rule for the ascendant (lagna) is stated.
Regarding the causes:
movable signs are considered the best, fixed signs are middling, and dual signs are remembered as inferior;
furthermore, all planets are avoided when situated in the eighth house (the house of death).

There shall be auspicious harmony between the teacher and the disciple when the signs of Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn are movable (cara); and when both signs are fixed (sthirā), they are excellent; when both are dual (dvisvabhāva), they are middling.
Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces are indeed dual-natured; Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius are fixed signs. The eighth house is called *naiḍhana*. As it is stated in the *Yogaja*:
"One should especially avoid all planets situated in the eighth house."
Or else, there may be the rising of Bṛhaspati, or even the rising of Śukra.
A specific detail is stated in the *Vīratantra*: "Either Taurus or Leo, Scorpio or Aquarius, or else Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, or Pisces."
These zodiac signs have been described; one should avoid the movable (cara) signs.
[The rites] should be performed in a fixed (sthira) sign or in a dual (ubhaya) sign where both [the sun and the moon] are rising.
Having commenced the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*), [one should perform it] there without the rising of the Moon; "the rising of the Moon" means the Moon [being present] at the ascendant (*lagna*).
Now follows the procedure for the yoga.
And the yogas are Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, Śobhana, Śubha,
Sukarman, Dhṛti, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Siddhi, and Harṣaṇa.
Śiva is the most excellent and perfected one, along with the sixteen Brahmins; all censurable things are to be censured, while those praised lead to liberation.
The eleven inauspicious yogas are: Viṣkambha, Atigaṇḍa, Vyāghāta, Vajra, Vyatīpāta, Parigha, Śūla, Gaṇḍa, Vaidhṛti, Sādhyā, and Śubha.
The sixteen yogas beginning with Prīti are not to be accepted [for auspicious rites].
In the Siddhāntaśekhara:
"One who desires worldly enjoyment (bubhukṣu) should not perform initiation merely by knowing the science of astrology;
however, for one who desires liberation (mumukṣu), initiation should always be performed, as there is no restriction regarding time and so forth."
Likewise, in the Devikālottara:
"Just as the fruit falls from the branch and the lotus [falls] upon the ground in due order, so too,
if there is devotion at the feet of Bhava, time is not proclaimed [as a limiting factor]."
On an auspicious day, when the woman has given birth to a son and the fetus is well-formed—
therefore, this time of renunciation is proclaimed as the proper time for initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Likewise, in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"The ripening of the thread is traditionally known as the birth of the pregnant woman; this ripening is the emergence of the disciple who contains the embryo of knowledge."
That day, which is the "womb of knowledge" (*jñānagarbha*), one should initiate [the disciple] during all months.
Thus, the specific time for initiation and the general time for the instruction of mantras have been set forth in the *Jyotiṣa*. As follows:
Commencing the practice of mantras and other rites in the month of Caitra bestows the fruit of many sons; likewise, doing so in Vaiśākha brings about prosperity and grants all forms of wealth.
In Āṣāḍha, there is the destruction of kinsmen; in Śrāvaṇa, an increase in lifespan;
and in Bhādrapada, the loss of progeny.
In Āśvayuja there is great prosperity; in Kārttika, the arising of jewels; in Mārgaśīrṣa, constant auspiciousness; and in Puṇya, the destruction of the place.
In the month of Māgha, he is constantly deluded; indeed, in Phālguṇa, he is an excellent Vaiśya. Having thus thoroughly purified him, the mantra should be given by the minister.
Regarding the timing [of initiation],

it was stated of old: "On the day of the disciple's birth, during the periods of conjunction or opposition, on the days of the lords of the signs, on auspicious days, and on days joined with yogas— the purification of the human body is prescribed."
The Procedure for the Time of the Master’s Initiation (Ācāryābhiṣeka)
In the glorious Mataṅga [Tantra]: "Having properly reached the northern solstice during an auspicious lunar day in the bright fortnight...
On the eighth or the fourteenth day, the consecration is praised.
In this very context, the Amṛtayoga is described:
"Either through the conjunction of the root [nakṣatra] with the Sun, or together with Śravaṇa; or, if that is not known, on a Proṣṭhapadā day when Mars is in an auspicious lunar mansion."
O Brahmin, having ascertained the day when the moon is situated in Kṛttikā,
or on a Thursday in the month of Bhādrapada, there is the conjunction with Punarvasu.

On the full moon day of Phālguna, on a Friday, or under one's own natal asterism, when the Moon is in motion; likewise, during the fall [of the Moon], the Mūla-nakṣatra, or Śravaṇa, and so forth—one should perform the Amṛta-yoga. Furthermore, on the second lunar day of Mercury and so forth, as well as on Fridays, one should recognize the Dagdha-yoga.

"One should avoid [the times] beginning with the *gurusttarā*," etc.; this is the rule regarding time according to the *Dīkṣādarśa*. Now, the procedure for the construction of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) for initiation (*dīkṣā*) is described.
For example—
the construction of a pavilion for the sun-gem (aṃśumati-maṇi).

O Pārvatī, I shall describe the sacrificial pavilion (maṇḍapa) as an auxiliary to the sacrifice; listen to its form. The letter *kṣma* is the constituent of earth (*kṣiti*), the letter *tu* is that of fire (*tejas*), and the letter *ṇa* is that of water (*ap*).
The letter *ṭa* is the fire principle (*agnitattva*), the letter *pa* is called wind (*pavana*), and the letter *ma* has the form of space (*vyoman*);
these arise in sequence from the five syllables.
The designation "five-colored" refers to the form composed of the five elements;
the form consisting of the five elements and the five kalās is called the maṇḍapa.
With mantras conjoined with the purification of the paths (*adhvan*), he [worshipped] the abode of Yama through the stages;
for he performed worship by means of those [mantras] and others, which have the paths and mantras as their support.
Therefore, that which is called the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa) is merely a name;
its defining characteristic here is stated to be the nature of the ritual action itself.

The wise one should design the pavilions (*maṇḍapa*) within the spacious area designated for Śiva; regarding the measurement and proportions of these pavilions, the *Kāśyapa-śilpa* states that there are six varieties of the *mānāṅgula*.
In this context, the measurement multiplied by eight is the best *mānāṅgula*;
a width of seven barley-corns (*yava*) is the middling *mānāṅgula*.
The measure of six barley-corns in width is the lowest *mānāṅgula*; however, four times the length of a *śāli* grain is designated as the highest *aṅgula*.
The middle finger is known to be three and a half *śālis* in length;
the *aṅgula* of Śākalya, which is three times that length, constitutes the inferior measure.
Thus, O best of the twice-born, the sixfold *mānāṅgula* has been declared;
indeed, the *mānāṅgula* is threefold: the *cintyāṅga*, the middle, and the excellent.
O Ācārya, in the middle of the middle finger of the right hand, the mountain is both long and wide; its circumference is three times the measure of the finger-joints of the creator.
The measurement of a cubit (hasta) is proclaimed to be twenty-four of those finger-breadths (aṅgula).
Alternatively, the determination of the dimensions of the pavilion (maṇṭapa) may be made by means of either the *māna-aṅgula* or the *mātrā-aṅgula*. [This applies to] the components of the sacrifice.
And one should have all [the components] made according to the measurement of finger-breadths.
In the *Suprabheda*, it is defined as follows regarding the measurement of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*):
"The palace, the pavilion, the enclosure wall, and likewise the gate-tower.
In the case of villages, roads, fields, and houses, [the measurement] is according to the rule of the *māna-aṅgula*.
In this ritual practice, one should employ the *kūrca*, the *pavitraka*, the *sruva*, the *sruc*,
and other implements according to the measurement of finger-breadths (*mātrāṅgula*).

Alternatively, one may have the sacrificial rites performed using the *māna-aṅgula* measurement; this includes the construction of arches (*toraṇa*) and banners (*patākā*), as well as the preparation of seats such as the tortoise (*kūrma*).
The forms of the eight fingers, the vessels such as the *sruc* and *sruva*, the bathing pedestal (*avagāhana-pīṭha*),
and the three-legged stands shaped like fruits, in due order.
The best of men should perform all these [rites] as occasion arises; however, for one's own sake, the measurement of a finger-breadth is prescribed for the purpose of procreation.
In the *Viśvakarmīya*:
"For one's own sake, one should have the measurements for domestic images made according to the *mānāṅgula*;
and for the household deities, the measurement should be slightly less than that, according to the prescribed rule."
In the *Suprabheda*: "The *pradeśa*, the *vitasti*, and the *gokarṇa*—these three should be employed in sacrifices and similar rites;
one should not employ them for temples and such."
Regarding the cause—
the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana) has been described: its width should be one rudrāṅgula, and one should not make it any greater than that.
In the case of craftsmanship—
namely, the Vasiṣṭha [mandala], the pavilion, the sacrificial pit, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the eight auspicious items, the mandala, the altar, and especially the fuel sticks and so forth.
O Brahmin, having performed everything again and again, whether deficient or excessive, and having performed these during the ritual progression,
one should subsequently perform the concluding rite.
Otherwise, for the sake of consciousness, it would cause disease to the sacrificer;
there would be fear of famine and an increase [in suffering]— of this there is no need for deliberation.

Therefore, one should have those pavilions and so forth constructed according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures; this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. As stated in the *Aṃśumat*: "The altar should be raised one cubit or half of that from the floor, or it may be made of stone."
Or even with bricks, or with fuel made of wood.
One should construct a pavilion as a support, either square or rectangular.
Thus, it is stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"It may be made of bricks in the form of lotuses, or of pure wood, or even of clay."
Having thus made the sacrificial pavilion pure,
In the Aṃśumatī [treatise], the characteristics of the common pavilion (maṇṭapa) are stated:
beginning from five cubits and increasing by one cubit up to thirteen cubits,
there are three sets of three sizes, starting from the smallest.
Beginning from five cubits and increasing by two cubits at a time,
up to twenty-one cubits, nine measurements are thus declared.
Having determined the measurement, one should divide the portion for the row of pillars;
the heights, starting from the best (uttama) and so forth, should be equal in the water-shed (prapā), while in the pavilion (maṇṭapa),
they should be equal to the middle length.
The pillars should be erected as appropriate, with one-third and one-half [of the height] for the middle section;
thus, sixty-four pillars are prescribed for the three superior types.
Endowed with thirty-six bodily parts in the three middle [mandapas],
and endowed with sixteen pillars in the pavilion of the three smallest [mandapas].
This has been stated as the general rule; now the specific details are being told. Alternatively, since initiation is the subject at hand, the pavilion for initiation is described.
In the section concerning the initiation for the purpose [of the rite]:
"The pavilion should be square, measuring twelve cubits, or eleven cubits,
or even ten cubits, and it should be provided with sixteen pillars."
It is said to be of nine kinds according to the distinctions of superior and so forth in the *Vīratantra*:
"In the three inferior [categories], it should be three cubits, five cubits, or six cubits."
Seven cubits, eight cubits, and nine cubits are the middle [sizes].
It should be ten or eleven cubits, and twelve cubits would be the best; it should be sixteen cubits in width and its height should be measured in the same proportion.
The pinnacle-ridge should be four finger-breadths in length and provided with a square base;
likewise, the pillars should be made of jasmine wood, campaka wood, or khadira wood.
The handle (nāha) shall be twenty finger-breadths (aṅgulas) long, made of betel-nut wood, bamboo, *vakula*, or *kesara*;
or else it may be made of *jāti*, *vakula*, *kesara*, *pantai*,
or from trees suitable for sacrificial use (*yājñīka*).
From the eighth part upwards, it becomes slender in successive order.
The queen [prepared] the supreme [ointment] produced from the *yava* tree.
It was as follows—(p.
The aśvattha, udumbara, plakṣa, and likewise the aśvakarṇa and khadira; the nyagrodha, śamī, bilva, mango, and likewise the kaṅkata.
The *asana*, the *śīrṣa*, and the *yajñavṛkṣa* are proclaimed [as suitable for the sacrificial post].
The *plakṣa*, *āṣāḍhi*, *yaikaṅkata*, *asana*, *veheka*, or *śirīṣa* [are used], but not in the *vīratantra*.
The wise man should bury one-fifth of that amount in the earth,
and then cover it with coconut leaves and bamboo in such a way as to conceal it completely.
The wise man should cover the top with a coconut leaf; he should then cause the pavilion or the sacrificial pit to be sprinkled with water.
The characteristics of the gabled roof (kūṭākāra) are stated in the Śāradātilaka:
"The distance between [the pillars] should be measured by five, seven, or nine cubits;
it should be constructed with sixteen pillars, starting from one finger-breadth less than the maximum."
Four at the corners and one in the center; having established it with a height of eight cubits from the base, those [pillars] measuring five cubits in length should be auspicious and free from holes.
Aṃśumatī:
These pavilions have been prepared according to their respective functions, endowed with auspicious dimensions and so forth,
and in accordance with the requirements of the patron.
One should construct a circular pavilion according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures, having measured its width and length as six, seven, eight, or more cubits.
Thus, the description of the location for the construction of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) is stated:
it is provided with four gates and adorned with four archways (toraṇas). [The four gates and the archways...]
Or rather, the method of installation has been stated in the Piṅgalāmata.

Based on the statement, "Having left two cubits outside, one should cause the archways (toraṇas) to be placed," one should leave two cubits at the front of each door of the pavilion and have the archways placed there. Likewise, a banyan-tree archway should be placed in the east, and [another] in the south.
The *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* states:
"In the west, there is one made of *aśvattha*, and in the north, a gateway (*toraṇa*) made of *plakṣa*.
[As stated] in the *Cintyaviśva*:"
In the absence of all four types of trees, there should be only one;
it is considered that a *plakṣa* tree should be placed in the east and a *nyagrodha* in the north.
Thus it is stated in the Śāradātilaka: "At the gates, there should be eight arches (toraṇa) made respectively from milky trees;
their pillar-heights are prescribed as being individually seven cubits each."
Its circumference is said to be ten finger-breadths (aṅgulas); the measurement of the horizontal plank should be from the middle of the pillars.
In the *Kāmika*:
"The rule for the tridents above the seat is that they measure five hand-fingers [in width]; beginning from seven fingers, they are increased by the measure of a void (one finger) at each step."
One should determine the length of the fruit to be one *pakṣa* (half-fathom) at most; and the base of all the arches (*toraṇas*) should indeed be one *hasta* in measure.
In the *Vijayottara*:
"In the absence of trees, one should construct archways according to whatever materials are available, whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others."
In the western gate of the Nivṛtti [Kalā], one should construct a front pavilion (mukhamaṇḍapa) of the same dimensions as that [main pavilion] in the region of the western door within the maṇḍapa.
There are also three other doors, or alternatively, the Kaṃpacāra; thus,
having conceived the door as being half a mātrā in height, as before—
this characteristic was stated by Kāśyapa.
It should be constructed as a cloth-like structure, well-proportioned and spacious;
from the base up to the upper limit, there should be an emergence of a door-like opening.
O Aṃśumatī,
if the site is constricted, the wise man should construct the door in this manner within the pavilion, either toward the east or the south.
On both sides of the doors and in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast (āgneya),
one should establish the water-pots (kalaśas) for the presiding deities of the pavilion (maṇṭapa).
The altar is seven times seven paces in extent and one palm-tree span in height.
Regarding the characteristics of the door-panels for the Kāśyapa [stūpa], it is said as follows:
"Then, the two door-panels were made firm with heartwood trees."
They are provided with three staffs within, and above, they are endowed with sharp-pointed crests.
(1340) Bound with pillars made of smooth, solid wood both externally and internally, it may have three, five,
or seven [pillars], or a desired number on one side.
Alternatively, having firmly fixed iron pegs on both sides,
one should attach a cloth or similar material to the door-panel on the right side.
Having constructed the door-panels joined together and made firm with wood and iron, they should be provided with bolts and other fittings,
capable of being both closed and opened.
A wise person, having secured the door-panel endowed with such characteristics,
should then perform the laying of the lines (sūtranyāsa) upon the radiant surface.
I shall now explain the various types of lines, each according to its specific distinction.
The number of threads in the rites beginning with Yama is five, twelve, and seven respectively.
The measurement should be performed according to the distinction of the ritual action; it is twofold, both for the installation of the *liṅga* and for the installation of the temple (*vimāna*).
During a festival and during initiation, after the wise one has performed the sprinkling of the preceptor and established the thirteen squares, he should proceed.
[These are used] for the installation of an image of the All-pervading Lord, as well as for sprinkling, for the dwelling of the sacred threads,
and also for the sprinkling of the temple.
In the case of the eleven-fold rite, the work should be performed with pavilions and ritual threads; likewise in the consecration of a *bāla-liṅga* and in rites such as expiation.
In the rite of the eightfold binding, as well as in the constant and occasional rites, the wise practitioner should perform these respective actions at the appropriate moments of play.
(1341) Since a specific type of initiation (*dīkṣā*) is the subject under discussion here, only that much is stated.
For there is indeed some distinction regarding the threefold classification of initiation and so forth. [The] pavilion...
Having performed [the preliminary rites] as before, one should likewise prepare the foot and the thread.

In the center, a nine-square altar should be raised to the measure of one cubit; in the east, a nine-square area is to be taken, and in its center, a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be constructed according to the prescribed rules.
In the western group of nine, the altar concludes with the worship of the Śiva-liṅga; to the right of both the sacrificial pit and the altar, there is a division extending toward the east.

The altar (vedī) is for the sake of the officiating priests and the people, and for the purpose of seating the disciples; to the north, there are nine squares for the purpose of installing the ritual jars (kalaśa).
For Vāyu, there are five medicinal herbs, five varieties of rice, and five types of earth.
As it is stated in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"Sahadevī, ekapatra, bhadra, vaikaṅkata, and likewise viṣṇukrānti."
These five are known as the "five-fold medicine."
Sahadevī, Ekapatra, Bhadra, Vaikaṅkata,
Suśālīka, Drava, Yavanīvāra, and Veṇuka— these are declared to be the five types of barley; one should prepare them in the jars accordingly.
Suśālī is on the mountain, at the lake, and at Vṛṣaśṛṅga in the ocean.
One should take earth from a field of merit and deposit it in sequence:
first the pitcher (kumbha) and the vardhanī vessel, followed by the ritual knife (kartṛkā) and the cord (sūtraka).

At the time of the formal acceptance (adhivāsana), however, one should likewise place the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in the northeast; there too, one should leave open a single space for the purpose of movement.

Then, one should perform the Vāstu-pūjā either at the front of the sacrificial altar or in the south-eastern direction; having placed the hearth (cullikā) to the south, it should be positioned in front of Dharmarāja.
The remainder is indicated as before; in that state and according to that rule, they perform three initiations:
the Śāmbhava, the Kauruka, and the Sēcana.
Therefore, the sequence is as follows:
in the pavilion prepared for initiation, one should lay out the lines by means of a moist cotton thread mixed with rice flour,
extending from south to north and from west to east.
It becomes one hundred and sixty-nine [squares]. In that outer enclosure area,

having separately constructed an altar (*vedi*) measuring one *bāla* in width and length for each of the forty-eight squares in order to establish the gates, the gate-pitchers (*dvārakumbha*), and so forth;

Having removed forty squares situated within that [area] on all sides for the purpose of circulation, one should prepare a sacrificial altar (*vedi*) upon the eighty-one squares remaining within that space— specifically on the nine-square area in the northwest—
for the purpose of consecrating the five medicinal herbs, the five types of rice, and the five types of earth.

Having prepared the altar in the manner to be described, and having first consecrated the nine-pada area for the purpose of placing the pitcher for the preceptor’s consecration, one should then prepare the pitcher (*kumbha*), the *vardhanī*,
and the *tanusūtra* within that same nine-pada area.

Having prepared an altar for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the knife and other implements, one should construct a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the center of nine squares to its south, and a mandala to its west for the purpose of worshipping the Bestower of Boons (*varapūjā*).

Having prepared the primary altar (pradhānavedi), one should prepare a second altar to its west for the worship of the chosen liṅga (iṣṭaliṅga); and to its south, two square units (dvipada) extending east-west, for the installation of the chosen liṅga and for the maṇḍala-worship of the Hotṛ and the disciple.
Having prepared a hearth for the sake of cooking the *sthālīpāka* in the presence of the Dharmarāja for the purpose of maintaining [the ritual],

and having constructed an altar to the west of that for the purpose of establishing the *aṅkurārpaṇa*, and [another] to the east of those two in the remaining space for the purpose of the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the disciples;

One should designate this area for the purpose of placing the substances required for the sacrifice. Having thus stated the division of the site by way of general rules, the characteristics of the principal altar (*pradhānavedikā*) are now demonstrated.
As it is said in the *Cintyaviśva*:
One should construct the altar specifically so that it resembles the surface of a mirror; or, in a cramped location, one may fashion it in a suitable form.
Its height should be one cubit (hasta), or even one forearm-span (ratni), or it may be made with a span (tāla) [of height],
provided with a secondary altar-platform (upavedī).
The height should be four finger-breadths and the width two finger-breadths.
This is stated in the *Kāmika-tantra*, in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā-prakaraṇa*).
The height is proclaimed to be either three finger-breadths or two finger-breadths; its width is equal to that, or one, two, three, four, or five [finger-breadths], or half of those.
In this manner, having determined the measurement for the height of the two altars to the west and north of the principal altar according to its characteristics,
one should construct the measurement for the height of the two side-altars (*vyaśāna-vedikā*) as half of that same height; such is the measurement for the height in the *Aṃśumatī* [tradition].
The construction of the pavilion for the installation of the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) has been previously explained.
It is as follows:
They construct altars and secondary platforms (upabhadraka) in the four directions; it is nine squares in extent, square in shape, with a height equal to half its measurement.
In the four corners starting from the southeast (āgneya), the height is half of that [measurement].

It should be understood that the three altars (*vedikā*) mentioned in the previously described procedure for initiation (*dīkṣā-vidhāna*) and the procedure for the consecration of the preceptor (*ācāryābhiṣeka-vidhāna*), as well as their previously stated measurements of height, are also applicable here. Thus...
Regarding the characteristics of the pavilion for all desires (*sarvakāmika-maṇḍapa*) on the prepared central altar (*pradhāna-vedikā*), it is stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the mandala that fulfills all desires. [This is] the mandala..."
It is called the essence; the wise know it to be the abode of all the gods.
This mandala was proclaimed by Śiva, the Supreme Self; by the mere sight of this mandala, one is liberated from all sins.
Prior to the time of initiation, the wise one should prepare the mandala according to the rules.
Regarding the characteristics of the measuring-line (sūtra), the *Kiraṇatantra* states:
"The instrument [for the line] may be made of cotton, linen, or derived from kuśa grass or bark; it should be free from knots and the like."
Then, that [number] minus the effect (kārya) shall be two, three, or six.
In the *Mṛgendra*:

"Formerly, for the one who has transcended the three qualities (*triguṇātīta*), [the thread] is made of silk, cotton, or hemp; for those who have not yet abandoned the defects of worldly life, it is a triple-stranded thread of threefold quality."
In the *Suprabheda*:
"Having perceived the vital breath within, one should observe Citrabhāga by means of Vāmadeva."
One should cause the thread-line to be drawn with the mantra.
Having fixed the thread in the eastern and western parts with a concentrated mind, one should then establish the auspicious thread there, extending from south to north.
There, having first established the thread from east to west, one should then extend the thread there, starting from the village and fashioned by one who has relied upon it.
Having extended a thread from the southeast (Āgneyī) to the northwest (Vāyavyā),
one should extend a thread from the northeast (Aiśānī) to the southwest (Nairṛtī).
Having made it square and even, let it be divided into nine parts; by means of one part for the palace, there shall be a lotus, and one should draw the pericarp.
That lotus is adorned with a pavilion consisting of four parts:
the first part is the pericarp, and the second is indeed the filaments.
The third [layer] is at the junction of the petals, while the fourth consists of the tips of the petals; the wise one should draw the first enclosure outside the lotus, reaching to its edge.
Regarding the cause—
or rather—
the square with its full extent, divided by the thread of the owl (kauśika), [is] by the sky (vyoma).
One should fashion the pericarp with one-fifth part [of the lotus], and the filaments likewise.

The remainder, however, should be for the *damanā* [pedestal], measuring half the size of the *karṇikā*; one should fashion the tips of the petals at that measure, and the space between the petals according to that same measure.
One should fashion the filaments joined with eight petals, and one should draw the line for each tusk according to the measurement of the petal-tip.

In a small [mandala], a five-petaled lotus should be made; in a large one, a large lotus. Alternatively, the outer path may be half the size of the lotus, or equal to the measurement of the lotus itself.
The beauty of the four gates is equal to that of the streets and is beautifully situated; the two guardians of those [gates] possess a splendor equal to that, occupying a portion of the sky.
The placement [of the deities] should be either equal to that of the lotus or in the four directions;
it should be two cubits or one cubit, and one should not construct it larger than that.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"Neither too thick nor too thin, not inferior, not crooked, and devoid of spots— having constructed the abode of the God of gods in this manner, it bestows the attainment of liberation."

A thick [line] is said to portend all kinds of fear; one should indicate quarrels at the mouth. A deficient [line], however, results in a lack of success, while a dot brings about the fear of enemies.
O Śambhu, when the thread is thin, disease arises; when it is of mixed color, there is famine; and when it hangs down with dust, there will be no presence [of the deity].
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform [the ritual] endowed with the proper characteristics. Regarding the causes:
it is traditionally taught that the *vītaśuklā*, *aruṇā*, *kṛṣṇā*, and *vartakānanā* are the varieties of *vacā*.
In the *Suprabheda*: "In that case, it is especially praised when mixed with pearls of various colors, particularly those of the color of a calf;
however, a red color produced by the powders of rubies is highly commended."
The black color is proclaimed to be produced by powders of sapphire,
while the yellow color is said to be produced by powders of gold.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"The colors are white, red, yellow, and black. Thus.
It is declared to be fivefold, consisting of the five jewels beginning with pearl.
With crystals, natural marks and the like, yellow-green stones, dark-blue ones,
and the five types of collyrium powders, according to the prescribed ritual.
Then, with the powders of lotus bricks and the powders of ten types of rice, one should fashion the *avaja* [image] using the powders of yellow myrobalan (*harītakī*) while reciting mantras.
With a pericarp of yellow color, resembling topaz and gold in appearance,
it has twenty-five petals, each raised by the measure of a barley grain.
The filaments resemble the [lotus] threads and are white at their tips;
the eight petals of the lotus are white, with black lines within the intervals between them.
On both sides of the lines, those two jewels should likewise be placed at every interval; the path around the lotus should likewise be of red color.
The doors should be made yellow in color, and on both sides of the doors,
one should cause the primary ornaments (śobhās) and secondary ornaments (upaśobhās) to be fashioned using all colors.
Another sūtra is said to be a barley-corn's length; it is remembered that the interval between two short [lines] should be even shorter.
For the sake of liberation, one should use the right hand (apasavya), but for the sake of worldly enjoyment, one should use the left hand (savyaka).
One who desires prosperity should draw with the tip of the hand that grants all accomplishments;
in the cause [of this], Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Bhavānī are the presiding deities of the *rajas* element. All defects...
One should extend the yellow-colored [light] for the purpose of withdrawal.
One should extend the white color for the sake of the manifestation of the form; however, for the sake of the downward breath (apāna), one should apply the red color for auspiciousness.
Having indeed withdrawn the *tamas*, one should extend the black-colored [element]; having conceived the *yogapīṭha* within the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), perform it according to the prescribed rite.
One should always worship the god Sadāśiva in the center of the pericarp; on the left side of the pericarp, one should worship the goddess Manonmanī.
Having invoked and worshipped according to the ritual procedure with perfumes, flowers, and so forth in due order,
one should perform the worship of the enclosures (āvaraṇapūjana) by means of the five-fold enclosure system.
Alternatively, having performed the first ritual action according to the prescribed rule;
or rather—
at the beginning of the initiation (dīkṣā) and so forth— one should employ a mandala upon the altar in the form of a svastika.
The Sarvatobhadra and the Gaurītilaka as well.
The Pārvatī, Kānta, Liṅga-abja-svastika, and likewise the Latā-liṅga-udbhava— thus the maṇḍala is said to be of six kinds.
In the *Śāradātilaka*, four types of maṇḍalas are mentioned, as follows:
"One should likewise cause the *Sarvatobhadra* maṇḍala, the *Śrāvaya* maṇḍala, the *Navanābha* maṇḍala, and the *Pañcābja* maṇḍala to be proclaimed."
For the purpose of worship during initiation, the fourfold mandalas have been described according to all the tantras; they grant success everywhere.
In this general initiation, the specific details are now stated: for Brahmins, it is the Sarvatobhadra; for Gaurīs, it is the Tilaka; and for kings, it is the Nṛpa.
For Vaiśyas, however, the *latā-liṅga* is prescribed; for Śūdras, it should be the *svastika*.
Regarding the *sarvatobhadra*:
as follows—in a grid of sixty-four squares, there is a lotus-pedestal (*padma-vīthī*) in the center, and the pedestal for the *liṅga* (*liṅga-pīṭha*).
The lotus has a pericarp and five pedestals.
Then, having adorned it sequentially with sixty-four eyes, six quadruples of feet, and the colors of the faces, and again with the four Vedas and their constituent words;
On the pedestal of the *liṅga*, one should construct a *svastika* with five squares in each of the four directions and one square in the corners; thus it becomes the *sarvatobhadra* [mandala].
The Gaurītilaka:
The incomparable Gaurītilaka [is made] with seventeen threads; in the center is the space-point (vyomapada), and there are four liṅgas in the four directions.
One should arrange leaves and flowers of various colors in the intermediate directions,
in each of all the corners, sequentially using twenty-five squares.
It should be fashioned in various ways with beautiful colors of creepers;
this is called the Gaurī-tilaka, which yields the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The pavilion arising from the vine-enclosure is as follows:
in this [space] divided into twelve parts, it is square on all sides; with six parts there is the fragrant flower, and with three parts the cloth-band (paṭṭa).
Likewise, one should fashion the path with one part, and similarly eight liṅgas; the door with two parts, along with creepers, extending for seven steps.
The *svastika-maṇḍala*, which bestows the fruits of all desires and is known as "Born from the Embrace of the Creeper," has been described.
For example—
one should stretch out five lines, one oriented toward the east and one toward the north. Know that the *liṅga* occupies one square, and the pedestal (*pīṭha*) likewise occupies three squares.
One should adorn it with four liṅgas and with threads of the prescribed colors; thus is described the svastika, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Aṃśumatī said:
"Nine squares should be taken in the east, and in the center, a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be constructed according to the rules.
Its characteristics have been described in the *Mohaśūrottara*:"
One should dig this [pit] horizontally and vertically along with the girdle;
outside the excavation, there should be a rim one finger-breadth wide—this is the rule for all sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
A triple girdle should be fashioned from gold, measuring one finger-breadth [in width];
its height from the navel to the deity [the waist] is twelve finger-breadths, while its breadth is one-third of that.
Resting on a single finger, it likewise enters within; joined with two "pots" (kumbhas), it is like the leaf of an ashvattha tree.
She is endowed with a girdle of big toes, like the support of clarified butter in the center;
she stands on the right during the first watch, and is swiftest in the west and north.
Having laid down the first cord from the east and the second extending toward the north, all fields shall be square; among fields, this is the perfection.
Regarding the cause:
having divided the navel-field into three parts, one should fashion the pericarp in the center;
with two parts on the outside, one should arrange eight petals.

One should fashion the navel in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the shape of a lotus, with a height of four finger-breadths (*dakṣāṅgula*) and a width of five finger-breadths (*bhūtāṅgula*).
The measure of the *daṇḍa* should be two parts, while the *karṇikā* is one part.
Above the *mekhalā*, one should fashion the *yoni* like an *aśvattha* leaf; as it is said in the *Kiraṇa*:
"One should fashion [the *yoni*] like an *aśvattha* leaf on a hand that is eight digits wide."
Its length is twelve finger-breadths, and its height is one finger-breadth.
Aṃśumatī:
"Having thus completed everything at the conclusion of the artisan's work, one should dismiss the craftsman there; perform the sweeping and sprinkling."
Having adorned the two sides of the doorway with flowering plantain and betel-nut trunks,
decorated with variegated cloths and embellished with betel nuts, flowers, and other offerings.
Adorned with mirrors and other objects in the shape of a crescent moon, and provided with a canopy, one should wrap the body in cloth and decorate it with four arches.
It was provided with lamps and banners, beautified by a canopy above, adorned with strings of pearls,
and hung with garlands of flowers.
Having constructed a pavilion provided with lamps, and having performed the sweeping and smearing [of the ground],
one should create a colorful design made of rice flour.
They perform three initiations: the Śāmbhava, the sprinkling by the Guru, and the examination of the disciple-lotus; the Guru should perform all of these.
Thus ends the procedure for constructing the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*) in the *Dīkṣādarśa*. (p.
1352) Now, the procedure for the worship of the site (*vāstupūjā*) is described.
The Vāstupūjā is prescribed for the subtle [rite],
for the installation, for the sprinkling, and likewise for the laying of the foundation (garbhanyāsa), for the installation of the temple (vimāna),
and for the festival pavilion of sacrifice (yāgamaṇḍapa).
In the maṇṭapa, in the assembly hall, in all places of installation,
at the site of the first stone or brick, and in the dance arena, one should indeed perform the sacrificial session (satra).
One should undertake rites such as expiation (prāyaścitta) and others, as well as the installation [of the deity]; the worship of Vāstu must be performed for the attainment of all prosperity.
If the worship of Vāstu is neglected, that kingdom shall perish;
therefore, one should undertake the worship of Vāstu with every effort.
Likewise, in the *Jyotiṣaratnākara*:
"If one enters a new house without performing the worship of the *vāstu* deity, one encounters various diseases, afflictions, and every kind of calamity."
In the *Śāradātilaka*:
"Thereafter, I shall describe the initiation preceded by the Vāstu sacrifice;
by performing which, the knower of mantras attains the fruit of initiation."
In the *Suprabheda*, in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā-prakaraṇa*),
regarding the ritual procedure for the worship of the site (*vāstupūjā-vidhāna*), one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).
In the *Kāraṇa*:

The Vāstuhoma sacrifice should be performed, provided with all necessary materials; it must be conducted by one who is perfected through initiation and consecration, devoted to Śiva from the beginning, and firm in his vows.
One who is endowed with all auspicious marks, proficient in the Śiva scriptures,
and pure in soul should perform the Vāstu-homa according to the rite for the site.
In the subtle [rite]:
the preceptor, joined with the disciple, should perform the bath as before;
having clothed them in pure garments, perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa.
In the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*: "Before initiation and consecration, especially during the installation [of an image],
at the commencement of all tantras, and for practitioners seeking various supernatural powers (*siddhis*)."
The coconut fruit, the plantain fruit, betel nut, betel leaf, sugarcane,
milk, and curd.
Having placed [the vessel] in a clean pot, one should perform worship there which bestows all accomplishments; one should worship Gaṇeśa there, for otherwise there will be no freedom from obstacles.
Aṃśumatī:
Having prepared the general arghya water, one should prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Then, having performed the placement [of mantras] according to the path of step-by-step deposition, one should perform the worship beginning with Brahmā.
The height should be one cubit and the width three finger-breadths; having worshipped the Vāstumaṇḍala-pitcher with the mantras beginning with the *samaya* [mantra], etc.

One should perform the fire-ritual according to the path described for the fire-ritual; at the conclusion of the oblation, the wise practitioner should perform the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa).
In this context, he teaches the worship of the site (*vāstupūjā*) many times through various methods;

here, at the beginning of initiation and other rites, one should perform the *vāstupūjā* after understanding the channels (*nāḍī*), cords (*rajjū*), bamboo-poles (*vaṃśa*), and so forth, according to the "frog-step" (*maṇḍūkapada*) pattern. Thus it is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
The sūtra is endowed with sixty-four steps, accompanied by eighteen [divisions], provided with a cord for the ear,
and adorned with eight strings.
The site is endowed with twelve vital points (marmas) and accompanied by the deities of the Vāstu.

Then the preceptor, adorned with five types of golden ornaments— namely, a golden ring, bracelets, armlets, a golden sacred thread, and earrings— and having gathered the materials required for the constituent parts of the Vāstu sacrifice, [proceeds].
To the southeast of the previously mentioned pavilion, or in each individual pavilion,
having prepared a site measuring one cubit in width and six finger-breadths in height,
one should construct sixty-four squares upon it, with lines drawn at the corners.

Having struck the lines with threads and having drawn tridents at their respective tips, one should draw circles in the directions starting from the east and perform the Vāstu-pūjā in the manner of a frog’s footprint.
The method for that worship is as follows:
One should know that the head is the Brahmakāya; it is further said, O Brahmin, that Āpa and Pāpavatsaka are remembered as the left arm.
Savitṛ and Sāvitrika are said to be the right arm;
Rudra and Rudrajaya are proclaimed to be the left foot.
Indra and Indrajapa are said to be the two right feet; Mitra is the penis, as well as the testicles and the back.
Having reached the earth face-down, he is known as Vāstu;
at the time of worship, his rising is said to be toward the north.
Because of his fierce nature and because he causes fear, he should be worshipped by those seeking fruits; he has four arms, wears a crown of matted hair, and holds a water-pot and a rosary.
The left hand is placed above the knee with the palm facing upward; she is golden-hued, holds a lotus,
and is worshipped with perfumes and other offerings.
"Oṃ, obeisance to the Brahmā-throne; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the form of Brahmā;

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the site"—having thus worshipped him with the eight purificatory rites beginning with invocation, [one should worship] within that, in the center of the six squares located in the east.
Salutation to Marīci in the center of the six squares within the south: *Oṃ Vivasvate namaḥ*.
In the center of the six squares within the west: *Oṃ Mitrāya namaḥ*.
In the center of the six squares within the north: salutation to Daṇḍarādharāya. Thus.

Having worshipped the four deities starting from the east, one should worship as follows: in the half-square of the two squares located in the southeast corner, "Oṃ, salutation to Savitṛ"; below that, in the half-square of the [next] square, "Oṃ, salutation to Sāvitrī";
in the half-square of the two squares located in the southwest corner, "Oṃ, salutation to Indra"; and below that, in the half-square of the corner...

In the [central] square: *oṃ indrajayāya namaḥ*. In the two half-squares of the northwest corner: *oṃ rudrāya namaḥ*. In the half-square of the corner below that: *oṃ rudrajayāya namaḥ*. In the two half-squares of the northeast corner: *oṃ āpāya namaḥ*. In the half-square of the corner below that: [oṃ āpajayāya namaḥ].
"Oṃ, obeisance to Āpavatsa. Having thus worshipped the eight deities in the corners, one should worship in the square surrounding them as follows:
in the southern half of the northeast corner, "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Īśāna";
in the [corner] to its right, "Oṃ, obeisance to Parjanya"; and [in the next], "Oṃ, obeisance to Jayanta."
Homage! Oṃ, homage to Mahendra; Oṃ, homage to Āditya; homage to Satyaka; homage to Bhraṃśa. To the north of that: Oṃ, homage to Dauvārika; homage to Hayagrīva; homage to Puṣpadanta.
