*Pracetase* namaḥ; *asurāya* namaḥ; *śoṣaye* namaḥ. In the southern square of the southwest corner: *Oṃ pāpākhyāya* namaḥ; in the western part: *Oṃ vāyave* namaḥ.
In those [spaces] to the east: *oṃ* homage to Rogāya, homage to Nāgāya, homage to Mukhyāya, homage to Bhallāṭāya, homage to Somāya, homage to Atithaye;
in the half-space of the northeast corner: homage to Inditaye; at the tip of the trident in the northeast direction: *oṃ*.

Salutation to Carakī; salutation to Vitārī; salutation to Pūtanā; salutation to Pāparākṣasī—at the four corners of the enclosure starting from the east: Oṃ, salutation to Skanda; Oṃ, salutation to Jambha; salutation to Balipiñcha; Oṃ, salutation to Gṛhakṣata.

Thus one should worship the eight deities. The individual meditations (dhyāna) have been explained in detail in the *Śivālayanirmāṇasthāpanādīpikā*; here, however, the meditation is stated concisely: "The remaining [deities] are endowed with four arms, holding a sword and a shield, with palms joined in reverence (*kṛtāñjali*)."
Endowed with their respective enclosures, they all abide in their own stations.
Having worshipped the Vāstu deities with their respective names ending in "namaḥ," one should offer a bali-oblation consisting of pure food mixed with curd, ghee, and jaggery.
In the subtle [practice],
one should not cause even a single offering to be presented with the size of a hen’s egg; the offering is prescribed here to end with "Namaḥ," whereas it is offered here ending with "Svāhā."
Prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with rice in the northeast of the offering pavilion,
adorned with parched grain, flowers, sesame seeds, darbha grass, and the five powders.
[One should offer] vessels together with water-pots, provided with sprouts, accompanied by cloths and gold,
furnished with *palāśa* leaves, and joined with coconut fruits.
Having established the Vāstu-pitcher along with its surrounding subsidiary pitchers,
one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, as prescribed for the ritual installation of the pitcher (kalaśa-sthāpana).

One should worship the deities of the site, beginning with Brahmā, with their respective mantras; one should cause an offering of food (naivedya) to be given to them, and likewise offer incense, lamps, and so forth.
To the east of the bali-maṇḍala, one should perform the fire-rite (agnikārya); there, one should especially worship the seat, the form, and the root-mantra.
In the causal rite— having offered fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood one hundred and forty times,
having offered clarified butter that same number of times, and likewise having offered the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) that same number of times.
Having offered oblations with sesame and rice mixed together in the previously mentioned number,
one should worship the deities situated outside the interior of the site (vāstu) by their respective names.

Then, one should offer oblations individually according to the sequence beginning with the *samid* fuel sticks; or, as stated in the *Sūkṣma*: "The wise one should offer ten oblations for the principal [deity], and one oblation each for the fires. [Using] *palāśa*...
Having thus offered the fuel-sticks with the mantras beginning with "brahmā," etc., [one should proceed].
Having offered clarified butter fifty-three times according to the names of the deities, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (caru) that same number of times.
The wise one should offer rice mixed with sesame seeds that many times; having offered the Vyāhṛtis at the end of the substances, he should offer the Mahāstra mantra one hundred times.
Having collected all the materials, one should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation;
then, whatever has been prescribed for this rite, one should offer the final *pūrṇāhuti*.
One should place [the fire] situated in the fire, situated in the foot, and situated in the pitcher within the heart;
[one should offer] leaves of the Aśvattha and Udumbara trees, withered by Brahmā, together with Darbha grass.

For the purification of that site, having bound [the mantra] there with clarified butter mixed with sesame seeds, one should perform the purification of that site by sprinkling it while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra.
Having placed the fire before that [mandala] and ignited it with the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ),
one should [visualize] the entire dwelling and sacrificial pavilion as being within the letter A.
Perform the circumambulation with fire accompanied by the *jayaghaṇā* chant; then sprinkle the site with water from the ritual jar while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having cast away the firebrand, one should perform the ritual bath outside of that according to the prescribed rules;
this is declared to be the Vāstu-homa, which cuts through all defects.
Thus ends the ritual for the worship of the site (vāstupūjā) in the Dīkṣādarśa.
Now, the procedure for the offering of the sprouts is described.
Regarding the cause— for this reason, I shall hereafter proclaim the supreme ritual of depositing the sprout (aṅkurārpaṇa), during festivals, ablutions, installations,
and likewise during consecrations (prokṣaṇa).

Whether for rites performed on specific occasions, for those desired for particular results, for expiatory ceremonies and the like, or for any other auspicious undertaking, this is called the "Auspicious Sprout" (Maṅgalāṅkura).
In the *Suprabheda* (p.
1359): "At the beginning of all auspicious rites and activities, one should perform the 'sprout of auspiciousness' (*maṅgalāṅkura*)."
In the *Śāradātilaka*: "One should perform the rite of sowing seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) during initiation, consecration, the entry into a new house, and at all festivals."
In the *Vijayottara*:
"On the night preceding the specified day, one should perform the offering of divine sprouts;
however, on the aforementioned auspicious night, one should offer the auspicious sprouts for mortals."
In the Kāmika:
"The wise man should cause a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to be prepared in the northeast direction of the pavilion, or specifically in its center, having eight petals and a pericarp."
In the *Suprabheda*, in the section on initiation (*dīkṣā-prakaraṇa*):
"Then, having offered the sprouts according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Also in the *Cintyaviśva*:
O Nandikeśvara, at the time of initiation (dīkṣā) and consecration (pratiṣṭhā), and indeed at the beginning of any other auspicious rite, one should perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇaka).
The Moon is the lord of seeds; one should sow the crops at night. It may also be done during the day, but if it is performed [at night], there will be destruction.
In the auspicious Brahma-sacrifice, it is always performed at the junction of the day and at both twilights;
a specific rule regarding the cause has been stated:
If the offering of fresh sprouts is to be made, one should perform it by day or at night;
[as stated] in the *Sūkṣma*: (p. 1360)
There is no sprout from a sprout without that specific intervening action; [this occurs] on the ninth or even the seventh day after the day prescribed for initiation.
One should perform [the rite] either five days, three days, or even immediately.
Herein is the sequence for collecting the earth: having gone to the bank of a river, a pond, flower gardens, forests, a cremation ground, or a pure spot of ground.

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the infusion of the deity’s limbs), having prepared the general water offering (sāmānyārghya) and sprinkled it with the Astra-mantra, one should offer there edible items such as cakes and coconut to Vighneśvara.
O Lord of Obstacles, salutations to you who are ever fond of modaka sweets; through your grace, may you dispel the many obstacles that have arisen so that I may be free from hindrance.
Praying thus, one should worship with devotion the supreme adoration of Vighneśa.
Having prepared a nine-square grid in that place, one should worship in the central square—starting from the center and extending to the northeast—with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā."
In the eastern and other compartments: *oṃ hāṃ anantāya namaḥ*— *oṃ hāṃ vinatāyai namaḥ*— *oṃ hāṃ bhadrāyai namaḥ*— *oṃ hāṃ jayantāyai namaḥ*—
*oṃ hāṃ bhramaryai namaḥ*— *oṃ hāṃ prasthitāyai namaḥ*— *oṃ hāṃ*.

Having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Parijṛmbhiṇī; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śūlinī," and having offered the *bali* in due order, one should dismiss them for their satisfaction with ghee, sugar-candy, curd, and boiled rice.

"O gods, this clay has been taken by my command for the purpose of producing the sprout; you may depart from this place as you please. Having made this request and dismissed [the deities], and having recited the *puṇyāha* (day of merit) in front of the sacrificial circle (*balimaṇḍala*), [he proceeds].
Having sprinkled [her] with the Kuntālī weapon-mantra and worshipped her with the heart-mantra, [one should visualize her] as resembling dark blue cloth,
with eyes like a shimmering lotus, wearing a golden sacred thread, and possessing two arms.

Having two eyes, endowed with all ornaments, and wearing a jeweled crown; the goddess is robed in red garments and holds a rosary in her right hand. Having meditated thus, one should worship [her] on all sides with the invocation and other ritual offerings, reciting: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhūdevī."
Having worshipped the world-protectors (lokapālas), facing either east or north,

and having recited the weapon-mantra (astramantra), he should dig three times with a spade or similar tool; then, taking the earth with the Tatpuruṣa mantra, he should place it in a vessel and sprinkle it thoroughly with water while reciting the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
Having worshipped with flowers and covered with cloth and armor, one should have that [image] carried by great lords mounted on elephants and so forth, or by those such as Rudrakaṇika and others,
accompanied by conchs and dundubhi drums.
Accompanied by shouts of victory, dancing, singing, and instrumental music, he enters the sacrificial hall in a clockwise direction; having drawn his own self in the northeast or southwest,
he [proceeds] upon the altars (sthaṇḍila) prepared for the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) in the positions beginning with Īśāna.
Having laid out five lines from west to east and from south to north,

thus dividing [the area] into sixteen parts, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with its stalk in the four central squares; then, in the squares starting from the northeast (īśāna), [one places] gold, silver, and copper.
Having placed twelve earthen vessels— either small bowls (*pālikā*),

jars (*ghaṭikā*), or shallow dishes (*śarāva*)— filled with powdered clay and provided with a single ear of *śirīṣa*, *aśvattha*, or *bilva* wood, upon the grain in the *avadhānī* vessel; or simply having placed the *pālikās* alone upon it.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa by means of the *candrahṛdaya* and other mantras, and having prepared the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*),
one should place within the four central squares a golden vessel with its cord, filled to the brim with consecrated water, provided with a cloth, a *kūrca*, and a lid of sprouts.
Having placed the water-pot (kumbha),
one should offer a seat with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Soma," and upon that [seat], [place the vessel] with "Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ."
"Salutation to the form of Soma. Having thus worshipped the form, one should praise the lotus in the midst of the water within the jar, and the form of the Moon in the center of that lotus.
White in color, with two eyes, seated upon a white lotus, having two arms,
holding a white water-lily, and draped in a white garment.
Adorned with a circle of light.
Having meditated upon the beloved of Rohiṇī, one should place [the mantra] in the middle of the pitcher.
Having thus meditated: *oṃ raṃ vaṃ saṃ hīṃ haṃ śrī someśvarāya namaḥ*. Thus [it is said].
Having invoked [the deity] into the center of the pitcher (kumbha), performed the rites of installation (sthāpanā), worshipped him along with his limbs (sāṅga),

offered milk-rice (pāyasa), and completed the recitation (japa), one should [visualize] the form of Vaikartana in the pitchers (pālikā) placed in the east and other directions: he has one face, two hands, and [carries] weapons.
And one who holds a golden flower with both hands.
Having meditated thus: "A golden [image] adorned with ornaments and clothed in garments of saffron," one recites:
*oṃ vaikartanāya namaḥ*.
Vivasvat, however, has his own natural form: two faces and four arms; with two hands holding weapons and lotuses, he is endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons.
The garment should be tawny and the ornament coral.
*Oṃ*, salutation to Vivasvat—
[the form] of Mārtāṇḍa [should be visualized] with coral, three faces, and endowed with six arms.
He displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, as well as a rosary, a water-pot, two lotuses in his hands,
a necklace, and other ornaments.
Oṃ, salutation to Mārtāṇḍa. As for the true form of Bhāskara, he has two faces and four arms; with two hands he performs the gesture of salutation, and his other two hands hold a pair of lotuses.
With crimson borders and crimson garments, adorned with blue gems;
"Oṃ, obeisance to Bhāskara. The form of Ravi is endowed with four arms, and specifically, [in this case] eight hands.
A rosary and a water-pot.
The trident, noose, goad, and lotus, as well as the gestures of fearlessness and granting boons—these are declared to be his weapons; he is red in color and holds them.
Having thus meditated upon the ornamented Amarataka, one should worship it with:
"Oṃ, salutation to Ravi—
the illuminator of the world, resembling the color of lapis lazuli (rājāvarta), ten-armed, five..."
The face and the lotus itself are formed with two hands.
He is endowed with hands bearing the trident, the goad, the staff, the rosary, the water-pot, the arrow, the bow, and the staff,
as well as the mudrās and the auspicious signs.
Blue and red in all his limbs, wearing blue garments—*Oṃ, salutation to Lokaprakāśa*. I shall now describe Lokasākṣī: he has one face and two hands.
One should visualize him with his hands joined in the *añjali* gesture, white in color,
wearing a single saffron-colored garment, and his body smeared with ashes.
Oṃ, salutations to the witness of the world—
[I worship] the form of Trivikrama, who has two arms and four arms.
Oṃ, salutations to Trivikrama.
The true form of Āditya has one face and two hands; in his pair of hands he holds a lotus, and he possesses the radiance of a pomegranate flower.
Having thus visualized the form of Āditya as having red ornaments, [one should recite]:
"Oṃ, homage to Āditya.
Furthermore, the true nature of Sūrya has one face and eight arms, [holding] two lotuses...
One should offer incense with sugar and a water-pot with a handle.
Endowed with the gesture of granting fearlessness and accompanied by a rosary, he wears golden garments, possesses a golden luster,
and is adorned with ornaments of pure gold.
Having meditated thus, one should especially worship the form of the Sun:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Sūrya!
His own form is garlanded with rays, possessing six faces and red in color, [with] twelve..."
Likewise, let there be two lotuses for the hands in front of the hand.

In the right and left [hands], he holds the *tomara*, the sword (*khaṭvāṅga*), the shield (*kheṭaka*), the noose (*pāśa*), the goad (*aṅkuśa*), the spear (*śakti*), the *vetāla*, and the gestures of fearlessness (*abhaya*) and granting boons (*varada*).
Homage to Aṃśumālin—[he] who has the nature of the sun, two faces, and four hands.
Holding two bilva leaves in one pair of hands and two lotus flowers in the other pair of hands.

Clad in garments of saffron and adorned with golden ornaments, one should meditate thus and worship [the Sun] with: *oṃ divākarāya namaḥ* (Oṃ, salutation to the Maker of Day), *oṃ ravaye namaḥ* (Oṃ, salutation to Ravi);
or alternatively: *oṃ hāṃ vai kartanāya namaḥ* (Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the Creator), *oṃ vivasvate namaḥ* (Oṃ, salutation to Vivasvat). *Oṃ...* [and so forth].
Salutation to Mārtāṇḍa—Oṃ, salutation to Bhāskara; Oṃ, salutation to Ravi;
Oṃ, salutation to the Illuminator of the World; Oṃ, salutation to the Witness of the World;
Oṃ, salutation to Trivikrama; Oṃ, salutation to Āditya; Oṃ, salutation to Sūrya.

"Oṃ, obeisance to Aṃśumālin; Oṃ, obeisance to Divākara"—with these [mantras], one should worship the twelve Ādityas starting from the east and ending at the northeast. In the case of eight [deities], one should worship Indra and the others with their respective seven mantras; in the case of five, having worshipped Nivṛtti and the others, [one should offer] incense, lamps, and so forth.

Having worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings, and having presented milk-rice (pāyasa) to them, one should worship the Śakti in the milk contained in a pure vessel with the mantra "Oṃ Hrīṃ Śaktaye Namaḥ";
then, into that [milk], one should place seven seeds located on the bank— namely, Nīvāra, Mudga, sesame, mustard, and Śiva.
Having washed those [vessels] five or three times, consecrated them with the four purificatory rites (catus-saṃskāra),
worshipped them with the Saṃhitā-mantras, and considering this to be the worship of Śiva, one should place them therein; then,
having worshipped the Support Power (Ādhāra-śakti) in the *pālikā* vessels and others, and having offered incense, lamps, and so forth.

Preceded by the auspicious sounds of conchs, kāhala trumpets, and drums, one should sow the seeds with milk while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra, or the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) along with its limbs (*brahmāṅga*),
and then water that pot every day with the water from the *soma*-jar.

One should fill [the vessel] with pure water until it reaches the level of the [intended] ritual day; having worshipped Soma, at the conclusion of the designated day, one should worship the *arghya* facing away from the pitcher situated within it and then dismiss it.
In the established doctrine (siddhānta):
one should examine the sprouts for the sake of the prosperity of the sacrificer.
And they were soft, having grown straight upward in perfect symmetry.
Sprouts that are auspicious are those that are white; those that are black bring inauspicious results.
One should avoid those that are smoke-colored, unprecedented, or otherwise inauspicious.
It constantly causes drought, brings about smoke-colored appearances and strife, leads to the destruction of non-worship, and results in famine and dark sprouts.

If the sprout moves horizontally, there will be disease, as well as hunchbackedness and fear of enemies; when an inauspicious sprout has arisen, one should perform a propitiatory fire-oblation (*śāntihoma*).
One should perform the oblation with the root mantra, together with the preceptor and disciples, in due order; or one hundred or a thousand times with the Aghora-weapon mantra and the Astra-mantra.
Whatever action is performed without the offering of the ritual sprouts shall all become fruitless; therefore, having performed the offering of the sprouts, one should perform the previous rites.
It brings prosperity, victory, merit, and increases longevity and health;
or else, the ritual of sowing the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) is described in another manner.
When the time has arrived and is urgent, one should immediately perform the offering of the *aṅkurārpaṇa* (germinating of seeds) in vessels such as *pālikās*, using coconut flowers.
One should fill [the vessels] with *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice, and sesame seeds, while reciting the root mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
Thus ends the procedure for the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇavidhi*) in the *Dīkṣādarśa* composed by Vedajñāna, the son of Vāmadeva. (p. 1367)
Now, the procedure for the worship of the pavilion (maṇḍapa-pūjā-vidhi) is described.
Namely:
the preceptor, having performed the two daily rites, having renounced food,
and having completed the evening twilight worship, should again perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) for the sake of a special satiation.
Having meditated upon the five Brahmās, the Vidyās and Vidyeśvaras, and the Tatvas and Tatveśvaras, one should perform a special libation (tarpaṇa) three times, twice, or once, as the case may be.
As it is stated in the Mṛgendra-tantra:
Then, having sipped water once more, with the tips of his hands he [should worship] all those beginning with Brahmā— the five [deities] as well as the Vidyās and Vidyēśvaras.
Meditating upon all the presiding deities of the principles (tattvas) within the mandala of half the [cosmic] time,
one should satisfy them with oblations ending in "svāhā" and preceded by their names in the dative case.
O Cintye,

having performed the ritual for his own sake according to the rules, the Guru should perform a special propitiation (*tarpaṇa*). At the conclusion of that special propitiation, he should be adorned with all ornaments.
Likewise, in the Māhendra [mandala]: "Having entered that pavilion with his body smeared with ashes,
he should first worship himself and then perform the occasional rite."
Aṃśumatī said:
O best of suns, I shall describe the worship of Maṇḍapā; listen. She is the womb of all tantras, the one who possesses all forms, and the embodiment of her own nature.
Perform the worship of the pavilion so that this abode of the mouth [of the teaching] may be protected by Indra and the other world-protectors, and for the sake of the emergence of the tantras.
Therefore, having meditated upon that pavilion according to the ritual procedures,
O Lord of Pārvatī, tell me what form the pavilion should be visualized as by those who are discerning.
One should fashion the pavilion as the form of Kalā, with the Sun as its four faces; having conceived the components of the pavilion as the embodiment of the five elements.
That pavilion has four doors and is adorned with four archways; it possesses eight elephants at the cardinal directions, banners, and the ten weapons joined with their respective powers.
Having established [the deity] in that pavilion within the area designated for the Maṇṭapa-vrata, the wise one [should worship] in the water-pot, the Liṅga, the image,
the sacrificial materials, and the flowers.
Those who travel the path praise all things as being non-existent in sequence;
one should consecrate the pavilion for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) with all mantras.
Therefore, having recognized that pavilion as the form of the *kalā*, one should meditate upon the Sun; for everything has arisen within the *kalā*, and thus its form consists of the *kalā*.

Therefore, the worship of that pavilion consists of the form of the *sākala* mantra; the path of words (*padādhvan*) is in the division of the words, while the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*) is situated in the middle of the words.

The path of mantra resides within the bellies of the jars and in the limbs of the image; the path of the principles (tattva) is situated, in due order, within the materials and the components of the pavilion.
The path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is directed upwards; having prepared everything to protect it, the path of kalās contains all within its womb, and the sixfold path is completely encircled.
Having known all this, O knower of the tantras, one becomes accomplished in the purpose of all rites;
thus has the sacrificial pavilion, which is a limb of the sacrifice, been described, and now the worship is being explained.
Likewise, in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Having worshipped the deities in due order according to the procedure spoken by Śiva...
Having performed worship according to the prescribed rite, one should then carry out the initiation.
For the destruction of all obstacles, an offering to Gaṇa should certainly be made; in the center is the Śiva-pitcher, filled with thirty-two *prasthas*.
The Vardhanī vessel should be half the size of that [kalaśa], and it should be filled with auspicious water;
there should be three threads wrapped around the pitcher (kumbha) and two threads for the small jar (karaka).

All the others as well are wrapped with a single thread. The Preceptor, leading with his right foot, enters the sacrificial hall and places the jar for the purpose of worshipping Śiva and Sūrya in the space between the feet of Indra and Agni, which will be described hereafter.
Having placed [the mantra] therein, one should meditate thus:

"The solar [deity], resembling saffron, with two supreme lotus-hands endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, adorned with all ornaments. Having meditated in this way, one should worship [him] as prescribed for the daily rite.

Having worshipped the hundred [mantras] rooted in the Sun with prostrations and other rites, one should rise and go outside; having thoroughly washed the feet and hands with fragrant water, one should [worship] in the center of the eastern archway with: *oṃ hāṃ śāntitoraṇāya bhadrāya namaḥ*.
On the trident: *Oṃ hāṃ*, obeisance to Pūṣan; *Oṃ*, obeisance to Dhātṛ; *Oṃ*, obeisance to Vidhātṛ. On the southern archway: *Oṃ*, obeisance to the victorious Bhūti-archway.
On the trident: *Oṃ*, obeisance to Bhava; *Oṃ*, obeisance to Parjanya; *Oṃ*, obeisance to Indra.
Homage! At the western archway: Oṃ, homage to the Vajra of the Strength Archway.
At the trident: Oṃ, homage to Aryaman; Oṃ, homage to Mitra; Oṃ, homage to Tvaṣṭṛ.
At the northern archway: Oṃ, homage to the Health Archway; homage to Nīlalohita.

At the trident: "Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu; Oṃ, obeisance to Savitṛ; Oṃ, obeisance to Aṃśumat. Having thus worshipped the deities of the archway's pillars and offered water for the feet and other offerings, [one should proceed].

Having sprinkled the eastern doors with the Astra-mantra, [one should place] the banner, the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), the rosary, and the lotus upon the eastern door and the subsequent vessels; [and one should place] Śānti, who wears the sacred thread (upavītinī) in all [the vessels].
Resembling pure crystal, she has five faces and four arms.
Having meditated thus, and having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the door of the Śāntikalā," [one should worship] in the southern foot-pot of the western door:
"She who has the luster of molten gold, adorned with four faces and the moon."
The goddess Nivṛtti is described as holding a mouth, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus.
Having meditated thus— having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the door of the Nivṛtti-kalā"—
one [should worship] in the southern foot-pot of the western door [the goddess]:
"She who has four faces and four arms, [holding] the Śānti [mudrā], the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), a rosary, and a lotus."
Holding a noose, the gesture of fearlessness, a rosary, and a lotus, she is the goddess Pratiṣṭhā, adorned with jewels.

Having meditated thus, one should worship with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the door of the *pratiṣṭhā* level," and having honored it with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, one should worship as follows: in the northern *pada*-pitcher of the eastern door—"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nandin"; in the southern *pada*-pitcher—"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mahākāla."
In the eastern jar of the southern [door]: *oṃ devyai namaḥ*. In the eastern jar of the door:

*oṃ hāṃ caṇḍāya namaḥ*. Thus, at each door, having prepared an altar (*sthaṇḍila*) on the ground or on the wall at the sides of those two jars, [one should perform the rite] preceded by the respective meditations (*dhyāna*).
Having worshipped the gatekeepers, honored the world-protectors, and meditated upon them, one should worship the eight banners.
In the same way, regarding this matter of worshipping the deities of the eastern gate on the two branches,
there are twenty-eight squares on both sides of the gates. Starting from the eastern gate, the sequence proceeds in order from Nandin up to Śānti.

Thus, in the words of Aṃśumat: having considered the description of the reversal of the positions of the gatekeepers, this [mantra] should be applied either as their installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) or as their object of worship. At the outer north of the eastern gate:
*oṃ hāṃ praśāntapatākāya namaḥ*. On the south: *oṃ hāṃ*...
Homage to Śirapatākā. To the east of the southern gate: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Parjanya-patākā. To the west: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Jayanta-patākā.
To the south of the western gate: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bhūtasañjīva-patākā.
In the north: *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Amṛtapātāla; *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Ināpatākā. In the east: *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Śrīpradāyaka.
[She is] red in color, peaceful, with two arms and two eyes, her palms joined in the gesture of reverence (*kṛtāñjalipuṭa*).
"Indeed, she is adorned with all ornaments.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the eight banners; likewise, one should worship the eight elephants:
*oṃ hāṃ kumudāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ puṇḍarīkāya namaḥ*; *oṃ*...
Hāṃ, obeisance to Śaṅkukaṇṭha. Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Sarvanetra. Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Ṣaṇmukha. Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Supratiṣṭha.
Meditation: [One should visualize] white, black, and dark-blue lotuses, possessing the luster of the moon and its rays.

Having meditated thus: "Two-eyed and two-armed, endowed with the staff and the gesture of fearlessness," and having worshipped them well with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, one should worship the gatekeepers at the western door as in the daily rite (*nityavat*).

Placing [the mantra] ending with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva" upon both eyes using the tips of the thumb and ring finger, one should gaze at the divine obstacles; having abandoned all obstacles, one should do so again with the nārāca-mudrā.

O Nandikeśvara, by casting the flower of the thumb and forefinger while reciting "oṃ hāṃ astrāya phaṭ," one dispels obstacles in the intermediate space; likewise, by drawing three lines with the left heel, one destroys obstacles situated upon the earth.

By means of the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, the expulsion of obstacles shall take place. Thus, having dispelled the three kinds of obstacles— those dwelling in the divine realm, the atmosphere, and on the earth— one should touch the threshold of the western door with the left foot.
Having taken hold of a branch and entered within with the left foot foremost,
one should then stand facing west in the center of an udumbara tree,
[visualizing] the four-faced, four-armed [deity], whose splendor is like a blazing fire.
With his right and left hands, he holds the spear, the trident, the gesture of fearlessness, and the gesture of granting boons.

Having meditated thus: "Adorned with a crown of matted locks, with the crescent moon as his crest-ornament," and having worshipped with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Guardian of the Weapon-Door," one proceeds by way of circumambulation, closes the other doors, and enters.
In the southwest, in a water-pot situated in the middle of three steps—
(p. 1373)— is Brahmā, four-faced, holding a water-pot and a rosary, mounted upon a swan.
When you are seated, [you are] twice-born.

Having meditated thus, [one should say]: "ĀṂ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the site (vāstvadhipati). Having worshipped him with these words and honored him with water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings, if the sacrificial hall is covered with grass and the like, one should [pray] over the pillars: "OṂ, obeisance to the earth-element (pṛthivī-tattva). Over the beams (triṇa): "OṂ HĀṂ, obeisance to the water-element (jala-tattva)."

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the fire principle (agnitattva); on the bamboo poles. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the air principle (vāyutattva); on the feet. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the space principle (ākāśatattva); on the canopy. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Moon; on the waves. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Gaṅgā (Jāhnavī).

In the *Darbhamālā*: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāsuki. Having thus worshipped [him], one should worship the auspicious objects prescribed for each respective caste—such as Brāhmaṇas and others—in the intervals between the sacrificial posts (*maṇḍapa-vedī-rāleṣu*). As it is said in the *Karaṇa*:
The eightfold measure of the gods, the eightfold measure of the twice-born,
the eightfold measure of the kings, the eightfold measure of the Vaiśyas,
and the eightfold measure of Indra— these are the eightfold measures for all.

The eight auspicious objects of the gods have not been mentioned here because they are already under discussion. The eight auspicious objects for the twice-born are: the banner, the conch, the discus, the full water-pot with its lid, the parasol, Lakṣmī, and the lamp.
The eight auspicious emblems of kings are Gaurī, the bull, the elephant, the two chowries, the lion, the mirror, the banner, and the lamp. Furthermore, the umbrella,
the banner, the conch, the drum, the jar, and the torch are also [auspicious].
p.
1374) And the auspicious turning of the day (kalyāvarta), as well as these eight auspicious objects for Vaiśyas today: the mirror, the full water-pot, the banner, the parasol, and the drum.
The *śrīvatsa*, the *svastika*, and the *padma* are the eight auspicious marks (*aṣṭamaṅgala*) for Śūdras. Having thus understood this rule of differentiation, a wise person should perform the rite.
He should have the eight auspicious marks fashioned either from metal or from wood. Furthermore, they should be eight finger-breadths (*aṣṭāṅgula*) in size.
The length of the *tāra* is sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
Now, the pedestal of the lotus should be one-fourth the measure [of the lotus]; above the lotus, one should have mirrors and other such items made, or else have them drawn.
A specific rule is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"Beginning from one *rudrāṅgula* and increasing by half an *aṅgula*,
these first three yantras consist of nineteen *mātrās* at their end."

Alternatively, having left a space of eight finger-breadths, one should worship them in that place; a devotee of Śiva should leave eight finger-breadths, or else [worship] the gods according to their respective names and colors.
In a village or even in one's own home, according to the capacity of the patron, there should be a mirror in the east and two jars in the south, as well as a bull and two chowries.
In the west, Svasti and Lakṣmī; in the north, the conch and the lamp—these are the rows of the eight auspicious symbols at the corners of the altar.
Or else, having set aside the eight auspicious objects (aṣṭamaṅgala), one should worship them in their place: Urvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, and Tilottamā.
Sumukhī, Sundarī, Kāminī, and Kāmavardhinī—
these are said to be the Apsarases; they attend upon him who wears the eight fingers.
In the mirror: *oṃ hāṃ skandāya namaḥ*. In the full water-pot: *oṃ hāṃ lambodarāya namaḥ*. On the bull: *oṃ hāṃ vīrabhadrāya namaḥ*. On the pair of fly-whisks: [oṃ hāṃ vīrabhadrāya namaḥ].
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gaṅgā; at the Śrīvatsa: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahālakṣmī; at the Svastika: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rudra; at the conch:
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Candra; at the lamp: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śauri. Having thus worshipped, [one worships] the Astra.

Having marked out the sacrificial pavilion by means of the two types of armor and the unsharpening [rites], one should place within the pavilion— upon a tortoise-seat (kūrma-āsana) to the right of the image— the deity in any one of the prescribed postures such as *prasanna* and so forth; then, one should cause the two knees, the two shanks, and the tips of the two feet to be positioned above.

The seeker of desires (kāmika) should finally perform the special offering (viśeṣārghya). It is rubbed; the gaze is slightly directed toward the tip of the nose, and there indeed the [breath] is long.
This is declared to be the beautiful posture (rucirāsana), which the wise know to be worthy of all worship.

Remaining thus, one should perform the ritual action. Accordingly, in the *Aṃśumatī*: "Standing on the southern side of the *vidikā*, facing north, perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) and so forth, as well as the ritual of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*), as if it were a daily rite."
One should perform the *dabhabhaṅgī*, *vaktrabhaṅgī*, or *ḍhābhabhaṅgī* according to one's capacity;
then, one should arrange the thirty-eight *kalā-bhaṅgīs* and the *mātṛkā* syllables as prescribed.

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the body of knowledge (vidyādeha), the eyes, and the heart and other limbs; one should likewise perform the internal sacrifice (antaryāga), the abode, and meditative absorption (samādhi).
In the *Kāmika* (p. 1376):
"At the end, one should prepare the special *arghya* offering with barley, white mustard seeds, and so forth."

The supreme eight-limbed [offering] has pervasion up to the level of Śivatattva; the *śivārghya* has pervasion up to the end of Vidyātattva; and that called *rodha* has pervasion up to the end of Ātmatattva. Having prepared these three—the sprinkling for the bound soul (*paśu-prokṣaṇa*), the *paśvarghya*, and the others—by means of the collection of mantras.

Having sprinkled oneself with the *śivārghya* water, one should sprinkle all the materials for the sacrifice with the *astra-mantra*, moisten them with the *kavaca-mantra*, consecrate them with the *hṛdaya-mantra*,
enclose them with the *kavaca-mantra*, and render them nectar-like (*amṛtī-kuryāt*). Then, one should apply a *tilaka* mark on the forehead with sandalwood paste.

Having recited the root mantra, having placed oneself [within the deity], and having performed worship, one should effect the purification of the mantra and the thorough adornment of one's own body with the uṣṇīṣa and other ornaments. Likewise, in the rites of blazing,
installation, sprinkling, sacrifice, fire-ritual, and recitation;
The twice-born seeker of auspiciousness should wear both a turban and an upper garment.
It should be white, fine, very smooth, with a fringe, and eight cubits in length;
its width should be one-fifth or even one-seventh [of that].
Having made one, two, or three folds, one should encircle it from the front; the wise man should then tie its tip at the right ear.
In the *Suprabheda*: "That which,
starting from just below [the forehead] up to the head, effortlessly covers both ears with soft white cloth, is called the *śiroveṣṭanaka* (head-wrap)."
When it is ablaze, one should take up half of the *uṣṇīṣa* and bind two [ends] together at the tail.
A wise person should wear an upper garment like the sacred thread; however, one should avoid there that which is burnt by fire, worn out, or torn.
In the *Kāmika*:
"For Brahmins, [the garment] should be with an upper cloth (*sottarīya*); for Śūdras, it should be a simple cloth (*kevala-vasta*).
In the *Kāraṇa*:
A woman and a Śūdra should avoid [wearing] the *uṣṇīṣa* and the upper garment (*uttarīya*).
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"One should place a white *uṣṇīṣa*, consecrated with the root mantra, upon the head; as for the upper garment..."
With the Gāyatrī, with that which is born at once, and with the garment.
One should adorn oneself with sandalwood mixed with camphor powder, as well as with flowers, fragrant ashes,
and ornaments.
And Aṅkura, especially the teacher who is utterly stainless, was endowed with linen garments,
pure clothes, and various ornaments.
O Aṃśumatī,
having covered the Arhat with a cloth while remaining composed, and having thus fully adorned his body,
one should thereafter perform the *śivahasta* rite.
For example:
having smeared the palm of one's own right hand with [sandalwood paste] using the left thumb,
and having placed the form of the seat in its center, [one should place] Īśāna and the others on the fingers starting from the thumb and ending with the little finger.
Having performed the placement of the pentad (pañcaka), having executed the placement of the body of the Vidyā and the eyes along with the root-mantra,

having invoked Śiva and placed the limbs (aṅgas) beginning with the little finger, having consecrated [the disciple] as supreme (paramīkṛtya) and envisioned the Hand of Śiva, one should meditate upon his form through that [Hand].
Having placed it upon one's own head with this [mantra], one should cut through that veil of ignorance.
Taking thirty-six blades of *darbha* grass, one should fashion the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*).
One should have it made one palm-span in size, bound like a braid of hair.
The tip should be two finger-breadths wide, and the knot should be one finger-breadth;
or, according to the *Upabheda-kāraṇa*:
"For the gathering of thirty-two blades of *darbha* grass, [the length] should be four finger-breadths."
It should be joined with two finger-breadths at the knot, resembling the shape of a braid.
The knot should be joined at the tip, with a length of one cubit (ratni) or a very long span;
it should be given as eighteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) or twelve finger-breadths.
On the trident, however, the measurement for the neck should be four finger-breadths; and for the upper and lower portions, it should be five or three finger-breadths respectively.

The preceptor, having consecrated the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*) seven times with the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), which is endowed with these characteristics, should fasten it to his right hip.
The jar, however, should be situated in the midst of the fire, located at the *liṅga*, and placed within the mandala. The preceptor...
Abiding in the heart and residing in the five, he is the liberator from bonds.
O Sadāśiva, you are the protector of the sacrificial rite for all, residing within the maṇḍala of karma;
you are present in the pitcher (kumbha) during the performance of the fire-oblation (homa).

Since it has been said, "O liberator from bonds, [place] my body for the disciple's destruction of bonds," one should contemplate the identity [of the disciple] with Śiva, thinking, "He is indeed I; I am Śiva. To the northeast or the southwest, a pit of one or two cubits in size should be prepared for the purpose of placing the *pañcagavya*.

Having smeared the sacrificial ground with cow dung, one should lay out five lines upon it—oriented toward the east and the north—and having intersected them at the center to form a single four-way junction:

Having arranged two squares each starting from the east, and one square each in the intermediate directions such as the southeast, thus forming nine compartments; then, having placed in each compartment rice— either one *āḍhaka*, half an *āḍhaka*, or half of that— according to the distinction of superior and so forth.
Having spread darbha grass over that [surface] with its tips pointing upward, one should offer obeisance in their midst:
*oṃ hāṃ śivatattvakoṣṭhāya namaḥ* in the east; *oṃ hāṃ sadāśivatattvakoṣṭhāya namaḥ* in the south; *oṃ hāṃ vidyātattvakoṣṭhāya namaḥ* in the north; *oṃ*... in the north.

"Hāṃ, obeisance to the chamber of the Puruṣa-tattva" in the west; "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the chamber of the Kāla-tattva" in the northeast; "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the chamber of the Prakṛti-tattva" in the northeast—having thus performed the worship of the chambers, they are installed therein.
In the vessels, in order from the middle and so forth: *oṃ hāṃ* obeisance to the vessel of firm establishment (*supratiṣṭha-pātra*);

*oṃ hāṃ* obeisance to the vessel of perfect peace (*suśānta-pātra*); obeisance to the vessel of generated splendor (*tejotpa-pātra*); obeisance to the vessel of blood-water (*raktodaka-pātra*); obeisance to the vessel of blood-water (*raktodaka-pātra*); obeisance to the vessel whose nature is nectar (*amṛtātma-pātra*). Unmanifest (*avyakta*).
"Salutation to the vessel. Having thus performed the worship of the vessels,

one should pour into them milk, curd, ghee, cow's urine, cow dung, and water with kuśa grass, and [worship] them respectively with the mantras of Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, Sadyojāta, the Gāyatrī, or the Mūla-mantra.

Having worshipped and offered the *arghya*, one should cast the seed-syllable (*bīja*) starting from the northeast; having consecrated it sixteen times with the root mantra repeated one, two, three, four, and five times respectively, and having cast in cow-dung and other materials by way of reabsorption while reciting the five Brahmans, one should finally pour *kuśa*-water into the central vessel with the root mantra.
Having placed a *kūrca* there and again sprinkled it with his right hand holding *kuśa* grass,
having consecrated it with the *Saṃhitā-mantra* or the *Gāyatrī*, and having protected, veiled, and rendered it immortal, he should offer incense, lamps, and so forth.

With the mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* used for the weapon (*astra*), one should scatter seven offerings consisting of sesame, mustard seeds, parched rice husks, flowers, *kuśa* grass, and unbroken grains. (p. 1380)
Having consecrated seven times the eye-cloth, the noose, the thread, and so forth—

the specific materials required for the sacrificial implements such as the knife— and having consecrated each one individually with the root mantra, [one should place them] in the southwest of the pavilion.
Standing facing northeast with the upper body erect,
having sprinkled the sacrificial hall with the *astra-mantra* using the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the two arghya-offerings,
one should perform the purification of the site through the fourfold rites beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*).
For all pavilions, eighteen consecrations are prescribed,
beginning with the inspection (vīkṣaṇa) and so forth, for the removal of the teacher's defects.

This has been stated in the *Sūkṣma*: "Observation is performed with the heart [mantra] alone; sprinkling, O Lord, is by means of the *Īśa* mantra; striking is with the mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*; and sprinkling [again] is with the head-mantra and the weapon-mantra."
Perform the extraction (*uddhāra*) by means of the *Ghananāśastramantra* and from the *Ghoramantra*; perform the filling (*pūraṇa*) with the *Vāmadeva*;
do not perform it with *Sadyojāta*, nor indeed with *Iśāna*.
One should perform sprinkling on the crest-lock (śikhā), pounding with the armor-mantra (varman),
cleansing with the eye-mantra (netra), and anointing with the person-mantra (puruṣa).
One should fashion the [deities] of the kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, according to their respective names; one should draw a circle with three lines using the mantra of the principal seed-syllable.

Having worshipped with the root mantra itself, one should lay down three lines for the Lord; [one should perform] the vajra-consecration with the weapon-mantra and the fourfold [consecration] with the root mantra.
Having scattered [the offerings] there and having sprinkled them with bundles of *kuśa* grass,
he should collect [the remains] with the *Śivagāyatrī* and enter the domain of Īśāna.
The knower of ritual procedures should prepare the seat with the weapon-increasing [mantra];

having performed the rite therein, he should scatter the *vikirās*— which have become blazing weapons— with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, for the purpose of pacifying obstacles in the intermediate space.

Having drawn a line with the *darbha* grass held in the hand, moving clockwise to ward off obstacles caused by spirits, and having gathered it together, one should place it in the northeast for the seat of the *vardhanī*; then, in the western *varuṇa* [vessel], in the northern jar—
Seated in the lotus posture, she possesses the luster of a lotus and holds a lotus in her hand;
her earrings are ornaments for the ears, blazing with gold and jewels.
Resembling beautiful garments, reddish-brown and free from defects, the girdle (mekhalā) with its waist-cord is considered to be Lakṣmī herself,
who increases prosperity.

Having meditated thus, [one should recite]: *Oṃ hāṃ mahālakṣmyai namaḥ*. Having worshipped with flowers and other offerings, [one should place] a mango, a *aśvattha*, or a coconut, or a citron fruit, upon a cloth spread over seven kinds of grain such as sesame and others, located in the northeast and filled with vermilion and ashes.

Having worshipped the pitcher— which has its mouth adorned with a *kūrca* mat and the like, which is filled with gold, gems, medicinal herbs, iron, and other materials, which faces west, and which has become the very embodiment of the deity— one should conceive of it as the moving seat (*calāsana*) consisting of the lotus of infinite virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty.
Having worshipped the form therein—
one who has four arms and three eyes, with black and tawny hair standing erect, the god holding a noose for the senses in one hand and endowed with the sword of knowledge in another—
Having meditated upon the Lord Pāśupata along with his limbs (retinue), the wise one should worship him;
thus, having invoked the Blessed One together with the enclosures beginning with Śakti, he should perform the worship.

To the south of that, having fashioned a seat for the Goddess Īśvarī in the form of a support— consisting of the previously mentioned ornaments, facing west with its nozzle, colored with half a *niṣka* of gold and other materials, separated by a distance of one fist, and having the nature of a *vardhanī* vessel shaped like a lion for the Hero— one should arrange it upon that.
Having worshipped the moving seat with "Oṃ pāśupatāstrāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ," and having thus fully worshipped the seat,
one should worship the form upon it with "Oṃ pāśupatāstramūrtaye huṃ phaṭ namaḥ. [One should meditate on the deity] whose hair is blazing red in color and who holds a sword and a shield.

Having meditated upon the Goddess Astrarīśvara, one should worship her with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. Having performed the invocation and other rites with the mantra "Oṃ ślīṃ paśuṃ phaṭ pāśupatāstramūrtaye huṃ phaṭ namaḥ," and having offered a pair of garments to each [deity], one should worship with water for the feet (pādya) and other offerings.
One should worship; or one should worship Śiva according to the method stated in the *Kāraṇa* up to the mirror. One should place the Śiva-pitcher and the *vardhanī* in the center of the lotus.
[The offerings are: water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and flowers—these fourteen.
And likewise water with fragrant flowers, water with bilva leaves, and water with kuśa grass.
The preceptor should then place [the vessels] in the intermediate directions in due order; having worshipped Śiva in the Śiva-kumbha and Manonmanī in the Vardhanī.
The best of installers should worship the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśvara) all around.
Having risen within the pavilion, he should establish [the deities] in the cardinal and intermediate directions starting from the east.
He should worship Indra and the others between Mahākāla and Sūrya, saying: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Indra."
In the Agni pitcher: *oṃ hāṃ kuberāya namaḥ*. In the Īśāna pitcher: *oṃ hāṃ īśānāya namaḥ*.
In the southern jar of that [central] jar:
*oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*. In the northern jar of the [jar of] Nairṛta: *oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*. Having specially worshipped all the world-protectors, beginning with Indra.
For Indra and his retinue, equipped with weapons and vehicles, one should worship their weapons:
the thunderbolt, the banner, the mace, the lotus, and the discus, according to the proportions of the hands; as well as the spear and the staff.
And from that ocean [arise] the sword, the noose, and the trident.
Since the weapons (astras) are to be produced here from their respective directions,
one who would undergo initiation should first worship them with devotion.
The vajra, the śakti, the staff, the sword, the noose, as well as the goad,
the mace, the trident, the lotus, and the discus— these are the weapons held in his hands.
Thus are proclaimed and celebrated the forms of the weapons:
Jāyā, Śakti, Gadā, Vidyut, Pāśa, Padma, and Napuṃsaka; the remaining ones are known and celebrated as male forms of the weapons.
He has one face and two eyes, is adorned with a crown and a casket, possesses two arms joined in the gesture of reverent salutation (añjali), and is endowed with all auspicious marks.
In this world, there are ten types of fierce metals, beginning with diamond; having fashioned [an image] from any one of these, one should worship it with one's own mantra.
As it has been said:
"One should worship these with the mantras 'Oṃ Bhrūṃ' accompanied by the two [syllables], likewise for Vajra, and with the mantras ending in 'Hūṃ Phaṭ Namaḥ'."
Oṃ hrūṃ vajrāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ. Having thus recited the mantra for the others, one should perform worship. Thereafter:
Taking the *guruvarddhanī*— which flows toward the tip of the *śivakuṃbha* and possesses an uninterrupted stream—
one should circumambulate it clockwise.
Having said, "O you who desire the Self," and reciting the root mantra while contemplating the *astra-darbha* grass: "Oṃ!
For the sake of protecting the sacrifice and for the purpose of destroying obstacles, you..."
Svāhā! Homage be to you; may you be girt with armor, O Protector.
This man is engaged in the Śiva-sacrifice; by the command of Śiva, you world-protectors must, with one mind, protect his devotees from those who stand above them.
Or rather:
"O Śakra, by the command of Śiva, you must remain vigilant in this direction until the conclusion of the sacrifice, in order to pacify all obstacles."

Having thus recited the Śivajñāna for each [deity] in turn, and having first established the *kumbha* (vessel) and afterwards the *vardhanī* (overflowing vessel) in their respective places, one should worship the Mūrti-vidyā-deha (the body of the form-vidyā), the Netra (Eye), and [the deities] from Śakti up to Śaktiparyanta within the Śiva-kumbha for the sake of a firm seat (*sthirāsana*).

If the initiation (dīkṣā) is to be performed together with the purification of the fire (agnivahni-śuddhi), one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the five kalās according to the order of emanation (sṛṣṭikrama). Having performed the invocation (āvāhana) and other rites with the root mantra (mūla-mantra), and having worshipped [the deity] along with the surrounding retinue (āvaraṇa),
one should worship a seat for the sake of a stable posture upon the *vardhanī* vessel facing west.
In the locations such as the heart and so forth: Oṃ hāṃ, to the heart, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ.
Oṃ ślīṃ, to the head, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ. Oṃ paṃ, to the crest-lock, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ. Oṃ śūṃ, to the armor, huṃ phaṭ namaḥ.

Oṃ hūṃ netrābhyāṃ huṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ astrāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ | Having thus performed the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), [one performs] the protection, the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and the transformation into nectar (*amṛtīkaraṇa*).

Having performed all the services beginning with the water for the feet (*pādya*) and having offered them, and having worshipped [the deity] together with the surrounding retinue (*sāvaraṇa*), one should contemplate the union of the *bhaga* and the *liṅga* with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ haṃ śivaśaktibhyāṃ namaḥ*. Then, forming a fist with the thumb pointing upward, one should encircle it with the left hand.
This is renowned as the *liṅgamudrā*; one should display it toward that water-pot (*kumbha*).
For the sake of worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*), however, one should touch it in the reverse manner. [The mantra is:
"To Māyā, who has the form of the *bhaga*, and to Śaṅkara, who bears the form of the *liṅga*."
Having praised him with "Obeisance to you, O Tumbhu," and having also said "Obeisance today."

"Oṃ! You are indeed the Lord of this sacrifice; this is your immovable form. This is your sword of knowledge; accept it as your weapon. Having thus informed the Goddess for the sake of protecting the sacrifice, [he places it] in her hand with the Astra-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.

Having offered the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*), having recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times and presented it to the water-pot (*kumbha*), and having recited with a portion [of the mantra] inside the *vardhanī* vessel and presented it, [one should say]: "The sacrifice has been commenced by me;
may the ritual of the sacrificer be successful."
"Therefore, you must protect him until his completion; for the Preceptor, having thus placed the burden of guarding the sacrifice upon him,"

Having thus requested protection for the sacrifice, and having offered the *nirodhārghya* with the *maghora* mantra, one should place that vessel and trample three steps toward the northwest from the east.
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, one should announce: "O Lord of the Gods, this sacrificial victim has been [prepared] by us."
"May that which was set in motion for the sake of [building] a house proceed to its conclusion, and may all obstacles remain in your presence. Having thus made this request:

Oṃ hāṃ, salutations to Gaṇapati. Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground before the pitcher situated in the middle of the three western steps in the northeast, and having made a formal request in the presence of the Guru, [one should worship] the God of gods.
"O Jagannātha, O cause of joy for the world!
This Śivādhvara sacrifice proceeds by your command; it is my own as well. Having thus informed [him]—

"Oṃ hāṃ, salutations to the seven gurus beginning with Sadāśiva. Having thus worshipped and obtained their permission, one stands to the south of the altar for the purpose of worshipping one's chosen *liṅga*, and as prescribed for daily rites, for the sake of the special worship of one's own chosen *liṅga*.

One should worship with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and so forth. Thus, it is stated in the *Kāmika*: "One should worship Śiva in a mandala, on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), or in a linga, accompanied by the special ablution and endowed with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*)."
One should worship Śiva especially with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); having prostrated and petitioned the Lord of Gods, the Guru likewise receives his permission.

For the purpose of performing the Maṇḍala sacrifice, one should construct an altar in the center; or else, a lotus that serves as a universal support and fulfills all desires, according to the specific requirements of its own class, or a Sarvatobhadra or other such Maṇḍala.
In this maṇḍala, one should worship [the deity] together with the enclosures, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and ending with the recitation (japa). Likewise, in the Suprabheda,
having worshipped Sadāśiva in the center with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings:
First, one should worship the womb-enclosure (garbhāvṛta), then the enclosure of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśāvaraṇa),
followed by the enclosure of Gaṇeśa, then the enclosure of the World-Guardians (lokeśāvaraṇa), and finally the enclosure of the Weapons (astrāvaraṇa).
And one should worship according to the prescribed rite.
In the *Sūkṣma-tantra*—just as for the deities mentioned in the tantras, so too should one sacrifice according to what is stated in the tantras. [The] pavilion...
Having worshipped with jasmine and other flowers, he performed the worship of the fire.
Then, having received permission for the purpose of the fire-rite (agnikārya),
one should perform the fire-rites either in a pit (kuṇḍa) or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) situated to the east or in the northeast of that [central area].
One should perform all rites beginning with the installation of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna) as prescribed for the fire-ritual (agnikārya).
Namely:
with the right hand [extended], placing the *kuṇḍanābhi* in front and sitting facing north; however, on level ground...
But on the back and the upper part of the head, there is a girdle.
Speak! [The deity] with hanging lips and a girdle upon the feet;
Padmanābha is said to be situated above the girdle; Pātāla.
They say that "kukṣi" refers here to the form of a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having thus meditated upon the form of the pit (kuṇḍa), one should gaze at the pit with eyes fixed by placing the ring finger and thumb together,

while reciting "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva. Then, using the weapon mantra ending in "huṃ phaṭ," one performs the digging and removal [of debris], and using the heart mantra, the filling and leveling [of the pit].
Having performed the sprinkling with the *varman* mantra and the pulverizing with the *astra* mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and having carried out the sweeping and smearing:
[one should recite] "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Śāntyatīta Kalā" in the center of the *kuṇḍa*, filling the interior of the *kuṇḍa*; and "Oṃ haiṃ, obeisance to the Śāntikalā" on the south.
"Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to the digit of knowledge (vidyā-kalā).
1388) Thus, having assigned the mantras of the digits (kalā-mantra) according to the sequence of emanation during the material initiation (bhautika-dīkṣā), [one prepares] the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

One should arrange the *kalās*. In the initiation for lifelong commitment (*naiṣṭhikadīkṣā*), one should recite the *kalā-mantras* in the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*)—specifically in the north-western direction and in the centers of the eastern pits: *Oṃ haiṃ kavacāya namaḥ*.

Having encircled the pit with three threads and worshipped it with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the pit consisting of the Kalās," one should draw three lines from west to east through the middle of the pit with "Oṃ hāṃ, huṃ phaṭ, obeisance to the Weapon," and likewise [one] line.

Having fashioned a vajra by means of three *kuśa* blades in the shape of tridents at both ends upon a square marked with horizontal lines, one should perform the deposition of the crossroads (*catuṣpathanyāsa*) using two *kuśa* blades with tips pointing east and north, reciting: *oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*. Then, *oṃ haiṃ*.

*Oṃ kavacāya namaḥ*. Having performed the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) by creating a protective mat (*akṣapāṭi*) with *kuśa* grass rising up on all sides within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), [one should offer] in the center of the pit: *Oṃ hāṃ vāgīśvarī vāgīśvarāya namaḥ*. Thus.

Having arranged the seat in the form of a *kūrca*, and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāgīśvarī and the forms of Vāgīśvara," one should meditate upon them:
"O Maheśvara, she is Vāgīśī, who is Gaurī; he is Vāgīśa."
The three-eyed, four-armed deity, possessing a luster like that of a ruby.
Her hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, while other hands hold a trident and a noose; Vāgīśī has the luster of a white lotus, four faces, and full breasts.
Having explained [the ritual], one should especially meditate upon her who holds a book, a water-pot, and a gourd, who has bathed after her menses, and is in the full bloom of youth.
The wise one should meditate [on her] as having the luster of the petals of a blue lotus, in accordance with what was stated regarding the ritual action.
Alternatively:
Vāgīśvara is red in luster, three-eyed, and four-armed; he is endowed with the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, and is equipped with a noose and a trident.

The wise man, dressed in fine garments and adorned with garlands, should duly invoke the Goddess, the Mother of the Universe, visualizing her as dark-complexioned, in her menses, and wearing ornaments.
Having meditated upon Vāgīśvarī, who has a serene face and the radiance of lotus-petal eyes,
one should invoke her with her own respective mantra.
Having meditated thus, one should invoke [the deity] and worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth. Thereafter, one should kindle the fire in the *kāraṇa*—
that produced from a *kānta* stone is best, while that produced from wood is middling.
It is proclaimed that a learned Vedic scholar is the cause for fire, while a maiden is the cause for peace.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"Sandhyā, sitting, recitation, fire-offering, worship of the deities,
hospitality, and the Vaiśvadeva— these are the six duties to be performed day by day."
A Brahmin devoted to the six duties is declared to be a *śrotriya*. Likewise, it is stated in the *Bhārata*:
"One who is learned is indeed called a *śrotriya*; a knower of reality is also called a *śrotriya*."
In the absence of arising from a sun-gem, it is inferior when produced from wood.
The procedure is stated here as follows regarding the causal [rite]:
one should first take a *śamī* tree, or a *pippala*, or a most excellent domestic tree.
In the *Cintyaviśve*:
"One should take a shoot from the interior of a *śamī* tree, or one with auspicious marks from an *aśvattha* tree;
in the central region, according to its own scripture, it should be cut slowly and steadily with a well-sharpened [blade]."
Having become sakalībhūta (endowed with all parts), one should cut [the wood] and then worship the flower;
its length should be stated as one cubit or twelve finger-breadths.
The practitioner of mantra should prepare an auspicious araṇī wood, eight finger-breadths in height, even, flawless, and clearly defined according to the rules.
A sacrificial ladle made of khadira wood should be fashioned with a handle twelve finger-breadths long;
it should be auspicious, tapering from a circumference of six finger-breadths at the base.
Likewise, regarding the cause:
one should wrap the tip of the base of the *maṇḍana* with a *svadhā*-strip; at the base, one should join it with a three-pronged pin measuring four finger-breadths.
In this manner, one should fashion a peg at the tip of a very firm staff; its width is said to be seven finger-breadths, and half of that is the thickness of the wood.
On both sides, the fist should be eight finger-breadths [in height]; its circumference should be five finger-breadths, and it should be perfectly round everywhere.
A triple-stranded rope made of cowhair, or alternatively of thread, should be twenty-five finger-breadths in length and as thick as the little finger.
In the *Kiraṇa*:
"Having addressed the wind, that which was spoken by Pradyumna should be performed with the cow-hair [brush].
Facing north, one should strike while recollecting the seed-syllable of Śiva."
One should offer the *gāyatrī* of the radiant *dhāriṇī* into the heart; one should gradually perform the circumambulation and join the parasol with the sword.
One should apply the crest-lock to the face and wrap the hands with the head-cloth; having thus produced the fire, one should offer oblations with the *dvija*, *madira*, and *gotha* mantras.
It may be produced from a sun-crystal (sūryakānta) or even by the general method of ignition.

Having thus prepared the fire and brought it into a copper vessel or an earthen vessel with the Pañcabrahma mantra, [one should place it] in the southeast, northeast, or southwest of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

Or, having established [the fire] with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, one should expel the flesh-eating portion of the fire toward the southwest corner (*nirṛtikoṇa*). Then, having purified the fire through the four purificatory rites beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*), one should [visualize it] as having a shimmering star-like form with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ haṃ vahnimūrtaye namaḥ*.
Having grasped the elemental fire with the *pūraka* breath using the *saṃhāramudrā*,

and having unified it with the fire of the *bindu* located in the middle of the forehead, one should unify it with the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) situated in the navel and throat— resembling a falling moth— by means of the heart through *kuṃbhaka*.

From the fire situated in vessels such as a shallow bowl (*śarāva*), one should extract the elemental fire— characterized by smokeless charcoal, a mass of flames, and resembling the sun at midday— through the *piṅgalā* channel using the *recaka* breath, with the mantra: "Oṃ hrūṃ,
obeisance to the consciousness of fire (*vanhi-caitanya*)," while employing the *udbhava-mudrā*.

Having consecrated [the materials] with the six-limbed mantra using the three fires of the belly and destiny, having worshipped them with the *saṃhitā*, and having performed the protection, veiling, and other rites, one should place them on the ground with the knees touching the earth facing oneself, either in a fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), while remaining with the head directed toward the northeast (*īśāna*).
Having visualized [the fire] within the central channel (*garbhanāḍī*) of Vāgīśvara, and having visualized it as being held by Vāgīśvara; then,
beholding the fire situated in the lotus at the navel, one should gather it from the navel with the heart-mantra, and visualize the laying of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
Having offered a drop of water as the *arghya* with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, having sprinkled it with the *kavaca-mantra*,
and having covered it with the *astra-mantra* ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, one should fan it with a fan or with the mind (*manas*).

Having kindled the fire and worshipped the embryonic fire (*garbhāgni*) with "Oṃ hrāṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to the embryonic fire," and having consecrated that *kuśa* grass or the bracelet seven times with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, [he places it] in the right hand of Vāgīśvarī.

For the sake of protecting that embryo, having performed the *garbhādhāna* rite immediately after birth, he should worship with the *hṛdaya-mantra* ending in *svāhā* and offer five oblations of sesame seeds. In the third month,
for the sake of the *puṃsavana* rite, he should worship Vāmadeva and offer an oblation of sesame seeds with the *śiras-mantra* ending in *svāhā*.

Having offered five oblations with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the body consisting of the eightfold city (puryaṣṭaka)," and having presented the general water-offering (sāmānyārghya), one should worship with the Aghora mantra on the sixth month for the occasion of the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana),
and offer five oblations of sesame seeds with the Śikhā mantra ending in svāhā.
Having offered fifteen oblations of sesame seeds ending with *svāhā* while reciting the *Avayasi-mantra* along with the *Śikhā-mantra*,

and having worshipped [the deity] with the *Tatpuruṣa-mantra* in the tenth month, one should offer five oblations ending with *svāhā* using the *Kavaca-mantra* for the purpose of removing the impurities of the fetus once it has been born.

Having kindled the fire with *kuśa* grass, and for the immediate cessation of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), having sprinkled both the interior and exterior of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) with water from the *arghya* vessel while reciting the Weapon mantra (*astra-mantra*) ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, and having struck it with a *darbha* blade using the Weapon mantra and sprinkled it with the Armor mantra (*kavaca*), one should remove the bracelet from the hand of the Goddess.
Having worshipped with the heart-mantra and meditated that the golden bracelet has been bound,
one takes up thirty blades of *darbha* grass; this is proclaimed as the *mātṛkā-bāhu-veṇī*,
which is also called the *veṣṭikā* or *piṣṭara*.
The fuel-sticks should be of the same measure as that [sacrificial post], including their leaves;
they are prescribed to have a circumference equal to that of the thumb.

Thus, for the sake of protecting the fire-child, having strewn darbha grass with tips pointing eastward and northward upon the eastern girdles using the Astra mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, one should place the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial seats (*viṣṭara*) upon them in sequence, starting from the east and west and moving toward the north, using the Hṛdaya mantra.

Having established [the deity] within the heart, and for the purpose of removing saliva from the faces and for nourishment, one should take five fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *palāśa* or similar wood, anointing the roots and tips with clarified butter, and offer them with the *astra-mantra* ending in *svāhā*. Then, on the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) situated to the east and other directions of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), first [at the eastern one], *oṃ*...

"Hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā" in the west; "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu" in the south; "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rudra" in the north; and "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ananta" in the north—having thus worshipped the deities stationed at the boundary (paridhi), [one should worship] upon the seats (viṣṭara).
In the order starting from the east and ending with the northeast: *oṃ hāṃ indrāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ agnaye namaḥ*,
*oṃ hāṃ yamāya namaḥ*, *nirṛtaye namaḥ*, *varuṇāya namaḥ*, *vāyave namaḥ*, *kuberāya namaḥ*, *īśānāya namaḥ* [in the northeast].

To the south: *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe namaḥ*. To the north, in the northwest: *oṃ hāṃ viṣṇave namaḥ*. Having thus worshipped and offered the *arghya* water, one should proclaim the command of Śiva: "O guardians of the directions! By the command of Śiva, ward off all obstacles and protect this Agnikumāra!"

One should cause [this] to be heard. Now, the procedure for the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *sruk* and *sruva* spoons, preceded by their defining characteristics, is described. Thus, in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"The *sruk* and *sruva* should be fashioned according to the rule; that rule is stated here. In the *Kālottara*:
Either a nyagrodha or a cūta tree, likewise a śamī or an udumbara;
or even one made of devadāru or red sandalwood.
In rites for pacification (śāntika) and nourishment (pauṣṭika), whether performed regularly or on specific occasions,
one should use the leaves of the king of beasts (mṛgendra)— the Brahmāśvattha, Śamī, Parṇī, Śiṃśupā, and other such trees.
Likewise, in the *Suprabheda*:
"Acacia, *śamī*, *bilva*, *palāśa*, *plakṣa*, and sandalwood; or else, among the sacrificial trees, fashion [the post] according to what is available."
In the *Kiraṇa*: "The *cūtacandana* [lineage] arises from the thirty-six *aṅgulas*.
In the *kāraṇa*..."
Having again divided the tree— which has a core to be grasped and a middle— into two parts,
one should place a firm and satisfied crane-offering (baka) at its side.
The handle of the *mūla-sruk* and *sruva* ladles is considered to be at the tip of a tree;
by the word "tip" (*puṣkara*), the end is meant— on that portion, the offering (*bali*) is prescribed for the left side of the tree, which is ever-awake.
The characteristics of the *sruva* ladle produced from the tree [of the sacrificial wood] have been described.
One should have the wooden planks made thirty-six finger-breadths in length, eight finger-breadths in width,
and six finger-breadths in thickness.
In the *Kāmika*: "One should lead [the thread] made of metal or mounted on wood for thirty-six finger-breadths.
And it is said in the *Parākhyatantra*:

The left [channel] is said to be thirty-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas) long, as is the northern blood [channel]; the middle and the smallest are to be known as being reduced by two finger-breadths each.
According to the *Kiraṇa*: "The circumference of the staff should be six finger-breadths, and its tip two finger-breadths.
Likewise, in the *Parākhya*:

For the three types beginning with the *uttama*, the staff shall be twenty finger-breadths [in length]; according to the *kāraṇa* system, it shall be one *karmāṅgula* in circumference, and at its lower end, it shall be joined with a foot-shaped base.
In the *Śāradātilaka*:
"The staff (*daṇḍa*) shall consist of twenty parts; the neck (*kaṇṭha*) shall be one part less than eight [parts];
the face (*mukha*) shall be measured by one part and seven parts."
The width of the neck is proclaimed to be one-thirtieth [of the total height]; the top should be equal to the neck, and one should fashion the opening at the mouth accordingly.
Regarding the cause:
having dug upward from the opening of the pit to the measure of a little finger,
one should join the tube and the flagstaff using either silver or copper.
In the Kāmika:
"The width of the pedestal (vedikā) should be eight aṅgulas and it should be very firm; its middle cavity is said to be three or four mātras."
Around the bilapāha, however, one should fashion an auspicious eight-petaled lotus with a width of one and a quarter finger-breadths all around the pit.
Regarding the cause:
around the altar (vedikā), there is a band (paṭṭikā) three barley-corns thick. In the Mṛgendra [Tantra]:
The *Vaṭā* [staff] has its base and end provided with the Vedas (4), the *vṛtta* (12), and so forth, and is established upon three tiers.
As stated in the *Śaradātilaka*:
"At the base and tip of the staff, there are two *kuṃbha* [vessels], measuring respectively three (*guṇa*) and four (*veda*) finger-breadths."
The *gaṇḍī* should be made from a portion of the *yuga* tree; it is said that it should be placed at the top of the staff.
In the *Sūkṣma*:
"I have stated that the staff (*daṇḍa*) is six finger-breadths long; it is called *gaṇḍa* and consists of three *gaṇḍikās*.
Its circumference increases by half a finger-breadth [at each joint], and its total width is four finger-breadths."
In the *Mṛgendrapaddhati*:
"The jar [of the breath] has a circumference of seven finger-breadths, and the staff [of the breath] has a circumference of six finger-breadths;
in the subtle [practice]..."
The water-pot (kumbha) should be two finger-breadths [in height], and one should know its circumference to be ten finger-breadths;
in the causal [form],
its circumference should be eight finger-breadths, and below that there should be a pedestal (vedikā).
Now, its back is shaped like a lotus with a pericarp,
its mouth resembles an elephant's trunk, and its back is tortoise-shaped.
Thus it is stated in the Śāradātilaka:
With six parts, the rear portion of the altar should be shaped like a tortoise;
it may also have the face of a horse, an elephant, or a boar.
As stated in the *Kāmika*:
The *sruva* ladle also has that as its source; its measure should be one cubit (*hasta*).
Thus it is stated in the *Vīratantra*: "I shall describe the characteristics of the *sruva*: its length is twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). Such is its length.
The circumference is declared to be exactly six finger-breadths.
The handle (daṇḍa) should be three finger-breadths in width, and there should be a gradual tapering [toward the top].
In the Śāradātilaka it is said: "At the base and the tip of the handle, there should be a gong (gaṇḍī), adorned with a ring (kaṅkaṇa)."
In the *Vīratantra*:
"O best of Brahmins, at the tip of the staff, there is neither a circumference nor a length of six finger-breadths.
In the *Mohaśūrottara*:

On the back, it is provided with two knobs; in its cooking [capacity], it is like a cow's footprint. They know its *puṣkara* to be two finger-breadths and its handle (*daṇḍa*) to be one finger-breadth.
p. 1397) *karṣadhāravaṭogaṇḍamūlegrahikagaṇḍikā* | In the *Kāmika*:
A new composition is superior because there is no prior one;
O best of the twice-born, the teacher should accept the composition of a Purāṇa.
Since the instrument of enjoyment likewise functions according to His command,
one should undertake the recitation of the Purāṇa after first performing a thousand repetitions of the Aghora mantra.
In whatever treatise an action is first set forth according to its proper place,
therein that treatise is established by the wise as the authoritative means (karaṇa).
One should accept [the implements] from another who is unsurpassed for rites such as festivals and ceremonies.
