Having taken up the *sruc* and *sruva* ladles— endowed with these characteristics, together with *kuśa* grass, positioned above the *ūrdhvapada*, and facing downward— and having performed the four purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) through the *astra-mantra*.

Having sprinkled [the wood] with the *kavaca* mantra and consecrated it, one should perform the *avaguṇṭhana* (veiling) ritual. To remove its status as mere wood, one should heat it over the fire three times with the *hṛdaya* mantra, rotate it, and then [heat it] with the tips, middles, and bases of *kuśa* grass using the *astra* mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
Having touched the tip, middle, and base of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles in sequence, [one should recite]: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-tattva;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the Śiva-tattva," at the tips of the *sruk* and *sruva*. Then:
"Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to the Vidyā-tattva; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the lord of the Vidyā-tattva..."

Salutation to Viṣṇu. Thus, in the center: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the self (ātmatattva)*; *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the principle of the self*. Having thus pervaded those three principles at their base, if one is desirous of liberation, one should worship them in the order of reabsorption [beginning with]: *Oṃ haṃ*.
Having worshipped with "I am Śiva and Śakti; obeisance to Śiva and Śakti, O Śivā," one should place the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles—

whose necks are wrapped with three threads— upon *kuśa* grass to one's right, first placing the *sruk*, which consists of *Śakti*, and then the *sruva*, which consists of *Śiva*, while reciting the *Kavaca* mantra.
One should worship with the heart-mantra using perfumes, flowers, and so forth. (p.
1398) Now follows the procedure for the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*).

In the *ājyasthālī* (clarified butter vessel) and the *praṇītā* (water-vessel), the dimensions are like those of the material vessels; in this [former], the interior should be six finger-breadths wide and the rim one finger-breadth thick.
The tip is said to be one finger-breadth and the belly twelve finger-breadths;

having thus prepared the vessel made of copper or other materials according to the prescribed rules, and having purified the "cow-vow" [the milk] by inspection and other means, one should meditate upon oneself as consisting of Brahman.

Having circled three times above the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should take a drop of clarified butter from the southeast corner of the pit and offer it with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe svāhā*. This is the installation (*sthāpana*). Then, having meditated upon one's own body as consisting of Viṣṇu, that clarified butter [should be placed] in the northeast corner.

Holding [the ladle], one should offer a drop of clarified butter with the tip of a *kuśa* blade while reciting: *oṃ hrīṃ viṣṇave svāhā*. This is the *adhiśravaṇa* (heating over the fire). Then, having meditated upon one's own body as consisting of Rudra, and holding clarified butter at the navel of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should offer a drop of clarified butter with the tip of a *kuśa* blade while reciting: *oṃ hāṃ rudrāya svāhā*.

One should offer oblations; thus it is said: "O you two, be lifted up! Reciting "Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the heart," one should take hold of two *kuśa* blades—one span in length and tied with a *brahmagranthi*—with the thumbs and ring fingers of both hands, and reciting "Oṃ haiṃ, svāhā to the armor," one should cause the fire, whose face is its own flames, to leap up three times.

Then, taking those same two blades of *kuśa* grass with both hands and reciting "Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the heart," one should divide them three times facing oneself; then, having untied the sacred knots (*pavitragranthi*) from those two blades of *kuśa*, one should cast them into the fire—this is the ritual bathing (*saṃplavana*). Of those very [blades]...
In some places, this triad is taught as the "approach to all obstacles," the "union," and the "immersion," [performed] with the heart,
head, crest, and subtle mantras: *oṃ hāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*.

Having thus consecrated a blade of *kuśa* grass with the *astra-mantra*, one should cast it into the fire after having dipped it in clarified butter; this is the *pavitrīkaraṇa*. With "Oṃ hai, obeisance to the armor (*kavaca*)", one should perform the lustration (*nīrājana*) by waving another blazing [blade] and casting that *kuśa* into the fire; this is the *nīrājana*. Huṃ.
One should cast [the oblation] into the fire with another weapon-mantra ending in *phaṭ* and a blazing *kuśa*-blade. This is the illumination (*udyotana*).

Likewise, for the clarified butter (*ghṛta*), having taken two *kuśa*-blades—one the size of a span and possessing a central knot—with the *praṇava*, [one offers them] to Agni, to the three [deities] beginning with Nairṛti, and to their mouths.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) for the sake of awakening that [wisdom]. Regarding the method of this *homa*, it is stated in the *Kāraṇāgama* as follows:
"With the right and left hands, one should bend the fingers at the joints; likewise, the thumb should be bent at its joint."
The index finger may be for me.
Joining two fingers while asking a question, and joining the little finger;
with these gestures and this mantra, one should perform the oblation with the sacrificial ladle.
In the absence of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, one should take *palāśa* leaves or other such materials and offer clarified butter (*ājya*) that has been consecrated.
Regarding this very point:
"In the absence of the *sruva* as well, [one may use] leaves of *palāśa*, *udumbara*, or *kiṃśuka*."
Or else, having poured [the offering] with leaves, one should pour it with a single leaf using a *sruva* ladle.

Having taken [the ghee] from the southern part of the ghee with the *sruva* ladle, one offers it into the right eye of the fire with "oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā. Then, having cast the remaining ghee into the portion of clarified butter with "svāhā," and having taken [a portion] from the middle part of the ghee, [one offers it] to Agni and Soma with "oṃ hāṃ agnīṣomābhyāṃ..."
Having offered [the oblation] into the fire at the forehead and the eyes with "svāhā" (p. 1400), one should offer the remaining clarified butter with "svāhā."

Having placed [the ladle] in the middle portion of the ghee and taken [a portion] from the middle part of the clarified butter, one should offer it into the fire at the forehead-eye with "oṃ hāṃ agnīṣomābhyāṃ svāhā. Then, having offered the remaining clarified butter, one should pour it back into the middle portion of the ghee with "hā. [This is done] with the left hand.

Taking the portion of clarified butter, one should offer it into the mouth with "Oṃ agnaye sviṣṭe svāhā," and then pour the remaining ghee into the three portions of ghee with "Hā. In the bright fortnight (śukla-pakṣa), one should perform this as described; however, in the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa-pakṣa), one should do so on the left and right sides as before. [Then recite] "Oṃ hāṃ somāya."

"svāhā" [is offered] in the left eye of Agni; "hā" in the left portion of the ghee; "oṃ hāṃ agnaye svāhā" in the middle portion of the ghee; "oṃ hāṃ agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā" in the left, right, and middle eyes of Agni, or in his mouth; and "hāṃ" [is offered] in the same places.

Having poured [the oblation] into three portions of ghee, consecrated it with the *astramantra* along with the clarified butter, protected it with the *kavacamantra*, veiled it with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*), rendered it nectarine by means of the *dhenumudrā*,
displayed the *mahāmudrā* with the *śaktimantra*, worshipped it with the root mantra, and thus refined the clarified butter;

One should cast [the offering] into clarified butter purified by washing for the sake of purification. In the *Ajita* [tantra], it is stated that what is offered into unrefined food or an unrefined fire becomes fruitless (*niṣphala*). Therefore, the preceptor (*deśika*) should perform the consecrations of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and so forth with the mantra.
Taking ghee with the *sruva* ladle, [one offers it] into the western face of the fire with "Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Sadyojāta";
into the northern face with "Oṃ hiṃ, svāhā to Vāmadeva"; into the southern face with "Oṃ huṃ, svāhā to Aghora"; and into the eastern face with "Oṃ heṃ, svāhā to Tatpuruṣa."
p.

1401) With the mantra *oṃ hoṃ īśānāya svāhā* for the upward-facing mouth, one performs the filling of the mouths with three oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) each. Then follows the joining (*sandhāna*): *oṃ sadyojāta*.
*Vāmadevābhyāṃ svāhā*. *Oṃ hiṃ huṃ vāmadevā-ghorābhyāṃ svāhā*. *Oṃ hūṃ heṃ aghora-tatpuruṣābhyāṃ svāhā*. *Oṃ heṃ hoṃ tatpuruṣeśābhyāṃ svāhā*. Thus, with these three [mantras].

Performing the *vasandhāna* or *mathavaktrasandhāna* with oblations of clarified butter (*rājyāhuti*): "Oṃ hāṃ hiṃ huṃ heṃ hauṃ, svāhā to Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna. Thus, starting from the southeast corner (Agni) up to the northwest corner (Vāyu), and starting from the southwest corner (Nairṛti) up to the northeast corner (Īśāna).

The unification with the *vajra* occurs through the falling of the stream of clarified butter (*ājyadhārā*). Regarding liberation: *oṃ hoṃ heṃ huṃ hiṃ haṃ īśāna-tatpuruṣa-aghora-vāmadeva-sadyojātebhyaḥ svāhā*. [This is for] the four faces beginning with Īśāna and ending with Vāmadeva, [and specifically] at Sadyojāta.

"One should contemplate dissolution" refers to the unification of the faces in the daily ritual (*nityakarman*). Having contemplated [the mantra] *oṃ hoṃ huṃ haṃ hiṃ heṃ* in the place of Īśāna, one should perform the occasional (*naimittika*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites and so forth.
Regarding the "unification of the faces," that face which possesses primacy is the [face] to be unified.
One should contemplate [the deity] joined with the gazing in one's own respective direction; or rather, the determination of the faces has been stated according to the specific ritual action.
In the *Kālottara*:
"Īśāna is for liberation; Aghora is for the person performing oblations and for powers such as *aṇimā*; likewise, Ghoratara is for rites of atonement and so forth, as well as for cruel actions."

For the purpose of the *vaśya* (subjugation) and *ākarṣaṇa* (attraction) fire-sacrifices, one should perform the oblation with the *vāmadeva* mantra; this procedure for the daily rite is beneficial in this western face.
Having understood this, O Mahāsena, one should determine the dimensions of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);
for the unification of the curves must be done in this way, and the son should not cause it to be done otherwise.
The fire sacrifice (*homa*) is indeed the primary mouth; all other [means] are secondary mouths.
Thus it has been said:
"Having meditated upon the five faces of the Fire-god, whatever rite is desired by means of [any one of] them..."
One should turn its face upward, and its mouth is directed upwards.
The other faces are included within that [central face], according to the measurement of the *kuṇḍa*; one should perform the insertion of the tongues into those very faces.
They are as follows:
Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Ratnā, Kṛṣṇā, and thereafter Suprabhā; Atiriktā and Bahūrūpā—these are proclaimed as the seven tongues of fire.
The tongue of Varuṇa is golden; the middle one is yellow; the northern tongue should be red;
and the one situated in the southern direction is black.
Sūprabhā is the eastern tongue, and Atiriktā is situated in the northwest (Anila); Bahurūpā is also a tongue;
thus the locations of the tongues have been proclaimed.
Where the tongue is designated, that should be the flame of the fire-eater (Agni). Hiraṇyā has the luster of molten gold;
Kanakā has the radiance of silver.
Suprabhā resembles a pearl, Riktā is like a ruby, Candrakāntā has the luster of the autumnal moon, and Bahurūpiṇī is multiform.
But he who, out of ignorance, places gold or other objects into the mouth of the Hotṛ priest while the fire is present,
shall become a slayer of a Brahmin.

The seed-syllables for the purpose of the sevenfold oblation are written here; they are as follows: those beginning with *ya* and ending with *ra*, excluding *ra* itself, combined with the sixty vowels.
The drops and the crest-mantras (śikhā), followed by the seed-syllables of the tongues in successive order,
are as follows: *oṃ iṃ hiraṇyāyai svāhā*, *oṃ hūṃ kanakāyai svāhā*,
*oṃ hūṃ raktāyai svāhā*, *oṃ ṣṭtaṃ kṛṣṇāyai*.
Svāhā! Oṃ ṣaṃ, to Suprabhā, svāhā! Oṃ huṃ, to Atiriktā, svāhā! Oṃ hūṃ, to Bahurūpā, svāhā! Oṃ lūṃ iṃ lūṃ, to Hiraṇya and Kanaka, svāhā! Lūṃ lūṃ, to Kanaka and Raktā, svāhā! Oṃ...
BRŪṂ ŚRŪṂ, svāhā to the red and black ones! OṂ ŚRŪṂ ṢRŪṂ, svāhā to Kṛṣṇa and Suprabhā! OṂ HRŪṂ SRŪṂ, svāhā to Suprabhā and Atiriktā! OṂ SRŪṂ HRŪṂ HRŪṂ IṂ, [svāhā] to Atirikta!

"Bahurūpābhyāṃ svāhā! Oṃ suṃ iṃ iṃ, to the remaining Bahurūpā, svāhā! Having thus worshipped the seven tongues, such as Hiraṇyā and the others, with these mantras during the application of the mantras for the seven tongues.

The kindling [of the fire] is performed by offering a single oblation of clarified butter with mantras ending in *svāhā*. The installation of the tongues [of fire] is performed by offering individual oblations with these seed-mantras enclosed (*saṃpuṭita*) within the mantras. (p.
Thus it has been said:
"One should perform the kindling by offering oblations one by one; having offered two by two for the reconnection, one should lead [the fire] to absorption in the center."

Having visualized a mouth of the desired shape and the dimensions of a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should visualize the six tongues, such as Hiraṇyā and the others, dissolving into the central tongue.
This is the unification of the tongues. For the purpose of naming [the deity], [one should visualize] within the fire—
Having visualized the Mother seated facing west, having worshipped her in the northeast and offered the *arghya* with flowers,
and having offered five oblations with the *astra-mantra* ending in *svāhā*,
one should perform the naming ceremony with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ, you are Śivāgni, O Consumer of Oblations," and [worship] the two parents.

Having worshipped with that mantra ending in *svāhā*, and having offered ten oblations for each [deity], he should worship the parents with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and dismiss them. Thus concludes the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*).

[The rites of] going out of the house (*upaniṣkrāmaṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*caula*), the initiation (*upanayana*), and the [sacrifices] dedicated to Prajāpati, Soma, and Agni—

For the sake of accomplishing the Vaiśvadeva, the *utsarga*, the funeral rites (*pañcatva*), the gift of a cow (*godāna*), the *samāvartana*, and the marriage— these bodily consecratory rites (*saṃskāra*)— one should offer three oblations for each with sesame seeds and water from the heart-mantra, and then perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root-mantra. This is the characteristic of the full oblation.
It has been explained by Ajita:

having sprinkled the *sruva* ladle with water using the *astra-mantra* and filled its cavity with clarified butter, one should then place a flower along with unbroken rice grains and *kuśa* grass into the tip [of the ladle] while reciting the *praṇava*.
Having placed [the vessel] and set the *sruva* upon it with its opening facing that center, one should then take hold of the base and tip of the handle, joined with the *sruc* and *sruva*.
Placing his hands in the *sevyatā* gesture like a conch shell,
he should sit with an upright body, having arisen and remained established in perfected being.
Having made [the lines] reaching up to the navel, one should then cause that root to be formed;
one should make them on the southern and inner sides of the ninth and the downward lines.
The wise practitioner should cast [the offering] all at once into the midst of the sacrificial fire; he should perform this correctly, beginning with the first oblation using the root mantra.
In the *Kālottara*, this threefold height resulting from the offering of the *pūrṇāhuti* is established through its divisions into "superior" (*uttama*) and so forth. As it is said:
"The oblation with a height of thirty-two finger-breadths shall be the superior; [that] of sixteen finger-breadths..."
And the oblation of one mātrā shall be the middling one.
O Six-faced One, one should know that offering of clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle, which is eight finger-breadths in height and uninterrupted, is the lowest.

Thereafter, having entered for the sake of all requirements— namely for incense, lamps, and food— one should divide the fire from the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and preserve it in another location. Then, with the sixteen vowels beginning with *a*, one should prepare sixteen fuel-sticks (*samidh*) made of *palāśa* or similar wood, each measuring sixteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

One should offer sixteen clearly manifest fuel-sticks (*idhmā*). Regarding this, it is stated in the *Kāmekī*: "Fuel-sticks are indeed said to be sixteen finger-breadths in length, pertaining to the divine. The characteristics of the sacrificial wood (*samit*) are also stated right here.
Fuel sticks made from sacrificial trees are recommended; they should be twelve finger-breadths long, possessed of their bark, cut evenly, and free from curvature, knots, and the like.
Likewise, regarding the implement: it should be the size of a thumb-joint and ten finger-breadths in length.
It is thick, glossy, even, cut straight, and free from the belly of worms.
Thus ends the meditation on the Śaiva fire. In the Kāmika [Tantra]:
"O Brahmin, listen as the Śaiva fire is described; be concentrated upon it. It is endowed with five faces and resplendent with seven tongues."
Ten-armed and three-eyed, adorned with all ornaments,
wearing red garments, and seated upon a lotus.
Seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), accompanied by the weapon of the arrow; then follow Kanakā, Bahurūpā, and Atiriktā.
Suprabhā, Kṛṣṇā, and another, Raktā, which is golden—these three are situated with their faces upward; the remaining ones are positioned starting from the east in due order.
We shall explain the nature of the other [fire] mixed with Vedic [rites] in the section on the final rites (*antyeṣṭi*).
Having thus meditated upon the Śiva-fire, one should worship it with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-fire," [reciting]: "O Fire, you are the splendor of Īśvara, considered the supreme purifier."
"Therefore, having established [thee] within the lotus of my heart, I shall satisfy thee.
Having prayed thus, one should worship that deity upon the *yogapīṭha* in the lotus of the heart; having performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*), one should meditate upon him.
The radiant form, both supreme and non-supreme.
Having brought that [deity] into presence within her [the image] by means of invocation and other rites, and having worshipped the causal [form],
one should worship the limbs of enjoyment externally upon it.
Having understood that the substratum has been destroyed, one should plant the individual radiant [seeds] separately,
having rendered them supreme within the fire of the mouth of Śiva.
Having established a connection with the fire, the light [of the disciple] emerges through the nose;
it enters through the *anudita* [breath], but exits through the *mudita*. The Guru should contemplate the entry [of the light] by means of the *anudita* breath of the self alone.

Thus, having established oneness with Śiva through the fire of the Kumbha-sthāyāga and having performed the union of the channels (nādī-sandhāna), one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times for each, ending with the word *svāhā* after the root mantra, for the sake of general and specific libations (*tarpaṇa*).

Having performed the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*— consisting of one-tenth of the [offerings] for the limbs of Brahmā— one should [recite] the root mantra accompanied by the syllable *phaṭ* in order to dispel ill omens arising from the regions, the falling of meteors, celestial, atmospheric, or terrestrial portents, and for the sake of bringing about auspicious omens.
Or, with the *bahurūpa* mantra, one should offer a hundred oblations for each [deity] together.
Likewise, in the *Kālottara*:
"The gods are seen in celestial chariots; that is always considered to be auspicious. [Regarding] the *asāma*s:
And when various [objects] fall through the sky.
The cutting of weapons and bows by men is especially distinguished;
or there may be a rain of falling dust, or birds may be ill-omened in the sky.
The sweet warbling of peacocks, swans, parrots, and other birds is desired; the falling of rain from the sun’s conjunction with the fire [planet] is auspicious.
The auspicious sound of conchs, kettledrums, clouds, and lutes, as well as the sight of the preceptor, Brahmins, women, and kings.
In the winter season, one should carefully avoid honey, meat, and the like;
likewise,
one should avoid seeing lotuses, flowers, and bulls.
Likewise, the sight of elephants and horses is highly commended;
while the sight of donkeys, camels, buffaloes, serpents, thorns, and those who eat raw grain is inauspicious.
When speech is praised, the wicked person does not desire it; sudden quarrel is undesirable, as is a terrible sound arising from negligence.

Likewise, the sight of virtuous men who are like trees of grace, as well as the performance of sacrifices and auspicious rites, [is favorable]; however, in the case of an inauspicious event, it pertains to the house.

One should pacify [the obstacle] by performing one hundred oblations with the Aghora mantra ending in *phaṭ*; having likewise offered one hundred oblations with the Astra mantra for the removal of that defect.
Likewise, in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"For the sake of place, time, and causal signs, one should pacify ill omens; a hundred oblations, indeed a hundred, should be offered with a full and unbroken ladle, O Śatakratu."

Thus, for the purpose of admitting the disciples, having offered one hundred oblations for each disciple with the root mantra accompanied by the final *pūrṇāhuti*, one should perform the satiation of the mantra (*mantratarpaṇa*) by offering individual oblations from the *svāhā* at the beginning of the root mantra up to the end of the *astra* mantra, concluding with the *śikhā*-enclosed *ārā* and ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
One should perform the kindling of the mantra with three oblations each, beginning from the root-mantra and ending with the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
It is as follows:
Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Śiva. Oṃ hoṃ, svāhā to the head of Īśāna. Oṃ heṃ, svāhā to the face of Tatpuruṣa. Oṃ haṃ, svāhā to the heart of Aghora.
Oṃ hiṃ, svāhā to the secret organ of Vāmadeva. Oṃ haṃ, svāhā to the form of Sadyojāta.
Svāhā! (p. 1409) Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the heart; oṃ hiṃ, svāhā to the head; oṃ hāṃ...

To the crest-lock, svāhā! Oṃ haiṃ, to the armor, svāhā! Oṃ hauṃ, to the eyes, svāhā! Oṃ haḥ, to the weapon, svāhā! Thus is the libation (tarpaṇa). Oṃ hūṃ hauṃ hūṃ, to Śiva, huṃ phaṭ! Oṃ hūṃ hoṃ hūṃ, to the head of Īśāna.

Hūṃ Phaṭ! Oṃ Hūṃ Heṃ Hūṃ, to the face of Tatpuruṣa, Hūṃ Phaṭ! Oṃ Hūṃ Haṃ Hūṃ, to the heart of Aghora, Hūṃ Phaṭ! Oṃ Hūṃ Hīṃ Hūṃ, to the secret part of Vāmadeva, Hūṃ Phaṭ! Oṃ Hūṃ Haṃ Hūṃ, to the form of Sadyojāta.

*Huṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hūṃ hāṃ huṃ hūṃ astrāya huṃ phaṭ |* Thus, one should perform the illumination (*dīpana*) starting from the root mantra and ending with the weapon mantra (*astra*). Likewise, in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"The libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the mantras beginning with the crest-lock (*śikhā*) and ending with the weapon should be performed once, ending with *svāhā*. [The *śikhā*...]
The kindling [of the mantra] is performed with mantras joined together, ending in *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*.
In the *Mohaśūrottara*:

"Having performed the satiation of the mantra, one should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and present the food offering (*nivedya*). Now follows the procedure for the cooked rice offering (*sthālīpāka*)."
Then, regarding the characteristics of the vessel in the *Dīptatantra*:

"I shall describe the ritual for the sacrificial ladle (*carupātra*): the belly should be six finger-breadths [in width], the circumference eighteen finger-breadths, and the depth four finger-breadths."
The lip is said to be one finger-breadth [in width], and the neck one finger-breadth in height;
the circumference of the neck is ten fingers, and the lid should be as described previously.
The width of the mouth of the shallow bowl (śarāva) is declared to be five finger-breadths;
its height should be two finger-breadths, and the thickness of the rim should be one finger-breadth.
Having thus prepared a vessel possessing these characteristics— either made of copper or clay, provided with a lid,

and free from defects such as cracks— and having washed it with water while reciting the Astra mantra, veiled it with the Kavaca mantra, and consecrated it with the four purificatory rites beginning with inspection (nirīkṣaṇa);
Having drawn [the deity] with sandalwood paste and other substances, having offered incense and lamps, and having recited over the sword, armor, and other implements,

one should take a triple-stranded thread, wrap it around the necks of those [images] along with *kuśa* grass and the armor-mantra, and place it on the southern side of the altar in the presence of the deity.
Joined at the two breasts and connected at the head in front, it should be made facing westward,
with each mountain measuring one finger-breadth.
In front of this, a hearth (cullī) one finger-breadth in width is fashioned;

having thus established the hearth endowed with these characteristics, one performs the rites such as the tracing (ullekhana) within its center just as in the case of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and thereafter [prepares] the five-fold sacrificial pap (caru) and cake (puroḍāśa).

Regarding the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the consecrated [fire]: having first offered clarified butter (*ghṛta*) into the *śivāgni*, and having placed a portion of that fire nearby on a mandala smeared with cow dung, which has been sprinkled with the *astra* mantra and shielded with the *kavaca* mantra, and upon which *darbha* grass has been arranged; having worshipped the sixfold arising seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) therein—on that [seat]...

Having placed the vessel as the embodiment [of the deity], one should worship Śiva along with his limbs within its interior, which has been wrapped with cloth at the opening, until the end of the dissolution (layānta). Then, having removed the flower, one should sprinkle [the vessel] with ghee consecrated by the Astra-mantra and purified with cloth, performing the rites of inspection (nirīkṣaṇa) and so forth.

Having recited the Śiva-mantra eight hundred times with pure water, and having filled [the vessel] with that [water], or with *kāpila* [cow's] milk or other milk, one should [place] sacrificial rice grains, *śyāmā* seeds, and so forth, for the initiation of a single disciple— or perhaps five.
Having taken those [offerings] equal to a *prasṛti* in another vessel— increased by one *prasṛti* for each subsequent disciple— from the heart, [one performs] the sixfold [rite].

Having washed [the vessel] and placed it within that oven, having sprinkled the hearth with the Astra-mantra and enveloped it with the Kavaca-mantra, having swept and smeared it, one should worship it therein with: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the hearth (cullikā). Then, on its right and left exterior sides, [one worships] "Oṃ hāṃ, to Dharma."

*Namaḥ*. *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Adharma*. Having thus worshipped and offered a seat consisting of the *praṇava* (Om) upon the western hearth, one should become facing eastward, place the cooking vessel upon it, and prepare it with wood free from worms, hollows, and other defects, using the *astra-mantra*.

Having ignited [the fire] and performed the extraction and removal with the Astra-mantra, while recollecting Ambhu, he should gaze with the Netra-mantra and protect [the vessel] with the Kavaca-mantra. Reciting "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śiva," he should cook the sacrificial porridge (caru) until it is well-cooked. Alternatively, [he may recite] the Hṛdaya, Śiras, and Śiva [mantras].
If the *pāka* [oblation] prepared with the *gāyatrī* is overcooked or undercooked, death or disease will occur.

To pacify that, one should offer a hundred oblations with the *astra-mantra*. Then, ending with *svāhā*, using the *saṃhitā-astra-mantra* and clarified butter (*ājya*), one offers into the *pāka-śivāgni* with the word *svā* and into the rice-pot on the hearth with the word *heti*.

Having performed the sprinkling with cold [liquid] and said, "Become cool," one should release the fire situated in the middle of the hearth by means of the heart-mantra and the *saṃhāriṇī* [mantra]. Thus it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"When it is hot, there should be sprinkling with heated [liquid]; when it is cold, there is sprinkling with cold [liquid]."
In ancient times, they employed the mantra ending in "svāhā" for the invocation of Agni.
Having said, "O Agni, carry the oblation," and also, "Become well-sacrificed," there should then be a stream of hot water in the second mandala.
Therefore, it should be the very same [deity] in the second maṇḍala; then, having been worshipped and installed after being joined with the sprinkling and other rites.
"Be very cool"—with these words, one should likewise perform the rite with the six sprouts; thus, through this collection of mantras, one obtains that which is called "coolness."
Then, having wiped the vessel on the outside with clay and water and washed it,
and having applied the *tripuṇḍra* mark, he should, as before,

mentally prepare the sixfold seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*) within the maṇḍala made in the western part of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and having placed the vessel there, [he should worship it] with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.

Having performed the worship, [he offers oblations] into the fire with the mantra *oṃ hoṃ heṃ huṃ hiṃ haṃ hāṃ hiṃ hūṃ hoṃ haṃ śivāya svāhā*. Reciting this, while shaking the *sruva* ladle over the remnants of the *caru*, he performs the *saṃpāta-homa* one hundred and eight times, one hundred and one times, or twenty-one times.
Regarding the procedure for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*), the *Kāmika* states:
"A thread made of three strands of virgin [wool], tripled again, sprinkled with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), rendered blunt by the armor-mantra (*varma*), and worshipped with the root-mantra."
When ignited,
it should be six finger-breadths in length and three finger-breadths wide, which is auspicious; however, when placed on iron, the tube should be four finger-breadths long.
A razor and a small knife, each measuring twelve finger-breadths in length and joined with a handle, are prescribed;
one should employ them in the rite of initiation.

Having thus endowed it with these characteristics, one should then consecrate the five-colored threads for the purpose of constructing the previously mentioned maṇḍala by the two thread-makers, as well as the sacrificial substances and so forth, by means of the fivefold purification. Thus it is said in the Mṛgendra:
A small wooden board for the fine threads, scissors, and colored powders;
likewise, a collection tray (saṃpāta) must be prepared for the sesame, rice, and other offerings.
Having thus consecrated all [the offerings] with the *saṃpāta* mixture, empowered them with the *vaṣaṭ*-ending mantra,

and performed the protection, the veiling (*avakuṇṭhana*), and so forth, one should contemplate that "this is accomplished" (*siddho'yam*) for the sake of the deities stationed on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*),
those in the pitcher (*kuṃbha*), the mobile liṅga, the retinue, the fire, and the Self.

Having divided the entire mixture into four parts with a ladle—one part for the vessel situated on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and the water-pot (kumbha), one part for the mobile liṅga and its retinue, and likewise [one part] for the deity; the other part, mixed with honey, is for the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa). The portion for oneself should be quickly mixed with honey.
One should simply prepare it mixed with ghee.
Likewise, in the *Kiraṇa*:

"Having fashioned the remainder for the fire of Śiva and the pitcher of Śiva according to one's own [prescribed] manner, and having performed the oblation and bowed to the Lord, one should perform the bali offering there."
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"One should offer [the oblation] to the *kumbha* and the *vardhanī*."
One should assign the second portion, together with ghee, to one's own disciples; and the third portion of the sacrificial porridge (caru), likewise accompanied by ghee and flooded with honey.
Having offered the oblation, one should give the inner *bali* while remaining composed in mind after sipping water;

then, according to the four-part division, one should assign one part to the deities residing in the mandala and so forth, the second part for the purpose of the fire-offering (*homakarma*), and one part for the retinue. The teacher [takes] one part.
Having offered one portion to the two disciples and given them water for their feet, and having completed the ritual actions from the incense offering up to the recitation of mantras,
he should preserve the remaining single portion for the consumption of the preceptor and the disciples.
Likewise, in the Kāmika [Tantra] (p.
regarding the initiation of the disciple:
The first portion is declared to be for the deity; in the second, the rite of homa; the third should be for the retinue;
and the fourth indeed belongs to the preceptor.
If one has moved away separately, one should cause the *naivedya* to be offered to the Lord of Gods.

For the sake of expiation, having performed one hundred and eight oblations with the *astra-mantra*, having given the *pūrṇāhuti*, and having made two offerings (*bali*), one should prostrate and ask for forgiveness.
One should contemplate: on the right side of the sacrificial pit, and also within the two mandalas, one should perform the inner and outer offerings according to the previously stated procedure.

Regarding the procedure for consuming the *caru*: in the initiation of *nirvāṇa*, one should have [the disciple] consume it as will be described later. Having gone near the chosen *liṅga*, and having worshipped Śiva residing in the fire and that residing in the *kalaśa* with the eightfold flower offering (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), one should address a petition to Śiva.
O Blessed Mahādeva, these sacrificial animals for whose sake this great sacrifice has been performed stand here at the gate, quiet and restrained.
"I have been commanded by you, who possess the form of a guru, regarding this task:
therefore, establish yourself within me now for the sake of bestowing grace upon these [beings]."
"May the Blessed Lord himself, the Sovereign who bestows liberation upon liberation, perform [this]," thus one should request. Thereafter, one should fashion the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta).
Then, with his right hand, the Guru [should take] pure [substances] with his own perfumes.
In the center of that, one should place Śiva together with Brahmā and the [five] limbs;
one should worship the Supreme Lord with perfumes, flowers, purifiers (pavitra), and other offerings.
Therefore, having meditated upon that [liṅga], one should worship the Supreme Lord;
having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the Śiva-mantra, one should remain established upon one's own head.
This is declared to be the "Hand of Śiva," auspicious for the destruction of fetters;
at that time, one should contemplate oneself as the agent, distinct from Īśa.
Acting as a witness, he should observe the ritual acts within the mandala;
likewise, he causes the water-pot to float in fire as the means of proof.
One should perform the binding and the purification of the bonds specifically for the disciple;
then, permitted by the words "So be it," he himself becomes presided over by Śiva.
One should contemplate non-duality (advaita) by means of that self which consists of the five bases.
[As stated] in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"Having bathed, being pure, and clad in clean garments, one should remain without food."
And having placed a faithful disciple before him.
Having recited the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should sprinkle the body of the disciple; then, one should fasten a protective thread upon his right hand.
Once the Lord of Sacrifice (Yāgeśvara) has been meditated upon in the nyāsa and other rites, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) must be performed.
According to the statement in the Pauṣkara, on the day prior to the sacrifice, one should perform the worship of the pavilion for the purpose of the preliminary consecration of the disciple.
Having performed the auspicious rite and having donned [the sacred thread], one should cause [the deity] to dwell [within the image].
It should be understood thus:
the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) takes place on the night before the appointed day, or in its absence, on that very day.
Or rather, the wise one should perform the rite preceded by ritual action.
The thread may be made of gold, linen, cotton, or other excellent materials; that is the supreme rule. Regarding fine [threads]—(p.

First, one should place a vessel upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), along with betel leaves and side dishes; in the center of that, one should set down a thread accompanied by the application of sacred ash (bhasma).
One should place upon the rice a white betel leaf combined with the *pūṭhā* seed and accompanied by a coconut fruit.
Having recited the Astra-mantra, one should sprinkle the auspicious ashes; one should place the Ātma-tattva in the vessel and the Vidyā-tattva in the unbroken rice-grains (akṣata).
Having placed the one named Māyā upon the ash-line, Lakulīśvara upon the ashes, and Ananta upon the thread,
one should worship them in sequence with the ghaṇṭā and other implements.
In the *Kāmika*:
"Having performed the washing of the feet in the southwest direction of the pavilion, and having stood there at that time, one should bind the protection-thread upon the disciple."
In the *Cintyaviśva*:

"Having recited the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), one should sprinkle [the area] with auspicious water (*śivāmbhas*). Facing north, the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) should assume the squatting posture (*utkuṭikāsana*)."
The ritual vessel made of clay should have its opening facing either east or west;
having filled it with consecrated rice grains, one should then fill the thread with ashes.
Having consecrated it with mantras and touched it with the guru’s thumb, excluding all other fingers,
one should triple that thread and extend it into the hand of the disciple.
That abode shall be protected by the armor-mantra and by ashes; having worshipped the causal deities beginning with Brahmā according to the scriptures, one should do so with the heart-mantra alone.
With the mantra of Naiṣikavīśa, [one should perform the rite] for the elemental body, but with the Puruṣa mantra for the crown.
1417) — [In the case of] the crown—
One should cause women and Śūdras to perform [the rite]; however, one should bind them with the left hand.

Since it is stated in the *Amara-kośa* that "left" (*savya*) refers to the left side and "right" (*dakṣiṇa*) to the right side, the avoidance of the [left] hand should be performed by that [right] hand; this is stated in the *Kāmika*:

Having fully performed the fire-rite (agnikārya) and worshipped [the deity], one should bind the protective thread (kautuka) in due order; having offered the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the same [mantra], one should effect the destruction of the enemy's seat.
The Guru, having taken the disciple by the right hand with his own right hand and by the left hand with his own left hand,
leads him out from the sacrificial hall to the north of the Brahmins and others; or, at the northern gate, this is common to all, [leading] to the west.
Or one may construct the mandala at the door; as it has been said:
"The northern door is for the Brahmin, the eastern door for the King (Kshatriya); the southern is to be known for the Vaishya, and the western for the Shudra."
One should perform [the ritual] at the western door for all, or else one should proceed correctly according to the rule.
In the *Makuṭa*, the remainder is stated:
"The eastern door is indeed praised, especially for Brāhmaṇas."
The southern gate is for the Kṣatriyas, and the auspicious northern one is for the Vaiśyas.
O Maheśvara, the western gate is for Śūdras; however, the southern gate is the most excellent for all the social classes.

Since the rule for the placement of the doors has been stated in this way, it was not mentioned in the *Kāmika* [Tantra] by way of a collective summary. Likewise, regarding the front of the door, there it says "there, upon the *praṇava* and the *kuśa*-grass mandala. In accordance with those respective [rules], the face of that [deity] at the front of the door should be measured as beautiful and square.

Having smeared two mandalas for the locations situated to the south and north with cow dung while reciting the mantra of the weapon (*astra*), one should place there *kuśa* grass and unbroken grains (*akṣata*) with their tips pointing toward the east or the north.
One should prepare either the sixfold seat (ṣaḍutthāsana) or the seat of the Praṇava. Or, as stated in the Suprabheda:
"Having smeared the ground in front of Śiva with flour-powder, making it square on all sides, and having adorned it and strewn it with *darbha* grass and flowers."
The wise one should place the face of Īśāna in the central position, that of Aindra (Indra) in the east, Aghora in the south, and Sadyojāta in the west.
One should worship Vāmadeva in the north, with the Hṛdaya-mantra in the southeast, Devaśiṣya in the southwest,
and Śimā in the northwest.
One should worship Kavacatvīśa in the various directions by their respective names; and for each one of these disciples individually.
Above that, one should station the disciples who are devoted to the meditation on Śiva.

The *bhautika* disciple should face either the east or the west, while the *naiṣṭhika* disciple faces the north; having positioned them thus, the teacher himself should stand facing the opposite direction from them.

For the sake of purifying the disciple’s body, having had him consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) along with *kuśa* grass three times, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) at another mandala, the Guru should, with divine vision,

look from the head down to the feet [of the disciple] while reciting the root mantra, for those who desire worldly enjoyment; [and likewise] from the feet up to the head for those desiring liberation.

Having gazed upon the seeker of liberation, one should sprinkle the site of the mantra with arghya water using the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*; then, having sprinkled it with the armor-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should trace three lines above the navel with the tips of darbha grass using the weapon-mantra for the purpose of purification (*mārjana*).
Having drawn three lines from the navel downwards with the root of kuśa grass while reciting the Astra-mantra for the sake of expiation,
[he addresses] the disciple—

Having visualized the three mandalas within the heart-lotus, and having visualized the life-force (*jīva*)— resplendent like a star, residing in the body as the primordial vehicle— strike oneself with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* for the sake of attaining all perfections: *oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ*.
Saying "Salutation to the form of the Self," having restrained that [breath] and performed the placement (*nyāsa*) upon that body according to the *Saṃhitā*,
he should worship the disciple’s head with eight flowers and apply a sectarian mark (*tilaka*) on his forehead.
In the *Santāna*:
Furthermore, one should have it bound here with divine silks, or with red cloth,
or even with cotton fabrics.
The binding of the eyes should be performed with the mantra of the Prāsāda;
one should know that white is the best, while red is middling.
The black garment is the lowest; therefore, one should avoid the black.
In the *Kālottara*:
"By a garment that is worn out, torn, or burnt, death shall occur. Therefore, all..."
One should bind it with effort using a clean cloth.
In the Vīratantra:
"The best is twelve cubits, the middling ten cubits, and the lowest eight cubits; however, five tālas has been forgotten."
One should always have the eyes bound with a ten-day-old cloth.
Its characteristics are now stated:
it should be slightly washed, new, white, possessing its full fringe, and unwashed.
That is the supreme worship for the mastery of all ritual actions.
p.
1420) One should sprinkle [the disciple's] continuum with the water of Śiva using the six-limbed mantra, and [recite] the eye-mantra.
The preceptor should perform the recitation here upon a new cloth.

O Goddess of gods, one should cause the eyes to be bound with a pair of garments. Having thus abandoned the impurity of looking at the cloth and so forth, one should consecrate it with the root mantra, veil it with the armor-mantra of the six limbs, and protect the eyes with the weapon-mantra.
One should cover it completely. Thereafter, one should have a golden flower made: ten *niṣkas* for the best, eight *niṣkas* for the middling, and five *niṣkas* for the lowest.
One should unite all those who are poor with whatever gains they may obtain; having thus reflected,
one should cast a flower and a piece of gold into the cupped hands of the disciples.
Having thus placed one of these, such as a golden flower, into his hand and having taken hold of his right hand, the Guru circumambulates the sacrificial pavilion three times and,
entering it through whichever door is appropriate for that particular caste, [proceeds] to the abode of the Deity.

On the sixfold seat, on the seat of the *praṇava*, having made the disciple sit facing east, one should cause him to sit. One should always show the eye-bandage to others for the sake of the seat of the bound state (*paśubandha-āsanāya*), which arises from the seed-syllable of bondage (*pāśa-bīja*). By that, the web of the thread [is formed].

"Having remembered that 'from bondage comes the severing of the bonds of the bound soul' (Paśupāśa-vighaṭṭana), he should spread out the blindfold. This Self, whose nature is Śiva, has its bonds loosened;
though surrounded by bonds, it is under my control through my own power, just as this [person] is."
That nectar, established in copper, possesses its own qualities and is fit for application.
I am Śiva, the supreme Lord, resembling a jewel;
by my touch, I shall quickly purify you, just as gold is purified.
"I shall perform [the rite] endowed with qualities, as prescribed by the scriptures and beyond reproach.

Having thus informed the Lord of the Mandala, one should station the Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas on the right and the Vaiśyas and Śūdras on the left. This has been stated by Brahmā, Śambhu, Vāda, and others.
Then, to his right should stand the Brāhmaṇa and likewise the Kṣatriya;
on the left side should be the Vaiśya and the Śūdra, for they are under the command of the Guru.
A specific detail is stated in the Viṣāsottara:
"Ascetics should be stationed in the northeast, and Brahmins situated to the north;
those born of the Kṣatriya caste should be stationed to the south of Śiva."
One should station the Vaiśyas in the western quarter, the Śūdras in the direction of Nirṛti, and the Śivas in the direction of the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), and then employ them.

Having thus established [the disciple] according to the rule, one should perform the rite of the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). Having stood according to the sequence thus described and having caused the throwing of the flower to be performed, one should show the maṇḍala to the disciple.
One should offer a handful of flowers with the Īśāna mantra; having performed three circumambulations, one should cause [the offering] to be given with the Vāma mantra.
In whichever mouth a flower—representing one's name and lineage—may rest, that person's mantra will be accomplished; therefore, it brings about the attainment of the desired goal.
On the petal of Īśāna, there is mental distress; in the south-east, it causes grief; in the south-west, it is said to bring prosperity;
and in the north-west, it brings a short life.
O best of Brahmins, when that flower falls upon the pericarp in one of the four directions,
then there shall indeed be happiness for those householders who have performed the purificatory rites of a single sacrifice here.
The appointment of those who have wives and children is proclaimed as *niyoga*.
In a sacrifice consisting of householders' rites, one should avoid the scattering of flowers; for that which is employed in this very rite, one should not perform it in a threefold manner.
When flowers have fallen upon the dog and the woman has slept with her husband, she incurs a great fault,
even though the sacrifice was well-protected.

One should offer oblations into the fire with clarified butter; one should perform a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra. By this procedure, the preceptor shall become free from defects, O Goddess.

One should perform the naming ceremony for all those who have fallen from their status—beginning with those residing in the Mantra stage and ending with the attendants (gaṇas) of Lord Śiva—as well as for those who live off them, for all base Śūdras, and for all women, using the name of Śiva or [the name] like that of a father. Thus it is stated in the Kāmika: [The text continues: ...the naming ceremony should be performed for all women using the name of Śiva or [the name] like that of a father. Thus it is stated in the Kāmika:
The name of the brahmin preceptor begins with the place indicated by his descent, followed by the word "Śiva-pada," and ends with "Devakaṇṭha-gaṇāntaka."
For women of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, [the mantra] known as "Śaktyanta" is prescribed; for all others, however, the name of Śiva is considered appropriate everywhere and at all times.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"In the case of a Śūdra born of a noble family, [the initiation] ends with the word 'deva'; in the case of an unworthy Śūdra, it ends with the word 'gaṇa'."
In the Śrīmanmṛgendra:
"The best of teachers should conceive of a Brahmin as Śiva, a Kṣatriya as Deva, and a Vaiśya as Gaṇa; for Śūdras, he should cause all [the aforementioned] names to be applied."
Regarding the cause:
for Brāhmaṇas it extends to Śiva; for a king, to the gods; for those of the Vaiśya caste, to Dharma;
and for a Śūdra, to the Gaṇas.
And you [have taught] the Siddhānta of Śiva for all [beings] in its progressive order, ending with Śiva for all,
or as it has been proclaimed otherwise.
For women belonging to those respective castes, the suffix should be in the feminine gender as before; however, according to the *Mṛgendra*,
for the best of the twice-born it ends in *-śiva*, while for others it ends in *-gaṇa*.
In the *Cintya-viśva*, a specific rule is stated:
"For all castes, the naming ceremony (*nāmadheya*) should take place at the end of the [first] year;
for the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya castes, the name-giving should occur at the end of the third month."
For those two who have attained union, their name should end with "Śiva";
for the sons of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, the name should end with "Devā".

Or one should cause [the mantra] to end with the *gaṇa*; likewise for others, it should be like that of the ancestors (*pitṛ*). The letter *a*, the letter *i*, and likewise the letter *u*— Please provide the text you would like me to translate. I am ready to assist you.
The letter *e* and likewise the letter *o* constitute these five vowels; they signify longevity, health, prosperity, decline, and even death.
Success shall be achieved according to the respective order; therefore, one should investigate the deity and determine the first syllable of the name of the disciple.

Having ascertained that the lifespan is three ten-thousand-year units, one should bestow [the initiation] upon those for whom it is one; however, one should avoid those two [units] which cause decay and death.
The supreme guru may give names to his disciples according to his own will; he should likewise cause the naming of his devotees and the members of his assemblies.
One should especially cause the names of the powers (śaktis) of the limbs to be given;
and the heart and other coverings [should be assigned] to their respective places, as well as the casting of flowers.
Thereafter, one should assign names to the Brahmins and others according to their respective qualities (*guṇya*).
Having thus performed the naming, one should prepare a mandala to the south or east of Śiva,
arrange a seat for the *praṇava* there, and [place it] facing the deity.

Having caused the disciple, whose body is upright, to enter, one should strike the disciple’s heart-lotus with a flower launched by the thumb and forefinger while reciting the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*; then, entering his body through the path of the channels (*nāḍī*), [one should proceed].

Having withdrawn that consciousness by means of the *saṃhāramudrā* with the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Self," and having restrained it within the pericarp of the heart-lotus, one should protect it; then, like the purification of the elements, one should purify the body through the five *dhāraṇās*, beginning with earth.
Having purified, flooded, and performed the ritual of total identification (sakalīkaraṇa), one should fashion the hand [as a weapon].

Merely by beginning with this, bound souls (paśus), due to the weight of their fetters (pāśa), depart from their state of bondage and, being free from fever, attain the state of Śiva through their own will.
Thus, having placed the Hand of Śiva— the bestower of the state of Rudreśvara— upon the head of the disciple,
and having meditated upon it as being of the nature of radiant energy (*tejas*), [one should sever] the bond (*pāśa*) while reciting the *Prāsāda* mantra.
Having led the *bindu* from the heart through the aperture of Brahma (*brahmabila*) at the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*) in accordance with the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*),
and having performed the destruction of the bonds (*pāśasaṃhāra*)— which wards off the entire multitude of bonds consisting of the qualities (*guṇa*)—
he places [the consciousness] upon the head of the disciple, removes the eye-blindfold, and [looks at] the right side of that disciple.
Having instructed him in the Śiva-mantra in his ear, having removed that cloth and performed the touching of all his limbs,

he should then cause him to offer a handful of flowers to the maṇḍala and to the [deity] residing in the jar with that very same [mantra], followed by three circumambulations and a prostration with eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma).

Having prostrated and led the disciple to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should prepare a maṇḍala with cow-dung in the southern direction; there, having seated the physical disciple upon a seat of the Praṇava,
one should place the root of a *darbha* grass in the disciple's hand with the root mantra for the purpose of joining the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*).
Having given that tip to the preceptor, he should join it at the joint of his own shank;

if he is a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika), having placed the root of the kuśa grass upon his own shank, he should give half of those kuśas— consecrated with the root mantra— under the guise of the kuśa grass.
Having emerged through the *piṅgalā* channel which resembles a spider’s thread, and having entered the disciple’s own *iḍā* channel,

one should contemplate that [the disciple's consciousness] has dissolved by means of *kumbhaka*; then, during the *recaka*, one should join their own channel with the disciple’s channel at the external sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) situated within the *kumbhaka*.
For the purpose of joining those [channels], one should satisfy the three channels with the root mantra: *oṃ hāṃ iḍāyai svāhā*, *oṃ hāṃ piṅgalāyai svāhā*, *oṃ hāṃ suṣumnāyai svāhā*;
then, having performed the *saṃpātahoma* with the *saṃhitā* over the head of the disciple.

For the sake of accomplishing the ritual procedures that bring about auspiciousness, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra, then offer one-tenth of that number for the Brahma-libations, perform the *pūrṇāhuti*, and then, for the sake of expiation,
offer one hundred and eight oblations ending with the *pūrṇāhuti* using the root mantra along with the *saṃhitā*.
Having instructed him in the mantras, having had him perform the worship of Śiva by means of those [mantras], and then having prostrated before the Guru, thereafter—
One should speak of the commitments (*samaya*) that must be practiced by one who has offered his body and so forth.
Thus it is said in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"The compassionate teacher should look upon the humble disciple; [this is] my command."
That triad, however, must be performed with faith.
The preceptor should cause [the disciple] to perform charity, religious duty, and the practice of austerity; he should likewise grant him his lineage, his tree, his clan, and his sphere of activity.
In this manner, the true guru [should impart] the lineage, the pentad, the "piercer of the vital points," the tree, the banyan, and likewise the clan to the disciple.
The pure reality is declared to be the auspicious sphere of experience; one should cause the disciples to hear the lineage known as Tandiśa.

The preceptor should cause the five [categories], such as the disciple and the monastery, to be proclaimed according to the specific lineage of these three— the Āmardaka monastery, the Abhadra-golakī monastery, and the Puṣpagirī monastery— and he should sprinkle them with water from the ritual pitcher and so forth using their respective mantras.
In the Kāmika:
"The general rule (sāmānyasamaya), however, is traditionally known as that of Māheśvara. He who is devoid of the extraction from caste (jātyuddhāra) is a general initiate (sāmānyasamayin)."
By the power of Śiva’s hand, one may go to the world of Śiva (Śivaloka) through the sky;
just as in initiation (dīkṣā), one becomes fit for the worship of Śiva and for service to the teacher. This is called the "general initiation" (sāmānyadīkṣā).
Likewise, in the *Bālajñānaratnāvalī*:
"In this manner, one who is a common initiate (*samayin*) should perform service and worship.
Likewise, he possesses the qualification for entry and other rites in the sacrifices of Śarva.

Thus ends the procedure for the initiation of observance (*samayadīkṣā*) in the *Dīkṣādarśa*, composed by Vedajñāna, the son of Vāmadeva, a resident of Vyāghrapura. Now, the procedure for the initiatory consecration (*saṃskāradīkṣā*) is stated:
how the disciple is purified through the extraction (*uddhāraṇa*) or the removal (*nirṇātyuddhāraṇa*) [of impurities].
For one who possesses the initiatory rite (*sāṃskāra-dīkṣā*) that leads to liberation (*nairvāṇikī*), there is no attainment of the state of the twice-born (*dvijatva*).
Therefore, his status as a twice-born is declared according to the scriptures: it is said that one born of a [low] womb is not joined [to the path], nor does he attain liberation. Now, for whom...
For one who lacks Vedic birth as a twice-born, it is appropriate to establish that status of being twice-born here;

however, for one who already possesses Vedic birth as a twice-born, it is improper to establish that status of being twice-born yet again, because it would lead to a lack of systematic order. True; that [status] is indeed Vedic birth as a twice-born.
That [purification] has been stated to belong to the body alone, and not to the self; and thus there is a Smṛti:
"The purification of the body must be performed, for it leads to purity after death.
And in the venerable Parākhyatantra: "By means of baths, oblations, birth-rites, tonsure, and the tying of the sacred thread..."
As long as a Brahmin has not undergone the purificatory rites, he remains equal to a Śūdra, since during that time he is not permitted to study the Veda.
Even a Brahmin who possesses [only] his birth, because he does not partake here of the food of a Svapāka,
would become equal to one who has fallen from his conduct by consuming it.
By this, the primacy of *saṃskāra* (ritual purification) is established in the Veda; how much more so,
then, in this Śiva-śāstra, which is supreme and free from all dependence?
Therefore, there is no purpose here in that refinement, because even when that Vedic status of being twice-born exists, one's destiny is dependent upon one's actions; and thus says the Smṛti:
"One may be a Brāhmaṇa by birth, or born of a Śūdra, or even an outcaste."
Overcome by future karma, they increase that very karma through their actions.
Both the peaceful and the cruel act for the sake of heaven and for the sake of hell; whether dead or born, such a person may become either a Cāṇḍāla or a Brāhmaṇa.
Likewise, in the Mahābhārata: "O God, even as beasts are to gods, so are gods to beasts; Brahmins are like dogs, and dogs are like Brahmins."

Therefore, even the refinement of the self (ātma-saṃskāra) is not intended here; for this body, being insentient, cannot undergo refinement through such Śaiva rites regarding its conjunction with or separation from inferior kinsmen and the like.
Thus, there is no refinement of these two states of connection and disconnection.

Because of the transformation into another state of birth (*jātyantara-pariṇāma*). Nor is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) intended for the production of the body and so forth—which are superior to the agent—through origination, nor for the destruction of that which is inferior; nor is the refinement enjoined for one who is already born.

Therefore, since initiation (dīkṣā) is possible for all [castes] on this earth, Brahminhood does not arise for the self merely from its own nature as a god or other being; rather, it arises through the conjunction with the *śrīrasa* (the essence of glory) associated with the [appropriate] caste, even for a conscious being endowed with the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).
It is the purification of that very embodied field (*kṣetra*), which is pure yet joined with the three impurities such as the atom (*aṇu*), and whose nature is that of an agent.
Likewise, in the *Kiraṇa*, the Blessed One said:
"The performance of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) for one who is not born, nor for a body, is not accepted; if [one were] born..."
When one among them has been initiated, the initiation of the others is considered complete.

Therefore, it is not said that [the grace] belongs to the birth of beings, for it is not considered to belong to the body; rather, the favor of the nature of consciousness is proclaimed, and Śiva is the bestower of grace upon all.

Likewise, in the venerable Raurava: "Neither the purification of the body, nor [the purification] of its conjunctions and disjunctions, nor through its birth and destruction, nor even of the genus (jāti) is it prescribed."
Volition also is held to be the refinement of that pure Knower of the Field, the embodied being, the agent whose very nature is consciousness.
Likewise, in the Kālottara:
"One should cause initiation to be performed for the Self— which is unimpeded by beginningless impurities— not for the sake of purifying the body, nor for caste, nor for ritual action."

His head must be placed beneath [the ritual vessel] by means of mantras, like the power of poison; initiation alone bestows liberation upon men, effecting the manifestation of both consciousness and the unconscious.

Thus, for the manifestation of the Śiva-principle within the distinguished self, there is the purificatory rite (saṃskāra). Now, regarding the purpose of the initiation by purificatory rites (saṃskāradīkṣā), if it is to take place on another day, it should be performed as prescribed in the Rule (samaya).

Having performed the entry of the disciple and so forth for the purpose of connecting the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*), one should commence the special initiation (*viśeṣa-dīkṣā*). In the case of a single-day rite, it should be performed immediately after the initiation of the rules (*samaya-dīkṣā*).
In the *Cintyaviśva*:

"Now, listen in due order to the characteristics of the consecration (*saṃskāra*) known as initiation (*dīkṣā*): the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*), the mandala, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*), and the worship of the liṅga."
Just as the initiation of the pledge (samayadīkṣā) and the consecration with the jar (kalaśābhiṣecana) [are performed],
one should perform the remainder as before, outside the circle of the eight Lords of Knowledge (aṣṭavidyeśvara).
If one has previously performed the purification rites as taught by the disciple with faith,
and is always endowed with these four qualities— freedom from anger, devotion, trust, and obedience to the guru’s command—
then he is liberated from all afflictions.

One who commits acts of treachery against the guru, treachery against Śiva, or treachery against the *samaya*, and who forms a bond of friendship with one who is uninitiated due to ingratitude and lack of discernment— [is excluded].
A disciple who is free from these eight faults of a guru is worthy of the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, one may initiate a disciple who possesses the opposite qualities during the ritual occasion; subsequently, he shall become a resident disciple at the conclusion of the initiation rite.
Having performed the rites from the construction of the mandala up to the worship of the fire, the supreme preceptor then sits upon a couch provided with a pillow of pure reality.
Upon the Kuṭilā-cloth, Sadāśiva always [worships] the goddess Vāgīśvarī, whose nature is the ritual illumination of Śuddhavidyā, and Vāgīśa.
Having spoken thus, and having sprinkled the disciple with water empowered by the weapon-mantra (*astra-ambunāstreṇa*),

he should strike the region of the disciple’s heart seven times with a flower consecrated with the mantra *oṃ haṃ huṃ phaṭ* in order to loosen the bonds (*pāśānām śaithilya-hetave*), [reciting] *oṃ huṃ*.
p.

1431) Having pierced the heart of Vāmana with [his] heart-mantra and entered the disciple’s heart by means of the *recaka* breath, one should contemplate that [disciple’s] consciousness as a shimmering star, and [recite]: *oṃ hāṃ haṃ hūṃ*.

Having separated [the soul] with the *jyeṣṭhā* mantra "phaṭ," and having grasped its consciousness with the *aṅkuśa* mudrā while reciting "oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ ātmane namaḥ," one should lead it to the *dvādaśānta* (the limit of twelve finger-breadths) and contemplate the individual soul (*jīva*) in the form of a drop on the tip of a blade of grass, [reciting] "oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ."
Having withdrawn [the deity] with the *saṃhāramudrā* while reciting "Salutation to the Self," and having established [it] within one's own heart by means of inhalation (*pūraka*),
one should, through retention (*kuṃbhaka*), cause it to become one in essence with the head of the Self; then, by piercing the knots of the heart and other centers,
[one perceives the deity] situated at the tip of the root-mantra, blazing and endowed with rays of fire.
Having led [the breath] up to the end of the power at the crown (*mūrdhva-śaktyanta*), and having passed beyond the causal deities beginning with Brahmā,
one should bring it to a state of equilibrium (*samarasīkṛtya*) at the *dvādaśānta* by means of inhalation (*pūraka*) and the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā],
reciting "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Self" (*ātmane namaḥ*) with the *udbhava-mudrā*.

Having gathered [the self] from the dvādaśānta, having brought it forth through the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), and having expelled it through the right channel (*dakṣiṇanāḍī*) with the mantra "oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ ātmane namaḥ," one should meditate upon oneself as the seed-syllable of Śiva (*śivabīja*) being cast by Vāgīśvara into the womb of Vāgīśī.

Having meditated upon the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*) in order to bring them about, and having worshipped Śiva, the [impurities] of the disciple's ground will be removed. Furthermore, his auspicious and inauspicious karmas are inferred by the characteristics of the fire’s color, sound, smell, and crest; as it is said in the *Śrī Kālottara*:
The sun possesses a luster with a dual color, a radiance like vermilion, resembling Indra’s peak,
and a brilliance like saffron.
These sixteen true entities grant success through the fire of knowledge (*jātavedas*);
there is the sound of the lute like that of a *kinnara*, as well as the resonance of the drum.
The Uḍukā-svara is preeminent, while the Phalakā-svara is supreme.
The sound of bamboo flutes is preeminent, while the sound of bells is auspicious;
the fragrance of camphor, agallochum, sandalwood, and pūrakīśaka [is likewise favored].
Kashmiri saffron, musk, kuṣṭha, and pālaka; jāti, tagara, kāla, kaṭuka, kuṭī, and mīnagandhaka.
The leaf, the flower, and the fragrance, as well as the fire with its auspicious scent, possessed radiant,
compact flames and shone like pure gold.
The sacrificial fire (jātavedas) that is smooth, curling to the right, radiant,
with a compact flame, and possessing the luster of pure rubies bestows success.
Having conquered death, one attains great siddhi; of this there is no doubt. The crest-lock (śikhā) may be on the east, the west, or even the north.
In the east, however, there is the accomplishment of wealth; in the west, there shall be pacification (śāntika);
in the north, indeed, the destruction of death; and in the zenith, it grants all desired objects.
In the southeast, there is death by fire; in the south, it bestows death;
in the southwest, death in battle; and in the northwest, there shall be strife.
The upward-pointing flame (śikhā) that indicates the bestowal of the yoga of knowledge has the characteristic of emerging [straight up];
when it has the sound of a bull (ṛṣabhadhvanika), it occurs upon approaching the unapproachable.
If there is a sound like that of a deer or a high-pitched cry, it indicates the arrival of a daughter-in-law;
if there is a sound like that of a frog, it indicates the arrival of a daughter.
If the sound "kha" occurs, it would be fire; if there is a mere measure (mātrā), it would be movement.
If the sound "bhaccha" has the resonance of a cat, one would incur the sin of violating the Guru's bed.
If the sound of a cart occurs, there will be the death of a good son; if the sound of gold occurs, it lasts for exactly seven days.
If one hears a sound resembling the crackling of lightning during the ritual oblation, or if fire [breaks out], the wife meets her death; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
Whether it be a sound like the roar of the ocean or even a great noise, she who encounters such [a sound] meets her death; thus it is true, O Six-faced One.
From the smell of garlic, one may incur a disease of the digestive fire; from the smell of asafoetida, one may incur jaundice.
Thus, O Six-faced One, the auspicious and inauspicious [omens] for the disciple have been declared here.
Likewise, in the case of a blazing fire: color, fragrance, sound, smoke, and the crest of the flame—these are the six signs.
And having understood the nature of fire, one should perform one's actions.
Color is to be known as elevenfold, and smell likewise as thirteenfold; sound is to be known as fivefold, and smoke has four characteristics.
The *śikhā* is indeed fivefold, and the *īṅ* is traditionally taught as twelve;
the signs of success (*siddhi*) and failure (*asiddhi*) are declared to be fifteen.
However, for fear of excessive prolixity, the defining characteristics are not written here.
Having thus recognized the impurity of the disciple through such signs, the preceptor should meditate upon the Lord who consumes sin and perform oblations with His mantra.
Likewise:
"The form of the deity Pāpabhakṣaṇa has the luster of crushed collyrium."
Licking his formidable lower lip, he addressed Meghanāda, who was exceedingly difficult to conquer.
With a wide-open mouth and large fangs, wearing red garments and possessing three eyes,
his matted locks were bound with red flowers and adorned with a circle of serpents.
Holding a trident and a sword, appearing fearsome, with hands granting boons and fearlessness,
clad in a tiger skin, and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread.
One should meditate upon [the deity] seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), who destroys even the most formidable sins.
Having thus meditated—
*oṃ sakṣahaṃ vidhāya svāhā*— [one should perform] the brief [offering] with the Navātman mantra.

One should offer one hundred oblations for the purpose of destroying sin. If [the sin] belongs to a teacher, one should offer one thousand oblations with this mantra: *oṃ khaḍgahasta kamalaṃ rūṇa khaṭ paṭ pāpabhakṣaṇāya svāhā*. [This is for] the self that has become weakened or bound.

The extraction [of the soul] from Śakti is the *rudraputratva* (the state of being a son of Rudra); the *garbhādhāna* (conception) is the manifestation of the qualities of the self through independence; the *puṃsavana* (male-rite) is the discrimination between the individual soul (*puruṣa*) and primordial matter (*māyā*); the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair) is the visualization of the reality of Śiva and other [deities]; and the *jātakarman* (birth-rite) is the attainment of the nature of Śiva.
The awakening to the state of Śiva is [effected] because it is spoken through the Śiva-mantras beginning with "Namaḥ.
One should perform the elevation from their respective castes for Brahmins and others by means of the mantras prescribed for those specific castes;
those of mixed castes are to be purified by the highly powerful Śiva-astra mantra.

A Śūdra should offer with the *varman* [mantra], a Vaiśya with the *śikhā*, and a Kṣatriya should have his [defects] purified by the wise with the *śiras* [mantra]; through the application of five oblations,
the two higher castes are purified of their births.
In the *Skandakālottara*,
it is stated that for those belonging to the intermediate Śaiva classes, after the elevation from their birth-status (*jātyuddhāraṇa*), there are sixteen ritual duties (*ṣoḍaśakriyākārya*).
Thus it has been said: "O Six-faced One, for the oblation that delivers one from birth, one should indeed milk each [cow] a hundred times by means of fire, even if she belongs to the Śūdra caste."
Having joined him with the status of a true Śūdra, perform the sixteen rites; he will directly attain the state of a Brāhmaṇa, after which you may then perform his initiation.
"A wise man should likewise cause the castes to be established according to the prescribed rule.
Regarding that method, it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"Even those who are Brāhmaṇas and so forth may become Śūdras due to their qualities; therefore, one should uplift them from that state."
Having extracted the *śūdra* caste from the root with [the mantra] ending in *svāhā*, [one should proceed].
Having subsequently offered three oblations, one should present [the offering] to Śiva; [this is done] because of the nature of food, the faults, and the womb, seed, and body.
"O Blessed One, Supreme Lord, may my self become pure and twice-born;
may the portions of the Śūdra fall away"—thus one should perform three oblations.

"O Lord, by Your grace, let this Śūdra become Rudra himself. Having thus petitioned, one should offer three oblations with the root mantra ending in *svāhā*, or five, for the purpose of removing the state of a Śūdra and attaining the status of the twice-born and a portion of Rudra respectively; or alternatively, one hundred [oblations] with the five Brahma-mantras.
One should offer oblations. Therefore, for those who practice the dharma of Śiva, the separate proclamation of their castes leads to rebirth in hell. Thus it is stated in the Svacchanda Tantra:
"For the spiritual sons (putraka), the sustainers (dhāyaka), and even the initiates (samayin)..."
A man who utters [the name] of a goddess belonging to a lower caste must perform an expiation.
For three days he is cooked in the stomach of Rudra, for five days in that of Keśava, and for a fortnight in that of Pitāmaha.
Whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, those who are appointed to the office of Ācārya by the Supreme Goddess are all remembered as Śivas.
Otherwise, those lowest of men who previously perceived [the Lord] as having a material form are cooked in hell together with their wives for three years.
In the Devikālottara:
"The man who deliberates upon what is permissible and impermissible regarding caste becomes a sinner.
In the Śivadharmottara:

The *liṅga* is said to be of two kinds: stationary (*sthāvara*) and mobile (*jaṅgama*). The stationary is known as the installed *liṅga*, while the mobile is understood to be the initiated [disciple].
Through the disparagement of the mobile [liṅga], the immobile [liṅga] becomes fruitless; therefore, a wise person should never disregard either of the two liṅgas.
"He who, out of delusion, shows contempt [for the deity] is a beast; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, in the *Cintya-viśva*:
"The worship of the *liṅga* is of two kinds: immobile and mobile. Beginning with the *liṅga*..."
O Nandikeśvara, the worship performed there is considered immobile.

In that regard, the worship of the *liṅga* and so forth is the supreme adoration of the mobile (*jaṅgama*) form; however, at the time of worship, the presence [of the deity] resides within the immobile (*sthāvara*) splendor of Śiva.
Śiva maintains his presence at all times within the mobile [liṅga]; however, when the mobile [liṅga] is treated with contempt,
the immobile [liṅga] becomes fruitless.

Initiation is appropriate for all castes, but especially for one who has already been initiated; indeed, there is always a distinction based on the specific differences among the castes of those who have been initiated.
O son of Śiva, because you have emerged from the inner sanctum of Vāgīśvarī and because you have attained the status of being her offspring, you are designated as "Śaiva."
Like a sinner who perceives a stone in a Śiva-liṅga, that initiated person possesses a state of excellence,
especially so.
He whose mind is fixed upon the auspicious *liṅga* need not consider his caste and so forth; whether he be of silver, copper, lead, or even iron.
The prior form, however, consists of cognition, its characteristic nature, and its differentiation by name; once the state of being gold is established, everything attains complete identity.
Therefore, for those initiated from the Brahmins down to the Śūdras,
a distinction of caste does not exist; through the initiation of humanity, all [castes] are one.
The ocean, fish, and tortoises, as well as Kumbhīka and Kaṭa;
For all beings, whether born from a womb, born of water, or otherwise, as well as for humans, this same rule is ordained for those who have been initiated.
In the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*:
"He who is born from the womb of Vāgīśī by means of the Śiva-mantras pervading the void, in the presence of Śiva, shall be a Śūdra."
