How could it be that things such as jars, which possess the nature of clay, [arise] from the conditioning of clay, just as [food arises] from clay?

In the same way, the castes that have abandoned their bonds are not merely natural (prākṛta) types; for if, through the purificatory rite of Śiva, the state of being Śiva were not attained by men, [they would remain as such].
Indeed, the teacher of the twice-born, gods, and others would not be fit [to act] unless he were always consecrated by the guru through the purificatory rites of mantra and initiation.
The moving and the unmoving would certainly attain the state of Śiva in that very moment.

Enough with excessive elaboration. Thus, in the initiation of purification (*saṃskāradīkṣā*), once impurity has been removed from birth through the elevation of caste, [the soul returns] for the sake of worldly activity once again.
Having offered oblations with the mantra of each respective caste, one should establish a pure caste.
Thus, in the *Kālottara*:
"For the sake of worldly transaction, a pure caste is established for all; [otherwise] impurity..."
Having destroyed the impressions of previous births, O Six-faced One.
One should conceive of Brahminhood, purity, Kṣatriyahood,
Vaiśyahood, and Śūdrahood for all [beings] according to the distinction of their respective fruits.
Isolation, absolute sovereignty, wealth, and the increase of grain and other assets—these should be known as the fruits in successive order; furthermore, liberation is common to all.
From that, O Guha, there occurs the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and the purification of their birth; furthermore, for all of them, there is now a re-emergence within that very [birth].
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the *puruṣa* [sūkta], one should effect the status of a Brāhmaṇa therein;
the status of a Kṣatriya with the *madhucchandas*, and that of a Vaiśya with the *vāmadeva*.
p.
1439) The state of being a Śūdra should be applied by means of the *sadyo-ja* [mantra], according to the previously described arrangement of oblations (*āhuti*).
Likewise, it has been stated by the venerable Brahmaśambhu:
The primordial material cause is the power Kuṇḍalinī;
that Self whose birth occurs within her is the first-born, and not any other.
Having cast off the state of a Śūdra, which is characterized by bondage, sorrow, and hostility, the Brāhmaṇa—
purified by the sacred mantras— is immediately born as the supreme being.

Because of its nature as Brahman, the body of Sadāśiva is Brahman; one born from that is a Brāhmaṇa, and he who knows it is so called because of that knowledge. When such a pure birth has arisen, the worldly lineage perishes. For the four [castes] beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, there is the fourfold division beginning with Śiva.
It will occur in sequence for those who have been initiated. Likewise, in the *Kālottara*:
"Śiva is the branch, and likewise Jyotis; that which is known as Sāvitra arises from Nāda at the time of initiation."
Just as a mantra dissolves into Śiva and the other deities.
By the power of those respective boons, there arose in sequence the four families;
this triad should be known as the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
Upon the arising of a pure birth, that which was established by one's [original] family perishes.
From the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*:
"The Brahmin is Śiva; the Kṣatriya is Śivā; the Vaiśya is Jyotis; and the Śūdra is born from Viṭ. These are the Savitras.
The phonemes [are] natural in the Śiva-āgama.
In the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"The branch situated in the lineage of Śiva is known as Kula; that which is in the lineage of Savitṛ is designated as Sāvitra.
On Krauñca, there is a settlement of the four castes according to their respective divisions;
on Śālmalidvīpa, that which is called Śiva; and Puṣkara is known as Jyotis. Thus, for the sake of favoring living beings, there are these four families.
In the Śaiva Purāṇa, it is said:
"The Śūdra-hood of the Śūdra has passed away, and likewise the twice-born status of the Brāhmaṇa; through connection with the Śiva-saṃskāra, no distinction of caste exists."
If you think that the status of being a Brahmin does not belong to the living soul here,
nor even to the physical body, then the sin of killing a Brahmin would occur simply from burning a clod of earth.
Even they, through prior deliberation, do not truly possess the status of the twice-born; therefore, one should certainly not deliberate thus regarding one's previous birth by the command of Śiva.
The distinction of caste was created by him at the command of Śiva; therefore, no distinction of caste should be made within the hermitage of Śiva.
Whether he be of noble birth or of low birth, upon seeing one who wears the sacred ashes and rudrākṣas,
if one rises from a high seat, one shall go to the Raurava hell.
One who has been born through the initiation of Śiva should not contemplate his former birth, just as there is no prior mental conception regarding a well-consecrated Liṅga.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"One who is committed to the lifelong vow (*naiṣṭhika*) should especially not contemplate distinctions of caste.
In that same work, the *Jātinirṇaya*:
O Nandikeśvara, even one who has been initiated according to the rules, whether he be a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika) or otherwise, still possesses a connection to his birth in this manner.

Because worldly custom specifically applies to one who is composed of the elements (bhautika), it is the settled conclusion of the scriptures that the [name] should be stated according to the previous caste.

Thereafter, having given the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*)— consecrated according to the respective caste of the Brahmins and others, or possessing an essence appropriate to their social class— he should offer oblations (*juhuyāt*) one hundred or one thousand times with the root mantra (*mūla*).
As stated in the *Kāmika*:
One should give the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) consecrated with the root mantra; having offered a hundred or a thousand oblations and having given the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Śiva-mantra.
The definition of that [thread] is stated in that very same place:
"A thread made of cotton, tripled and then folded three times over—such a single thread is for Śūdras; for Vaiśyas, there should be two."
For Kṣatriyas, there should be three strands, while for Brāhmaṇas, the number is seven;
or else, for them, there may be five or even nine threads.
The mantras for the *aghora*, *vāma*, and *jāti* [faces] are used respectively for the Brahmins and the other castes;
the sacred thread (*upavīta*) should be worn with the mantra prescribed for one's own specific caste.
Regarding the sacred thread (*upavītaka*) prescribed for those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes:
it should be used only at the time of worship and similar rites, but it must not be worn [as a constant ornament].
Having deliberated upon what is appropriate and inappropriate regarding the *anuloma* and other [arrangements] of the syllables, it is likewise stated in the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*:
The *mātṛkā* consisting of the worship should be maintained; no other method of maintenance has been taught for them.
In the Aṃśumat division of Māhendra,
the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) should indeed be bestowed by the group of Brahmins upon the disciples;
for Kṣatriyas it should have three strands, and for those of the Vaiśya caste, two strands.
For Śūdras, a single-threaded cord is prescribed at the time of initiation; however, at other times, it should specifically be made for those of the Śūdra caste.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"One should wear the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*); indeed, that sacrificial thread increases one's splendor and strength.
[Worn] above the navel it does not increase longevity, but below it there is a loss of ascetic merit (*tapas*). Therefore, it should be level with the navel."
O best of the twice-born, one should perform the rite of wearing the sacred thread.
In that regard, since the wearing of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is established for the *śūdra* by the general scripture,
the regulation of the time for its wearing by a householder *śūdra* has been stated in that very same [text].
Namely:
during worship, in the fire ritual, or at the time of the twilight junctions; it is not otherwise.
As stated in the *Suprabheda*:
Furthermore, the thread may be spun by a Brahmin woman, a princess, or a Vaiśya girl,
or else by a Śūdra girl— thus it is fashioned from three [types of women].
One must diligently avoid any sūtra fabricated elsewhere; however, a Śūdra may wear a sacrificial thread and even perform ritual acts.

One should not diligently practice the lineage, the sphere of activity, or the mental continuum; however, one who is committed to the ultimate goal should always perform these, whereas a householder should never do so.

Since this has been stated, the lineage (gotra) of this householder must be constantly maintained and reflected upon; let it be understood in detail from the *Kṛtaśaivasamayācārapaddhati* which we have composed.
Furthermore, in the *Kālottara*:
"This is the duty for the twice-born; one should prescribe it for women in the same way."
And for the sake of favoring all women, Śiva shall become [manifest].

Because all women possess a portion of Umā, they know this [to be so]; and for those of the twice-born status, there is the initiation (upanayana) at the proper time, as well as the marriage ceremony during the consecration (dīkṣā).
O Six-faced One,

one should cause the initiation ceremony (upanayana) to be performed according to the rules of worship, including the topknot and the sacred thread; for all twice-born women as well, there is likewise the topknot and the sacred thread.
Śiva has declared that the entitlement [to this rite] belongs especially to women; therefore, with every effort, men too should wear the sacred thread (upavītaka).
Performing sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma together with his wives,
he casts the fuel-wood into the fire with a mantra and consumes the sacrificial porridge (caru) with a mantra.
Indeed, in all sacrifices, one who has undertaken the vow of age performs the sacrificial rites with the mantra,
even without the topknot and the sacred thread.
The root mantra, the deity, the ritual authority, and the sacred thread (upavīta); without the sacred thread, every sacrifice performed by women is fruitless.
The topknot and the sacred thread—everything is ordained in this manner. Having first adopted this procedure, one should thereafter perform the sacrifice.
In this context, the characteristics of the location of the crest (*śikhā*) are also described as an incidental discussion:
from the midpoint between the eyebrows up to nine finger-breadths, that is the eastern location of the crest.
The station of the crest (śikhā) is thus proclaimed; Śiva [resides] in the sequence of the east and the west.

This has been indicated as the general rule, and the specific details have also been stated; their number and measure have been declared. Likewise, there are one hundred and eight feminine qualities, or even more.
Even among the hairs on his body, a single lock of hair is proclaimed.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"The vow is indeed of two kinds—Vedic and Śaiva.
The Vedic [vow], consisting of the sacred thread (*upavīta*) and so forth, is to be performed by those belonging to the three higher castes."

The initiation of Śiva (Śivadīkṣā) is indeed the primary [requirement], for the Śaiva path is exceedingly supreme. Therefore, for the initiate who desires to enter the stage of life of Śiva (Śivāśrama), there are the garments, the sacred thread, the deerskin, the tooth-stick, the staff, the loincloth, the ashes, the crest-jewel, matted hair, and so forth.

Having purified [the items] individually through inspection and other rites, and having placed them in separate vessels— or, as stated, in a single vessel— up to the end, one should consecrate them with the *Sadyojāta* and other mantras. Then,
having performed the purification by means of a *saṃpātāhuti* (a drop-off oblation) using the *saṃhitā* mantra ending in *svāhā*, [one prepares] the ritual substance for the limbs (*aṅgadravya*).
Having displayed [the image] in the presence of the Lord of the Altar (Sthāṇḍileśa), one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) before the jar.

In the case of the "immediate consecration" (sadyodhivāsa) method, having established it for only a moment and consecrated it with the Sadyojāta and other mantras, one should give the vow to the Blessed One, having commanded him, saying: "Please grant it."
Having requested permission and received it, one should bestow the ancillaries of the vow upon him.
Thus, in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "Then, by means of the ancillaries of the vow, the practitioner seeks to conquer the five elements."
The staff, the loincloth, the ashes, self-restraint, and the crest-jewel.
The vessels, beginning with the *kuṃbha*, are purified by inspection and other rites, consecrated with mantras, and cleansed by the offering of *saṃpāta* oblations for even a moment.
Having placed [the items] for the purification of the inheritance, one should present them to the one who has prostrated.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"This is an ancillary part of the vow; all [these things], such as matted hair, deerskin, ash, and staff, are indeed appropriate."
As well as a loincloth and a water-pot.
Having recited the five Brahmans and the six limbs as prescribed, one should place them into the vessel together with the *svāhā* ending and the *saṃhitā* mantras.
Likewise, in the *Kālottara*:
"The staff, the sacred thread, the deerskin, the tooth-stick, the girdle, the turban,
the loincloth, and indeed the ashes."

Because it is the cause for manifesting the vow, this is the vow of the ascetic. One should cause the sacred thread (*upavīta*) to be given with the *Vāmadeva* mantra and with the *Aghora* mantra; one should cause the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) to be given with the *Tatpuruṣa* mantra alone.
One should cause the loincloth to be given with the Vāmadeva mantra, the sacred ash with the Īśāna mantra,
and one should oneself wear the rudrākṣa beads with the Tatpuruṣa mantra.
"This is the duty for the twice-born and others; one should prescribe it for women in this same way.
Having said, "This too is a great favor," with eyes filled with tears of joy, he should accept it, wear it, and bow down.
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground, filled with devotion and firm in his vows,
the disciple as well, being composed, should take up and wear the components of the vow.
Now follows the procedure for wearing matted hair (*jaṭādhara-vidhi*). The sequence for the wearing of matted hair by the four castes, beginning with the Brahmins, is stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
The golden [threads] of a Brāhmaṇa are proclaimed to be smooth and fine;
those of a Kṣatriya are to be known as thick and twice as many, with intervals between them.

For a Vaiśya, one [tuft] is prescribed in the place of the top-knot; likewise for a Śūdra. Having removed [the hair], joined with smooth eyes, he should remain self-controlled and have his senses conquered.
Now, some say that for Brāhmaṇas there is no wearing of matted hair, ashes, and so forth;
that is incorrect, because it contradicts the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas. Thus, in the Gautamīya Sūtra:
"The *caula* ceremony is specifically for the three twice-born classes..."
In the first year, the wearing of matted hair (jaṭā) should also be performed as enjoined by the Śruti.
Likewise, in the Vāyavīya-Sāvarṇya-Saṃhitā:
"The fourteen Manus, beginning with Svāyambhuva, [attained] great glory."
Their entire bodies were adorned with gold, and they wore bright sacred threads.
Their limbs were adorned with the triple mark (tripuṇḍra), and they wore matted hair, rudrākṣa beads,
water-pots, and were all resplendent with rosaries.
Thus it is stated in the Lokākṣi-sūtra: "A learned Brāhmaṇa should wear ashes consecrated with the *mānas-tokā* mantra; he should not, even in his mind, transgress the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*)."
"Because it is enjoined by scripture, therefore one who abandons it becomes fallen"—
by such scriptural statements, the wearing of matted hair, ashes, and so forth, must necessarily be maintained.
In the *Mṛgendra*:

"Neither one with matted hair, nor a Śūdra, nor one lacking discipline, nor one who is ignorant, nor one who is negligent; nor a woman, nor one whose age is extreme, nor one afflicted by disease, nor one who is excessively corpulent."
In the determination of castes, for a Śūdra there is but a single lock of hair on the head; he should not wear matted locks like Rudra, though he may wear a single lock.
O Goddess, listen to the supreme secret, the excellent characteristics of the matted locks (jaṭā), which are eight tālas in length and three aṅgulas in width.
The hair on the heads of those devoid of locks is called *kabarī*; the matted hair (*jaṭā*) is declared to be the cause of the universe, consisting of manifold powers.

He who knows this is called "one with matted hair" (jaṭin), for one is not a jaṭin merely by the binding of matted locks; [he is so called] by virtue of the number of the principles of Time, the purifiers, the Śaktis, the Mantras, and the Īśvaras.
Having divided the *śoka* and combined it individually with the *saṃhitā-aṇus*, one should bind it with *tejas* before the Lord of Thought (*mateśvara*).
By the word *kalā*, thirty-eight are denoted; by the word *tattva*, thirty-six;
by the word *pavitrāṇu*, the five pure [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta; by the word *śakti*, the nine powers beginning with Vāmā; and the eleven lords (*īśas*) beginning with Mantreśa and Viśveśa.

The Lord of Mantras, having understood [this], becomes the most excellent Guru; otherwise, he would incur fault. O son, regarding the suitability of the practitioner and the mantra to be mastered through the heart-mantra, a specific rule has been stated therein for the purpose of increasing the matted locks of those observing the vow.

O ascetic devoted to the elements, you shall not attain nourishment by mixing ashes with substances containing worms, nor by using eye-salve made from the three myrobalans (triphalā), nor by means of a refined complexion.

The meaning of this is as follows: having placed substances such as pungent oil, viṭaṅka, and banyan wood into the interior of the vessel, having sprinkled it with the Astra-mantra and enveloped it with the Kavaca-mantra, having wiped it and covered it with a stone slab,
one should worship that [vessel] with "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the hearth (cullikā)," and then [worship] its right and left [sides].
Having worshipped [the deity], and having provided a seat consisting of the *praṇava* (oṃ) upon the western hearth,
he should face eastward, place the cooking pot upon it, prepare it with wood free from worms and insects using the *astra-mantra*, and generate the fire with the *astra-mantra*, [invoking] Śambhu.
Observing the essence with the Netra-mantra and again with the Kavaca-mantra, while reciting "Oṃ Hāṃ,
obeisance to Śiva," one should cook the *caru* until it is properly cooked; otherwise,
if the head or the crest [of the fire] is used with the Gāyatrī, death may occur if the cooking is overdone or underdone.

And disease occurs. For the sake of pacifying that, having offered a hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra, then with the Saṃhitā-Astra ending in "svāhā," one should perform the *pātahoma* (offering of falling) into the cooking-pot situated on the hearth with clarified butter, saying "svāhā" and "pākaśivāgnaye. Then, having removed [the vessel] from the heat, [one should offer] to each its own [deity].

Having said "Become [cool]," and having placed the vessel upon a seat consecrated with the syllable *praṇava* within the circle of the ritual ground, he should perform the cooling sprinkling (*śītābhighāra*) over the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the combined mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*,
saying "Become cool" while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
With the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā], one should release the fire situated in the middle of the hearth.
Thus it is said in the *Kāmika*:
"When [the fire] is hot, there should be sprinkling with warm water; when cold, sprinkling with cold water."
In ancient times, they employed the fire in the collection of mantras ending with "svāhā."
Having said, "And indeed, [be] the oblation," and also, "Be not in me," he then [places] the heated water itself upon his second mandala.
Once it has been consecrated with sprinkling and other rites and worshipped, it should be lowered [into the fire].
Having said, "May you become very cool," one should release the fire situated in the middle of the hearth by means of the *hṛdaya-mantra* and the *saṃhāriṇī-mantra*.

Likewise, in the *Kāmika*: "In heat, there should be a pouring of hot [liquid]; in cold, a pouring of cold. Having concluded the mantra with 'svāhā', one should indeed say 'bhava' for the six-petaled [offering]."
In this manner, one should obtain the vessel named Śītā through the recitation of the mantra.

Then, having wiped the exterior of the pot with clay and water and having washed it, and having applied the *tripuṇḍra* mark, [one should perform the rite] as before upon the mandala made in the western part of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

The sixfold rising posture (ṣaḍutthāsana) is resolved. Having placed the vessel (sthālī) and worshipped it with the heart-mantra, [one recites]: "Oṃ hoṃ heṃ huṃ hiṃ hāṃ hīṃ hāṃ hīṃ haiḥ hoṃ haḥ | Śivāya svāhā. Thus, one offers the oblation (heti) into the fire; [then follows] the remainder of the sacrificial porridge (caru), the clarified butter (ājya), and the dipping-spoon (sruva).
Shaking [the vessel] in this manner, having performed one hundred and eight or twenty-one times the *saṃpāta-homa*,
according to the *Kāmika* in the section on *adhivāsana*:
"A thread made of a maiden’s [spinning], tripled and then tripled again, [consecrated with] the *astra*..."
My armor has been sprinkled with water, yet it remains blunt and unadorned.
The length should be six finger-breadths, and its auspicious width half of that;
the tube, however, should be made with a seat of four finger-breadths.
Measuring twelve finger-breadths and joined with a slight curve, these two— the *kṣurikā* and the *kartarī*— are prescribed; one should employ them in the rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Thus, endowed with these characteristics, one should prepare the previously described maṇḍala using a thread and two compasses; and for that purpose, one should gather five-colored powders, sacrificial materials, and so forth,
along with *harītakī*, strength, the ashes of *vīhitaka*, and a mixture of weapons and full vessels, according to the ritual manual.
Then, for the sake of perfecting the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the perceived particularities, one should cause the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation) to be offered.
Afterwards, having withdrawn the self— which resembles a flame of fire— by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*,
and having placed it within the lotus of one's own heart as before while reciting the root mantra with breath-retention (*kuṃbhaka*), [one should proceed].
Having established the state of oneness between himself and Śiva, O disciple, he should again take [the disciple] by means of the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā],

lead the self up to the end of Śiva through the sequence of abandoning the causal deities beginning with Brahmā by means of the *rejayoga*, and [unify them] with the *udbhavamudrā*, reciting: *oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ*.
At the end of "ātmane namaḥ," having placed [the deity] within the perfumed body in the pericarp of the heart-lotus,
and having sprinkled a drop of water on the head of the disciple, having offered the *caru* oblation,
having worshipped the two ancestors (*pitṛ*), and having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, [one should perform the rite] with the root mantra for the sake of expiation.
Having offered a hundred, a thousand, or half of that— or until completion— with clarified butter (*ājya*),
and having worshipped Śiva residing within the fire according to the ritual path, and having caused the *praṇiti* (the leading forth) to be performed for himself,
[he should apply it] to the worship of Śiva and the Guru, to the study of the Śiva Āgamas, and to the initiation into liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*).
Having declared that [the disciple] has attained fitness (*yogyatva*), the preceptor should place the Śiva-liṅga into the hand of the disciple.

He should then cause the disciple to hear the previously mentioned rules (*samaya*) according to his stage of life (*āśrama*). O best of gurus, he should grant to the disciple the Liṅga-mantra together with its mudrās.
Until that day, however, you must make a vow to perform worship three times a day,
twice a day, or even once a day.
p.
1451) One should worship especially according to the sequence of rites prescribed for worship.
[As stated] in the *Cintyaviśva*:
The best of gurus should cause the disciple to hear those [teachings] which were previously [taught];
he should not disparage the cause, and thus he should practice knowledge free from disparagement.
Endowed with devotion toward the elder— the practitioner who is advanced in knowledge— one should not step on the shadow of the preceptor or the shadow of the Liṅga when they are present.
One should not consume the remains of offerings to Śiva, nor should one feed those devoted to Śiva [only such food]. Worship of the Śiva-fire and the Guru must be performed for as long as one lives.
Absence of anger, devotion, faith, and likewise the observance of the guru’s command— these four must be practiced with constant discipline.

Thereafter, for one capable of performing the observances of the *samaya*, following initiation, one should purify the bonds (*pāśas*) equally according to one's capacity, [even] for children, women, the elderly, those enjoying worldly pleasures, and those afflicted by disease. It is as follows: *oṃ hāṃ nandaye namaḥ*.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mahākāla. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Bhūrī. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Gaṇapati. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vṛṣabha.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Devī. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Caṇḍa. Having thus worshipped in the southeast (Agni),...
One should satisfy the fire with each [mantra] ending in *svāhā* and purify the bonds (*pāśa*) of the disciple’s conduct according to the rules (*samaya*). Thus says the Āgama:
"Having worshipped the groups [of deities] beginning with Caṇḍa and ending with Caṇḍa, as well as those beginning with the river [deities] and ending with Caṇḍa, one should satisfy them in the fire."
Having offered five hundred root-mantras, one should dissolve that [visualization] at the conclusion of the full number. O Blessed One, this observance of the rules of conduct is not appropriate.
Therefore, perform the fire-oblation with this [mantra] and ask forgiveness for all of that, with the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), the Lords of the Ganas (Gaṇeśas),
and the World-Protectors (Lokapālas) as witnesses.
Having done this, the supreme preceptor should purify him according to the rules, so that he, having become a *samayin*, becomes worthy of the ritual consecrations.
He is fit for hearing and study, and likewise for honoring and offering worship;
for one thus established in steadfastness, the descent of power (śaktipāta) becomes irreversible.
Having understood this, one should then perform the supreme initiation that bestows liberation;
for he who is thus endowed with the purificatory rites of the *samaya* is fit for the worship of Śiva.
Whether at home, during study, or even while listening to the Tantras,
a human being who is worthy attains the supreme state of Rudra.

"A twice-born man shall become qualified for that initiation into Nirvāṇa. Thus ends the procedure for the special initiation in the *Dīkṣādarśa*, composed by Vedajñāna, the son of Vāmadeva, a resident of the illustrious Vyāghrapura. Now begins the *Karmanirvāṇa*.
The ritual procedure for initiation.
In the *Kāmika*: "I shall now proclaim the initiation called Nirvāṇa, which bestows supreme liberation.
Now, regarding the ripening of the impurity (*mala*) of the disciple who has been consecrated by both [initiations]:

Having recognized the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and having examined those whose intended goals are complete according to the sequence beginning with the Brahmins, one should again perform the purificatory initiation (*saṃskāradīkṣā*).

If it is to be performed at a single time, the preceptor should complete the rites from the libation (*tarpaṇa*) up to the drinking [of the consecrated substance] as before, and then perform the initiation of liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*). This is stated in the *Cintyaviśva* regarding the locus of authority;
namely:

The initiation by refinement (*saṃskāradīkṣā*) for disciples excludes the eight [impurities]; it is said that nineteen [initiations] should be performed, beginning with the one endowed with good qualities (*sadguṇa*).
One endowed with virtues should perform what is to be done by those who possess pride in being twice-born and so forth;
O son of Rudra, one who is devoid [of such] should perform the duties associated with worldly existence.
If one is devoid of these qualities, he is utterly unfit for nirvāṇa;
therefore, having again performed the initiatory rite of refinement (saṃskāra-dīkṣā), he should practice for nirvāṇa.
Now, if the ritual is to be performed separately, one should perform it preceded by the construction of a pavilion; one should prepare a separate mandala, adorned with various ornaments.

The initiation (dīkṣā) may take place within seven days, five nights, three days, or even immediately; however, the previous [preparatory rite] must be performed, as well as the offering of the sacrificial cake (kurārpaṇa) on an odd-numbered day.
In the Kāmika:
"The preceptor, having performed his daily rites, then performs the libation of mantras and so forth;
having worshipped the Sun, being pure, and having made his body possessed of all [deities] (sakalīkṛta)."
Having performed the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) and opened the door,
he should enter the temple through the western doorway.

Having performed the worship of Brahmā in the sacred field (*kṣetra*) and having provided protection according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), the mental placement (*nyāsa*), and the special offering of water (*viśeṣārghya*) as in the daily rite.

Having fashioned the sword called "knowledge" (jñāna-khaḍga) and prepared the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should then consecrate the sacrificial site with mantras and perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having scattered [the flowers], the Guru should collect them within the circle of the monastery; there, having worshipped the Kumbha and the Vardhanī on all sides, he should proceed.
Having worshipped the guardians of the world (Lokapālas) and having caused their command to be heard,
he should whirl the water from the jar-weapon and worship the sword of knowledge (Jñānakhaḍga).
One should perform all the rites beginning with the installation of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna) as prescribed for fire-rituals;
one should then pour the sacrificial oblation (caru) into that fire of the homa using that very fire.
In the Kāmika:
Having established the disciple's entry within his own portion, one performs the rite of joining the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna),
as well as the libation (tarpaṇa) together with the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having performed the kindling with the *śivādi* mantra, one should properly carry out the rite; having formed the *saṃpuṭa* of *aghora*, [the mantra] is *śivaṃ saṃ gaṃ* ending with *phaṭ*.
One should perform three oblations accompanied by the mantra that kindles [the power of] the mantras, which is joined with arched eyebrows and possesses a formidable face.
In the section on ritual action (kriyākāṇḍa)—
one should perform the illumination in this manner for every cruel rite; in rites of pacification (śāntika),
nourishment (pauṣṭika), and subjugation (vaśya), one should use the mantra ending with *vauṣaṭ* and so forth.
When the syllable *ka* is situated above [the vowel], accompanied by *vaṣaṭ* and *dhvauṣaṭ*,
one should create a world with the *śambaras* in all cases, such as in the rites of subduing and so forth.
Likewise, in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"Initiation (dīkṣā) indeed effects the severing of bonds; its function is thus fierce.
In all fierce rites, the 'kindling' (dīpana) of the mantras is performed at the beginning."
In rites for nourishment, subjugation, and pacification, one should employ mantras ending in *vauṣaṭ*,
accompanied by *vausaṭ* and *dhvauṣaṭ*, and situated above the seed-syllables.

And with mantras, the fire-oblation (homa) must be performed everywhere, including during the seasonal transitions (ayana) and other rites. In the *Kālottara*, it is stated regarding the extraction, sprinkling, and likewise the striking [of the ritual substances]: "Huṃ Phaṭ."
It should be performed in due order, joined with the ritual actions.
Likewise, it is set forth in the section on the initiation of Mataṅga, as follows:
"One should arrange [the ritual] during the withdrawal and the seizing."
Indeed, the *phaṭ* syllable is prescribed for the head; one should join it with the *kavaca*.
*Vaṣaṭ* is used for the conjunction, while *vauṣaṭ* is considered for the withdrawal.
The utterance of "svadhā" belongs to the ancestors; therefore, he should constantly worship them with offerings of food, incense, and lamps.

O great sage, the leader of mantras ending with "svāhā" must be employed by the lord of teachers; for the rites of ritual placement (nyāsa), worship, recitation, and meditation are indeed made manifest [by it].
The mantras ending with "namaskṛ" accomplish all purposes.
Then, proceeding by way of circumambulation, he went into the presence of Śiva together with the disciple.
Having worshipped Śiva and shown [the disciple] to him, one should make this request in his presence:
"This person has been tested and proven capable; he has approached for the sake of liberation (*nirvāṇa*).
He is of noble birth, devoted to the Lord, established in the observances (*samaya*), and though afflicted by suffering, he yearns for liberation."

"Existence has suffering as its purpose; therefore, let my favor be bestowed upon this [disciple] for the sake of liberation. Having been thus authorized by the Supreme Lord, he should contemplate: "So be it. Then, having purified the thread fashioned by the twice-born maiden through inspection and other rites, [he should proceed].

Having purified [the vessel] with the *saṃpātāhuti* offering, one should place it in the presence of Śiva residing in the *kumbha*; having sprinkled it with the *astra-mantra* and enveloped it with the *kavaca-mantra*, one should worship it with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*). As stated in the *Kāmika*:
A thread spun by a maiden, tripled and then folded three times, sprinkled with the Astra-mantra, protected by the Varma-mantra, and consecrated with the root mantra, remains unimpaired.
In the *Mṛgendra*: "The knot of pride, beginning with lack of affliction (*akleśa*), is described as equal by the Maiden (*Kanyā*);
one should extend [the hands] to the tips of the crests, reaching as far as the two thumbs."
When [the fire] is blazing,
one should forget that it was six finger-breadths in length and half of that in width; the tube, however, should be made of iron and four finger-breadths long.
A certain distinction is stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"Its length should be eight finger-breadths, and its width half of that;
the tube, however, should be made of iron and four finger-breadths [in length]."
Measuring two finger-breadths in width and joined at the tip of its three prongs,
the razor and the small knife are thus described; one should employ them in the rite of initiation.

In the *Mṛgendra*: "The measurement of the threads should be one *ghatikā*, and likewise the application of the powder; in the same manner, the application of the three types of rice and so forth should be performed."

Thereafter, in the southern mandala of the Śiva-fire, having prepared a seat of *praṇava* made of *darbha* grass and a sixfold raised seat (*ṣaḍutthāsana*), one should establish the disciple facing north with his body upright and hands in *añjali*. Then, [one should apply] the [mantras of] Śāntyatītā and the others to the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet.
Having deposited the seed-syllable of the *kalās* according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhāra-krama*), one should visualize the thread consisting of the *suṣumnā*,
discern the crest at the front and back, and having fixed the tip of the twelve-finger-long crest at a height of four fingers or one finger, one should grasp it with the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā].

Having bound [the thread] from the big toe to the topknot with the root mantra, one should hang it over the right side for the sake of worldly enjoyment; having bound it by the process of reabsorption (saṃhārakrama) for the sake of liberation, one should hang it over the left side.
Having worshipped the thread with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śakti," one should bind it on the left side with that same [mantra].
One should suspend [the thread]. In the case of immediate consecration (*sadyodhivāsana*),

having performed the offering of the meeting-point (*saṃpātāhuti*) for the thread, the *kartavyā* [rite], and so forth, and having consecrated it, one should present it to Śiva residing in the *kumbha*, bind it as before, and omit the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) and the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
Likewise, in the Pauṣkara:
"When the consecration has been performed by you, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) should be carried out immediately according to the previously mentioned procedure,
having overcome [all obstacles] with a tooth-stick."
In the case of sacrifices, beautifications, and so forth, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) must be performed; then, that [consecration] is applied to the body of the disciple with:
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Iḍā."
"Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Piṅgalā. Having thus worshipped and visualized a lotus within the Suṣumnā, [one should worship] with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Suṣumnā," [thus for the disciple].

Having taken [the deity] from the body, joined it with the thread, worshipped it, restrained it, and veiled it, one should offer three oblations with the root mantra for the sake of its presence, saying: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāmā;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā; Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Raudrī."

Having reflected thus with "Namaḥ," having worshipped [the deity], and having also fully honored [him] in the fire for the sake of gratification and for the sake of bringing about his presence, one should offer five oblations for each [deity] ending with "svāhā.
Then, having again restrained [the deity] within the thread and veiled [it], one should recollect the loosening of the bonds and so forth by means of those [mantras].
Then, in the region of the heart within the thread that corresponds to the entire continuum of the body thus permeated, [one should recite]:
"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lotus of the heart, endowed with the orbs of the sun, moon, and fire;
salutation to Mahākartṛ therein."

Having performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*), worshipped, and concealed [the deity], and having offered libations into the fire, one should meditate upon the manifest form of light as the "Body of Knowledge" (*vidyādeha*) with the mantra *oṃ hāṃ vidyādehāya namaḥ*, worship it,
and then sprinkle the disciple with water while reciting the weapon-mantra (*astra*) over flowers consecrated seven times.

Having entered his heart with "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ ātmane namaḥ," and having struck it with "haṃ huṃ phaṭ" while uttering the syllable "huṃ," one should imagine the Self emerging through the disciple's exhalation (*recaka*) from the bud of the disciple's heart-lotus, slightly moved. Then, of that [Self]...

Having entered that heart by means of inhalation through the left channel (vāmanāḍī), one should [visualize] that which is to be severed, having the form of a shimmering star and consisting of the seed-syllable *svam*: "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ, I seize the self;
haḥ huṃ phaṭ. Then, having separated [it] with Jyeṣṭhā: "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ."

Saying "svāhā," having drawn [the life-force] upward with the *kuśa* mudrā and led it to the *dvādaśānta*, one should contemplate the life-force (*jīva*) in the form of a drop at the tip of a blade of grass; then, having grasped it with the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā] and the self-mantra, one should establish it in one's own heart by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), and meditate upon it as being well-composed during retention (*kuṃbhaka*).
p.

1459) Recollecting the root mantra, having led oneself to the *dvādaśānta* by means of one’s own mantra through the sequence of abandoning the causes beginning with the mantra, and then, for the sake of the disciple's creation, [one proceeds] from the middle of the eyebrows and so forth.

Having expelled [the breath] through the right nostril with a single cycle, one should join it to the thread with the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ ātmane namaḥ*. Having thus addressed the Self as pervading the thread and having bound it, one should offer three oblations with the root mantra for the purpose of its presence (*sannidhāna*).
Likewise, there is beating, separation from the body, dragging, and seizing;
then union with Vāgīśī, and again birth within Māyā.
From that [state], there arise authority, enjoyment, dissolution, and expiation; then the severing of bonds, the casting down, the lifting up, and one should cook [the final purification].
Those bonds are to be severed and broken while they remain within the thread, but not in a physical struggle;
therefore, one should diligently cultivate the body as being composed of the thread.
Then again, having contemplated that the impurity (mala) in the form of Kṛṣṇa is upon the head of the disciple:

"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the worldly and other karmic bonds (*pāśas*) which are the causes of being the experiencer of pleasure and pain. Now, [one contemplates] the variegated and multiform effect of *māyā*.
Having meditated thus: "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the noose of Māyā, the cause of the body, the senses, and the objects";

and "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śiva-śakti, the presiding deity of the noose"—and having then visualized the form according to these distinct limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), [the teacher] takes [it] from the body of the disciple.

Having joined the thread, having worshipped it, and having restrained it, one should worship the *vakuṇṭha* and the fire; then, for the sake of [their] presence, one should offer three oblations for each with the word "svāhā" at the end.
Here, how is it that Śiva and Śakti become of the nature of bonds? Truly, [it is so].
It is stated figuratively that [the soul] is bound by attachment through the relationship of the purified (*śodhya*) and the purifier (*śodhaka*).
Likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*: (p. 1460) [text follows]
Among them, the power of Maheśvara is Śivā, who bestows grace upon all;
by virtue of following the path of dharma, she is metaphorically designated as "bond" (pāśa).
Then, having placed [the mantra] upon the thread for the Vidyā-deha with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Vidyā-deha," and having offered three oblations of clarified butter with "To the Vidyā-deha,
svāhā" for the purpose of its presence, one should pervade the mantras of the Śāntātīta-kalā and so forth, as well as the words, syllables, and so on.
Having understood the state of pervasion, one should unite consciousness with that which abides in the thread (*sūtra*).
Thus it is said in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"One should know [the self] as both the pervaded and the pervader when the time for initiation has arrived."
The path of words consists of mantras contained within the *pata*s, situated in the midst of the phonemes.
The phonemes contained within the worlds, the expanded principles (tattvas), and the medicinal herbs; the principles situated within the digits (kalās) are established in their proper sequence.
Those which pervade while manifesting differentiation therein are called *kalās*. These five divisions of the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*) are established as distinct.
In the Kāmika:
"The wise one should establish the relationship of pervader and pervaded therein; [this includes] mantras, words, phonemes, principles (tattvas), and worlds."
The objects of pervasion (vyāpya) are the impurity of action (karmamala), the substrate (ādheya), and the bond (bandhana);
furthermore, the impurity of the objects (vyāpyamala) and so forth are also [pervaded], while Kalā is remembered as the pervader (vyāpaka).
Therefore, by the inclusion of those [mantras], all [deities] are here accepted;
though they were previously established by means of the Viśvaśuddhā [mantras], they become pure even when established here [by these].
Therefore, it is maintained that purification occurs for everyone.
The purpose of this [work] has been stated by Svāyambhuva:
"Now, for the sake of removing the state of being a bound soul within the continuum of the self, and for the manifestation of Śiva-nature,
the sixfold [reality] is proclaimed above."
The path of reality (tattvādhvan), the path of words (padādhvan), the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) consisting of worlds, the path of mantras (mantrādhvan),
and the path of kalās (kalādhvan)— these constitute the twenty-one states of Śiva.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:

"The path of principles (*tattvādhvan*), the path of words (*padādhvan*), the path of phonemes (*varṇādhvan*)—which is indeed the phoneme itself—the path of worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), and the path of energies (*kalādhvan*): one should deposit these six paths in their proper sequence."
Having placed the seed-syllable *tāram* at the beginning of the [mantras] ending in the dative case and followed by *namaḥ*,
and having projected the paths of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) upon the thread, one becomes endowed with the state of Śiva.
Likewise, in the *Kālottara*: "One should worship the path of words (padādhvan) in Tatpuruṣa, joined with its respective Brahma-mantras;
one should worship the word beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with the salutation (*namaḥ*) in the middle."

In this sūtra, it is called "puruṣa" because it is to be bound by means of the cultivation of the puruṣa. Here, in the order of emanation (sṛṣṭikrama), the binding should be performed at the location of the sūtra. One should contemplate: *oṃ hāṃ śāntyatītakalāyai namaḥ*. [Then] *oṃ hāṃ śivatattvāya*.
Salutation! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Śakti-tattva. Thus are two tattvas. Oṃ hrāṃ, salutation to Anāśritā; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Anātha; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Anantā.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to her whose form is space (vyomarūpā). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Pervasive One (vyāpinī). These are the five cavities of the power-aspect (śaktikalā). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the one who moves upward (ūrdhvagāminī). Oṃ...

Hāṃ, salutation to Mocikā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rocikā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Dīpikā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Iddhikā. Thus are the worlds of the Nādakalā within the Śiva-tattva; [there are] five. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śāntyātītā.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Śānti. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vidyā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Pratiṣṭhā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nivṛtti. Thus are the worlds of the *bindu-kalā* within the principle of Śakti. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the letter A. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the letter I.
Salutation! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the letter Ī; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the letter U; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the letter Ū; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the letter Ṛ; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the letter Ṝ;
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the letter Ḷ; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the letter Ḹ.

Salutation to the letter *kā*. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the letter *e*. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the letter *ai*. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the letter *o*. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the letter *au*. Oṃ hrāṃ, salutation to the letter *aṃ*. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the letter *aḥ*. Thus.

There are sixteen syllables. *Oṃ hāṃ oṃ namaḥ*—this is the first word. *Oṃ hāṃ śivāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ hāṃ īśānāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ haḥ astrāya namaḥ*—these are the mantras beginning with the weapon (*astra*). *Oṃ hāṃ nādāya namaḥ*, *Oṃ hāṃ*...
Homage to the letter *ha*. Thus are the two seed-syllables. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Śākhinī. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Āhyā.

Thus, two channels: *oṃ hāṃ sañjayāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ devadattāya namaḥ*. Two organs of action: *oṃ hāṃ śrotrāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ vācāya namaḥ*. Thus, two sense organs: *oṃ hāṃ śabdaviṣayāya namaḥ*; *oṃ*... [text ends]

Hāṃ, obeisance to the quality of sound (*dhvaniguṇa*). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the one whose nature is white (*sitāsvarūpa*). Obeisance to the mandala of space (*vyomamaṇḍala*) marked by the vajra. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the state beyond the fourth (*turyātītāvasthā*). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sadāśiva, the Lord of Causes (*kāraṇeśvara*).
Having meditated upon the Śāntyatīta-kalā conjoined with these [syllables], one strikes the disciple’s head with a flower while reciting: *oṃ hāṃ śāntyatītakalāyai haḥ huṃ phaṭ*.
Then, having grasped it by means of the *pūraka* breath-retention in the mode of withdrawal (*saṃhāriṇī*), one recites: *oṃ hāṃ*.

"Oṃ, obeisance to the Śāntyatīta Kalā. Having thus joined the thread from the topknot to the forehead, worshipped it, restrained it, and enveloped it, one should offer three oblations for the purpose of its presence with the mantra: "Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the Śāntyatīta Kalā. Thereafter—

In the Śāntikalā: Oṃ aiṃ, obeisance to Śāntikalā; Oṃ, obeisance to the principle (tattva) of Sadāśiva; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Īśvara; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Śuddhavidyā. These three principles [are to be worshipped] in them respectively.
The worlds (*bhuvanāni*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the world of the *Sadāśiva-tattva*. Thus is one world. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sikhandin. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Trimūrti.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ekarudra. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ekanetra. Oṃ...
Hāṃ, obeisance to Śivotthāya. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sūkṣma. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ananta. Thus are the eight worlds within the principle of Īśvara (Īśvaratattva). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Manonmanī.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Sarvabhūtadamanī. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Balavikariṇī. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Balapramathanī. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Kalavikaraṇī.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kālī. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Raudrī. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāmā. Or, [one may worship] the worlds by means of the principle of Śuddhavidyā: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the letter Ka. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the letter Kha.

Salutation! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gakāra. These are the three syllables. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vyāpinī; salutation to her whose form is space (Vyomarūpā). Soṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sarvavyāpin. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śiva. Oṃ Anuya... salutation. Oṃ hāṃ.

Salutation to Anāthā. Salutation to Anāśritā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Dhūpa. Salutation to Śāśvata. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to him who is established upon the Yoga-pīṭha. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Eternal Yogi. Oṃ, salutation to Dhyānahāra. Thus.

There are twelve words: *oṃ hoṃ tatpuruṣāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ kavacāya namaḥ*. There are two mantras: *oṃ hāṃ bindave namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ dhakārāya namaḥ*. There are two seed-syllables (*bīja*). *oṃ hāṃ alaṃbuṣāyai namaḥ*. There are two channels (*nāḍī*).

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kṛkara. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kūrma. These are the two winds (vāyu). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of skin (tvak-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of the hand (pāṇi-tattva). These are the two Indras. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the object of touch (sparśa-viṣaya). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to sound (śabda).
Salutation. Two qualities. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Turyā. State. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the hexagon whose nature is Kṛṣṇa.

*Oṃ, salutation to the maṇḍala endowed with the six dots and the kalās.* *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śabdā.* Having meditated upon the *śāntikalā* together with these [deities] and the Lord of Causes (*kāraṇeśa*), [one should recite]: *Oṃ hyai,
to the noose of the śāntikalā, huṃ phaṭ*, from the forehead to the region of the throat.

Having struck [the breath] with the *pūraka* function and having gathered it with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*, one should join it to the "mouth-thread" (*mukhasūtra*), worship it, and offer three oblations for the presence (*sannidhāna*) ending with *vaṣaṭ* and *svāhā*. Thereafter, in the *vidyā-kalā*: *oṃ hrūṃ vidyākalāyai namaḥ*.
Thus one should contemplate: *Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Māyā; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kālā;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Niyati; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kālā; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vidyā; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rāga; obeisance to Puruṣa.* Thus.

There are seven principles (*tattvas*) in the *vidyā-kalā*. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Tvaṣṭamatrā. Obeisance to Īśāna. Obeisance to this one with tawny eyes (*piṅgalekṣaṇa*). Obeisance to Udbhāvā. Obeisance to Vidyā. Obeisance to Bhavā. Obeisance to Vāma. Oṃ hāṃ.

Salutation to Mahātejā. Thus, there are eight worlds (*bhuvana*) within Māyā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śikhedā; salutation to Ekavīra. Thus, there are two worlds within the principle of Time (*kāla-tattva*). Salutation to Pañcāntaka; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to * * yāntaka. Thus [there are two] within Niyati.

In the *tattva* [of Māyā], there are two worlds: *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Saṃvartaka; *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Jyotiṣikā. Thus, in the *tattva* ending with Kalā, there are two worlds. *Oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to Piṇḍa; salutation to Krodha. Thus, in the *tattva* of Vidyā, there are two worlds.
Salutation to Ekaśikha. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ananta. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Aja. Salutation to Umāpati. Salutation to Pracaṇḍa.
Thus, there are five worlds belonging to the principle of Rāga: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vīra; obeisance to Īśāna; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhava; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ugra;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhīma; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Cāra. Thus, there are six worlds of the Puruṣa-tattva. In this way, there are seven [groups of] worlds with names identical to those of the Rudras. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ya;
oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Da; oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Ca.

Salutation to the letter Cha. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the letter Ja. Salutation to the letter A. Thus are the seven letters. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śiva. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Source of All. Salutation to Śiva. Oṃ hāṃ, to the Head of Īśāna.
Salutation! Salutation to the face of Tatpuruṣa. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Aghora, the heart.
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vāmadeva, the secret part. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sadyojāta, the form. Oṃ, salutation to Namaḥ. Oṃ hāṃ, Oṃntamaḥ. Oṃ hāṃ.

Homage to the Lord of all Vidyās! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the one whose form is light! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the secret of the secret! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the protector! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the one who is deathless! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the one appointed over all yogas! Oṃ hāṃ...

Salutation to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the conscious and unconscious (*cetanācetanāya*); oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the sky of skies (*vyominvyominnamaḥ*). These are the twenty-one words. Oṃ huṃ, salutation to Aghora; oṃ hi, salutation to the Crest (*śikhāyai*). These are the two mantras. Oṃ hāṃ.
Oṃ hāṃ ram namaḥ. Oṃ hāṃ ram namaḥ. These are the two seed-syllables. Oṃ hāṃ puruṣāya namaḥ.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Hastijihvā. Thus, two channels (nāḍīs). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Antagā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vyāna. Thus, two [vital breaths]. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of sight (cakṣus-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of the feet (pāda-tattva). Thus, two sense organs (indriyas).

Two: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the object of form (rūpaviṣaya). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the qualities of sound and form (śabda-rūpa-guṇa). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the fire-maṇḍala (vahnimaṇḍala), whose nature is red, whose essence is burning, and which is marked by the svastika and the lācchinā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the state of deep sleep (suṣupti-avasthā). Oṃ...
"Hāṃ, obeisance to Rudrākāraṇeśvara. Having meditated upon the Vidyā-kalā together with these [mantras],

one should strike from the throat to the navel with a flower while reciting "Oṃ hrūṃ vidyākalāyai haḥ huṃ phaṭ," and then withdraw [the energy] by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā* through the practice of inhalation (*pūraka*).
Reciting "Oṃ hrūṃ, obeisance to the Vidyā-kalā," one should join [the mantra] to the thread, worship it, restrain it, and envelop it;
then, ending with "svāhā," one should offer the oblation for presence (*saṃnidhāna-huti*). Thereafter, reciting "Oṃ hlīṃ, obeisance to the Pratiṣṭhā-kalā," one should gaze [upon it]. Oṃ hāṃ...

Salutation to Prakṛti. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Guṇa. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Buddhi. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Haṃkāra. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ahaṃkāra. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śrotra. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Tvak-tattva. Oṃ hāṃ...
Oṃ, homage to the principle of the eye. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the tongue.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the nose. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of speech. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the hand.

p. 1468) Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the feet (pādatattva). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of wind (vāyutattva). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the generative organ (upasthatattva). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of sound (śabdatattva). Oṃ...
Hāṃ, obeisance to touch. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to form. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to taste. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to smell. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to space.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of speech. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of fire. Oṃ hāṃ...

Salutation to Aptatva. Thus are the twenty-four principles (tattvas). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Auma; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kaumāra; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vaiṣṇava; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā.
Salutation! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Bhairava; oṃ krū, salutation [to him].
Thus is the group of eight [deities] of the womb (yony-aṣṭaka). In Prakṛti and Gaṇa: oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Brahmā;
oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vrajeśa; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Saumya; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Indra.

Salutation! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Gandharva; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kṣaya; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rākṣasa; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Paiśāca. Thus ends the group of eight divine origins (*devayony-aṣṭaka*). In the *prakṛti*, within the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*): oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sthaleśvara.
Salutation! Salutation to Ahaṃkāreśvara. Salutation to Sthūleśvara. [Salutation] to the mind and the five organs of perception. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śaṅkukarṇa.
[Salutation] to the five organs of action. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kālāñjana. Oṃ hāṃ...
Salutation to Kuṇḍaleśvara. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mākoṭa. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Dviraṇḍaka. Thus [are the deities] in the pentad of subtle elements (tanmātra). The five worlds (p. 1469).

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sthāṇu. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Svarṇākṣa. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhadrakarṇa. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gokarṇa. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Mahālaya. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Avimukta. Obeisance to Mahendra.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Aṭṭahāsa. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vima-leśvara. Oṃ, obeisance to Khala. Obeisance to Kurukṣetra. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Gayā. Thus is the group of eight in the element of air (vāyutatva). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhairava. Oṃ hāṃ...

Salutation to Ketāra. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Mahākāla. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Madhyameśvara. Salutation to Śrīśaila. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Hariścandra. Thus [ends] the eightfold [salutation] in the principle of fire (tejas-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ...
Salutation to Lakuleśvara. Salutation to Bhārabhūtika. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ḍiṇḍinī. Salutation to Muṇḍa. Salutation to Āṣāḍha. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Puṣkara. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Naimiśa. Oṃ.
Salutation to Prabhāsa. Salutation to Amareśa. Thus is the group of eight in the seventh [category].
In this way, by seven groups of eight, each consisting of eight, it should be understood that the fifty Rudras are to be honored equally with the forests. Om Hāṃ, salutation to Ṭakāra. Om...

Hāṃ, obeisance to the letter Ḍha. Obeisance to the letter Ḍhu. Obeisance to the letter Ḍha. Obeisance to the letter Ṇa. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the letter Va. Obeisance to the letter Tha. Obeisance to the letter Da. Obeisance to the letter Dha. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the letter Na.
p. 1470) Homage to the letter *pa*. Oṃ, homage to the letter *pha*. Homage to the letter *ba*.
Homage to the letter *bha*. Homage to the letter *ma*. Homage to the letter *ma*. Homage to the letter *ya*.

Homage to the letter *ra*; homage to the letter *la*; homage to the letter *va*; homage to the letter *śa*; homage to the letter *ṣa*; homage to the letter *sa*; homage to the letter *ha*. Thus, these are the twenty-three phonemes. *Oṃ hāṃ*, homage to the Pervasive One (*vyāpin*).
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the formless one who possesses form! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the first of the first!
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the splendorous one of splendor! Homage to the light of lights! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the formless! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the non-fire! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the smokeless!
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Ashless (Abhasma). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Beginningless (Anādi). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the one named "Various" (Nānānāman). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Dhū Dhū Dhū Dhū.
Oṃ Bhūnamas. Oṃ Bhuvannamas. Oṃ Suvannamas. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Undying (Anidhana).

Salutation! Oṃ, salutation to Nidhanodbhava. Oṃ, salutation to Śiva. Oṃ, salutation to Śarva. Oṃ, salutation to Paramātman. Salutation to Maheśvara. Salutation to Mahādeva. Oṃ, salutation to Sadbhāveśvara. Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Tejas.

Namaḥ | Oṃ, homage to the Lord of Yoga (yogādhipati). Oṃ, homage to the One who Releases (muñcamuñca). Prathama, prathama, homage to the First (prathama). Oṃ, homage to Śarva-Śarva. These are the twenty-eight words. Oṃ hiṃ, homage to Vāmadeva. Oṃ hīṃ.

"Śirase namaḥ"—thus there are two mantras. "Oṃ hāṃ ukārāya namaḥ," "Oṃ hāṃ vakārāya namaḥ"—these are the two seed-syllables (bījas). "Oṃ hāṃ gandhāyai namaḥ," "Suṣumnāyai namaḥ"—these are the two channels (nāḍīs). "Oṃ hāṃ udānāya namaḥ," "Oṃ... [The text continues].
"Hāṃ, salutation to Samāna.
1471) Thus, there are two [mantras] for Vāyu. "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Rasa; salutation to Vāyu. Thus, [there is one] for the sense organ.

The Sākhya is not the object. Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the one whose qualities are sound, touch, and form. Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the maṇḍala marked by a white half-moon and a lotus. Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to the state of dreaming. Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the Lord of Causes.

Endowed with these [qualities], having observed the portion of the *pratiṣṭhā* [kalā], one should strike the disciple with a flower from below the navel to the end of the knees, saying: *oṃ hiṃ pratiṣṭhākalāyai haḥ huṃ phaṭ*. Then, having grasped [the essence] by means of the *pūraka* [breath] and the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā], one recites: *oṃ hlīṃ pratiṣṭhā*.

"Oṃ *kalāyai* namaḥ. Having joined this to the thread, having worshipped and enveloped it (*avakuṇṭhya*), one should offer three oblations for the purpose of bringing [the deity] into proximity (*saṃnidhāna*). Thereafter: "Oṃ *hāṃ* *nivṛttikalāyai* namaḥ"—with this, one should untie [the knot]. "Oṃ *hāṃ* to the *pṛthivī-tattva*, namaḥ"—one [oblation]. Oṃ...

Hāṃ, obeisance to Bhadrakālī. Thus, above the Brahmāṇḍa, there are two worlds: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Trilocana; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Lipsā; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nabha; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vivāha; obeisance to Svāhā; Oṃ.
Hāṃ, obeisance to the Lord of the Thirty-three; obeisance to the Three-eyed One; obeisance to the Chief of the Gaṇas;
Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Vibhu; Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Śambhu—thus for the ten directions above. Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Daṃṣṭra; Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to Indra.
Salutation! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lord of Serpents (phaṇīndra). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Audumbara. Salutation to Īśāna. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Grasana.
Salutation to Mārutāśana. Salutation to Krodha. Salutation to Ananta.
Salutation to Viṣadharāya—thus ten [below]. Oṃ, salutation to Balipriyāya; salutation to Bhūtapālāya; Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Jyeṣṭhāya.
Salutation to Śarva. Salutation to Sureśa. Salutation to Vedapāraga.
Salutation to Jñānabhugeśa. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sarvajña. Salutation to Prasāda. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Īśāna. Salutation to Vidyādhipa.
Thus, in the Īśāna [direction], there are ten: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Prakāmadāya; obeisance to Prasādāya; obeisance to Śrīdharāya; obeisance to Raktadharāya; obeisance to Lakṣmīdharāya;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jaṭādharāya; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Samyadehāya; Oṃ...

Hāṃ, salutation to Dhānya; salutation to Rūpa; salutation to Nidhīśa—thus ten [names] in the north. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Medhavāhana; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kapardin; salutation to Pañcaśikha; oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Pañcāntaka; oṃ...
Hāṃ, obeisance to Kṣayāntaka. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Tīkṣṇasūkṣma.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vāyuvega. Obeisance to Laghuśrīghra. These are the ten [gods] of Wind. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sunāda. Obeisance to Meghanāda. Oṃ...
Hāṃ, homage to Jalāntaka! Homage to Dīrghabāhu! Oṃ Hāṃ, homage to Jayabhadra! Oṃ Hāṃ, homage to Śveta! Homage to Mahābala! Homage to Pāśahasta! Oṃ Hāṃ, homage to Atibala! Homage to Bala!
Thus, there are ten [mantras] for Vāruṇa: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Daṃṣṭra; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Lohita; obeisance to Dhūmra; obeisance to Virūpākṣa;
obeisance to Ūrdhvaśeṣa; obeisance to Bhayānaka; obeisance to Krūradaṃṣṭra.
Namaḥ! Oṃ hantre namaḥ! Oṃ hāṃ māraṇāya namaḥ! Oṃ hāṃ nirṛtaye namaḥ! Thus, ten [offerings] in the southwest (nairṛta). Oṃ hāṃ dharmapataye namaḥ!
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Dharma. Homage to Viyoktr. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Saṃyoktr. Homage to Kartṛ. Homage to Vidhātṛ. Homage to Dhātṛ. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Hāra. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Mṛtyu. Homage to Yāmya. Thus.
In the south, ten [offerings]: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kṣayāntaka; obeisance to Bhasmāntaka;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Babhru; obeisance to Dāhana; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Jvalana; obeisance to Hara; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Khādaka; [obeisance] to Piṅgala.
Salutation! Salutation to Hutāśana (the Fire-eater)! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Agnirudra! Thus are the ten [offerings] to Agni.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Lord of the Thirty-three (Tridaśādhipa)! Salutation to the Wielder of the Pināka bow (Pinākin)! Salutation to the Teacher (Śāstṛ)! Salutation to the Imperishable (Avyaya)! Salutation to Vibhūti!

Homage to Pramardana! Homage to Vajradeha! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Buddha! Homage to Aja! Homage to Kapālīśvara! These are the ten in the east. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Rudra! Homage to Viṣṇu! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Brahmā!

Salutation to Hāṭakeśvara. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kūṣmāṇḍa. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kālāgni. Thus is the group of ten. In the very center of the Brahmāṇḍa is the forest of Maṣṭā, containing a hundred [deities] whose names are identical to those of the Rudras. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the letter Kṣa.
Thus is the color. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Bhavabhava. Obeisance to Bhavodbhava.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Sarvabhūtasaṃprada. Obeisance to Sarvasānnidhyakara. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmaviṣṇurudrapara. Oṃ hāṃ.

Salutation to the one who is unhonored yet honored; salutation to the one who is unstudied yet studied. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the one who was previously situated, to the previously situated; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the witness, to the witness.

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Kururu! Salutation to Pataṅga, the bird! Salutation to Piṅga, the tawny one! Salutation to Jñāna, the knowledge! Salutation to Śabda, the sound! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sūkṣma, the subtle one! Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śiva! Oṃ hāṃ...

Salutation to Śarva. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śiva. Oṃ namo namaḥ. These are the twenty-eight words. Oṃ, salutation to Sadyojāta. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Heart. These are the two mantras. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the seed-syllable A.
*Oṃ* to the seed-syllable *la*, *namaḥ*. Thus, two at the *cau*. *Oṃ hāṃ* to Piṅgalā, *namaḥ*.
*Oṃ hāṃ* to Iḍā, *namaḥ*. Thus, two for the *nāḍīs*. *Oṃ hāṃ* to Apāna, *namaḥ*.
*Oṃ hāṃ* to Prāṇa, *namaḥ*. [These are] in the wind. *Oṃ hāṃ* to the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*), *namaḥ*.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the organ of procreation. There are two [senses] in the sense-faculties: homage to the object, odor.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to sound. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to touch. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to form. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to taste. Homage to odor.
The yellow, square water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) is the waking state.

*Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the Lord of the Cause.* Having meditated upon the *nivṛtti-kalā* pervaded by these [mantras], one should perform the pacification below with: *Oṃ hāṃ, to the *nivṛtti-kalā*, haṃ huṃ phaṭ*.

Having struck with a flower, gathered [the deity] with the *saṃhāra-mudrā* and the *pūraka* breath, one should join it to the thread with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Nivṛtti-kalā. Having thus joined it, worshipped it, and performed the *avaguṇṭhana* (veiling),
one should offer three oblations for the purpose of bringing it into proximity (*saṃnidhāna*), and [place it] on the left and right sides, which are the abodes of the Moon and the Sun.

The abandonment of the flow [of the breath] consists of the Suṣumṇā-nāḍī, which is of the nature of bonds and serves as the locus of the presence of the Self, extending from the seat of Bhūta to the end.

Having recollected the thread consisting of all the ritual acts (sūtramayī), one should not [perform them] upon the body; therefore, in that very [thread], one should perform the inspection, striking, grasping, seizing, and joining of the constituent parts (kalās).
In the case of initiation with seed (sabījā-dīkṣā), it is desired that the properties of the body's commencement and so forth [be applied].

Having internally recollected other binding karma-fragments— such as *pūrta* and other works, along with their consequences, the bonds of conventional conduct (*utsamayācāra*), and so forth— one should contemplate them as contained within the thread (*sūtra*).
In the case of initiation without seed (*nirbīja-dīkṣā*), one should likewise contemplate the dharmas that initiate the body and their consequences.
One should meditate upon that which is contained in all the sūtras together with the conduct of the observances (samayācāra). Thus it has also been stated by the venerable Somaśambhu:
"In initiation involving seeds (bīja-dīkṣā), [one is freed] from the bonds of the conduct of observances; [it is] the initiator of the body..."
And from the Dharma, as well as from the fruit of mantra-accomplishment.

One should contemplate that which is distinct from the merit of sacrifices, charitable works, and so forth— a continuous bond that obstructs consciousness, existing within the midst of the subtle kalās.
In the *Samānatantra*:
"The first [noose], which is to be cut, resides in the thread and not in the physical form.
Thus, one who desires liberation should contemplate the state of the pervaded and the pervader as residing in the thread."
For the purpose of igniting the *kalās* (energetic constituents) through the pacification (*śānti*) and other rites of initiation (*dīkṣā*), one should offer an oblation for each.
Likewise, their ignition should be performed with mantras beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *phaṭ*: *oṃ hrūṃ*.
Reciting "haṃ haṃ śāntyatītakalāyai huṃ phaṭ," one should mark that thread at the locations of the kalās with either saffron or gorocana;
having worshipped Śiva along with his limbs (aṅgas) therein, [one recites] "oṃ hāṃ astrāya huṃ phaṭ."

Having struck the disciple’s head with the *nārāca* mudrā while holding a flower on the thread, and having entered [the mandala] with the mantra "oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*"), one should take hold [of him] with that same mantra.

Having offered three oblations ending with *svāhā*, one should tie a knot in the thread while reciting: *oṃ hauṃ hauṃ hauṃ bhagavan śāntyatīta-kalā-pāśa-mala-karmamaya-śākta-tattva-bhuvanādi-vyāpakam baddhabaddha huṃ phaṭ*. Thus [it is done].
One should form a knot at each of the locations beginning with Śāntikalā and Kalādi.
Thus it is stated in the Kāmika:
"O Lord, that which is called Śāntyatītā is pervading, associated with impurity (mala) and karma, and of the nature of Śakti."
The two words "pāśabaddha" (bound by fetters) [follow] after "tattva" and so forth.
Having uttered [the mantra] ending with *huṃ phaṭ*, one should tie a knot in the thread; [one should also recite] one's own respective seed-syllable enclosed by *śivaṃ* and the word *bhagavan*.

Having uttered the four digits (kalā), the fetter (pāśa), and the pervasive principles of impurity (mala-tattva) and so forth, together with the word "bound, bound" (baddha baddha), it is endowed with the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ* at the end.
Having recited [the mantras] individually, one should tie a knot in the thread. As stated in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"Then, having instructed him regarding that thread, one should cause the disciple to enter it. [Regarding] "vismṛtādya" (forgotten, etc.):
And for the destruction of dense [obstacles], one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra.

One should strike the person with a hundred [strokes] and carry them away from all sides; immediately thereafter, one should place [the victim] within the heart-mantra and the weapon-mantra joined in a *saṃpuṭa* (enclosure).
In the *Mṛgendra*:
"Then, having informed Śambhu of the snares that have been cast," (p.
Saying "Protect [her]," the learned husband should place her near the water-pot.
Having released the darbha grass and risen, the disciple should worship Śiva with prostrations and circumambulations before the preceptor, who is seated upon the jar that is the abode of fire.
In the *Kāmika*:
"The preceptor, together with the disciple, should give the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and the tooth-cleaning stick (*dantadhāvana*) to those who have come to the sacrificial pavilion."
To those who are purified and have washed their hands and feet, one should offer the specific internal recitations (antarjapa) in due order,
while holding kuśa grass in the right hand.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"Having taken the arghya water consecrated with the *praṇava*, the preceptor should go outside the sacrificial hall and then construct three pavilions in sequence."

Having sequentially caused the naiṣṭhikas, the bhautikas, those with gentle faces, and those with faces like Indra to enter [the state], listen to the procedure for having the disciples consume [the offering] as it is to be performed.

O Lord of the Vidyādharas, one should first take the five products of the cow with the hand along with kuśa grass; and at every interval, O Lord, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
The second *caruka* is said to consist of three morsels,
or even eight morsels in measure, and it is devoid of sight and touch.
For the purpose of liberation, one should use leaves of the *pālāśa* tree; for the purpose of enjoyment, one should use leaves of the *pippala*.
A specific distinction regarding the material has been stated.
In each case, there should be five morsels (*piṇḍas*), measured according to the size of a mouthful.
And having consecrated the rice-balls with the Brahmāṅga mantras, one should do so once for each.
Having sipped water according to the rules for *ācamana*, and having eaten without touching with the teeth,
one should feed [the guest] accompanied by the five mantras beginning with *prāṇa* and *apāna*.
In the Kāmika [Tantra]:
"First, one should present the fivefold food offering (*naivedya*)... The practitioners who await the [final] time should perform the Prāṇāgnihotra."
If these [elements] exist otherwise, everything becomes otherwise; it is not otherwise.
In the *Cintyaviśva*, it is said:
"Thereafter, one should perform the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) again with pure water; thus is the knower of purity."
And the tooth-stick should be endowed with auspicious marks.
One should chew a tooth-stick that is as thick as the knuckle of the little finger, straight, of good quality, free from defects,
auspicious in appearance, and eight finger-breadths in length.
Having given the tooth-stick for cleaning the teeth with the *hṛdaya* mantra,
one should afterwards rinse it with water and throw it away after washing it, with the face turned upwards.
One who possesses the discernment between the desirable and the undesirable should know that regarding those fallen and others situated in the directions of Hari (East),
Indra (South), Varuṇa (West), and Īśāna (North), there arises the attainment of desired fruits.

Thereafter, one should offer a hundred oblations with the *asinā* mantra to ensure that no obstacles arise; then, for the pacification of the three wombs (*triyoni*), one should offer three hundred oblations.
With the *śiva-mantra*, which possesses six limbs and destroys obstacles,
the propitiation of the principal mantras is considered complete at the conclusion of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

In this context, as an incidental discussion, the Bhīmasaṃhitā sets forth that if a teacher, through negligence or for some other reason, fails to rise from his seat and so forth, or if he utters something improper, an oblation (homa) must be performed.
Namely: when rising from one's seat, when angry, when sneezing, when spitting, in the movement of wind,
when fear has arisen, during the impressioning (vāsana), and for one who has been initiated by pervasion (vyāpidīkṣita).
When a clod of earth or heated water has been cast out, and when the performance of the ritual action and the recollection of the mantra have occurred,
one should perform an oblation with the *vyāhṛtis* upon the utterance of the mantra during the mantra-rite.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:

Having purified the ground with the root mantra, one should offer the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) into the fire; then, having worshipped the guardians of the world (*lokapāla*) and the water-pots (*kalaśa*), and having performed the ritual confinement (*niruddhya*).
He who desires external protection should dispatch the Gaṇapālakas; he should offer the bali-oblation to the Lokapālas both concisely and in due order.
Having bathed either in the Āgneya or Vāruṇa [tīrtha], one should enter the sacrificial hall; as stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"Having recited the ten-syllable mantra together with the limbs of the Vidyā and the Brahma-mantras..."
Then, having recited the primary seed-syllable, one should especially do so with the razor.
Then, having returned and separated the roles of disciple and preceptor,
and having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should sleep at night by the side of Śiva.

O Lord, this continuity of non-sacrificial acts must be brought to an end by you; for the destruction of the fetters of bound souls, the oblation must be offered here, for there is no other presence [of authority] than yours.
On the southern side of the deity, having smeared the ground with cow dung,
one should cause the disciples to dwell in the mantras on the southern side of the pavilion.
Covered with cow-dung ashes and a cloth, the Guru should place the child, with its head toward the east or south, with a view toward both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Likewise, in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"The lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika*) who sleep on ashes should have their heads toward the south;
those who follow the householder stage (*bhautika*) should be placed on a bed of *darbha* grass, previously protected by the *mālya* and *astra* mantras."
Having again bound the topknots of all those who had been protected by tying their tufts,
the Guru should then impart the mantra of the Lord of Dreams.
