Thereafter, with a knife consecrated seven times with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should sever the bond of the *śāntyatīta* level by means of the mantra "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ śāntyatītakalāpāśāya haḥ huṃ phaṭ," pronouncing it with its vowels. Then, for the sake of removing the bondage:

Having rubbed [the object] with both hands using the Astra-mantra and having rolled it into a ball, one should place it in a ladle (sruvī) filled with ghee and offer it into the fire along with the clarified butter using that same mantra;
one should burn it, reducing it to ashes with three oblations of the Astra-mantra alone. The Blessed One [says]: "Not for oneself..."

Having requested, "Perform, perform, perform the severing of the bonds of the kalās that have passed beyond peace," and having offered five oblations with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* for the cessation of the sprouts of the bonds,
one should offer eight oblations with the weapon-mantra for the sake of atonement, [and then] for the destruction of the entire body...
One should cause the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) to be performed.

When the capacity for the conduct of the observance (samayācāra) exists, one should deposit the bond (pāśa), which consists of the nature of the observance; while reciting the mantra, one should [deposit] the observance, the conduct of the observance, and the hosts presiding over the bonds.
The wise preceptor should worship the fourth [syllable] preceded by the Praṇava and ending with "Namaḥ"; he should offer three oblations for the purpose of invoking the presence [of the deity].

O Maheśvara, having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the *śi* mantra, [perform] the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), the observance (*samaya*), the conduct of the observance (*samayācāra*), and the purification of the bonds (*pāśaśuddhi*).
p.
1519) By saying to the disciple, "Do it, do it," one should offer [the initiation] free of fee; repeatedly reciting the seed-syllable of Śiva, "Sadāśiva."

One should perform three oblations with the mantra: *mano gṛhāṇāsvāhā*. Having thus paid the bride-price (*śulka*), one should make this request: "This supreme Śivakara has transcended the origin of worldly existence; having now accomplished his purpose, he seeks the soul (*āṇu*)."

One should cause [the soul] to cease out of compassion. Thus, having visualized the self as the extremely pure and fierce Śuddhatatva, one should afterwards offer three oblations with the root mantra for the sake of its extraction, saying: "O Blessed One, of this self..."
Having brought the *brahmahṛdaya* [mantra] with the *recaka* breath and the *udbhavamudrā*, one should join it to the body of the disciple's thread, worship it,

and perform the rites of nourishment (*āpyāyana*) and leading (*ānayana*). Then, having sprinkled drops of *arghya* water upon the head of the disciple with the root mantra (*mūla*), one should offer three oblations (*āhuti*) with the root mantra for the sake of stabilization (*sthirīkaraṇa*).

Thereafter, having worshipped the parents and offered three oblations, Yama said, "O parents, you have been distressed for the sake of the disciple's initiation; out of compassion, please forgive that of mine. Having thus informed them and dismissed them with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, he established me in his own place.
One should offer full oblations.
Thus concludes the purification of the Kalās beyond Peace (Śāntyatīta). Now follows the procedure for the cutting of the topknot (śikhācchedavidhi).
Initiation for liberation (nirvāṇadīkṣā) is of two kinds: that which follows the way of Śiva (śivadharmiṇī) and that which follows the worldly way (lokadharmiṇī).
This initiation for liberation is twofold: the worldly is to be known as pertaining to householders, while that which follows the way of Śiva pertains to those who bear the sectarian marks (liṅgin).
That initiation in which there is no cutting of the top-knot (*śikhā*) is one characterized by worldly dharma;
that initiation which is joined with the unbroken [mantra] as before is one characterized by the dharma of Śiva.

Oṃ hāṃ hauṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Śāntyatīta-kalā and its two Śaktis. Thus, having united the pure Śāntyātītā with the pure Śakti in the form of the tuft (śikhā) for the purpose of concealment, [one perceives] the Ātma-tattva, which extends from the subsequent Māyā-tattva down to the end of the Ātma-tattva.

"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śiva, the principle of the Self. Having thus performed the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) and worship with the root mantra, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations according to the rule for the sake of purifying any deficiency in the ritual procedure, while reciting the commentary, [addressing] the principle of Sadāśiva and the principle of Knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*). Oṃ hīṃ.
"Obeisance to the principle of Vidyā.

Having thus performed the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) and worship, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra, recited in a whisper (*upāṃśu*), for the purification of any deficiency in the recitation of the mantras, up to the end of the principle of Śakti.

Having presented [the offering] with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Śiva-tattva" and having worshipped it with the root mantra, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations for the purification of mental deficiencies. Then,
for the cessation of the power of concealment (*tirodhāna-śakti*) which causes obscuration, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra.
One should perform the oblation. In the *Kāmika*:

"Having meditated upon Śivā, who stands before [the practitioner], resembling pure crystal, and who is the path of all levels situated within the half [of the universe]—she who is the cause of the fulfillment of desires."
Having contemplated the consciousness of the disciple, he should obtain the *kartarī* (scissors) from Śivā.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"The *kartarī* is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*); by means of it, he cuts the bonds (*pāśa*). That is the crest-lock (*śikhā*)."
The supreme, most subtle [power] of mantras is the awakener of the ultimate.
The scissor (kartarī) should be understood by the best of teachers in its form as the agent (kartṛ). In the *Niśvāsa*: [p. 1521]

The mantra-practitioner should consecrate the scissors seven times with the *śikhā* mantra; then, the wise one, having grasped that very [scissors] with the appropriate mudrā, should employ it upon what is to be cut.
O you of virtuous vows, the four [fingers] beginning with the thumb should be urged forward;
likewise, one should cut the crest-lock (śikhā) with the Śakti [finger], which is the very form of the obstructing power (rodha-śakti).
One should cause the cause of all fetters to flow from twelve finger-breadths;
for another, it is eight finger-breadths above, which is called "seedless," yet one should indeed seed it.
Having brought honey and clarified butter mixed with clarified butter, Golaka offered them to the fire; having given the *pūrṇāhuti* to the crest, he offered five oblations with the weapon-mantra.

With the mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ* and using clarified butter, one should reduce the topknot to ashes; then, having drawn the topknot outside, [one should likewise treat] the *sruk*, *sruva*, and the scissors as well.
Having rinsed his mouth and become pure, the disciple should perform the ritual bath; he should do so with particular care, endowed with sincere devotion.
Then the Guru, having entered within and beheld Śiva, spoke: "By your grace, the purification of the paths (adhva-śuddhi) and the severing of the crest-lock (śikhā-ccheda) have been performed by me."
O Blessed One, O Supreme Lord, since this disciple is now united with that supreme light,
he should now be joined with the clarified butter according to the prescribed rite.
Having been thus authorized with the words "Do so," the preceptor, joyful and with palms joined in reverence,
should summon the disciple and proceed toward the fire accompanied by the Śivamantra.

Having consecrated both the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles for the purpose of application and for their own luster, one should likewise perform the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of the disciple and the ritual integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*).
Then, having joined the name and the joining [of the mantra], there is the satiation of the mantra and the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa by means of offering individual oblations with the mantra.

Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and purification, the preceptor should unite [the disciple] with Śiva. Then, for the sake of the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), another preceptor—being of the nature of Śiva—should duly perform it.
The virtuous preceptor, having cast the *bindu* while seated upon his seat, [proceeds].
Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, and likewise Mocikā; then Ūrdhvagāminī, Sūkṣmā, Sūkṣmā, Mṛtā, and Mṛtā.
O twice-born ones, it is said that the power of the drop (bindu-śakti) is the power of sound (nāda-śakti), which is the digit (kalā);
the supreme teacher, endowed with a body, is fully fashioned by these digits.
Pervasive, of the nature of space, infinite, and indeed considered supreme;
she is the Unmanā of the principle of the Self (ātmatattva) in Śaivism, joined with a body that is completely filled.
Having performed the *kumbhaka* and *pūraka* breath-retentions and established the connection with the vital breath (*jīva*),
one should slightly turn [the gaze] upward, not touching the teeth with the teeth.
With the body properly erect, having united Śiva with the self, one should remember the Suṣumnā channel as being made one with the vital air called Prāṇa.
Having conceived the consciousness of the disciple to be like pure crystal,
and having uttered the mantra through the yoga of abandoning the causal [body], [the teacher should perform the rite].
One should unite the disciple with Śiva during the *pūrṇāhuti* by means of breath-retention (*kuṃbhaka*).

At this juncture of union, one should contemplate the reality of the five substrates (*pañcādhikaraṇa*) residing in the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, as well as the manifestation of the *kalās*. "I am indeed that very Lord Sadāśiva, who consists of the five substrates."
This water-pot (*kalaśa*) belongs to Daṇḍa; O Daṇḍa, O Daṇḍa, O destroyer of the arts (*kalāntaka*).
At the tip of the staff (*daṇḍāgra*), Māyā is known to be joined with the *vea* and *vidyā*, together with variegated leaves (*citra-patra*).
The mantra has departed; it is bound by the flow of the corners.
That hollow which is the support, situated as the lotus-throne, is the ear; it is the locus of the primordial sound (nāda), its opening being the form of Śakti.
The power that pervades all time is conceived as the *sruc* (sacrificial ladle); the staff of the *sruc* has the form of a thread, and its movement consists of the revolving of the *bindu*.
In the designation of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, Sadāśiva is not merely a mass of power (*śaktipiṇḍa*). Or, as stated in the *Mṛgendra*:
"Having superimposed the path of the *sruc* upon the jar, its shoulder is the *gaṇḍī*, and its neck is the altar."
Having withdrawn from the openings of the mouth, it pervades [the body] according to its divisions.
Having thus visualized the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, grasping them with the conch-like mudrā according to the method taught by the Guru, and having known the seven equinoxes (*viṣuva*),
one should [perform the offering] at the end of the seventh equinox, within the *śāntyatītā* kalā at the *dvādaśānta*.
One should contemplate the self as dissolved into the nature of supreme bliss.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"First is the equinox of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), then the equinox of the mantra, and then the equinox of the channel (*nāḍikā*)."
Thereafter, the Viṣuvat [day] is perfectly tranquil.
The fifth is the power-equinox (śakti-viṣuva); the sixth is the equinox known as the digit (kalā); they know the seventh to be the supreme equinox of reality (tattva), called dissolution (laya).

As for the method of reciting the root mantra, among those belonging to the Prasāda mantra, there is the pervasion of Kāla together with the syllable *hau*, beginning from the *mūlādhāra* up to the heart-lotus.

Immediately after that, there is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of Brahmā; above that, the pervasion of Yāgaṣaṣṭha; immediately after that, the pervasion of Viṣṇu; and above that, [the pervasion] of Sakadra.

Having arrived at the center of the palate, its pervasion extends upward from there to the *bindu* of Īśvara, reaching as far as the space between the eyebrows. Above that, for one finger-breadth (*ekāṅgula*) in the middle of the forehead, is the pervasion of the half-moon (*ardhacandra*). Above that, for one finger-breadth, is the pervasion of the *nirodhinī*.

Pervasion (*vyāpti*): Above that, within the aperture of Brahma (*brahmabila*), there is the pervasion of *nādānta*, which denotes Sadāśiva. From the aperture of Brahma, the pervasion of *nādānta* extends for a measure of one finger-breadth (*ekāṅgula*).
Three finger-breadths above that is the pervasion of Śakti. Two finger-breadths above that—
Pervasion by the pervasive [power]. Above that, for two finger-breadths, is the pervasion known as *amā*.

Beginning from *nāda* and ending with *unmanī*, within the station of power (*śaktisthāna*), and above that, one should contemplate Śiva—the abode consisting of dense consciousness, established in himself, and beyond all that is to be contemplated.

That is known as the equinox (viṣuva); at that time, one should separate [the breaths]. Having meditated upon inhalation (pūraka) and retention (kuṃbhaka), and having drawn in the vital airs through the mouth, one should proceed.
One should gradually recite the root mantra until the mind of the disciple is dissolved; the firm conclusion of the scripture is that liberation occurs upon the dissolution of the mind.
The sensation of an ant's touch arises there in an instant; having experienced all of that, one [proceeds] from there gradually to the dvādaśānta.
In that which is devoid of qualities, stainless, pure, free from the expressed and the expresser, eternal, infinite, subtle, and devoid of both existence and non-existence.
One should describe Kaivalya as the tranquil and auspicious mass of consciousness;
therein, one should visualize the disciple’s self as the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), and [visualize] the stream of clarified butter (*ājyadhāra*).
One should offer oblations at the end of the flames into the supreme Śiva.

Then, for the sake of stabilizing the state of union (sāyujya), one should offer oblations with the root mantra; having uttered it ending with "vauṣaṭ," one should perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) according to the prescribed rule.
In the Kāmika:
"O you whose mind, breath, sound, power, and limited agency have been withdrawn, release the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles near me quickly with the *saṃhāra-mudrā*."
I salute the pure one who has raised his crest-lock like a ritual formula; the individual soul should worship him with the seed-syllable *dastra* in his body as before.
Even though he was joined with him there, he was not made equal in qualities;
for as long as [the qualities remain], the pervasion of the Pradhāna remains all-pervasive, like space.
O Prince,
even the attainment of supreme sovereignty does not shine for one who is ignorant of the sixfold policy, even if it were to be shared by a hundred kings.

For the manifestation of the six qualities, one should offer six oblations of clarified butter with that ladle; likewise, the wise man should offer the qualities as a sacrifice by means of this ritual application.

Oṃ hāṃ ātman, become omniscient; svāhā! Oṃ hīṃ hīṃ, become completely satisfied; svāhā! Oṃ hāṃ ātman, become awakened from beginningless time; svāhā! Oṃ haiṃ ātman, become independent; svāhā! Oṃ hauṃ ātman, become one whose power is attained; svāhā!

Svāhā! Oṃ hiṃ! O Self, become possessed of infinite power, svāhā! Having thus grasped the Self endowed with the six qualities from the Supreme Imperishable, the preceptor, joined with the state of the ritual procedure, should unite it with the body of the disciple.
Thereafter, having beheld with divine vision the solar disc as the supremely pure Self,
he draws it into his own heart by means of the *saṃhāra-mudrā* and, through exhalation (*recaka*), brings it into the heart of the disciple by means of the *udbhava-mudrā*.

One should again unite [the disciple] for the sake of experiencing the fruits of the karma that initiates the body, in order to pacify the exhaustion produced by the descent of the intense power (*tīvra-śakti*). One should sprinkle drops of the nectar-water from the *arghya* vessel upon the head of the disciple, as well as those from the *śiva-kumbha* and other vessels.
And the guru should cause [the disciple] to step upon all [of them] in succession.
Having placed that [image] within a mandala on the right side of the Lord, one should oneself face north and visualize [the deity] facing south.
And thus favored, having resorted to the root [mantra], he said: "O Lord, since you are the fire-god (*vanhi*), therefore, O Master, show favor to this [devotee] through your consort."
"O Lord, by your grace, may this [bird] whose wings were severed and whose actions were brought to an end become whole again.
Alas! Through my negligence, an offense has occurred that became the cause of his bondage."

Having thus informed the deity and bowed down himself, the Guru should then respectfully say to the disciple, "May there be prosperity for you both. Then, for the sake of pacifying obstacles such as those arising from the house and so forth, the Guru, through the kindling of his own power, should perform the rite.
One should initiate oneself by recollecting that which is bound by the fetters of the *kalās* through knowledge; by the single utterance of the root-mantra, one should contemplate union with Śiva.

Then, having gratified Śiva residing in the fire, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra for atonement; having offered the food offering (naivedya), one should offer *nama*, *kaṭukā*, and then the rinsing water (*camana*), sandalwood paste, betel leaf, and so forth.
Having worshipped with the eight flowers on the altar and offered the *arghya* as before, one should bid farewell to Śiva (p.
perform the inner and outer *bali* offerings, and [again] [worship] the Śiva residing in the maṇḍala with the eight flowers.

Having performed worship, offered the fruit of the accomplished rite, and prostrated, he spoke as follows: "Having gathered [the essence] and joined it within the vessel, and having united it with that mantra into Śiva, one should say 'Forgive me' with due consideration and then restrain [the deity]. Now follows the procedure for the Caṇḍayāga.

For the purpose of the Caṇḍayāga, having worshipped Caṇḍa as usual upon a seat marked with the syllable *praṇava* on a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) or within a half-moon-shaped mandala in front of the Caṇḍakumbha, one should offer the remains of the previous offering (*nirmālya*).
In the Bhīmasaṃhitā:
"Now I shall describe the Caṇḍa-sacrifice, which is the means for accomplishing all rites; the worship of it bestows fruit even upon all the Gaṇas."
One should have a lotus, a *sarvatobhadra*, or a *svastika* drawn;
likewise, in the *Mṛgendra*:
"Then, having prepared the city of Lord Caṇḍeśa, devoid of five parts..."
The mandala sacrifice should be performed by means of the word "Śiva."

The meaning of this is as follows: having taken a square field-measure devoid of the five [outer] parts, one should, by means of a cord of that same length, draw a mandala in sequence and place a lotus in its center;
then, according to the primary ritual procedure for sacrifice, the Caṇḍayāga should be performed. Thus it is stated in the Svāyaṃbhuvatantra:
Having set aside the fifth part of that square’s side,
one should rotate the remaining equal area like half a Veda.
In the center of that, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp,
measuring thirty-two finger-breadths or else one cubit in size.

Having placed the yoga-pīṭha, one should place [the deities]; establish Sarva and Śarva in their respective positions, and likewise establish Caṇḍeśvara. Then, one should again place the limbs of the Vidyā upon him according to the prescribed rule.
One should then place the Astra-mantra again upon the petals starting from the southeast (āgneya) in their respective directions,
having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, as well as with various kinds of food and ornaments.
One should satisfy all [the deities] beginning with the heart, one by one in sequence, with the remnants of the sacrifice, using one hundred and eight [offerings].
Having gratified [the deity] with twenty oblations, one should ask for forgiveness; and whoever prepares what is appropriate for Caṇḍeśvara through worship alone.
Let the food for those desiring success be free from dust and impurities; therefore, one should also offer other substances to the deity.
One should cast that flower into deep water for Caṇḍeśa; otherwise, for those who act contrary to this and cause a violation of Śiva’s command, [the same penalty applies].
Caṇḍeśvara is their teacher and the lord even of those who have been initiated;
he causes Caṇḍeśvara to manifest himself as the cause of fear for them.
Therefore, having been refined through propitiation, one should resort to the Śaiva path;
as it is said in the Kālottara:
"Having first performed the Caṇḍayāga according to the rites seen in the scriptures..."
Through the sacrifice to Caṇḍeśvara, one becomes free from disease and free from calamity.

At the conclusion of the initiation (dīkṣā), one should diligently perform the sacrifice (yāga) to Caṇḍeśvara; having established the disciple before him, one should then cause him to hear the rules (samayas).
The Guru should not offer the sacrificial fire of Śiva, the scripture of Śiva, the practitioner,
or himself to those who are censurable, especially not to women.

One should avoid eating the remains of offerings (nirmālya), giving gifts, and fasting; one should also avoid the food of a woman who has recently given birth, of a menstruating woman, and of a woman in her courses.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, freedom from guile, absence of anger,
service to the teacher, purity, contentment, and straightforwardness.
Thus, even though this conduct is common to all, O Gaṇeśa, it should be observed according to one's capacity by those who desire the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In this regard, O Lord of Beasts, the reason has been established:
by that [power] which brings about the manifestation of Brahmā and the others,
and which possesses the nature of a fierce form, one wards off the state of being possessed by delusion and effects purification.
For those who perform the *laṅghana*, *nandīkṣita*, *chāyāśiva-arcā*, or offer *aṅga-bali* [to Śiva],
and for those who consume what has been given by them, as well as for that which is understood through its own specific designation, [the Lord is the cause].
"One who lives off that [wealth] is not auspicious during childbirth, death, or menstruation;
these are like a great pit of sand— fearing a fall into them, one should avoid them and distribute [the wealth] accordingly," thus the Lord himself declared.
Other rules of conduct for those established in the Śaiva self are described in the Caryāpāda,
because conduct (*caryā*) is indeed the practice (*caraṇa*).
Then, having gratified Agni with the remnants of the sacrifice— either with a thousand or a hundred [oblations]— one should dismiss Caṇḍanātha, saying, "Forgive me."
Then, having offered oblations with the *bhūr* and other vyāhṛtis and having dismissed the Śiva-fire, one should dismiss the guardians of the world (*lokapālas*).

Having prepared an auspicious and excellent maṇḍala marked with a svastika, one should first sprinkle the disciple—who has been strengthened—with the Śiva-pitcher for the sake of the purificatory bath (*avabhṛthasnāna*). In that very place:
Then, on a ground marked with lines in an auspicious direction, one should perform the concluding bath (*avabhṛtha*) by filling the vessel of Śambhu with the water of the weapon-mantra (*astrāmbu*).

Let that [rite] which destroys misfortune stand aside; for even the mere drops arising from it, through the power of the perfected recitation of mantras, bring about auspiciousness and the pacification of all creatures.
Likewise, in the *Svāyambhuva*: "Then, upon the completion of the sacrifice, on a ground marked with svastikas,
the initiated one, being himself consecrated, should perform the purificatory bath (*avabhṛthasnāna*)."

Then one should perform the Guru-yāga. Thus it is said in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*: "O son of Pārvatī, I shall explain the Guru-yāga in brief; it is to be performed upon the vision of the deity, as well as for the accomplishment of siddhi."
At the time of a wedding procession, upon seeing an evil dream, when such a dream occurs, during the recitation of mantras, at the commencement of a sacrifice, and at its conclusion;
The word "should be performed" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Having conceived of the seat of the previously mentioned thirty-six-finger-width *yogapīṭha*, one should place the image upon it.

One should invoke Śiva there, accompanied by Brahmā and his limbs (the deities of the limbs), having worshipped him with effort using scents, flowers, and other offerings, while reciting the *hṛdayamantra*.
Having meditated upon the Guru as Sadāśiva and having prostrated before him again and again, or else— as stated in the Svāyambhuva—
the wise one should afterwards worship the Guru along with his attendants.
In the *Kālottara*:
"There, one should worship the preceptor with a crown, earrings, and so forth;
one should cause him to be given other household requisites with the *hṛdaya* mantra."
The best of preceptors should worship with the Īśāna mantra; having worshipped according to this procedure, he should prostrate and ask for forgiveness.
In the *Kiraṇa*:
"At the end of the sacrifice, there should be a sacrifice to the Guru; one should worship [him] at the beginning of the sacrifice.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
All initiation and knowledge arise from the grace of the Guru;
therefore, with every effort, service to the Guru is supreme.
Furthermore, there should be service characterized by uninterrupted devotion;
thereafter, one should receive the grace of the guru, provided that such service continues to the highest degree.
A disciple who has been initiated into Nirvāṇa and is fit for association with the Guru possesses the qualification for the worship of the Liṅga intended for the benefit of others.
Mataṅga said:
For a living being whose mind has been purified by the fire of initiation, [the supreme reality] known as Sva attains manifestation through yoga;
and by the power of the All-pervading One kissing the region of his heart, it brings about the cessation [of bondage] for other beings as well.
Thus concludes the ritual procedure for the initiation into Nirvāṇa.

1533) Here, it should be understood that by the word *pratiṣṭhā* (consecration), only those entitled to the consecration of a mobile liṅga (*calaliṅga*) are intended; among these [categories], this ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is not to be performed.
According to the methods taught by the wise, one should meditate on Him as Śiva alone and attain full realization.
Thus it is said in the *Kālottara*: "Among all castes, the householder is declared to be the most excellent guru."
Thus it is stated in the Siddhānta:
"In this Siddhānta, the status of being an Ācārya has been established by Śiva for all four castes, as well as for those who bear the sectarian marks (liṅgin) and those who are seekers (grahin)."
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"One who is devoid of the initiation of consciousness (*vijñānadīkṣā*), lacking devotion to the Guru, arrogant,
ungrateful, and a defiler of the conduct of the rules (*samayācāra*)."
One who is not endowed with such qualities as these is indeed not worthy of worship on this earth; one should not perform the consecration for such a person, nor grant him the title of *ācārya*.
If an initiation is performed through negligence, one incurs fault.
Likewise, in the *Tridhāsārapaddhati*:
"The Guru may, according to his own will, initiate a disciple with an initiation involving transgression (*vyabhicāra*)."
Being a preceptor, yet [acting] like a disciple, one is cooked in the ocean of hell.
Disciples who have been initiated by a teacher endowed with the qualities of Śiva but fallen from his own virtues—what initiation could that be? Such a person goes to hell.
The preceptor who is endowed with his own virtues and the initiated who are free from transgression—both go to heaven; the initiated go to hell, while the teacher attains the state of Śiva.
Thereafter, for a disciple who has been initiated into Nirvāṇa by the Guru but whose conduct was deficient,
one should perform the consecration of an Ācārya preceded once again by the initiation into Nirvāṇa.
Likewise, in the *Kāmika*: "If the disciple, who has performed the prescribed rites and is endowed with [proper] conduct, is initiated after being praised,
one should perform the desired ritual procedure after offering the outer and inner oblations."

One should begin the consecration for one who has been initiated into Nirvāṇa according to their respective [lineage], who is free from deficiencies in conduct, and who is complete in the performance of what has been taught. Even for a disciple who desires both the initiation into Nirvāṇa and the consecration at one time, the [Nirvāṇa initiation] must come first.

Having completed the initiation for individual liberation (pṛthak-nirvāṇa-dīkṣā) in that pavilion, all the ritual vessels and other implements required for the initiation are set out, as the Caṇḍayāga has already been performed.
Now follows the procedure for the construction of the pavilion for the purpose of consecration.
Having performed the purification of the pavilion preceded by the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*),

and having again withdrawn the new pitcher and other items as before, one should commence the worship of the pavilion, the preparatory rite (*adhivāsa*), the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and the initiation (*dīkṣā*). Thus it is stated in the *Suprabheda*:

Thus, having completed the initiation (*dīkṣā*), one should then perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*). Likewise, it is stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "In a noble place and at an auspicious time, having performed the rites during the [proper] lunar mansion (*lagna*), one should carry out the sacrifice (*yāga*) as before. Similarly, in the *Bālaratnāvalī*:
On the following day, having performed the daily rites and the occasional worship (*naimittikapūjā*),
the knower of mantras should consecrate a disciple who has mastered the *Saṃhitās*. Having performed the sacrifice as prescribed, he should complete the initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Then one should consecrate the one who lacks discernment of the proper method by means of the thread-technique.
In a temple, in a monastery, or likewise in the house of the preceptor and disciple,
one should construct a pavilion at the site of initiation.
In the Raurava [Tantra],
it is specifically stated that in a temple, one should construct either a pavilion (maṇḍapa) or a water-shed (prapā); in its center,
there should be an altar (vedikā) and a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), arranged according to the sequence previously described.
In the *Niśvāsa*:
"One should indeed construct a square in the eastern direction of the pavilion.
Likewise, in the *Kāmika*, in the section on the hundredfold consecration (*śatābhiṣeka*):
On a mountain peak, or at a water-station, or in a pure and delightful place, measuring between five and fifty-five cubits in extent;
Or else, in a [mandala] with ten thousand faces, provided with four gates, and adorned with one to fifty-five divisions;
Whether it be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra, or a woman born of any of those respective castes, or one who worships Śiva—
In that very place—
in the northeast of the east and then in the western direction— on the northern face of the pavilion, which is adorned with canopies and other ornaments.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*, there is a specific detail:
"Having been thus authorized with the command 'Do so,' [the preceptor] should go outside to the east, the north, the northeast, or the west, into a pavilion facing west."
Adorned with the five ornaments, one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
Likewise, in the *Santāna*:
"The pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) or the enclosure (*trapā*) should be exactly thirty-two cubits."
It should be sixteen, ten, nine, or eight cubits in size.
O Goddess, it should be provided with pillars and adorned above with a canopy;
one should encircle it with garlands of *darbha* grass and suspend banners in all directions.
On the level ground spread out beneath a vast canopy,
Mataṅga [beheld it] adorned with variegated banners and auspicious, white flags.
And also by censured archways situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions; as stated in the *Niśvāsakārikā*:
"By four archways, adorned with banners and flags."
And the site of the altar was beautifully adorned with canopies and water-bubbles.
Adorned with flowers and leaves, beautified by mango sprouts,
and provided with svastikas, lotuses, and white mustard seeds.
In the *Kāmika*:
"Likewise, the support for the altar (*vedikā*) should be half a cubit high, quadrangular, four cubits in width,
and extending toward the south and north directions."
And the *parājita* [altar] is adorned with svastikas in the four directions;
or, as stated in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"One should have an altar made eight finger-breadths high and two cubits wide."
In the Raurava [Tantra]: "The height should be four finger-breadths and the length two cubits; or as it is stated in the Kriyāsārapaddhati:"
A pair of auspicious altars (vedikās) should be established in the east and west; it is stated in some places that they should be four cubits [in length] and twelve finger-breadths in height.
Smeared with ointment and adorned with various kinds of flowers such as lotuses and the like,
the procedure for the construction of the consecration throne is now described.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Indeed, thirty-two finger-breadths in width and that same height; square, even, pure, and adorned in the center with a single lotus."
Having arranged the pedestal (pīṭha) as before, one should install and worship [the deity] upon it. As stated in the Mataṅga: "On a pedestal made of heartwood or produced from the Śīparṇī tree..."
Having displayed his former deeds with the ostentation of white garments, he settled there.
Likewise, in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"Having placed a seat made of *śrīparṇa* wood and so forth there, one should arrange the seat of Ananta; other wooden seats are said to be unsuitable."
Likewise, in the Kāmika:
"On a noble pedestal, one should consecrate [the deity] with water produced from a milky tree, or from another such source; or from a jackfruit tree, a bilva tree, or a brahma tree."
A specific measurement for the breath has been stated.
The pedestal should be four cubits in circumference and beautifully adorned; it should be made with great concentration to be one cubit in height.
On the altar-platform of the sacrificial pavilion mentioned previously, one should construct the Anantavijaya maṇḍala. Likewise, in the Svāyaṃbhuvatantra:
"Now, for the purpose of the consecration of the preceptor, one should worship Anantavijaya, as well as those [deities] intended for specific desires."
For this is the invocation of the treasure for the sake of accomplishment.
Within the interior of a pedestal measuring two cubits, one should draw a lotus in the center; six finger-breadths from the front edge,
one should first draw the pericarp.
One should fashion the filaments in the second [circle], the joints of the petals in the next, and the tips of the petals in the fourth;
thus one should construct the lotus itself.
One should draw the ritual diagram measuring two cubits, situated around the pedestal;
the outer deity Varuṇa should be made separately with half the width of the pathway.
The main street is divided into eight sections by eight interruptions;
it extends from the mouth of the street back to the outer door, joined with its half.
Having then marked it out with a cord, one should subsequently cut away the layers of skin;
these very parts are indeed to be distributed according to their actual requirements.

One should cast the lines according to the prescribed path, starting with white and so forth in due order; the white lines constitute the inner enclosure, while those of red and other colors form the outer parts.
Possessing the eightfold straight path and characterized by infinite victory, merely by the sight of this [teaching],
even those who are great sinners—
Having attained the state of Rudra, they became stainless; yet, regarding this, they were filled with apprehension, [saying]:
"O Lord, Sovereign of the hosts of gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas!"

Those standing outside the sacrificial ground behold the victory over the infinite. In the construction of the pavilion for the initiation of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), one should fashion a nine-navel mandala at the intermediate direction.
Thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*.
Then, for the purpose of the master’s consecration (ācāryābhiṣeka), one should fashion a nine-naved [mandala];
for all rites performed for specific desires as well, the nine-naved [mandala] bestows the fruit.
Listen, O wise one, as the mandala known as the nine-naved is being described: it should be a square field of eight cubits, or even ten cubits.
One should divide the city on all sides by means of seventy-four [lines] called *darbha*;
if there are eight [lines] on all sides, there will be strife in the center.
The *pathika* [type of temple] has its door at the end of the *vīthikārya* [section], measuring half a *padma*;
it is provided with *karṇa* and *upakarṇa* [projections], and possesses a neck-like (*kaṇṭhavat*) upper frieze (*adhipaṭṭikā*).
Thus, one lotus together with its path and gate has been described by him;
outside of that, a pathway is prescribed.
That [central area] shall measure five parts, while the space extending ten parts on all sides— toward the cardinal and intermediate directions and the zenith and nadir—
should be made into eight lotuses as previously described.
According to the ritual procedure for the eight lotuses, it should be provided with paths and gates; in the center is that white lotus, and the eastern lotus is yellow.
Outside of that is a five-tiered pathway adorned with leaves; the neck of the gate is like a lotus, while the tier is like a royal thorn.
The cheek-panels should be clearly fashioned with three doors for the directions of activity; the corner-binding and the tripod-base should be like a thunderbolt.
In the center is that white lotus; the eastern lotus is yellowish-green, or else pale like a lotus, or even pale red.
Pervading the sky, it is beneficial for the rite of the nine altars (navādhvara) of Śiva alone; it is declared to be the "nine-navelled" (navanābha),
belonging indeed to the temple (prāsāda) of Śiva.
Alternatively, one may proceed according to the method taught by Mataṅga:
having divided [the area] into seven parts, one should fashion a lotus in the center;
it should measure thirty-two finger-breadths and be well-proportioned as before.
Having set aside one part, one should draw eight lotuses of the same size as the central lotus, in due order, within the eight directions.
One should properly fill with colored powders the auspicious mandala, which is radiant with four paths, eight doors, and the aforementioned [ornaments], so that it becomes beautiful.
And likewise it has been stated by the Teachers:
"In the field, having divided [it] into seven parts, one should draw a path for the feet of Śiva all around;
in the eight directions, lotuses with their stalks [should be placed], and the path [around them] should be made with one part."
With the feet situated within the eight doors, the body is established inside; there shall be a lotus with nine pericarps, thus declared in the venerable Mataṅga.

Now, the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa). Thus, in the *Kāraṇa*: "One should fashion the pot in this manner with a thousand pots, or even with half that number of pots, or even with fifty pots."
Likewise, in the *Santānasaṃhitā*:
"One should perform [the rite] a thousand times, or two hundred, or even half of that;
or else one hundred and eight times, or even eighty-one."
p.
1541) Or with twenty-five, or nine, or five, according to the *Suprabheda*:
"And up to one thousand [mantras], according to one's wealth, for the ritual bathing (*snāpana*)."
One should indeed establish the water-pots according to the prescribed rite.
In the *Vīratantra*:
"In the center, one should place the Śiva-pot with the Śiva-mantra; [and] the *vardhanī* for it..."
One should place [the seed-syllable] on the left from the bīja of Gaurī.
One should place eight water-pots starting from the east and ending with the northeast;
one should place Īśa in the portion of the principal pot and Manonmanī in the *vardhanī* vessel.
Ananteśa, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetraka,
Rudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍika.
Likewise, in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"O Śiva, one should place the *kuṃbha* pitcher in the center upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*);
O Śiva, one should place the *vardhanī* vessel, joined with it, to its left."
One should place the jars of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) outside of that [central jar],
filled with the essences of the salt ocean, the milk ocean, clarified butter, sugarcane juice, and *kādambarī*.
And within the womb, eight rivers should be placed;
or else, in the jars at the four directions, [the colors] red, blue, white, and orange.

Furthermore, in the jars starting from the southeast (Āgneyī), [one should place] those beginning with Ananta and ending with Ekanetra; and those beginning with Ekanetra and ending with Śikhaṇḍin, who are white, blood-colored, blue, and red respectively.

One should worship [the deities] with five faces or four faces, bearing the weapons of Śiva. The installation accompanied by the *vardhanī* vessel pertains to the sphere of desires for worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*). In the *Vīra-tantra*:
The presiding deities have been fully described; now hear about the ritual substances, O Brahmin: there are nine [substances] in the primary pitcher, namely kṣaya and citta.
One should cast gold into the *vardhanī* vessel using the seed-syllable of Gaurī; likewise, silver, copper, iron, tin, and lead.
Then, one should place abundant brass and bell-metal in the eastern [vessel], and there, in the southeastern jar,
one should deposit the nine grains.
Haritāla, Gandha, Gandhaka, and manaḥśilā; mākṣika, rāṣṭra, rasa, and likewise gaurīka.
O best of Brahmins, one should especially place mercury (rasendra) and the ninth [substance] there; and one should place the bark of the Akṣa tree in the southern pitcher.
The bark of the Palāśa, Āmra, Khadira, Plakṣa, Nyagrodha, Pippala, Panasa, Bilva,
and Śirīṣa trees.
When the water-pot has been placed in the southwest, one should deposit nine types of earth: from both banks of a river, from a mountain, from an anthill, and from a cow-pen.
In a field, a lake, a mountain, a planet, or the ocean, one should place fresh flowers upon a water-pot (kumbha) consecrated to Varuṇa.
The *candrapaṅkaja*, sandalwood, the white water-lily, the blue lotus, the *pāṭala*,
the *karavīra*, and the red lotus.
The *nandyāvarta*, the *vyāghāta*, and the *navapuṣpa* are mentioned here; when the water-pot (*kumbha*) has been placed in the northwest, one should deposit the ninefold collection of fragrances.
One should place sandalwood, saffron, iron, the khaṭa plant, elephant, and monkey, as well as black pepper, kaṭaka, and leaf, each according to its own name.
When the water-pot has been placed in the north-eastern direction, one should deposit nine seeds:
barley, bamboo-seed, priyaṅgu, śāli rice, and nīvāra rice.
One should place wheat, sesame, mung beans, and mustard seeds respectively, and then arrange the nine medicinal herbs in the pitcher situated in the northeast.
Lakṣmī, sahadevī, viṣṇukrāntā, nṛpa, balā, indravallī, śaṅkhapuṣpī, sūryāvarta, and gaṇḍikā.
One should specifically install [the items] with their respective names according to the mantra; in the absence of gems, one should install a vajra, and in the absence of metals, gold.
In the absence of seeds, one should establish Yama; in the absence of the four elements, Tālaka;
and in the absence of medicinal herbs, one should employ Sahadevī.
Now, following the procedure for the consecration of the poor, the ritual rule is stated:
"In the case of all those who are poor, the jar should be made according to whatever materials are available."
Having performed it with twenty-five, or else with nine fives.
Likewise, in the Sarvajñānottara:
"Or else, with five jars prepared according to the previously mentioned procedure...
There, one should arrange the jars as before, beginning from the east, according to the ritual for the Śiva-jar,
conjoined with the respective mantra-deities.
One should apply the mantras of the eight Lords of Knowledge (Aṣṭavidyeśvara) in the first [lotus]; the five Brahmans in the second; and the four Aṅgas in the third.
The fourth [vessel] is joined with the Astra-mantra, and the fifth is the Śiva-kumbha; having consecrated them as before, one should perform the bath according to the prescribed rite.
Furthermore, having bowed again to those twenty medicinal herbs beginning with Sahadevī,

as well as the grains beginning with Brahma-grain, the metals such as gold and iron, the ores such as cinnabar, and the fragrant substances such as mercury and sulphur— all as previously mentioned— *pa*.

Having placed the five medicinal herbs, the five sounds, and the five *śālinīs* one by one in sequence into the five jars, one should first perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the *kalās* beginning with Nivṛtti, and then place the five Brahmans beginning with Sadyojāta. Thus it is said in the *Mṛgendra*:
As before, one should place [the herbs] beginning with Īśāna in the pitchers at the cardinal directions; then, in the pitcher of Sahadevī, one should place Brāhmī, Trāyantī, and Lakṣaṇāvatī.
Śaṅkhapuṣpī, balā seeds, jyotiṣmatī, aparājitā,
viṣṇukrāntā, balā, moṭā, bilva, dhātrī, bhārṅgī, and amṛtā.
Śatāhvā, pāribādā, ūrvā, kuśa, vyāghrī, punarnavā, the seeds beginning with barley,
and the juices such as salt and the like.
The gems, all the fragrances, and even the metals are [to be understood] according to the treatises.
By the word "rasa," the six flavors beginning with salt are expressed. As stated in the *Cintyaviśva*:
One should place two Vidyeśas in each of the five jars;
likewise, one should also place two Samudras and the deity in the same manner.
In the center, upon the Śiva-pitcher (śivakuṃbha), one should likewise place the Ocean of Śiva;
and beside it, the Vardhanī vessel, accompanied by the Ocean of Śakti.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*, another method is stated:
"The knower of mantras should perform the consecration with four jars,
as before, [consecrating] the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*s) and the limbs of Brahmā."

The third [mantra], joined with the weapon-mantra (astra), should be applied to a single jar; in the *Niśvāsa*, one jar is prescribed. Alternatively, one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) with a single jar.
Endowed with all the principles (tattvas), mantras, and oceans,
one should perform this rite here using a single jar; or else, the consecration may be performed with a single such vessel.
Alternatively, if [the materials] are unavailable, there should be only one consecration by the preceptor;
it may take place either in a vessel made of birch bark or in a conch-shell or a mother-of-pearl shell.
One should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) and thereafter should not inform [others].
In the case of the causal [rite]—
on a prepared pavilion, on an altar, or on a sacrificial mound fashioned from rice.
One should draw a lotus provided with a pericarp and eight petals.
Having strewn it with rice, sesame seeds, and likewise with *kuśa* grass, [he should place] earthen vessels free from defects, filled with half a *droṇa* of water.
The pitchers, arranged in groups of three, joined with nine vardhanīs,
filled with water scented with all kinds of perfumes, and provided with kūrca-grass tufts;
In the *Kāmika*:
"Or else, one should place jars— either ninefold or fivefold— situated upon all kinds of grain."
Or else, [he should place] water-pots together with blades of kusha grass and with lids.
[He saw] jars bound with cloths, filled with water, scented, and resplendent with gems and gold;
their mouths were adorned with mango, *aśvattha*, and *palāśa* leaves, and they were provided with seeds, flowers, and fruits.
One should consecrate [the thread] with the Vidyeśa known as Sadeśākhyā during the nine-fold division, or with the kalās beginning with Nivṛtti during the five-fold division.

Having placed the jars, which were obtained from Śiva in a hundred ways, worshipped, and deemed fit for the ritual bathing, in their respective positions as before, one should perform the worship of Śiva as previously described.
Having thus gathered the materials for the sacrifice on the previous day, one should offer the sprouts.
As stated in the Kāmika:
"Then one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka), preceded by the offering of the sprouts."

In the Raurava [Tantra]: On the previous day, having performed the worship of the Sun while adorned with the five-fold ornaments, the Preceptor, with hands washed, [should proceed] from the pavilion toward the northeast or the north.

Having stood outside, worshipped the gatekeepers of the archway, and entered within, one should perform the worship up to the end of the *ācārya-pūjā*, and then worship the Lord of the Disciple-Maṇḍala (*śiṣya-maṇḍaleśvara*) in the midst of the Guru. In the *Anantavijaya* [maṇḍala], beginning from the central lotus, one should worship Paramaśiva and the others. Likewise...
In the Svāyaṃbhuvakalpa:
one should place the supreme Lord Śiva in the pericarp in its center;
having assigned Īśāna to the head, one should place his face upon the eastern petal.
On the south, however, is Aghora; likewise, Vāmadeva is on the north. On the western petal is Sadyojāta, according to the sequence of the petals in the array of the words.
By this very [method], one should properly commence with the limbs and so forth in the intermediate directions; one should then place the Praṇava at the root of the southeastern petal, in the heart.
One should place the head in the northeast and the crest-lock in the southwest; likewise, one should place the armor on the tip of this petal in the northwest as well as in the north.

One should place the mantra *sarvātmāna* at the tip of the eastern petal, *śiroṣṭārṇa*, *jvālinī*, and likewise *piṅgalā* on the southern petal, and the *netra* mantra on the tip of the eastern petal.
One should then duly assign the *astra* mantra to the south.
Having established Gāyatrī in the west, one should place the limbs of the Vidyā as before; then, one should install Pāśupata upon all the intervening petals.
One should then place the Aindra-pīṭha in the east and the Sūkṣma-pīṭha in the south;
having invoked them with arghya-vessels, one should place Śivottama in the west.
Then, having established and worshipped the god Ekanetra in the north, one should place these [deities] in the northeast,
beginning with the composed Ekarudra.
One should worship Trimūrti in the southeast, Śrīkaṇṭha in the southwest, and Śikhaṇḍin in the northwest on the pedestal, in due order.
Thus, one should worship the power Vidyeśvarī, who is heard of as the primordial Vidyeśvara;
she is the first form of Śiva and is to be worshipped in the ritual of sacrifice.
One should worship the two groups on the right and left sides of Ananta, and then worship the Goddess in her distinct forms, beginning with Sūkṣmā, in their proper sequence.
Thus, the state of the eight groups is established in the four directions; having worshipped them, one should worship the weapon situated at the eight door-panels.

Alternatively, in the ninth maṇḍala, one should worship Śiva, the world-protectors (lokapālas), and the weapons (astras) in sequence within the nine lotuses beginning with the central lotus. Thus it is said in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*:
"Having worshipped Śiva in the central lotus, [one worships] the world-protectors in the others, and the weapons [in the remaining]."
Having worshipped with devotion and diligence in the outer path, however, [he should proceed].

Thereafter, having gone to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should perform the rites ending with the satiation (*tarpaṇa*) of the mantra. Having performed the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta-homa*) for the sake of pacifying defects related to place, time, and the ritual signs, one should inform Śiva: "O Lord, today I have been thus commanded by you, who are the embodiment of the Guru. [The initiation and the exposition...]"
This is the injunction for the sake of non-interruption, O observer of excellent vows.
This [initiation] should be given to one's own disciple, who possesses the conduct of the thorough knowledge of birth,
immediately after Śiva.
"By the power of that [previous experience], this has now come to me; therefore, by your command, I shall bestow this yoga upon him."
Having given the command, "Do so," and having caused the disciple to enter,

he should have him worship Śiva as previously described; then, having performed the binding of the *pratisara* (protective cord), he should [place the disciple] near Śiva upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) made of rice grains, covered with a new cloth, and situated at the tips of *darbha* grass.
One should cause the bed to be prepared as before. Likewise, in the Raurava [Tantra] (p.
"And likewise, both dreaming and the good dream."
One should bind it with the root mantra of Śiva; having offered a gift, one should likewise wrap the bed with a new cloth.

Having recited the Śiva-mantra one hundred times, he should go to sleep; or else, having performed the "immediate sprouting" (sadyāṅkura), he should immediately perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) for the disciple.
Thus concludes the procedure for the preliminary consecration and the rite of perfuming for the initiation of empowerment.

Then, at the proper time, the preceptor and the disciple shall rise and perform their daily rites such as bathing; the disciple shall destroy his bad dreams by reciting the Astra-mantra one hundred and eight times, and having first performed the worship of the pavilion (maṇḍapa), [he shall worship] Indra and the others, the five Brahmans, the six limbs, the Mūla-mantra, and the Vyāhṛtis.
Having performed the oblations with the root mantra and the primary substances,
one should examine bad dreams as well as good dreams in the Raurava [tantra]; [one should then remove] their defects.
Perform one hundred and eight burnt offerings for the purpose of pacification.
At the time of dawn and during the day, one should perform the daily rites (*nityakarman*).

Having established [the deities] from Indra to Īśāna, one should thereafter place the ritual jars (*kalaśas*) upon the altar (*vedikā*) constructed within the sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*) as previously prepared.
And one should offer the *vyāhṛtis* in sequence with barley,

rice, parched grain, cakes, white mustard, and black mustard. Having placed these substances upon the Vāyavya altar and having established the deities therein according to their respective suitability, [one should proceed].
Having worshipped [the deities] in the sequence beginning with Sadyojāta and so forth for the sake of the preliminary rite (*prādhānika*),
and having performed the construction of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) preceded by the prescribed rules, one should [perform] therein the pervasion up to the principle of Vidyā (*vidyātattva*).

Having arranged either a noble seat (bhadrapīṭha) or a lion-throne (siṃhāsana), and having spread a white cloth upon it, one should station the Brahmins and others in their proper order and consecrate them; O twice-born ones, know that [the officiants] are in the eastern direction, in the north-eastern direction, and in the direction of Yama (the south).

One should place the Śūdras in the western direction, or all [the castes] situated in the northeast; or else, having constructed a pavilion for the consecration (abhiṣeka) facing every direction starting from the east, one should arrange two altars there, south and north, as previously described. ... [with] the water-pot (*kalaśa*).

Having established [the altar] and stationed the disciple to the north, one should consecrate him. Thus it is said in the *Mṛgendra*: "In the northeast, on a prepared seat made auspicious by the presence of the sun, having attained the status of the 'Mantra-seat' (mantrapīṭha), when the degree of the ascendant is aspected by a benefic [planet]."
In the Kāmika:
"Having placed [the disciple] upon the southern altar together with the nine and five jars joined by Śiva, one should establish the child upon the northern altar."
Likewise, the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) is presided over by Śiva himself along with his limbs.
Then, in the Raurava [Tantra], there is the lion-throne (siṃhāsana), and above that, the lotus-seat (padmāsana); such is the seat.
One should perform worship there and likewise initiate the disciple.
Having placed [the disciple] facing the eastern direction, having sprinkled him, and having established him with the recitation of mantras;
as stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"One who has performed the prescribed ablutions, is dressed in white garments, has observed a fast, and is facing east before eating."
With a gentle countenance, he stood facing the disciple with his face turned toward the east.
p.
1551) In the *Cintyaviśva*:
Having seated the disciple facing east, his body having been rendered fully manifest (*sakalīkṛta*).

First, for the purpose of purifying the body, one should apply an ointment made from the *aśvattha* tree and so forth; subsequently, having fetched each of the eight substances, such as sour gruel and rice, and having meditated upon them as being of the nature of the weapons beginning with the *vajra*, one should cast the unmixed substance [upon the body] while reciting the *varman* mantra.
Likewise, in the Raurava-tantra:
"One should take the wood of the *aśvattha*, the *vaṭa*, and the *bilva*, as well as *kuśa* roots and earth; mixing these with cow urine, one should apply them while reciting the Sadyojāta mantra."
Thereafter, one should perform the cleansing (nirmārjana) with sour gruel,
water, ashes, dūrvā grass, cow-dung balls, cow-dung balls, white mustard seeds, curd, and water, using the *vajradaṃṣṭra* mantras respectively.
Thereafter, having wiped it with protective garments, one should cast them out in the directions starting from the east;
and having wiped it again and again with various auspicious items, [one should proceed].
In the section on the *nīrājana* ceremony in the *Kāmika*:

"The consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the preceptor (*deśika*), however, is performed without lamps and the like; rice grains are prescribed for that [consecration], but if it belongs to Rudra, it is joined with lamps."
The teacher, facing either north or east, having joined the *prāṇa-śakti*— in its essential form— within the Supreme Lord who is the self of the sacrificer, through the Suṣumṇā or the Iḍā [channel],
by means of the perfect retention of the nectar (*amṛta-dhāraṇā*), and while reciting the Śiva-mantra, [he becomes] one whose power is dissolved (*kṣībdha-śakti*).
Visualizing the water issuing from the jar in the form of thick, flowing nectar,
and in the case of nine jars, first sprinkling the water of the *vardhanī* with the *astra-mantra* for the removal of obstacles—

In the case of the water-pot (kalaśa), while reciting the mantra of Śiva along with his limbs, one should [perform the rite] with pots consecrated by Brahmā, beginning from Sadyojāta and ending with Īśāna.

One should consecrate [the disciple] with those respective mantras. However, in the case of the "four-plus-one" (caturādhekānta) position, one should consecrate him with the very mantras deposited there in that nectar (*amṛta*). Thus it is stated in the *Mṛgendra*:
"The Supreme Lord has entered into either the *suṣumnā* or the *iḍā*."

Having placed [the vessel] in the *kumbha*, the wise one should sprinkle it with the *Sadyojāta* and other mantras from the northeast to the west, while reciting the mantra of Śiva along with his limbs (*aṅga*), each separately.
In the *Kālottara*:
"O Six-faced One, with a non-conceptual state of being, the preceptor, established as before, should perform the consecration with all the mantras."
At that time, whoever recites this hymn in the eastern direction,
having thus performed the study amidst the sounding of conchs and trumpets;
With loud shouts and resonant cries, as well as with auspicious utterances, with shouts of "Victory! and hymns of praise accompanied by dance and song.
Especially for the Brahmins, with hymns and auspicious recitations, [he honored] the Śaivas,
the Pāśupatas, and likewise those who observe the Great Vow (Mahāvrata).
And likewise for the Buddhists, the followers of Arhat, and all other heretics, as well as for the wretched,
[this protection] shall be provided by means of this iron bar.
In Raurava—
there is the sound of conchs and horns, filled with the music of lutes and flutes, and the resonance of trumpets.
It is joined with hymns of praise and auspicious utterances.
One should cause the *maddalī*, *paṭaha*, *ādamallī*, bell (*ghaṇṭā*), and *ḍhaṅka* drum to be sounded.
As stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"First, having lifted [the deity] from the jar with alkaline water and the other substances in due order..."
By practitioners and other noble ones, and by the forms of the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyārājas).
This sprinkling must be performed for the sake of the chariot-race by those who follow the path of Śiva;
they, following the ways of the world, shall shatter the [obstacles] beginning with Ananta using water-pots.
Thereafter, with the water from the Śiva-pitcher by the Guru, who is the very embodiment of Śiva,
[the disciple receives] the lineage-consecrations (gotrābhiṣeka) accompanied by the "Sumaṅgalī" verses from the Raurava[-tantra], and other various [mantras].
Having established [the deity], one should perform the consecration with water-pots.
In the Kāmika [Tantra]:
Having established [the deity] in pure water, and then again in another place,
one should provide [the deity] with changed garments and so forth, along with an upper cloth and beautiful flowers.
His body should be smeared with white sandalwood paste or likewise dusted with ashes.
Regarding the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*): it may be made of gold or silver; in its absence, it may be made of cotton.
Twice the number of threads, tripled [in weaving].
Having put on divine garments, one should also adorn oneself with ornaments: a crown, earrings, necklaces, and armlets.
Having likewise offered a bracelet, a new hero’s thread, and a waistband, one should hang a fragrant garland of divine scent from the Gandhamādana mountain.
O child,
one should fumigate and illuminate [the area] accompanied by shouts of victory; furthermore, the Guru should constantly contemplate therein, "I am Śiva."
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:
"Having adorned the disciple, one should worship him with elaborate rites beginning at night;
[offering] balls of turmeric-rice, curd, dūrvā grass, and unbroken grains."
Having untied [the thread], one should cast it in the directions; the wise one should wrap it three times.
[The substances are] gorocana, water for rinsing the mouth, dūrvā grass, flowers, curd, and milk-rice.

The preceptor, having grasped the disciple's left hand with his own left hand, should cause him— who is dressed in white linen and holds white *siddhārtha* seeds— to pay homage for the sake of auspiciousness.
Taking [the vessel] clockwise, one should place it in the abode;
on the southern lion-throne called Śivapīṭha, [one should place the deity] seated upon the seat of the Praṇava with water.
Having filled the conch with this metallic mineral, that wise man [proceeds].
Taking gems, seeds, and fragrances, he should place them; the five digits beginning with Nivṛtti, together with Brahmā and the others acting as assistants for the tastes.
Having established the Root-Vidyā along with Śiva and His limbs, together with the fivefold acts (pañcakṛtya):

Oṃ, salutation to the act of creation (sṛṣṭikṛtya). Oṃ, salutation to the act of maintenance (sthitikṛtya). Oṃ, salutation to the act of withdrawal (saṃhārakṛtya). Oṃ, salutation to the act of concealment (tirobhāvakṛtya). Oṃ, salutation to the act of grace (anugrahakṛtya).
Homage to Kṛtyā!

Endowed with the aforementioned meditative visualization, the Guru should lift up the conch and perform the consecration. Thereafter, having drawn a mandala to the west of the deity, [he should proceed] in the sequence beginning from its center.
One should worship the Guru who belongs to the lineage of both the supreme and the non-supreme.
As stated in the *Sarvajñānottara* (p. 1555):
According to the path taught in the scriptures, one should place the lotus-seated seat of the Lord in the western direction within the mandala of mantras; this is the prescribed seat.
Sadāśiva and Ananta, Vidyārudra together with Umā, the god Viṣṇu,
as well as the god Brahmā and Skanda.

One should worship one's own guru precisely according to the path taught in the scriptures. To the true gurus, one should offer one's body, wealth, and life-force. Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground with the head placed toward the north, one should remain there.
Once the disciple has been initiated, one should place the foot of Śiva upon his head;
at that time, one should especially bestow the hand of Śiva.
While reciting the Śiva-mantra into his right ear and uttering all the mantras,
he should initiate the disciple who stands with palms joined in reverence.
Thereafter, one should address Śiva:
"O Lord, by your grace, you who are the embodiment of the Guru, this disciple has been consecrated by you; he is now made fit for initiation."

"Now, the Master, being impelled by the consideration that [the disciple] is fit for initiation, shall grant [it] upon being thus commanded. Here, the qualification is stated. To the disciple who is thus endowed with qualification, he should give the *uṣṇīṣa* and so forth. As stated in the *Kāmika*:
Then the preceptor should give to the disciple the uṣṇīṣaka and other items, as well as the *karaṇī*,
the *kartarī*, the *ghaṭikā*, and furthermore the *sruva* and *sruc*.
Darbha grass, books, rosaries, a crown, earrings, sandals, a fly-whisk,
a parasol, elephants, horses, palanquins, and so forth.
To whom else could a king endowed with faith give [this] at that time?
A specific distinction has been stated regarding the expectation of both worldly enjoyment and liberation for the *Cintyaviśva*.
There, the worldly disciples should indeed bestow upon the excellent lifelong teacher the uṣṇīṣa, the crown, the parasol, the sandals, and the fly-whisks.
One should cause the elephant, the *ākañcakaraṇī*, the *kartarī*, the *ghaṭikā*, and likewise the conjunction (*yoga*) of both to be given; therefore, one should indeed bestow them.

One should also [prepare] a rosary, kusha grass, a large and small sacrificial ladle (sruk-sruva), books, and so forth. According to the *Suprabheda*: "One should bind on a fine, white turban with pure cloth."
The forehead mark (lalāṭapaṭṭa) should be applied as proclaimed by the king.
One who knows the ritual procedure should provide a crown, adorned with all ornaments such as earrings and the like,
as well as a parasol held above and a fly-whisk.
But in the absence even of these [materials], one should prepare them with *darbha* grass;
or else, one should mentally contemplate everything as auspicious by means of the Śiva-mantra.
In the *Kālottara*:
"From that point beginning, one should always perform the auspicious *uṣṇīṣa* [covering] which envelops the throat and neck, as well as the *uttarāsaṅga*."
One should always wear two sacred threads together with an upper garment; as long as one wears them, even if they are not washed, they do not become defiled.

In the *Cintyaviśva*, it is said that the preceptor of authority should communicate [the teachings] to that disciple; therein, he should cause him to hear the rules of conduct (*ācāra*). In the *Kāmika*:
And having understood the command through faith, as well as initiation, exposition, and so forth, up to the present day, perform the examination according to the prescribed rule.
In the *Suprabheda*: "The rites of worship to Śiva and so forth, as well as recitation (*japa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*), should be performed according to one's capacity;
likewise, a commitment to exposition (*vyākhyā*) must always be undertaken."
Regarding the cause:
one should not touch any twice-born who have not been initiated;
with great effort, one should not touch a Caṇḍālī woman who has not been initiated.
In the presence of the Guru, one should not wear the sandals out of excessive zeal;
this is explained in the Sarvajñānottara as follows:
"An umbrella must not be held in front, nor a turban, nor sandals."
Furthermore, one should not wear a crown or similar ornaments while in the presence of the Guru during a period of ritual impurity.
One should not engage in teaching, nor in exposition, nor in disputes with disciples;
rather, staying in the presence of the teacher, one should provide instruction to both the teacher and the disciple.

In the presence of his guru, he should not ascend a seat, a bed, or a vehicle that is higher than the guru's. Remaining on a lower seat than the guru, he should stay there with him as his sole refuge.
The things to be avoided by these [practitioners] have been explained in detail in the *Kānyācārapaddhati*; let that be understood from there. In the *Suprabheda*:
"Always remembering my form, one should always recite the mantra of Śiva."
He should cause him to discard the rudrākṣa beads, the sacred thread, and even the disciple's status itself.

A woman and a Śūdra should avoid the sacred thread (*upavīta*) and the upper garment (*uttarīya*). If it is asked how the fourth [caste] can wear the sacred thread despite such prohibitory statements based on specific reasons: a Śūdra [may wear] the topknot and the thread for divine purposes with divine mantras.
It is merely a matter of retention.
By the reversal of the sequence at the end, the king and his kingdom perish. This prohibition pertains specifically to the retention of Vedic mantras, and not to those of the Āgamas.
The state of being the object of wearing [the sacred thread]. As stated in the *Kāmika*:

"The mantras of Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Jyeṣṭha correspond respectively to the Brahmins and the other castes; they wear that sacred thread with the mantra prescribed for their own respective caste."

Then, one should instruct the disciples. Thus it is stated in the Niśvāsa: "From this day forward, you are considered the teacher of your own self and of the Śiva-mantra; you must constantly bestow grace upon those dwelling in the four stages of life (āśramas)."
The exposition, the worship, and the instruction of the teacher and disciple— he too,
having replied "So be it," should indeed receive that command upon his head.

If it is the formal transfer of authority (*adhikāra-samarpaṇa*), one should, after having thoroughly honored the disciple as oneself, hand over the book to the *kartṛ* (the officiant) during the day;
from today onwards, whatever authority has been transferred by me to you, that must be exercised by you.
Meanwhile, [the transition occurs] from elsewhere through the transference of the sacrifice.
In the Niśvāsa [Tantra],
having worshipped Karaṇī, Kartarī, along with the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and so forth, together with the [mantras] beginning with *asya*, one should offer the office of authority (*adhikāra*).
The specific distinction of the teacher who confers authority (*adhikāra*) is stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"In this way, one possesses authority as long as it is transmitted from one [teacher] to another."
But one who has transferred his authority should perform the accumulation of ritual actions.
Thus it is said in the Kālottara:
"Having then surrendered one's own office, one should always practice one's own yoga in a desolate place or in a forest,
remaining self-restrained and free from desire."
However, in the case of a dependent dedication, the verse beginning with "The authority of others... (*anya-prabhṛti-yaścitādhikāra*) should be recited;

yet, in that instance, a formal salutation (*namaskāra*) is not to be performed. Even though the dedication of authority has been made, when once again seeking to discharge that authority, one should obtain the *icchāsechavajra*.

Having performed the self-initiation (*ātma-dīkṣā*), and having offered a thousand oblations with this [mantra], one should become [the deity] in form and perform the concluding rites of initiation. Or, one should offer a thousand oblations with the [mantra of] Śiva; [thus one attains] authority.
Then, having given it back by way of Śaṅkara’s path.
Whatever office you wish to perform, you shall do it according to your desire,
until the end of this body, as granted by me according to the prescribed rite.
In the *Jñānaratnāvalī*, the fruit of the two offices (*adhikāra*) is stated:
"Therefore, through the office, there is union (*sāyujya*) in the supreme state;
the office-state is his enjoyment in the state of Sadāśiva; at the end of that, eternal liberation is declared."
Thus, according to the certainty of the treatise.
Then, having prostrated before the Guru Śiva—
[who is] the Guru in embodied form who has commanded the initiation from beginning to end— he [is one] who has reached the further shore of the Saṃhitā.
O Śiva, you have been consecrated by me.
"By your grace, may he perform his office without obstacle"—thus one should inform [the deity].
He too, having worshipped Śiva, should inform him: "May there be no obstacle. Then the Guru, having brought that fire into proximity, [should offer] five [oblations] with the *saṃhitā*...

Having satisfied the pentad of kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti and ending with Śānti, along with their presiding deities, by means of five oblations for each, and having likewise offered five oblations for each of the five [faces], one should speak as follows. Thus it is said in the Mṛgendra:
"By this, all the levels (bhūmis) become the domain of this [initiate] who holds authority. Regarding the state of being an object...
Take refuge [in him] and grant permission; he is the leader.

Then, the preceptor should offer the *pūrṇāhuti*. Regarding the meaning of the mantra "kṛtamoma": "O you who consist of the subtle elements (*bhūtamaya-tattva*), whose forms are the worlds, the kalās, and the [levels of] authority—by the command of Īśvara, you [should bestow] upon this initiate the initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth desired by him."

"O you who are intent on activity, resort to the range of this [deity]; likewise, O Kalātattva, O Lord of the World, grant permission for [him] to perform his own duties and so forth. Having thus spoken with the mantra, [the officiant], together with the Śiva-mantra, [places] the hand with fingers fully extended...

To remove the state of being saline (ūṣaratva), for the purpose of cutting the cord with the tip of a bamboo splinter, and for the sake of illuminating the mantra, one should perform the kindling of the hand that has been scorched like a sword-blade. Thus it is said in the *Mṛgendra*:
One should touch the tip of the root-mantra with the tip of the Śivādi-bhikara; this is for the purpose of inflaming the mantra like a sword and for the sake of severing the bonds and so forth.
Therefore, having performed the *homa* here with that hand, the preceptor, for the sake of completing the entire *homa* rite,
should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Then, having placed flowers and other offerings into his hand, [he should place them] upon the pitcher, the flame, and the mandala.
Having caused him to prostrate before himself and led him to the presence of Śiva, one should announce his name, lineage, and so forth. As stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"Having placed [the disciple] within the maṇḍala while recollecting the Prāsāda mantra, [one should perform the rite] with whichever mantra..."
Then the flower, consisting of that very name and lineage, shall fall.
Īśāna, Vaktra, Vidyeśa, Ghorabrahma, Sadyojāta, Rudra, Vāma,
and Huṃkāra— these nine are said to be the ninefold [forms].
Surrounding Śveta and the others are the hosts of Rudras ending with Gaṇāntaka; in Raurava,
their names should be proclaimed in succession according to their respective order.
One should especially avoid women, eunuchs, and those of neuter gender.

O wise one, one should never proclaim the male gender (*pulliṅga*) for all [the names] through verbal expressions; however, there is a specific distinction regarding the Śvetas, namely the supreme *gotrasūtra*.
The crest-lock of Śiva is likewise light; Sāvitrī is the one who moves through the sky. The group of sages beginning with Kaśyapa is said to be their lineage (gotra).

That which was previously declared at the time of the descent [of the teaching] in the language of Śiva is here prescribed as the lineage (*gotra*) within the sphere of experience (*paryāgocara*), according to that very Sūtra.
In the *Kāmika*: "The characteristic of the lineage (*gotra*) for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas is the preceptor (*ācārya*);
there can be no lineage for a Śūdra. Such is the doctrine regarding the rule of lineages."
"You should favor him with action prescribed by the scriptures; you should listen to auspicious knowledge and cause it to be heard by those who seek it."
After a disciple has resided for one year, the wise teacher should perform the initiation (*dīkṣā*).
This *Mṛgendra* [Tantra] should be explained to seekers; it must be heard by you with devotion, and [the teaching] should be practiced extensively.
Abundant knowledge, duty, what is to be done, and great splendor.
Having abandoned laziness, O Teacher, one should act for the benefit of devotees; having established the images of Śiva and others, one should pray to them most fervently.

Even with very little fire-offering, recitation, and worship, one who does not neglect the daily observances may dwell there; and even with worldly [offerings], there is a delightful fragrance that is free from conflict.
Whatever has been prescribed as beneficial and whatever has been prohibited shall be taught;
all that must be followed by those who conform to what ought to be done.
In Raurava, by the command of Śiva, one should perform [the rites] beginning with Kṣaṇa and ending with Pratiṣṭhā; from Pratiṣṭhā up to Utsava; and from Utsava until the end of Niśā.
