Having thus promised "So be it," the wise one, with the consent of the preceptor, should then perform the *prāyaścitta* (expiatory rite), beginning with the *pūrṇāhuti* (final oblation).
At this point, one should dismiss the sacrifice.
Having circumambulated the fire clockwise, one should pay homage to the teacher. As stated in the *Suprabheda*:
She gave a sacrificial fee into his mouth, free from any desire for wealth; likewise, she offered him a vajra-ornament, a crown, and earrings.
One should cause the preceptor to receive a golden sacred thread, golden flowers as an offering, and items such as a deer-skin bed and seat.
Whether in a chariot, a palanquin, on a horse, an elephant, or in a carriage, he should then enter his own home after performing the circumambulation of the village.

If he is silent, observing silence, bathing three times a day, well-versed in the doorways [of ritual], self-controlled, a bestower of boons, peaceful, and adorned with white garlands and unguents— then he is Śaṅkara.
One who possesses a yogic belt, a rosary, a girdle of muñja grass, a deerskin, and the sacred grass—
such a person should worship the lineage of Śiva there with garments, gold, and finger-rings, as well as the Brāhmaṇas.
One should feed the devotees of Śiva there; at that time, one should cause them to be well-fed.
One should feed the members of the *samaya* and cause all the goddesses (*devījana*) to eat as well.
Thus, having received initiation, the *ācārya* should perform [the rites] for the sake of attaining success in the mantra. Likewise, in the *Svāyambhuva*:
One should observe the vow of the preceptor, the supreme among all vows.
One should meditate upon the collection of mantras from Sadyojāta up to Śiva.
For three fortnights, one should sleep on the ground, eat only at night, and always consume *caru* (sacrificial porridge).

One should perform the recitation daily, a thousand times, without distraction; at the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) every day, being protected according to the sequence.
With ghee, or with sesame seeds mixed with milk, or with rice grains, or with *vrīhi* rice,
or with sacrificial fuel-sticks, or even with curd or barley.
One should worship with bilva fruits, bilva leaves, or auspicious flowers fit for sacrifice;
then, upon the completion of the vow, one should first worship the mandala.
And for three days at both the beginning and the end, one should consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
As stated in the *Kāmika*: p. 1564) [End of citation]

The Guru should practice the form of Śiva together with His Power (Śakti) and His limbs according to his capacity; this alone shall be the vow of the Ācārya, the most excellent among all vows declared. At its conclusion, having worshipped Śiva within the Maṇḍala as Anantavijaya, he should [worship] himself with one [offering].
One should perform the consecration with the Śiva-pitcher as prescribed; then they shall obtain that fruit.
Likewise, at the time of undertaking the vow in the Kriyā-āgama, the wise preceptor and the practitioner should likewise consecrate themselves for the sake of infinite victory.

In the *Kālottara*:
"I shall proclaim the initiation of yoga (*yogadīkṣā*) in brief, and not in detail.
Likewise, in the *Cintyaviśva*:
In the sense of the verbal root *yuj* as "union," the conjunction of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Śiva is called *yoga*; it is clearly stated that this is the path of the self (*sahamārga*).
The knowledge that brings about the destruction of non-existence and the manifestation of existence, joined with the principle of Śiva— this is called the initiation of yoga.
The mandala, the pavilion, the ritual pitcher, the worship of the deities, and so forth, should be performed according to the previously mentioned rules,
accompanied by self-restraints and observances.
One should initiate an excellent disciple who is endowed with such qualities as being free from greed and possessed of the desire to attain ultimate auspiciousness.

O Nandikeśvara, the illumination of the mantra, the satisfaction [of the deities], and so forth, should be performed as before; furthermore, one should carry out the entire fire-ritual according to the previously stated rules.
The Guru should worship Vāgīśvara and Vāgīśā as before; and [perform] the piercing and so forth upon the chest of the disciple with a flower, as previously described.
One should perform the purificatory rites (saṃskāras), beginning with conception (garbhādhāna), according to the previously prescribed rules;
thereafter, one should also contemplate the ten channels (nāḍīs) within the body of the disciple.
Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and likewise Suṣumnā; Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Pūṣā, and Yaśasvinī.
Alambuṣā, Kuhū, Śaṅkhinī, and Daśamī, as well as the fourteen vital airs beginning with Prāṇa, were all present together.
The first wind is prāṇa, as well as apāna and vyāna; udāna and samāna, and nāga and kūrma as the seventh.
Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya are thus declared; likewise Vaiśānta and Mukhyaka constitute the internal ruler (antaryāmin) of the phenomenal world (prapañcaka).
Thus, these fourteen vital airs, beginning with prāṇa, have been described;
and these winds circulate within those channels (nāḍīs).
The stabilization of the winds and the channels in their respective locations occurs through the recitation of the Praṇava, Śakti, and the seed-syllable of Śiva, and so forth.
One should establish, worship, and meditate upon it, and contemplate it as having the form of Śiva. Among the channels (nāḍīs), three are principal: Suṣumnā, Iḍā, and Piṅgalā.
Among those [channels] as well, the preeminence of the Suṣumṇā is proclaimed; in its center is the Brahma-nāḍī, the supreme abode of Śiva and Śakti.
Beginning from the *mūlādhāra* and ending at the *brahmarandhra*, its location should be understood as characterized by nine supports (*ādhāras*).
Then the space between the anus and the penis, followed by the base of the penis, then the navel, the heart,
and thereafter the base of the throat.
The root of the palate, the bow (the space between the eyebrows), the center of the brows, the forehead,
and the aperture of Brahma— these are declared to be the nine streams.
The mūlādhāra has four petals, and above that there are six petals;
its location is considered to be at the distance of one finger-breadth from the anus.
The throat is declared to be the twelfth, and the root of the palate the sixteenth;
likewise, the forehead and the space between the eyebrows are the station of Śiva immediately following.
One should sequentially recollect three hundred and sixty [deities] according to their distinct colors:
first the golden-hued, then the crystal-hued, and immediately after that the fire-colored.
Resembling the rising sun and possessing a brilliance like that of the sun,
it was composed of the splendor of rain and was beyond the reach of mental conceptualization.
In these locations, one should designate the causes such as the killing of a Brahmin;
[the presiding deities are] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
One should contemplate right there the supreme Śiva, who consists of the power of action, the power of knowledge, and the power of will, as the locus of the orbs of fire, sun, and moon.
The fire-maṇḍala is at the two nāgas, the sun-maṇḍala is at the heart,
and the moon-maṇḍala is said to be between the two bows.
The *bindu* is in the *kriyā-śakti*, but the *nāda* is not in the *śakti*; in the *icchā-śakti*, *kalā* is said to reside, and therein alone is the supreme nectar (*paramāmṛta*).
Above that, in the abode of Śiva, is the supreme nectar of bliss; having meditated thus, one should contemplate the ninefold mantra within its center.
Having sprinkled the body of the disciple with this water,
the preceptor [should perform the rite] so that it becomes like the blazing of the fire within the sacrificial pit fanned by the wind.

In the same way, one should utter that mantra situated in the location of the support; and in the support of the rosary, one should utter the *tāra* (oṃ), the *marāla* (haḥ), and [the seed-syllables] joined with Śakti and Śambhu.
Or, one should recite [the mantra] nine times in sequence at the tip of a fresh blade of *darbha* grass,
joined with the *bindu*, *nāda*, and *kalā*, extending as far as the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
The supreme teacher should cause a light resembling a spider’s thread to emerge;
he should contemplate it as the form of the mantra, having the appearance of a blazing lamp-flame.

One should visualize them as flashing like lightning against one another, strung together on a thread; having meditated thus and performed worship, one should worship [the deity] within oneself and in the disciple.
Having performed worship according to the prescribed rite, one should carry out the laying out of the lines; one should then contemplate the dimensions of the five lines beginning with the *śikhā*.
One should lay down five lines: ending at the *bindu*, ending at the heart, ending at the navel, extending to the body of Viṣṇu, and reaching the region of Brahmā.
Thus, the fivefold Sūtra, which is conjoined with the heart of the disciple, consists of the ear and so forth,
speech and so forth, sound and so forth, and utterance and so forth.
One should place the twenty principles upon the face-thread; on the heart-thread, one should place the triad of mind, intellect, and ego.
Mind, passion, and illusion are at the thread of the navel;
destiny, necessity, and time are always at the thread of the foundation.

One should sequentially place the pure Māyā and the pure Kalā, which constitute the two principles (tattvas), followed specifically by sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and striking (tāḍana) with the weapon-mantra (hetimantra).
Having entered the *kāra* through the practice of proper exhalation (*recaka*),
one's own consciousness, ending with the *ajapā*, becomes distinct as before.
One should apply [the mantra] with the *saṃhāramudrā* to the three faces as well:
*oṃ hāṃ hāṃ ātmane namaḥ*. This constitutes the pervasive protection, as well as the offering for presence (*saṃnidhāna*).
The visualization of the emanation and the worship should be performed as before; in this same way, one should apply it to other channels that have become [manifest] in the sūtras.
O Nandikeśvara, having drawn forth the consciousness of the disciple, one should unite it with one's own self; as before, there is the union with the vessel—thus one should contemplate.
One should perform the purificatory rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* according to the previously prescribed rule; then, one should likewise dismiss both Vāgīśī and Vāgīśa.
Having invoked Brahmā, who is seated upon a lotus, one should then worship him; one should offer white barley-grains to him until the bliss of the ears and other senses is attained.
One should place twenty *tattvas* upon the face-thread (*mukhasūtra*).
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃ, to the one with Brahmā, the nose, so'haṃ svāhā. Oṃ hrīṃ haṃ, to the one with Brahmā, the skin, so'haṃ svāhā. Oṃ hrīṃ haṃ, to the one with Brahmā...

The eye is I, svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ haṃ, together with Brahman, I am that, svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ haṃ, together with Brahman, the skin is I, svāhā! Speech is I, svāhā! The hands are I, svāhā! The feet are I, svāhā! The anus is I, svāhā!

Oṃ so'haṃ svāhā! Oṃ so'haṃ, the arrival, svāhā! Oṃ so'haṃ, the departure, svāhā! Oṃ so'haṃ, touch, svāhā! Oṃ so'haṃ, form, svāhā! Oṃ so'haṃ, taste, svāhā! Oṃ so'haṃ, smell, svāhā! Oṃ so'haṃ, speech, svāhā! Oṃ so'haṃ, grasping, svāhā!
"To movement, I am; svāhā! To emission, Soma; svāhā! To bliss, I am; svāhā!
With these twenty mantras, one should offer the bride-price (*brahmaśulka*).
"For this child whose bonds have been completely burnt away here, one should cause him to hear this command of Śiva once again for the sake of his awakening."

Having taken the thread from the mouth [of the vessel] and coiled it as before, one should place it into the *sruva* ladle filled with clarified butter and perform the oblation (*homa*) with the *astra-mantra*.
Then, O Nandikeśvara, one should release Brahmā through the left channel from the *kumbhaka* state, establish him in the *mūlādhāra*, and worship him there.
One should join the lunar orb, freed from its fifth part consisting of the stain, back into the Viṣṇu-thread from the waking state into the dream state.
As before, one should perform the striking, the entry into the womb of Vāgīśī, and the consecration as previously described; then, one should again invoke Viṣṇu.
O Nandikeśvara, all the worship and libations are as before;
by virtue of your authority over Viṣṇu, I shall initiate you for the sake of liberation.
"You should be favorable; thus you should inform Viṣṇu. Then one should make Viṣṇu the mind, the intellect, and the ego-function.
Oṃ hrīṃ saṃ saḥ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, so'haṃ svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ haṃ saḥ, the intellect of Viṣṇu, so'haṃ svāhā! Haṃ-kāra, so'haṃ svāhā!
In this manner, one should offer the bride-price (śulka) and then bid farewell to Govinda.
Having invoked [the deity] into the consecrated site, one should establish and worship it in due order;
then, having brought the thread from the heart and made it circular as before.
Having placed a sruva ladle filled with clarified butter, one should perform the oblation (homa) with the *heti-mantra*.
One should visualize [the deity] as auspicious, resembling the moon, free from the five stains (*kalaṅka*).
Then, one should apply [the consciousness] to that which is in deep sleep;
one should worship the consciousness with water for the feet at the cord of the navel. All the preliminary rites and consecrations are to be performed as before.
Having invoked Rudra, [he said]: "For this child, whose bonds have been entirely burnt away by you, [grant] stability..."
Furthermore, one should not bind him; rather, one should cause him to hear the command of Śiva. For the sake of his welfare, one should cause the bride-price to be given with devotion, as before.
One should cause the mind, passion, and the māyā-portion to be offered right there:
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃ rudrāya cittaṃ sohaṃ svāhā | Oṃ hrīṃ haṃsaḥ rudrāya rāgaṃ sohaṃ svāhā |
In this manner, one should cause the mantra to be bestowed along with devotion; then, one should sequentially establish it ending with Rudra in the region of the Maṇipūraka.
Having invoked the deity, who possesses a luster equal to the orb of the moon when devoid of its three parts and its dark spot,
during the state of deep sleep (suṣupti), one should worship with the heart-mantra (hṛdayamantra).
"Since this child, whose bonds have been completely burnt away, is to be bound by you once again,
you should cause him to hear this command of Śiva."
Furthermore, O Nandikeśvara, the Lord shall cause the bride-price to be given, as well as the knowledge of destiny and time, with the mantra-encasement as before.
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃ saḥ vidyā sohaṃ svāhā | Oṃ hrīṃ haṃ saḥ īśvarāya niyatiṃ svohaṃ svāhā ||
p.
1587) Oṃ hrīṃ haḥ saḥ kālaṃ sohaṃ sva * *. Endowed with devotion, one should perform the offering of white [substances] with these [mantras]. Therefore, having invoked the Lord (Īśvara)...
One should cause [the deity] to sleep in the heart-lotus.
Having established [the deity] according to the prescribed rite, being endowed with devotion and having conquered the senses,
one should take the thread located at the base and wipe it as before.

Having placed a vessel full of clarified butter at the tip of the sacrificial ladle, one should perform the oblation with the Astra-mantra; then one should carry out the procedure for the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) beginning with the removal of the sprouts of bondage (*pāśāṅkura-nivṛtti*).
One should fashion a mark that is fourfold, inferior yet possessing a luster equal to the moon; at the end of the fourth part, one should join it with the form of the Self.
The performance of the rites such as striking and the purificatory consecrations (*saṃskāra*) are as before;
having invoked [the deity] up to Sadāśiva, one should worship with devotion.
Being composed, one should offer pure māyā and pure kalā as the bride-price;
having united them with the root mantra, one should first perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the mantras.
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃ saḥ oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Sadāśiva; [I am] the pure Māyā, so 'haṃ, svāhā! Oṃ hrīṃ haṃ saḥ hauṃ, obeisance to Sadāśiva; [I am] the pure Kalā, so 'haṃ, svāhā!
In this manner, O Nandikeśvara, the offering of the white [substance] should be performed.
"Having united with this young animal whose sins have been entirely burnt away by you, you must not depart again;
rather, you should cause him to hear the command of Śiva."
Having invoked the supreme state of Sadāśiva into the purified body,
one should perform the installation and worship with devotion.
Then,
having taken up the thread and coiled it as before,
one should offer oblations into a vessel filled with ghee at the tip of a deer-horn, using the *hṛdayāṇu* (heart-mantra).
Then, one should again meditate upon consciousness as being free from all blemishes, possessing a luster equal to the king of autumns, and consisting of a mass of pure splendor.
Having taken up the Haṃsa-mantras, one should join them with the Praṇava; then, having joined the Praṇava and the Śakti-bīja, one should join them with the Mūla-mantra.

Having recited this mantra— *oṃ saḥ oṃ hrīṃ hauṃ caitanyāya hauṃ*— one should apply it to the *mūlādhāra*. Having recited this mantra— *oṃ saḥ oṃ hrīṃ hauṃ caitanyāya hauṃ*— one should apply it to the *mūlādhāra*.
One who is united with the state of Śiva should also join the pure Self to that which is the wealth of consciousness— immaculate, tranquil, eternal, and devoid of all [attributes].
Beginning from the *mūlādhāra* and extending to the end of the *dvādaśānta*,
one should contemplate the form of the *Navātman* mantra, joined with the resonance (*nāda*) as it is being uttered.
With this very mantra, one should touch [the body] with the tip of a blade of darbha grass; beginning from the *mūlādhāra*, one should join it at the *dvādaśānta*.

Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, the Guru should cause [the disciple] to perform prostrations and the like; then, having performed the consecration, he should contemplate, "I am Śiva."

Having worshipped again with perfumes and other offerings, the knower of the ritual procedure should perform the remaining rites as before; he should then bestow the meditation belt (yogapaṭṭa) and so forth with the *kavaca* mantra.
In the initiation of yoga through knowledge (jñāna), no preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) is required;
one should perform the sacrifice to Śiva and worship the feet of the Guru.
"One who is endowed with the initiation of Yoga is Śiva himself on the surface of the earth.
Thus ends the section on the procedure for initiation in the *Dīkṣādarśa*, composed by Vedajñāna, the son of Vāmadeva.
Now, the ritual procedure for initiation into the knowledge of yoga is described.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"I shall now proclaim the initiation of knowledge (*jñānadīkṣā*), which is the true means for liberation; it is an effort that makes manifest the pervasiveness of Śiva and is free from delusion."
Likewise, for disciples who are endowed with previous initiation, this is the most excellent;
it consists merely of the non-differentiation of Śrī, wherein there is no differentiation of the vital breaths whatsoever.

Thus, through devotion to the Guru, one should cause the initiation of knowledge (jñānadīkṣā) to be performed; it is of three kinds: that born of the individual soul (āṇava), that born of power (śākta), and that born of Śambhu (śāmbhava).
The initiation of Śakti and Śambhu is performed by means of the [five] Tattvas;
whereas the Āṇava initiation is performed by others according to the distinctions of "dull-intense" and so forth.
O Nandikeśvara, having constructed a variegated pavilion for the mandala and other rites as previously described, using especially the aforementioned materials;

Especially on the night of the curd-offering, one should avoid the rite of formal acceptance (adhivāsana) and instead honor the disciple with fragrant flowers, incense, ornaments, and other such items.
Fragrant unbroken rice, flowers, incense, lamps, and likewise food offerings— endowed with all these materials and accompanied by virtuous associates.
Having thus performed the purification of the ritual substances according to the previously stated procedure, one should worship the mandala there, especially at midnight.
Having adorned and placed [the deity] upon the seat, especially as one called Vajra, one should likewise contemplate the mind of Śiva as it is attained,
as well as the temporal path to its end.
Then, the teacher, through constant yoga and devotion to Śiva, should enter the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā) and perform the installation, which is nectar itself.
O leader of the path, one should recite with the Śiva-mantra and with power until knowledge arises through the intellect; that state of stability is the end.
Having recited [the mantra] and attained supreme bliss, the Guru, seated at a distance, should place that which has been meditated upon into the mouth of the disciple.
The *Kāritatantra* itself is flavorful and within the scope of disciples; the temple is the *Śivamantra*, and Vāgīśī is the *Śaktimantra*.
Having first accomplished [the practice] for a month, one should perform oblations with the mantra;
from that which is self-evident, great knowledge arises, like the brilliance of the sun.
Yogas joined with the essences, the mandala accompanied by mudrās, dance, song, and instrumental music— play according to one's own will proceeds.
In the body where perpetual bliss has arisen, there is neither hunger nor sleep; one should perform dancing, bathing, and running with pure clarity.
It is endowed with seven steps and possesses the qualities of stairways; the first is said to have three strands, while the second has five parts.

The five superknowledges (pañcābhijñā) are in the third [section], while the eightfold accomplishment (siddhi) is in the fourth. There are ten [units] for each of the two fives, and the sixth shall consist of ten palas.
Ānanda is the seventh; they are to be accomplished through reflection. Āṇava consists of trembling and so forth, while Śānta consists of the two: poetry and [the rest].
The Śāmbhava state, which is the mind devoid of hair and other [sensory objects], is considered to be threefold:
like a mirage, like the first opening of the mouth, and like the spreading of a lamp's light.
Through one's own seeking, the entire pentad of lamps enters; this is the transformation of increase, consisting of knowledge and preceded by the memory of what was previously sought.
The divine eye and ear, the five superknowledges,
and the eightfold siddhis beginning with *aṇimā* are accomplished in the form of gnosis.
Likewise, the seedless cause, the striking with poison,
the blazing with fires, and the conquest of the wind through the channels.
The stainless *bindu* and *nāda*, as well as the transference of the body,
the vision of smoke and light, and the independent performance of the act of death.
Now listen to the eighteen powers of the Ten Powers, which consist of [the knowledge of] lifespan, karma, requisites,
liberation, and the inclination of others' faculties.
First, there is birth and power; then the fruit consisting of supreme reflection on the Dharma;
and thereafter, greatness and so forth, which are indeed to be accomplished through the sequence of the truths.
The wise know that from these, one attains tenfold increase in knowledge and so forth; it is innate, beyond deception, unbroken, and full of splendor.
p.
1592) Within the lake, all the leaders of the three worlds [are present]; and the yogic accomplishment of the disciple shall become intense and even more intense.
And Nipati, along with Daṇḍa, Kalāvati, and Guṇa, were destroyed by the Veda of the Vidyādhara through the power of his commenced karma.
This is declared to be the Śāktopāya; the Śāmbhava [is taught] by you... Indeed, the one called Sadāśiva shines equally upon the staff of the arrow.
The Śāmbhavopāya has been proclaimed by Brahmā, the bearer of pure knowledge; the bestower [of grace] acts in accordance with whatever kind of devotion the disciple possesses.
Having understood and observed the individual souls (āṇava) and other [impurities] through the signs of those worthy of the twice-born,
one should, out of compassion, bestow the hand of Śiva.
Afterwards, the preceptor should cause him to perform prostration and have his name bestowed; he should then cause the Padmadaṇḍa and other rites to be performed as before.
Even if one has performed the fire-rite, it would not truly be considered a fire-rite performed;
one should offer the circle of the body and the vital breath to the Guru.
Having first obtained the permission of the Guru,
one should, endowed with constant devotion, experience the realization of that [instruction] according to his command.
He should offer his entire wealth to that guru; at that time, his own autonomy is relinquished.
The wise one should act for the sake of the guru through both speech and deed; then, O Nandikeśvara, having performed the consecration as before.
(1593) With all ornaments, perfumes, and so forth, as well as garments and other decorations,
the Guru should further adorn the disciple and cause him to perform prostration.
O Ānandikeśvara, one should also dismiss the deities of the sacrifice and so forth.
Thus ends the procedure for the initiation of the knowledge of Yoga. Now, the procedure for the initiation of higher realization (vijñāna) is described.
Likewise, in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"Henceforth, I shall explain initiation (*dīkṣā*) combined with higher knowledge (*vijñāna*),
because it is preceded by specialized knowledge and because of the manifestation of the state beyond the waves [of dualistic thought]."

That is declared to be the initiation of consciousness (*vijñānadīkṣā*), the most excellent of all initiations; for one who has been initiated, it is free from [the need for] mantras, free from ritual actions, and free from meditation and the like.
Because it accomplishes full perfection, initiation is indeed purifying; for that state of Śiva is bestowed, which is ever eager for hearing [the teachings].
Always desiring service to the Guru, free from impurity, and intent on obeying his commands,
whether in happiness or even in suffering.
And there is a lack of independence in that place, like clay and other materials belonging to a potter; this is likewise true even when falling into the ocean or leaping into fire.
Even in the face of falling upon tigers or snakes, the command practiced in the Vedas must not be cast aside;
if one possesses devotion, that has been declared by him.
One should always remain proficient in one's duties and free from attachment;
having cast away wealth and other possessions upon the ground, one should pursue the path of knowledge.
Mother, father, son, brothers, and so forth— by whose grace the Guru is fulfilled and the bestower of all goals.
That which exists sequentially through the mantra of mental activity is the initiation of knowledge; indeed, that which is called "higher knowledge" (vijñāna) shall possess all sovereign power.
In a beautiful and auspicious place, at a delightful time, and during pleasant circumstances—
when both [the practitioner and the consort] experience an equality of happiness.
At that very moment, that initiation—which destroys all impurities—is established in the five supports; likewise, the Guru is established within the body.
And within the circle of the head is the supreme circle of the Guru, which consists of all witnesses and is Śiva,
the ultimate cause.

Afterwards, by the grace of the Guru, one should perform the placement of the mantras (*mantranyāsa*) in its entirety; indeed, all sacred pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*) reside upon the palm of the Guru’s hand.

The Brahma-tīrtha is indeed at the base of the thumb; that of the gods and the mantras is at the tips of the fingers; but the Devarṣi-tīrtha, which should be well-served, is at the joints of the finger-segments.
The *kaniṣṭhāmla* is the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) of humans and sages; that which is at the base of the hand is called the sacred bathing place of the spirits (*bhūta*).
The *pitṛtīrtha* (ancestral sacred site) is situated between the index finger and the thumb;
one should understand that the seven sacred sites (*saptatīrtha*) exist in the hand for the purpose of giving gifts.
Having meditated upon the sacred fords (*tīrtha*) as being in the form of the *bindu*, [one should contemplate] the moment;
his right hand, moreover, is pervaded by the *śiva-mantra*.

The Guru should cause the disciple to visualize [the deity] pervading [himself] by means of the mantra of attraction (vāmanayukti), and he should have the disciple honored with perfumes, flowers, lamps, and forms.
Having seated him in a comfortable posture with his gaze fixed [between the eyebrows], the disciple should become such as this; immediately thereafter, he shall become a guru.
Then, one should contemplate the fire of Śiva arising from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) at the root-stream (mūladhārā),
as well as the clarified butter in its place and the nectar situated within the lunar orb.
The preceptor, having established the fire within the mandala, should prepare the ladle (sruk),
the small ladle (sruva), the fuel-sticks (samidh), and likewise the ritual portions (kalās).
Raising his arms, which are like bows with roots for arrowheads, up to his throat, he should meditate upon the pure,
the tawny, and the moon and sun.
And having brought about prosperity by means of the thread of the nature of *nāda*, [one proceeds] because the fire has already been established previously,
and likewise without the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*).

The *tāra* (om), the power (*śakti*), the *ajapā*, and *śiva* (hauṃ), with another [syllable] as a *saṃpuṭa*, ending with the word "flower" (*puṣpa*)—this indeed shall be the mantra; it is the unsurpassed oblation of knowledge (*jñānāhuti*).
Oṃ saṃ seṃ sūryasoma śā na tatpuruṣābhyāṃ sohaṃ hauṃ svāhā | Oṃ hrīṃ haṃ saḥ oṃ; one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) in the mūlādhāra by means of the piṅgalanāḍī path.
Oṃ hrīṃ haṃ saḥ oṃ hāṃ īśvaramaya sohaṃ svāhā.
One should subsequently offer oblations to Umā and perform the fire sacrifice (homa) in the water-vessel.

One should perform that which brings happiness and pleases Śiva in the presence of Śiva. In this way, the initiation of women is described among the five types of teachers.
Either in the house of the preceptor or in one's own delightful home,

Having placed a water-pot before that [image], provided with its own cloth and other offerings, one should consecrate the water a hundred times with the five-syllabled mantra.

Having informed Viṣṇu for the sake of removing obstacles, the ritual dismissal (visarjana) should take place; having withdrawn the consciousness into oneself, it should especially be absorbed into one's own self alone.
O Nandikeśvara, one should join it in the middle of the thread upon the head; one should then sprinkle drops of the nectar-water of the arghya upon the disciple's head.

For the sake of purifying the *vidyā-tattva*, one should perform the rite of the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*); at the junction of the twilight, one should contemplate the *śiva-tattva* for half that duration.
Having placed [the mantra] from the head to the topknot, it becomes a sixfold pervasive [protection].
Having struck [the disciple], having taken up the *tattva*, and having cast it into the fire, one should offer libations.

in this section concerning Rudra, I shall initiate those seeking liberation.

One should perform the fire-oblation with the root mantra, the weapon mantra, and the five [mantras], specifically for the concealment of the fetters and for their purification.

With the mantra "Oṃ haṃ śikhāyai huṃ phaṭ," recited over the knife and the weapon (*heti*), one should cut off the topknot (*śikhā*) as previously described.

Having seated her upon a cow-dung seat, one should offer oblations according to the prescribed rite into the fire from the tip of her crest-lock while she remains with the sacrificial ladle (sruk) filled with clarified butter; then one should wash both ladles.

Then, for the sake of unification, one should again employ the clarified butter as being identical with that [Self]; having taken it according to the previously stated rule, one whose form is above the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.

A liṅga made of collyrium, one produced from clay, one arising from cow-dung, a seed-liṅga produced from sand,

Just as it is here, so by that very means is its stability.

Listen attentively to the specific rites for the release from vows and the attainment of the Śaiva state: the Buddhists are established in the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva), while those with matted hair [the Śaivas] reside at the summit of the qualities (guṇa).
O Blessed One, those who follow the command of the Vedas are born from that [source], O Puruṣa; the Māyā-pāśupatas are in the principle of Vidyā, as are those of the Great Vow (Mahāvrata).
The symbols of their vows are as follows, according to the procedure for the extraction of the *liṅga*:
the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*) and the false principles (*vithātattva*) each have their own distinct vow.
Having established them with their respective names, one should worship each one individually;
and having offered oblations with the mantra of each by its own name, one should honor the leader of the path.
Having first joined these channels externally,
one should perform their striking and separation, [placing] the self-mantra established within one's own self.

With that root-mantra, one should offer a thousand oblations into the fire while reciting the *Tadyoḥ* mantra; this worship of the deity, when performed as a sacrifice (*homa*), destroys the fruits of merit.

With the Astra-mantra, eight thousand [oblations] are offered for each individual possessing a *liṅga*; and with the Mūla-mantra, five for each, for the sake of liberation from every principle (*tattva*).

Having extracted the intellect (*buddhi*), the principles (*tattva*), and so forth, one should apply each of those [to their respective places]. Having extracted the ancient tradition (*pūrvācāra*) and the [lineage] born [therefrom], one should apply them.
One should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* with the root mantra one hundred and eight times; then, having offered water as an auxiliary to the vow, one should do so with the *pāśupata* mantra.
Afterwards, having given him a pair of garments, he should perform the rite of initiation; and he should establish him in the stage of the ascetic or in that of the householder.
Having extracted both the traditional practice and that which has arisen [in the lineage], one should apply it;
one should worship with the root mantra a hundred and eight times, ending with the full oblation (pūrṇā).
One should especially initiate him according to his respective initiation; having cast the primary mantras upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila), one should purify them with the Astra-mantra.
Likewise, the procedure for the extraction of the *liṅga* (the central channel) of Pañcārddhakāla, Vaktṛ, and the others is demonstrated in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*. As follows, the Lord states (p.
O Six-faced One, I shall now proclaim the extraction of the *liṅga* for those who are lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika*),
as well as for those with five, three, or two faces, and even for all heretics (*pāṣaṇḍin*).
Having spent five nights or three nights [in preparation], the wise one, mindful of the requirements for the vow, should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) using the Heart-mantra.
One should place the *mātṛkā* there according to the ritual procedure prescribed by rule; one should draw an eight-petaled lotus adorned with the prescribed characteristics.
One should worship the Mātṛkā there by means of the yoga of the thousand-spoked wheel; having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the fire-oblation as before.
The wise man should offer five oblations for each of the five castes in due order; he should perform this with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantreṇa) or with the saṃsāra-mantra.
Having done thus as before, one should generate the ultimate [deity] therein;
having formed the aggregate of the ultimate by means of the reabsorptive [process].
Having performed [the practice] through the yoga of creation and dissolution, one awakens to the ultimate state; even if attached to sense objects, one is not stained by the defects of karma.
Thus, for heretical ascetics who have cultivated their souls, the removal of their sectarian marks (liṅgoddhāra) must be performed;
and for householders, it must be done until death.
Thus ends the procedure for the removal of vows in the *Dīkṣādarśa*. Now, the procedure for initiation on behalf of the deceased (*mṛtakī-dīkṣā*) is described.
Likewise, in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"In the case of a devotee who died without initiation, and one who died having received initiation...
And even while still alive, if there is a desire, the initiation of the deceased is prescribed.
Likewise, in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Even one who has not received the supreme initiation, if he is devoted to the Guru and prostrate before him,
since the individual soul remains [in bondage] for a time, how could there be liberation for him?"
What is the use of that affliction which was undertaken for the sake of liberation?
For how could there exist any action belonging to him that serves as a means to liberation?
O Skanda, for one who is devoted to the guru, self-controlled, of truthful conduct, and firm in his vows, the rite of initiation is prescribed even for one who is dead.

In the event that this very person dies between deities, even if he has not yet received initiation, one should perform the "initiation of the deceased" (mṛtakadīkṣā) and the funeral rite (antyeṣṭi) according to the standard procedure.
Even for one who has died between deities, there is the funeral rite; however, for one who was initiated, [one should perform] the effigy of the deceased.
Having performed [the rite], it should also be performed with *kuśa* grass.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"Then, one should fashion the characteristic marks of the image using thirty-six [types of materials], such as *kuśa* grass, trees, *palāśa* leaves, and the sprouts of the *aśvattha* tree."
One should sprinkle that [image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) ground into a paste.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"Alternatively, O Six-faced One, in the space of the sky, [one should prepare it] with cow-dung mixed with the five products of the cow."
Having performed [this], one should employ it upon that.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"Having placed [the deity] upon a seat of flowers on the right side of the image, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) using buds of *karavīra*."

Alternatively, [one may perform] the "abiding in space" (*vyomasaṃsthā*) with cow-dung and ashes; having bathed [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should then meditate upon it there with the *Sāman* chants.
One should place the triad of powers—Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—in the heart;
one should also assign Yama, Dharma, and all ritual actions.
Having established [the deity] somewhere with the Mahājālaka mantra—

*oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ hūmātmane namaḥ*— one should, by means of this mantra, draw forth the three impurities known as *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārma*. This is for the purpose of binding them through libation (*tarpaṇa*).
One should perform the oblation (homa) with each respective name; having offered five oblations for each, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) beginning from the head.
As stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*:
Then, one should place all the principles (tattvas) starting from the crown of the head down to the feet, as follows:
at the top of the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), *oṃ hāṃ namaḥ to Rodhaśakti*.
Brahmāṇḍa: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śivatattva, whose form is the Bindu. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śiva, who is the Śiva of Śivatattva.
At the top of the head, below the Brahma-randhra: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Śaktitattva. Oṃ hāṃ...
Salutation to Śaktimān, the lord of the principle of Śakti (śakti-tattva).
Above the forehead, at the level of the hairline: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Sadāśiva (sadāśiva-tattva).
Salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the principle of Sadāśiva. Below the uvula (ghaṇṭikā).
Up to the limit of the aggregates: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of Īśvara.
Homage to the one possessing power, the sovereign of the principle of Īśvara. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Śambhu, the sovereign of the principle of Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā).
On the left side: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Māyā (māyā-tattva). Obeisance to Garhaṇeśa, the lord of the principle of Māyā.
On the right side: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Time (kālatattva).
Obeisance to the one named Kāla, the lord of the principle of Time.
On the chest: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of Portion (kalātattva). [Obeisance] to the lord of the principle of Portion.

Salutation to Jñānabindu. At the heart: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Niyati (Destiny). Salutation to the Lord of the principle of Niyati, the Controller. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Vidyā (Knowledge).

Salutation to Consciousness, the lord of the principle of knowledge (*vidyā-tattva*). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of passion (*rāga-tattva*). Salutation to the Giver of Desires, the lord of the principle of passion. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the person (*puruṣa-tattva*). Salutation to the subtle body (*sūkṣma-deha*), the lord of the principle of the person.
In the abdomen: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Prakṛti (Prakṛti-tattva); salutation to Vṛṣāṅka, the presiding lord of the principle of Prakṛti.
In the spinal column: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of Guṇa (Guṇa-tattva); [salutation] to the presiding lord of the principle of Guṇa.
Salutation to the Three Bodies (Trideha).
Between the navel and the genitals: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of intellect (buddhitattva). Salutation to the Buddha, the lord of the principle of intellect.
At the three junctions: *Oṃ ahaṃkāratattvāya namaḥ*.
Homage to Ahaṃkṛta, the lord of the principle of ego (*ahaṃkāratattva*). *Oṃ hāṃ manastattvāya namaḥ*.
Homage to Saṃkalpa, the lord of the principle of mind (*manastattva*).
In the ears: *oṃ hāṃ* homage to the principle of hearing (*śrotratattva*); homage to the Lord of the principle of hearing, the Sky-walker (*vyomacara*).
In the skin: *oṃ hāṃ* homage to the principle of touch (*tvaktattva*); [homage] to the Lord of the principle of touch.
Salutation to the entire body.
In the eyes: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of sight (cakṣustattva). Salutation to Prakāśa, the lord of the principle of sight.
On the tongue: *oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the principle of the tongue (*jihvā-tattva*). Salutation to Mahāvaktra, the lord of the principle of the tongue.

In the nose: *oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the principle of the nose (*nāsā-tattva*); salutation to Viliṃpaka, the lord of the great nose. In speech: *oṃ hāṃ*, salutation to the principle of speech (*vāk-tattva*); salutation to Dundubhi, the lord of the principle of speech.
Homage! To the two hands: *oṃ hāṃ*, homage to the essence of the hand; homage to Samādāna, the lord of the essence of the hand.
At the two feet: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the feet (pādatattva). Salutation to Gamanā, the presiding deity of the principle of the feet.
At the anus: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of the anus (pāyutattva). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the presiding deity of the principle of wind (vāyutattva).
Homage to Kukkṛta. At the genitals: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of the genitals (upasthatattva). Homage to Ghanānanda, the lord of the principle of the genitals.

At the navel: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of sound (śabda-tattva). Salutation to the principle of sound, the subtle resonance (sūkṣma-nāda). Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of touch (sparśa-tattva).
Salutation to the most powerful lord of the principle of touch. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the principle of form (rūpa-tattva).

Homage! Homage to the Lord of the principle of form (rūpa-tattva), Bhānumat. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of taste (rasa-tattva). Homage to Jalada, the Lord of the principle of taste. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the principle of smell (gandha-tattva). Homage to Gandhāṅga, the Lord of the principle of smell.
In the womb (yoni): *oṃ hāṃ* homage to the principle of space (*vyomatattva*). Homage to Sūkṣma, the lord of the principle of space. *oṃ hāṃ* homage to the principle of air (*vāyutattva*).
Homage to Mātariśvan, the lord of the principle of air. [These are] in the intermediate directions within the womb.
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the fire element (agnitattva). Homage to the Lord of the fire element, the treasure-house of splendor.
[This extends] from the base of the womb down to the kneecaps. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the water element (jalatattva).
Salutation to the Lord of the water-tattva, the Lord of Waters.
[Below the knees: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the earth-tattva;
salutation to Śrīkaṇṭha, the Lord of the earth-tattva.
In the gulpādi-lake: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the world of Brahmā; obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the world of Brahmā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the world of Viṣṇu;
obeisance to Viṣṇu, the lord of the world of Viṣṇu. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the world of Śiva.
Salutation to Śiva, the lord of the world of Śiva.
On the back of the feet, beginning from the ankles: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Pātāla;
salutation to Hāṭakeśvara, the lord of Pātāla; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Naraka.

Salutation to Kūśmāṇḍa, the lord of hell, on the big toe—Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Kālāgni. Salutation to Īśvara, the lord of Kālāgni. One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) in sequence from Paraśiva down to Kālāgnirudra.

Having meditated in this way and worshipped according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), one should perform the rite starting from the feet according to the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) for the sake of purification, as previously described. Likewise,
in the *Sarvajñānottara*:

Beginning from the feet, one should place all of them in the fire and purify them; having performed the sacrifice appropriately with those various [substances] in their proper sequence according to the *yoni-mantras*.
Having visualized [the deity] as before, one should withdraw [the visualization] with *paṃ* and *vaṃ* and then rejoin it;
having performed the rites beginning with the impregnation (*garbhādhāna*), one should carry out all the rituals as previously described.
Having thus established [the mind] within all principles, one should likewise unite it with Śiva, [visualizing] milk, ghee, and curd mixed together,
situated upon the tip of a needle.
Having performed this, the wise one should subsequently offer that small image into the fire, after having worshipped it in due order within the center of his heart.
p.
1619) This sequence of awakening is well-established based upon the sacrificial animal (paśu). Having contemplated its form as before, one should contemplate the channel (nāḍī) accordingly.
O Six-faced One, one should deposit the three powers (*śaktitraya*) and both merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) into them;
then, having invoked the Self through the application of the "Great Net" (*mahājāla*), one should firmly establish it as before and worship it.

Having performed everything up to the union with the beloved as before, one should burn [the body]; then, having joined the fire of reality (tattvāgni) and performed the rites accordingly, one should lead [the soul] to Śiva.
In the *Kālottara*:
"From wherever the preceptor (ācārya) may be situated, one should then, at the end of that [mantra],
remember the deceased along with Vyomaśena."
Having extinguished the fire, one should cast those ashes into the waters of the Gaṅgā. Thus, O Six-faced One, the threefold initiation for the living soul has been described here.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for initiation into the deceased.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the funeral rites (antyeṣṭi).
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"O Śaṅkara, you have thus described initiation even for those who are dead;
yet one who is joined with initiation becomes devoid of [proper] conduct."
In the Śrī Kālottara:
"Whether among Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, Praśceśas, or other castes—for all of them, initiation is indeed not [restricted];
that initiation is the Prathameṣṭikā."
The funeral rite (antyeṣṭi) is prescribed to be performed at the very end of life;
but if one passes away without having performed expiation (prāyaścitta), how can such a person be liberated?
Henceforth, O Six-faced One, I shall proclaim [the procedure] regarding the transgression of the conduct of the *samaya*; by this, even one whose body has perished is purified.

Whether performed through ignorance or even with knowledge, when the rite of the final oblation (antyēṣṭi) has been completed, the embodied soul is thus liberated, even from the transgression of the rules (samaya) and other obligations.
In the *Kāmika*:
"A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or likewise a Vaiśya or one born in the direct order from a Śūdra—these may be the Ācāryas or the Sādhakas; the Putrakas are those who abide by the rules."
When their life-force has departed, the final rite (antyēṣṭi) should be performed for those three—
the disciple, the preceptor, and the [other] teacher— endowed with the purification of reality (tattva-śuddhi).
The funeral rite for another person is devoid of the purification of the reality (tattva-śuddhi);
likewise, these three—the preceptor and the others—are devoid of the prescribed conduct.
For one who dies without performing expiation, the funeral rites (antyeṣṭi) are performed;
likewise, the purification of the elements (tattvaśuddhi) and other daily obligatory rites (nityakarman) are properly executed.

For those who have avoided what is forbidden and are free from negligence, the *antyeṣṭi* (funeral rite) is prescribed as consisting solely of the purification of reality (*tattva-śuddhi*), without anything else.
The locations, the rites, the knowledge, and the upward departure (utkrānti) through the distinctions of the Brahma-aperture and so forth have been established;
now the purification of their essential principles (tattva-śodhana) as distinguished by the knowers of Yoga is being described.
Regarding this, the characteristics of the departure [of consciousness] (utkrānti) are stated in the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*: "Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), or otherwise as is comfortable..."
The wise one should break the skull-cup.
Having sequentially transcended the principles (tattvas) and burned them away with fire,
one should enter the imperishable state through the yoga of upward breath (*nāda*) and exhalation (*recaka*).
Thus, O you of excellent vows, the process of departure (utkrānti) has been briefly explained to you.
In the *Sārdhatriśatikā*:
"Having fixed the mind upon the crown of the head, one should slowly utter the name of Hara with the mind."
Having drawn it back, it is established within the external channel.

With devotion to Rudra, one should meditate on the presence [of the breath] as having the reddish luster of the fire within the *kuṇḍalinī*; once it has filled the path of the *ghaṭikā*, one should then cause the *hikkā* (hiccup-like sound) to arise.
Having performed worship, O Skanda, one should cast out the wind situated in the ear;
having thoroughly purified it, one should direct it upward until it reaches the svastika.
Above that is Sadāśiva, and beyond that are Bindu and Nāda; having transcended Bindu and Nāda, one should then follow Śakti.
"Abandoning power (*śakti*), go to the end, to Śiva, the supreme cause; having gone there, O son, one is not born again—this is my promise."
In the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*:
"One should perform neither the rite of offering a funeral ball (*piṇḍakriyā*) nor the rite of water-libations (*udakakriyā*) for him;
rather, the worship of Śiva must always be performed by his disciples in order to discharge their debt."
In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*, it is established that there is no rite of cremation for those who have fallen [from their caste]. As it says:
"For those who have fallen, there shall be no cremation, nor the funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*), nor the collection of bones."
In certain cases, such as at śrāddha ceremonies and the like, one should also shed tears and offer a funeral ball of rice (piṇḍa).

Even for one who has received the specific initiatory observances (*viśiṣṭasamayin*), who seeks the initiation into Nirvāṇa, is devoted to service toward the Guru, and has died before receiving the [final] initiation, the purification of the paths (*adhvaśuddhi*) must be performed together with [the other rites].
As it is stated in the Kāmika:
"For one who possesses the distinguished *samaya* but is of inferior status, and whose mind is intent on 'May *nirvāṇa-dīkṣā* be performed for me,' the *uttara-dīkṣā* must be performed."
Even for one who has failed, the state of being a *pātaka* (one fallen) is addressed; here it is said that purification occurs through an *iṣṭi*.
In the *Niśvāsa*:
"When death has arrived, for one whose body is completely purified by initiation, [there is no fault] regarding the transgression of the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*)."
And for one who has stumbled through negligence.
The funeral rite (antyeṣṭi), however, is performed by Śiva himself for the sake of purification through expiation.
As stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*: "Especially for those who have not been liberated from doubt regarding the observances (samaya)."
Likewise, for those who have resorted to other scriptures, as well as during states of deep sleep or inactivity.
The funeral rites must then be performed; otherwise, one shall not attain the supreme state.
Thus it is stated in the *Sārdhatriśatikālottara*:
"But one who has been initiated, yet violates the rules (*samaya*) at a later time, [offends] the God..."
And one would incur the guilt of a mortal sin against the gurus.

O Guha, for those others who have not abandoned doubt and whose natures are still impure, the funeral rite (antyeṣṭi) is ordained for the sake of removing their sins; the etymological explanation of this is shown in the Vātula [Tantra].
The final rite is the supreme state; it is the entry into reality. When performed according to the prescribed method through the path of yoga, it is called the ultimate funeral rite (atyantyeṣṭi).
In the *Kāmika*:
When the time for the departure of this living being’s vital breath has arrived, the ritual bath of fire (*āgneyasnāna*) is prescribed.
His body was girt with armor.

Likewise, for one desiring liberation, having performed the ritual action of the mantra, that which is to be known is expressed by the term "mantra-body" as the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa) and so forth.

Having worshipped the Lord with the eightfold offering of flowers, for the sake of one desiring liberation, [he should worship] with sandalwood paste and other substances using his own hands or hands made by others.
Having firmly established Maheśvara in the form of a *liṅga* within his heart,
and having touched [the disciple's] head with joined palms, he should cause [the deity] to be present there.
For that purpose, this statement was made in the presence of the Lord of the gods: "O God, this man has been initiated by you and is an observer of Śiva’s command."
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods that the deity has attained the state of Śiva through the performance of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, one should install him in his own place.
One may perform this rite either once or many times; at the time of the departure of the breath (utkrānti), one should recite the Saṃhitā into the vicinity of the ear.
Especially the Śiva-mantra or the five-syllabled mantra (pañcākṣara)— all this should be performed by the preceptor or by another.
By this very person born of that lineage, and by the ritual action which will be described, [it is said] in the *Kālottara*:
"At that time, one should place the mantra into the right ear of the deceased; and for women..."
The oral instruction is prescribed for the left ear.
In that very same *Dattānugraha-paṭala*:
"The man whose body is presided over by Śiva, even if he meets death...
That person shall indeed become Śiva himself, completely liberated from all bonds.
Therefore, at the time of departure, one should clearly touch the *liṅga*;
he who effects the release of the vital breaths becomes Śiva—of this there is no doubt.
In the Kālottara:
"One should perform the rite for the deceased, endowed with all ornaments; having prepared a bed of sand and rice, provided with darbha grass."
In the case of the causal [rite]:

one should accomplish the propitiation of Śiva upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), with the tips and roots of *darbha* grass joined together, the head toward the south, and the feet toward the north.
In the Vātula:
"And thereafter, for the sake of purifying the deceased, one should specifically perform the shaving of the hair.
In the Kāmika:
Having taken up water from a sacred bathing place for the purpose of bathing the deceased whose life-force has departed,
and having bathed him with hundreds of jars of water and other such substances;
If he is a householder, he should cause them to bathe; otherwise, he should perform the ordinary bath. Or, he should prepare various jars or pitchers according to the rules for their installation.

In the case of a deficiency in the establishment and the increase [of offerings], one should provide only water; likewise, the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and so forth, along with cloth, gold, and a bundle of kuśa grass (kūrca).

One should bathe the image with water mixed with unbroken grains (akṣata) according to the prescribed rite, accompanied by the limbs of the Vidyā and the Heart-mantra; or one may perform the initiation (dīkṣā) either under the planets or in a cremation ground.
In the Kālottara:
Having bathed [the image] with cow dung, clay, ashes, fragrant paste, and *āmalaka* fruit— all consecrated by the recitation of the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*) and others—
one should then envelop it with various flowers.
Having likewise performed the purification of the body with turmeric, *āmalaka*, and so forth, according to the *Cintya* (p. 1625), by means of all water and knowledge.
In the *Sarvajñānottara*:
"The knower of mantras, having purified [the image] with clay and water consecrated by the Astra-mantra,
and having smeared it with turmeric and myrobalan, should bathe it with auspicious water."
Having performed the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) in reverse order, one should clothe [the deity];
having adorned [him] with perfumes and flowers, one should offer the sacrificial food (anna).
In the Kāmika:
"Having performed [the ritual] by way of withdrawal (saṃhāra), one should wear a loincloth or a garment;
then, having turned [around], one should adorn oneself with rosaries and other ornaments suitable for decoration."
Having anointed it with sandalwood paste, one should surround it with various flowers; there, on a cloth that is either deep red or white, [one should place] the Vāstu-deity upon the upper garment.
The sacred thread (*upavīta*) should be worn with an upper garment (*sottarīya*), just as if it were new.
In the *Sarvajñānottara* it is said:
"But for Śūdras, the upper garment is excluded there, as is the sacred thread (*pavitraka*)."
He who [places] darbha grasses at the end of those two joints.
In the *Vidveṣaṇasaṃhitā*:
"Then, having bound the feet and likewise the hands with the heart-mantra, and having adorned them with perfumes, flowers, canopies, and garlands of darbha grass..."
In the Vātula [Tantra]:

Having constructed a water-shed (*prapā*) in the courtyard of the house and a walkway in front of the house, one should adorn that water-shed according to the prescribed rite with garlands of *darbha* grass and other ornaments.
Then, having performed purification by bathing, one should smear [the ground] with cow dung;
having adorned it with lamps, flowers, canopies, and garlands of *darbha* grass.

Then, the preceptor, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with sand according to the prescribed measure, should perform a powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*) adorned with every kind of ornament.
Having placed *darbha* grass upon it, one should place [the vessel] on top of that; then, having bound the feet and hands with threads, one should do so while reciting the Heart Mantra.
Now, the procedure for the powder festival (cūrṇotsava) is described.
Likewise, in the *Araurava*:
"Now I shall explain in detail the sequence of the ritual for the powder-festival (*cūrṇotsava*), both for those who have been initiated and for others who uphold the teaching of Śiva."
And for others, as appropriate, there should be a night-powder mixed with oil;
the funeral rite (antyeṣṭi) shall be the initiation of the deceased, through the purification of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan).
One should also perform the powder festival for one who has died, even if they were initiated; however, this dismissal (visarjana) should take place at the conclusion of the festival of the deity.
One should perform this powder festival (cūrṇotsava), which consists of the sacrifice to Śiva, the sacrifice to Vāk, and the sacrifice to Mṛtā,
for the purpose of performing auspicious rites.
If the preceptor does not perform [the rite] there, then no auspiciousness will occur; therefore, for the sake of all auspiciousness, one should cause a powder festival (cūrṇotsava) to be held.
In the Kālottara:
"And at the end of one's life, one should cause the Śivotsava to be performed, wherein the full [offering] is bestowed;
the service beginning with the Pāṇḍava [flowers] and so forth is for the sake of all goals."
The funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi*) shall be the initiation for the deceased (*mṛtadīkṣā*), because it purifies the sixfold path;
and for that person who has become Śiva, the Guru [provides] the attainment of the state of Śiva.

For the purpose of auspiciousness and for the sake of ritual prostration, this powder festival (cūrṇotsava) should take place; one should perform it according to the sequence of the Vedic, Śaiva, and Āgamic traditions.
One should contemplate: one should perform the powder festival at the threshold of the house door, or alternatively,
one should perform the powder festival at the site of a funeral pyre.
Having performed the washing of the feet, the preceptor receives the mantra; [the disciple provides] nine garments and a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).

The wise man, having placed his upper garment over his left shoulder (in the *apasavya* manner), and having performed the smearing with ashes and other rites, as well as the *tripuṇḍra* mark according to the prescribed rule;
The placement for reabsorption has been stated here; perform the purification of the locations.
I shall now describe the procedure for the powder festival: three mandalas in front of the preta.
In the Kālottara:
"The wise one should have a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) made according to the measurement of the teacher's hand;
it should consist of eight *droṇas* of rice and be provided with eight petals and a pericarp."
Having placed the mortar in the center of that [space], and the drum joined with it to the east,
the wise man should place the water-pot in the west, at the four corners.
The most excellent preceptor should place the form of the weapon (astramūrti) in the pitcher;
likewise, he should place Indra’s ashes, Varuṇa’s oil, and Tāmbūla.
Some, however, place a washed loincloth for each of the guardians of the directions;
or alternatively—
durvā grass, unbroken rice, betel leaf, oil, and turmeric powder.
One should place gold ash and a loincloth, starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
In the *Kālottara*:
"On the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should fashion a mortar and likewise a pestle."
Regarding the measurement: twenty finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in length is proclaimed as the best; that which is according to the Smṛti-aṅgula is the middling, while the inferior is in kalā-aṅgulas.
Having tripled the length, the circumference is prescribed; one should divide the length into four parts, and a third part of that is said [to be the width].
The circumference at the base of the two [pillars] should be half the measure of their height;
specifically for the best type, the lip and chest are said to be one finger-breadth [in thickness].
The measurement for the middle and the lowest [types] is said to be one-quarter and one-fifth less than that of the mortar;
now hear the rule for the mandala.
The lowest [measure] is three and a half tālas; the middle is two tālas; the highest is five tālas;
and others are one finger-breadth (aṅgula) less than that.
The circumference of the base and so forth is declared to be circular in all cases;
one should firmly wrap it at its root with a thickness of exactly two finger-breadths below.
Having placed a pestle in the middle of that, with its tip pointing eastward and its base facing north, one should contemplate:
"Likewise, the *plakṣa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, and *vaṭa* trees [are used for] the mortar; thus, nine [parts]."
Having adorned the mortar and the pestle likewise with garments.
Having made the mental resolve, one should worship the Power named Ādhārā in the mortar; then, having worshipped the Lord in the pestle, one should place the turmeric there.
Having thoroughly ground very white, pure chalk into powder,
that which is half of that amount is declared to be middling, and half of that again is the lowest.
p.
1629) Regarding the cause:
having recited the *vyomavyāpin* mantra, the supreme preceptor should grind the *musalī* plant with *bādira* wood.
One should know [the mantra] and sprinkle [it] with the heart-mantra.
Born of yoga—
the mortar has Brahmā as its presiding deity, the pestle has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity, and the ritual vessel (vasu) has the deities of the eastern direction and others as its presiding deities,
provided with *darbha* grass and flowers.
In the Vātula [Tantra]:
Having adorned the mortar and pestle with nine cloths,
he [the officiant], accompanied by devoted people and courtesans, [proceeds].
Having worshipped Śivadāsī with garments, perfumes, and other offerings,
one should place the pestle, joined with the hand, into the mortar.
At midnight, for the purpose of severing the bonds, one should grind [the ingredients] with the axes of Śiva in the middle of the mortar.
Thereafter, one should cause betel-leaf to be offered to the devotees and the followers of Maheśvara;
likewise, having performed the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) over the corpse, one should perform the binding of the fetters (pāśabandha).

Having thus given [the offering] with the Astra-mantra, one should cause the mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa) to be given. According to the Kāraṇa: "The mortar has the Earth as its deity; the pestle has Skanda as its deity. But in the case of the powder..."
One should consecrate the damana plant, which has Rudra as its presiding deity, with the mantras of Vyoman.
Having worshipped each respective deity, one should begin the beating of the drum.
Its characteristics are stated here:
it may be made of *āsana*, sandalwood, *vakula*, or *śirīṣa* wood, or of *uśīra*.
Or the wise man may fashion a drum from a tiger-tree.
Likewise, in the Vātula: "Uśīra and ghee are said [to be used], endowed with the proper characteristics.
In the Dīpta [style],
the length is four tālas and its width is five tālas; the diameter of the opening is prescribed according to the measure of an āditya-gula.
And its interior is hollow, especially extending from the opening to the end;
it is well-rounded, measuring four finger-breadths in diameter from the opening to the end.
It is joined with new pegs, wrapped at the bottom with a cloth-band, having a circumference of one finger-breadth in the middle,
movable, and wound with a cord.
One should especially bind it with ropes made of cowhide; the characteristic of the drum (bherī) has been declared, and its measurement should be determined according to the *mānāṅgula*.
In the Siddhatantra:
"The crown is said to be the resonance (nāda), and the trident is accompanied by recitation;
with his hands, he holds the conch, discus, trident, rosary, and likewise the staff as weapons."
One should meditate on the form of enjoyment, endowed with all the primary marks, having three feet and resting upon a lotus, while always contemplating its nature as the resonance of *nāda*.
In the Vīratantra:
"Then one should worship the drums and wrap them with new cloth; in their midst, on the right and left, [one should place] Śambhu, Viṣṇu, and Caturmukha."
Mātṛkā, Saptakīlā, and Āsyā; the Moon and the Sun as the lords of the [two] sides; the Lord of Serpents on the leather-thread; and Skanda as the presiding deity of the corners.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using their respective mantras, the preceptor—
In the Bhīmasaṃhitā:
The preceptor should strike the drum while facing either the east or the north.
In the *Kāmika*:
"One should strike the drum while recollecting the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*). One [should perform] that single blow.
The first two are of two kinds.
The third [rite] is performed in three ways, and likewise the threefold method. Having summoned the Ajita-vādya, one should sprinkle it with the auspicious water (śivāmbhas); then, into his hand—
One should cause water, flowers, and so forth to be offered.
He too, having cast a flower and lifted up the drum, should play it;
the drummer himself should strike it with the Tatpuruṣa mantra.
One should perform [the rite] endowed with all its limbs and accompanied by the Śakti; however, one must especially avoid that which is deficient in its limbs.
Regarding the cause:
the instrumentalist should play with the *acchapuṭa* rhythm; specifically for the Brahmins and others, one should strike [the drum] with Vedic mantras.
One should first strike the auspicious [target] with the *tryambaka* mantra and the syllable *ḍama*;
then, with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," one should strike again with the syllables *ḍa-ḍa-ma*.
Having performed the *nyāsa* of the *ḍaḍha* and *mañca* mantras according to the knowledge of the mantra,
one should strike the drum while recollecting the *astra-mantra*.
One is preceded by a single blow, the second by two blows, and the third by three blows;
or alternatively, all three may arise from a single blow.
In the *Kālottara*:
"By striking with anything else, the king and his kingdom perish.
In the *Vidveṣaṇasaṃhitā*:
At the conclusion of the powder-offering, one should cause [the offering]— preceded by *śuṇṭhī* oil and accompanied by the sound of a conch— to be placed upon the head of the deceased (*preta*).
In the Vātula [Tantra]:
One should cause oil, betel-leaf, and lime to be given to all the devotees,
especially to the singers, accompanied by various musical instruments.
In the Kāmika:
"For those who have been initiated, as well as for others who uphold the teaching of Śiva,
and for others as appropriate, [the offering] consists of āruṣkara oil mixed with powder."
One should cause fresh betel-leaf, along with lime, to be given to all people; then, upon the conclusion of the powder festival, follows the descent of the deceased.
Having given Śiva’s sacred ash and the like, as well as perfumes, garlands, fine garments, and so forth,
and having adorned that deceased person, quickly lead him to the cremation ground.
In the *Saṃhitā* on the characteristics of the time for joining and the rite of inciting enmity:
having taken a sacrificial tree, one should proceed with the joining; or else, using trees of the sages, or a *kramuka*, or a bamboo.
Having spread a cloth over it and having especially adorned it, [it is said] in the Vātula:
"One should cause a seat to be made of udumbara wood, measuring the size of a corpse; the peak should be shaped like a garland."
Or by others, or especially so.
Whether in a chariot, a palanquin, or any other vehicle according to one's preference,
a person should exert themselves by increasing [the distance] by six finger-breadths at a time.
The length should be three cubits, and the width should be one-fourth or one-fifth of that; the seats (viṣṭara) should be provided in odd numbers.
Having performed the ritual of erecting the *kuṭa* after having entered into the *āsandhika* [meditative absorption],
it is adorned with red garlands and garments, with canopies hanging down from above.
This has been revealed according to the *Śrīśaivasamayācārapaddhati*;
however, for fear of excessive prolixity, it has not been described here in full detail.
In the *Vidveṣaṇasaṃhitā*—
having spread out a cloth and especially adorned [the area]—
a certain specific rule is stated regarding the Śiva-yogin.
Likewise,
by means of the departure of the other [mind], the yogin should thoroughly extract even that which is well-stabilized,
having adorned it with auspicious ornaments.
Then, one should place the corpse upon a palanquin constructed from moist bamboo and other materials, adorned with the son's ornaments, and provided with steps leading to heaven.
He should maintain [the ritual] together with those of the same caste who wear the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), who are initiated (dīkṣita), who possess equal status,
and who are engaged in the recitation of weapons-mantras (śastra-mantra).
In the Kālottara: "One should especially provide a garment and a loincloth."
In the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*:
"Having taken [the bones] together with those of his own kind who have been initiated and are well-initiated, he should remember the site; the bones and limbs are to be avoided."
In the *Vidveṣaṇasaṃhitā*:
"The preceptor, in particular, should designate a site for the funeral rites on a riverbank, by a pond, or even in a grove or garden."
In the Vātula:
[one should offer] the fire of the deceased, wood, *darbha* grass, unbroken rice, sesame seeds, boiled rice, and parched grain.
Together with pieces of gold, water-pots, and a vardhanī vessel.
One should carry before [the practitioner] into the cremation ground clarified butter, flowers, cloth, thread of five colors, a water-pot, and all the sacred ashes.
The materials for the fire sacrifice (homa) are rice grains, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
the large and small sacrificial ladles (sruk-sruva), along with incense, lamps, a bell, and ornaments for the five limbs of the body.
The sacred thread and the purifier (pavitra), or else accompanied by a ring, together with two red garments and likewise an upper cloth.
A coconut fruit, sacrificial fuel, a copper vessel, betel leaf with fragrance,
and oil mixed with sesame seeds.

The water-pot (kumbha) and the prosperity-pot (vardhanī) should be joined with sixteen smaller jars according to the prescribed method; within the main pot, one should place a gold coin (niṣka), or half of a niṣka, or a sixteenth part of a niṣka.
Silver is prescribed for the *vardhanī* vessel according to the measure of a *mukta*; the *kalaśa* should be made of ten pieces of gold, or according to one's capacity.
Two bhāras of rice, one *droṇa* and half a *droṇa* of husked grain (*taṇḍula*),
half as much sesame as the husked grain, and one *droṇa* combined with parched grain (*lāja*).
Yellow, white, red, dark-brown, and black—these are the five colors for the two powders; one should prepare each of them in the measure of two *prasthas*.
Thus it is said in the Vidveṣaṇasaṃhitā:
"Now I shall describe the five colors: red ochre and sugar likewise.
The powder of *rajanī* (turmeric) produced from charcoal,
and the powder of *śaṅkhinī* leaves, five parts each— according to the *Vātula*.
One *prastha* each of *pañcagavya*,
along with *mudga*, *māṣa*, *kulattha*, *śivaka*, *kāṣāḍha*, and mustard seeds.
Provided with materials for the fire sacrifice, there should be auspicious ghee in measure of one *prastha* each;
and its height on all sides should extend to fourteen cubits.
The wise one should present to the preceptor a covered cloth-casket, eight *tālas* in width and of that same proportion in length.
That foot [of the vessel] shall be the *kumbha* cloth; half of that is known as the *vardhanī*;
half of that is the *lūkhala*; and the *bherī* cloth—these are said to be the characteristics.
Having the shape of a ripe bimba fruit, devoid of a black spot,
and filled with thirty-two prasthas— that is called the Śiva-kumbha.
An exceedingly dark complexion, a water-jar, and a small pitcher; for the ten [deities] beginning with Vajra, there are three *prastha* measures of jars.
The unstable jewel is the vein, the thread is the flesh, and the marrow is the water; by means of these, the wise man [perceives] that which is red-copper-colored, and it is exactly like this.
It is known as Kūrcajihvā, wrapped in a skin garment;
it consists of the seven constituent elements and is placed within jars and pots.
Matted hair, the leaves of the mango tree, and likewise the coconut crown— these are said to be the "substance" (dravya), while they are called the "limb" (aṅga) of the ritual actions.
All the materials for the fire-oblation (homa) should be brought near by the performers; accompanied by various musical instruments, one should lead them before the deceased.
In the Vīratantra:
"Endowed with various long [vowels], accompanied by the lamp of the trident, joined with the lamp of the wheel,
and provided with the support for the lamps."
One should then perform a circumambulation of either a village or a city.
As stated in the *Kālottara*:
"From the house to the middle of the cremation ground, one should successively offer oblations to the spirits of the region using a conch and a *kāhala* drum."
And with sounds, the wise person should mutter the Śiva-mantra.
A wise person should construct a pavilion in the northeast on auspicious ground.
As stated in the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*:
"One should lead [the remains] to a consecrated site that is free from bones and charcoal."

In the *Sarvajñānottara*, it is said: "Having performed the *śaṅkarī* initiation, one should place [the disciple] in a purified location. Regarding the method for constructing the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) here, it is described in the *Vidveṣaṇasaṃhitā*.
I shall describe the cremation pavilion (antyeṣṭimaṇḍapa), measuring six or five cubits; it should be provided with twelve pillars and be joined in its center with a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
In the Kālottara:
"The pavilion for the five [deities] should be nine, seven, or five cubits in size;
it should have sixteen, twelve, or even four pillars."
Alternatively,
in the Cintya [tantra],
it says: "The width and length should be twenty-four *tālas*, and there should be four gates."
Likewise, a nine-square grid is joined in the center.
Alternatively, in another manner, it is provided with four doors and eight corners. As stated in the Vātula: "Having divided the pavilion into nine parts, it should be joined with nine compartments."
In the middle of that, however, is the air-chamber (vāyukoṣṭha), and the altar (vedikā) is one cubit [in measure].
