In the northeast, within the *vardhanī* vessel, one should place the *pretaka* in the fire-compartment; the *pañcagavya* is in the southwest, and there is one *kuṇḍaka* in the center.
In the *Kālottara*:
"In the center of that [mandala], there should be a fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*) with only a single rim; the pit should be six finger-breadths in height and its width likewise six finger-breadths."
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be one cubit in measure, and above that, it should be joined with a womb (yoni).
A specific detail is stated in the Vātula:
"I have prescribed only one [pit] according to the measurement of one cubit, having made it provided with a navel (nābhi) and a womb."
The pit was the size of a palm tree.
In the *Kāmika*:
"Having constructed a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) according to the rule, one cubit in size, in a copper vessel.
In the *Kālottara*:
Having mentally conceived an altar at the locations of the winds, measuring one cubit in size,
one should make it six finger-breadths in height, free from any depressions or elevations.
In the northeast, one should likewise place a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and a vessel for increasing [the offerings].
In the *Vidveṣaṇasaṃhitā*:
"In the ten locations beginning with the thunderbolt (vajra), one should firmly fix the wall."
It should be one *vitasti* in length and perfectly square.
One should fashion its height at six finger-breadths according to what is aesthetically pleasing;
it may have four doors or one door, with the southern door being the most excellent.
The eastern and western [gates] are called the middle gates;
that which is joined with the northern gate is called the inferior gate.
One should worship the Lord of the Weapon (Astra-īśa) at each door with specific rites for the sake of liberation;
or one should worship the archway, the door-pitcher, or the ritual weapon.
In the Kālottara:
"The wise one, having established ten pitchers within the pavilion,
[should arrange them] in an anti-clockwise sequence starting from the trident and ending with the vajra."
Having encircled it with high waves and adorned it with canopies and banners,
one should designate the cremation ground as extending from south to north.
Its length should be eight tālas, and its width half of that;
the length is from south to north, and the width from east to west.
The excavation should be eight finger-breadths deep, free from depressions and elevations; it should have six lines with the southern end and likewise the western end [marked].
One should strike a stake right there at the center of the square; likewise, one should place stakes made of dry wood in the corners starting from the southeast.
One should repeatedly encircle those [offerings] arranged with their tops upward and bases downward using a five-colored thread and a protective amulet (*kavaca*).
Thus, if one is unable to construct a pavilion [in the full manner], one should construct a pavilion using stakes and so forth.
As stated in the Kālottara:
"Alternatively, [it may be] provided with a dug-out pit and stakes, endowed with three threads, and joined with four pairs."
One should not associate with the Saṃgha.
Regarding the characteristic of its length, it is stated in that same source: "The stake made from a milk-tree should be twelve finger-breadths in width and twelve finger-breadths in length,
with a thickness equal to that of a thumb."
The root of the lower [structure] should be struck outside the pavilion;
having thus constructed the pavilion, one should perform the ritual actions without indolence.
Thus ends the procedure for the final rites (*antyeṣṭi*).
Now, the procedure for the final rites according to the Samaya tradition is described.
Having smeared the ground situated near that [object] with cow dung, the Guru— pure in his offerings, possessing the mantra-body, and acting as the increaser of the *vardhanī* vessel— [proceeds].
In the Vidveṣaṇasaṃhitā: Taking water in the vardhanī vessel, standing with the left arm raised,
one should [proceed] from the pavilion in the order of the apasavya (anti-clockwise).
Taking water from the *vardhanī* vessel with an unbroken stream,
one should place the *vardhanī* in that location, starting from Īśāna and ending at Īśa.
One should perform the visualization: seated comfortably on the left side of the altar in the northeast.
From the *Vidveṣaṇasaṃhitā*:

One should perform the placement of ashes (*bhasmanya*), the placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*), and thereafter breath control (*prāṇāyāma*). Then one should perform the placement of the digits (*kalānyāsa*), and after that, the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*).
Indeed, this is the sequence of reabsorption (saṃhāra) conjoined with the deposition of the Mātṛkās;
here, the order of deposition is reversed. Having purified [the hands] with the Weapon-mantra on the palms and backs in reverse order, and having rendered them immortal—

Having placed the forms of the seats upon the palms of the hands, and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) from the two little fingers to the thumbs, corresponding to the deities from Sadyojāta to Īśāna, one should then place the limbs of the Vidyā-body and the root mantras of the eyes.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantras beginning with the Heart-mantra, and having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*) counter-clockwise with the Weapon-mantra preceded by three claps of the hands (*tāla*), one should display the Great Mudrā (*mahāmudrā*) with the Root-mantra.
Having performed the internal worship, one should sprinkle the Weapon-vessel (*astravardhanī*) with the Weapon-mantra.
Having performed the ritual visualization of worship within oneself with substances sprinkled with that water;
Having prepared the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in the Ūrdhvaretas fire, the supreme preceptor should recite the Saṃhitā mantras according to the method of the withdrawal of the kalās.
Having placed within himself the causal principles beginning with Brahmā,
the preceptor should perform the hand-gesture of withdrawal (saṃhāra-hara-hasta) and meditate upon Śiva once.
Then, having scattered kusha grass, ashes, and other materials there, and having gathered them back together according to the rule,
one should perform the rite for the *vardhanī* vessel and for the seat.
Then one should worship the site of the funeral pyre.
As stated in the *Kālottara*:
"In the center of that [site] is the Pāśupata [mantra], with Earth as its presiding deity (adhidaivata)."
And having visualized the yellow-colored seed-syllable *laṃ*.

Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the earth element (pṛthivī-tattva). Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the presiding deity of the earth element. Having visualized the southwest direction (nairṛti), the white seed-syllable *va* is declared to have Viṣṇu as its deity; it is shaped like a half-moon and consists of four parts. Oṃ.
Salutation to the state of water (aptatva). Salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the state of water.
Thus, the red [element] of fire is the bath; it is triangular and forms a dot (bindu).
One should worship the four-footed Rudra, the divine, in his proper place.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the principle of fire (tejas-tattva). Obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the principle of fire.
Having mentally projected this at the location of the wind, one should visualize the wind-element as having four feet, six corners, and the color white, with the syllable "ya" as its seed-syllable.
One should especially worship Īśvara as the presiding deity (adhidevatā).
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the wind element (vāyutattva). Salutation to Īśvara, the lord of the wind element.
In the northeast (īśa), there is a four-petaled [lotus]; the sky (ākāśa) is white in color and circular.
The seed-syllable *hakāra* has Sadāśiva as its presiding deity (*adhidaiva*).
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Ākāśa-tattva. Obeisance to Sadāśiva, the lord of the Ākāśa-tattva.
One square in the east is yellow; in the south it is remembered as black. In the west, however, one...
To the north of that is a white foot of red color.
Having first worshipped Indra in the east, one should worship Yama in the south; having worshipped Varuṇa in the west, one should likewise worship Soma in the north.
Having placed [the offerings] within the corners of the mandala, ending with *svāhā* in due order:
*oṃ hāṃ indrāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ yamāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ varuṇāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ kuberāya namaḥ*, *oṃ hāṃ brahmaṇe*.
Svāhā! To Viṣṇu, svāhā! To Rudra, svāhā! To Īśa, svāhā!
To Sadāśiva, svāhā! To Indra, svāhā! To Yama, svāhā! To Varuṇa, svāhā! To Kubera, svāhā! Having thus offered the bali-oblation,
One should begin the worship of the weapons (*astra*) at the *vardhanī*.
1642) Having worshipped the *Pāśupata* [weapon] at the *vardhanī* in the northeast (*aiśānī*), thereafter—
He initiated [the disciples] from the trident up to the vajra, and likewise initiated them in the eightfold manner.
One should worship the second [deity] above and below, as well as the husband’s two attendants.
Herein is the sequence:
*oṃ hāṃ pāśupatavastrāsanāya huṃ phaṭ namaḥ*. Thus is the seat.

Having worshipped the form [of the deity] with "Oṃ *hūṃ* phaṭ *namaḥ* to the embodiment of the Pāśupata weapon," [one worships] the root mantra with "Oṃ *ślīṃ* *paśuṃ* *phaṭ* to the Pāśupata weapon, *hūṃ* phaṭ *namaḥ*. [Then one worships the limbs:
"Oṃ *oṃ* to the heart, *hūṃ* phaṭ *namaḥ*; Oṃ *ślīṃ* to the head, *hūṃ*..."

Oṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | Oṃ phaṭ śikhāyai huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | Oṃ śuṃ kavacāya huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | Oṃ hāṃ netrebhyo huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | Oṃ phaṭ astrāya huṃ phaṇṇamaḥ | Having thus meditated upon the weapon-mantra as previously described, [one should proceed].
Having performed worship, he should then [worship] those located in the directions starting from Īśāna: Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Trident;
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Mace; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Banner; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Noose; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Sword; Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the Staff.
Homage! Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Śakti. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Vajra.
To the north of Nairṛti, Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Cakra. To the south of Īśāna, Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Padma—one should worship thus.
In the *Kāmika*:
"When the pitcher is placed upon seven grains and endowed with all ornaments," or else—
One should properly worship Bhava upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) amidst sesame seeds and *darbha* grass with:
*oṃ hāṃ ādhāraśaktaye namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ anantāya namaḥ*.
In the corners starting from the northeast and ending at the southeast, [one should worship] with: *oṃ hāṃ aiśvaryāya namaḥ*; *oṃ hāṃ*.
Salutation to Jñāna.
1643) Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Sarva. Having thus worshipped, [one should worship] in the directions starting from the north and ending with the east with "Oṃ..."

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Aimanaiśvarya; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vairāgya; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Prajñāna; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Dharma. Having thus worshipped [these] in the northeast (īśāna) and southwest (nairṛtya), [one worships]: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Ūrdhvacchadana. Oṃ...

"Hāmadhacchadanāya namaḥ. Having thus worshipped, [one should worship] in the center the bulb (*kanda*), the seeds (*bīja*), the stalk (*nāla*), the filaments (*kesara*), the pericarp (*karṇikā*), and the seed-lotus (*bījapadma*): "Oṃ hāṃ padmāya namaḥ";
"Oṃ hāṃ bījebhyo namaḥ."
Having thus propitiated [the deity] in the pericarp, one should worship in the northeast (īśāna):
*oṃ hāṃ manonmanyai namaḥ*. Then, on the filaments of the eight petals from the northeast to the east: *oṃ hāṃ sarvabhūtadamanyai namaḥ*.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Balapramathinī. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Balavikariṇī.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kalavikariṇī. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kalavikaraṇī. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Kālī. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Raudrī. Oṃ hāṃ...
Salutation to Jyeṣṭhā. Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vāmā. Having thus worshipped, one should worship in the center of the pericarp: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the Śakti-maṇḍala;
salutation to Īśvara, the lord of the Śakti-maṇḍala.
At the tip of the pericarp:
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the fire-maṇḍala; salutation to Rudra, the lord of the fire-maṇḍala.
On the pericarp-tip:
Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lunar maṇḍala; salutation to Viṣṇu, the lord of the lunar maṇḍala.
On the tip of the petal: Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the solar disc; salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the solar disc.

Having worshipped thus— saying "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva"— and having worshipped the seat, one should place the image upon it and [install] Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna, beginning from the feet and ending at the head.

Having performed the placement of the Vidya-mantra according to the sequence of the staff (daṇḍabhaṅgī), one should perform the placement of the "eye of the body" (dehanetra) regarding the purification of the paths (adhvaśuddhi) in the locations beginning with the feet, such as Nivṛtti and the other kalās.

Having performed the placement [of the mantras] with the root mantra and having invoked Śiva as before, one should worship Him with the ritual services beginning with installation (*sthāpanā*); then, having worshipped the limbs of dissolution (*layāṅga*) with the *sadyojāta* and other mantras, and having offered prayers and requested permission for the worship of the limbs of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*), [one proceeds] to the north-west.
Having worshipped Sadyojāta and the others in the petals starting from the southeast, northeast, and so forth— with the outer eyes in the northeast—

and having worshipped the Heart-mantra and the others in the petals of the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest, as well as the Astra-mantra in the four cardinal directions, one should perform the oblation and conclude with the recitation.
One should worship and offer oblations either in the eight jars of the enclosure, or in them together with the central jar, or in the central jar alone;
or alternatively—
Since Kālāgnirudra has authority over the act of burning, one should invoke and worship him therein. As it is stated in the Vidveṣaṇasaṃhitā:
"One should fashion eight covered jars, or even a single pot, with its respective mantra."
Then, having meditated upon him likewise accompanied by the guardians of the directions.
In the *Kālottara*:
"Having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in its center with a water-pot (*kuṃbhaka*) upon a lotus,
one should invoke Kiālāgni and Rudra by means of the counter-clockwise sequence."
Likewise, it is stated in the *Cintya*:
"Having invoked Kālāgnirudra, one should worship the pitcher in the northwest;
it is red-robed, three-eyed, two-legged, and adorned with anklets."
He is endowed with four arms, his head is slightly bent toward Lord Śiva, and he holds the base of a trident and a rosary in two of his hands.
Having meditated thus upon [the deity] who grants fearlessness, is endowed with the boon-granting gesture, and is adorned with all ornaments,
one should especially worship him with particular distinction.
p.

1645) Because the connection with the protection of the funeral rite (*antyēṣṭi*) is inappropriate here, there is the absence of the installation of the *kuṃbha* accompanied by the *vardhanī*, which is the cause for the creation and protection; this is *saṃhāra*.
The application of the primary vessel alone, which serves as the cause for the increase of the [spiritual] stream, is sufficient.
Thus, O Guardian of the Quarter, there is no need for the installation of the directional jars (*dikpāla-kuṃbha*). There is also no application of the ten weapon-jars (*daśāyudha-kuṃbha*).
Only the installation of the Śiva-vessel, which is worthy of the five-fold enclosure worship (*pañcāvaraṇa-pūjā*), is required.

The procedure for worship through the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*) is indeed appropriate; furthermore, since the practical application (*prayoga*) must be explained, one should not apply logical reasoning to matters established by the words of the supreme scripture, according to the maxim that "this sequence is not suitable for that which is based on scriptural authority.
Thus, regarding the meanings set forth in the words of the supreme tradition, logical arguments are not to be deliberated upon.
Having meditated thus, "The object of awakening," one should thereafter perform the sequence of the fire-ritual (agnikārya) according to the path taught for the fire-ritual.
Regarding the establishment of the fires.
The sacrificial fuel-sticks of the appropriate trees are offered with the *sadyo-mantra*;
one should offer oblations with their respective names, using *caru* as the sacrificial material.

Having offered sesame seeds with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), one should cause [the disciple] to purify [the body] by means of the *sākantana* [mantra]; one should offer oblations (*āhuti*) one hundred times, fifty times, twenty-five times, or for each [limb] individually.
One should perform the oblation in the heart with the mantra one hundred times;
and for the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should offer it with the head [of the fire] while reciting "sviṣṭam agne."
The procedure here is as follows: having gone near the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and sat down, one should consecrate it with the purificatory rites beginning with inspection (nirīkṣaṇa),
worship Vāgīśī and Vāgīśa, and then circumambulate the consecrated fire three times.
Having cast [the seed] into the central channel (*nāḍī*) of Vāgīśī, and having performed the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*) as is customary,
[he should place] darbha grass upon the girdle (*mekhalā*) with the Weapon mantra (*astra*).

Having spread [the grass] in reverse order over them, having placed the sacrificial ladles with their tips pointing south, west, north, and east respectively, and having offered five fuel-sticks for the sake of generating the fire,
[he worships] Ananta and Rudra in the northern, southern, western, and eastern directions among the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
Having worshipped Viṣṇu and Brahmā, one should worship Īśāna and the others—
Soma, Vāyu, Varuṇa, Nirṛti, Yama, Agni, Indra, and Viṣṇu— from the northeast (Īśāna) to the east, upon their respective seats, with Viṣṇu situated to the south of Īśāna.

Having worshipped Brahmā and requested Agni’s protection, one should sprinkle the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with the mantra "Oṃ haḥ astrāya phaṭ," whirl them three times over the fire as before, perform the remaining consecration (*saṃskāra*), and carry out the sprinkling of the clarified butter (*ājya-saṃskāra*), the smearing of the mouth (*vaktrābhidhāra*), and the joining of the mouths (*vaktra-sandhāna*).

Having performed the five purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), such as the unification of the faces and the unification of the tongues, as previously described; and having performed the naming ceremony and the dismissal of the ancestors as before; one should then invoke [the deity] into the heart of the fire as if onto a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) and worship it.

Having performed the satiation (*tarpaṇa*) of the mantra, one should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). Then, for the sake of the place, time, and other factors, having offered oblations according to one's capacity with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) in accordance with the available materials and time, and having satiated [the deity] with the mantra-complex (*mantra-saṃhitā*) and offered the concluding oblation (*sadgīpya*), one should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇā*). Alternatively, [it may be] fashioned from five colors.

Having consecrated the site with purificatory rites such as the inspection (*vīkṣaṇa*) and so forth, one who is free from passion (*vītarajas*) should draw a square with white powder for the purpose of constructing the city of Indra (*māhendra*) in its center;
then, having drawn a red triangle within that square with red powder, [one should worship] "Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Indra" in the square.
Having worshipped in the triangle with "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Agni," according to the *Kāmika*: "There, having spread sacrificial wood upon a bed of corpses,
mixed with sandalwood and agallochum, and covered with an inverted cloth..."
Having worshipped with the King of Mantras (Astrarāja) upon the ground with flowers and kuśa grass,
and having worshipped with the King of Mantras upon the ground with flowers and blossoms.
Having prepared nectar cleansed with earth, along with cow-dung and water,
it was bathed and fumigated there with ashes according to the prescribed method.

Wearing the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) over the left shoulder, disregarding his previous caste status, and having worshipped the Fire-god with the *āgneyī-śakti* mantra, he sits upon a *kuśa* grass seat to the south of the fire.
Through the purification by means of gazing and so forth, and by the five types of concentration (dhāraṇā),
the work of mantra then takes place within the hollow of his heart-lotus.
Unattached to the latent impressions of karma that are yet to be experienced, having cast off the body commenced by past actions—
herein lies the application of the Great Net (mahājāla): for the purpose of depositing [the consciousness] into a dead body,
one should lead the *nāda* supported by the resonance (*ūrca*) of the *praṇava* to the *dvādaśānta*, and by means of that...

Then, having conceived the Self as moving here and there according to its own karma by means of the *nāda* (the primordial sound), one should contemplate the mantra of the Self as being grasped on all sides like a net, spread forth by the power of that *nāda*.

Uttering it very subtly, rotating three times within the space between the index fingers, and having visualized oneself as being far away and then near, one should grasp [the consciousness] with the goad-mudrā (*sṛṇimudrā*) by placing [the hand] at the base of the thumb and joining the fingers, while reciting the mantra into one's own heart.
Having drawn [the self] inward to the end of its own sound and divided it, one should grasp it with the *saṃhāramudrā* using the self-mantra "Oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ to the Self, obeisance," and then,
having emerged outward through the flow of the vital breath, [place it] again externally at the *dvādaśānta*.
Having grasped [the deity] with the *udbhavamudrā*, one should join him to his heart and cast [him in]. Thus,

having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) by means of the application of the Great Net of the Tortoise (*kūrmamahājāla*), and having offered three oblations (*āhuti*) with the root mantra while contemplating the three bonds (*pāśa*), one should [invoke] the Brahmās, beginning with Sadyojāta, in the sequence starting from the feet.
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*), one should then connect the channels (*nāḍī*) and offer three oblations with the root mantra.

Having offered oblations for the purpose of bringing him into proximity, and then having offered a hundred oblations with the root mantra to purify any deficiency in the conduct of the initiate, and having united him with Śiva, the presiding deity of Rudra, by means of the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should unite the Lord of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍileśa*) with the fire and place the corpse upon the funeral pyre.
In the *Kāmika*:

"Having worshipped Īśa, who has brought all bonds to their absolute end, the Guru should abandon [the disciple's] body; having withdrawn the *vidyā-deha* into that body, he [places it] in his own station."

Having placed the corpse upon the sacrificial ground and withdrawn it into his own station, the wise Guru, acting as a father, should worship the constituent letters in their respective places and cause them to marry.
In that place, having established the funeral pyre, the placement of the deceased (pretanyāsa) is performed upon it.
As stated in the *Suprabheda*: "On the southern side of the deceased, the wise one should [establish] the Śiva-fire as before, with the *hṛdaya* [mantra]."
Having offered one hundred oblations, he should then offer a hundred oblations in the name of that person.

Having performed the fire sacrifice with the desired oblation, one should place the *caru*— prepared with milk, unbroken rice, and other ingredients— into the regions of the navel, heart, and mouth by means of the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
For having applied a portion of mercury to the nine gates— the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the mouth, and the anus— the wise man [attains success].
One should deposit the *liṅga* at the nine gates with the heart-mantra; then, having offered milk mixed with rice, one should [place it] on its head with the left hand.
In the *Vidveṣaṇasaṃhitā*:
"One should indeed join the [mantra] related to the gods and that of Śiva with the Astra-mantra alone.
In the *Kāmika*:
One should have the thumb struck off and severed with a sharp weapon;
then, together with the paternal kinsmen and brothers, one should perform the offering of unctuous water.
Then, with the tip of the weapon, they all performed circumambulation of it; and taking the full jar that causes burning, they performed the circumambulation in the reverse direction.
Having performed the threefold [rite], one should pour that water from the left with the Astra mantra; then, the water remaining in the vessel should be poured back into its original place.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"From the crown of the head down to the feet, one should apply ghee very beautifully; then, touching both feet and recollecting [the deity], one should offer it into the fire like an oblation."
In the *Cintyaviśva*:

"Thereafter, one should inflame the fires with the fire situated in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*); when they have blazed up in the region of the head, one should again offer oblations from the north."
In the *Kāmika*:
"Having sprinkled clarified butter mixed with honey into the blazing fire, and having lifted up the worshipped *sruc* ladle filled with clarified butter, honey, and milk..."
Standing with his head toward the Guru and facing the eastern direction, he should pour the stream [of water] into the mouth of the fire while uttering these words: "Thus..."
O Agni, you are the southern time; accept this great oblation, purified by mantras and offered by Śrāvī, presented by Time itself.

The meaning of this is as follows: by the word "Agni" is meant Rudra, the lord of fire; by the word "Kāla" is meant birth and the duration of birth; he who is the "taker" (harer) of that [duration]—the destroyer—is Kāla.
Or rather:
Śiva, who consists of all things, limits the sixteen-fold universe— from the atom up to the great dissolution— by means of his power.
"O God, you are Time itself," according to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of this mantra; for this very reason, from the injunction regarding the "Aghora" [face] on the right,
he is the agent of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) for the one whose form is Aghora.
Because [the Lord] acts as the agent of creation, maintenance, destruction, restraint, and grace respectively through the forms of the mantras beginning with *Ṣya*,
He possesses the state of being the enjoyer of the karma that has been brought about by Time,
together with those things brought about by Time, such as food, medicine, and so forth, through their presence.
"Having prepared her, purified by the mantras as prescribed for initiation and cleansed through the placement of mantras (*nyāsa*) and other rites,
accept now this great oblation (*mahāhuti*), which is the very form of a human corpse, along with the worship and the consecration of mantras performed for you."
The meaning of the mantra: in the *Cintyaviśva*,
it says "there, facing the tree."

For the great Śaivas who perform the practice of Vedic Śaiva mantras, one should generate the Vedic fire as previously described, merge it into the Śaiva fire, and perform the funeral rites with that mixed fire. This is stated in the Kāmika:
The characteristics of the Śaiva fire have been previously described. O twice-born ones, hear now the nature of the mixed Vedic fire: it should possess a single body, two faces, and two nostrils.
He has six eyes, is girt with a belt, and is endowed with three feet; he is considered to be possessed of four limbs, two heads, and matted hair.
Wearing the sacred thread and the girdle of muñja grass, endowed with seven hands, possessed of seven tongues of flame,
and accompanied by the bull as his vehicle.
Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, and Jihvākāṇī are on the right; Suprabhāvātiriktā and Bahurūpā are on the left.
Thus the tongues have been described: Miśrā is in the Agni-fire, the Vaidika fire; Hiraṇyā is the tongue in the Vāruṇa-fire; Kanakā is situated in the middle.
The northern tongue of the mouth is red, the one situated in the southern direction is black,
the eastern tongue is Suprabhā, and the one situated in the southeast is intensely red.
The tongue of Bahurūpeśa is proclaimed as the locus of the tongue;
one should employ the mantras of Śiva only in the Vedic fire.
Vedic mantras or others that have been proclaimed are used in the Śiva-fire;
likewise, in the mixed fire, it is said that the Vedic fire is employed.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World (Śiva), and whatever other gods are established [there], as well as Vyāsa,
Bodhāyana, Āpastamba, and Vātsyāyana.
Satyāṣāḍha and others likewise [composed their works] after having heard the meaningful doctrines of the gods,
as well as other scriptures, the Purāṇas, and the Smṛtis.
In the Sūtras, however, Vyāsa, the compiler, has provided this for the sake of restriction; the Vedic fire-sacrifice performed according to his opinion is what is recited here.
That which is prescribed solely by Vedic mantras is Vedic;
that which is prepared with the Brahmakūrca is recorded in the Vedic tradition as being likewise Vedic.
In the same way, for the Miśravahni, there is the Śaiva [fire] joined with those two,
together with three enclosures (paridhis) and provided with two fuel-sticks (samidhs) above.
The Vedic fire is thus designated, while the mixed fire possesses the nature of both; furthermore, Brahmins and others who are uninitiated may employ either the purely Vedic fire alone.

Those who have been initiated and are fit for all [rites] are called "eligible" (adhikārin). As for those who are "mixed" (miśrin), having first performed the Vedic [rite] separately for both, [they are eligible].
The Śaiva fire, preceded by the consecration of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), belongs to the most excellent practitioners;
this is designated as "mixed" (miśra), being suitable for those belonging to both stages of life (āśrama).
Having thus prepared the mixture, one should offer it into the fire without sloth;
such is the characteristic of the purificatory rite (saṃskāra) here at the beginning of the funeral ceremonies (antyeṣṭi) and so forth.
Elsewhere, however, the rite should be performed separately according to one's wealth and faith.
In that very [text] it is said:
"Having brought [the victim] without circumambulating and having seized the sword, one should act without sloth."
Lifting her up and placing her upon his shoulder, he covered her head while she turned her face away.
Relinquishing the core [of the thread] while remaining attached, perform a circumambulation to the right with those established in their own dharma;
then, proceeding with the steps in reverse order, place the *vardhanī* vessel face down.
One should cast the *śastravardhanī* (the ritual dagger), which has been extracted from the region of the head, into that [fire].
In the *Vidveṣaṇasaṃhitā*:
"Then, having removed the archway and other items, one should cause [the victim] to enter onto the bank of water."
Likewise, in the *Kāmika*:
"Then, having gone to a body of water and bathed, one should spread out excellent *kuśa* grass;
thereafter, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), one should first utter the *praṇava* and the heart-mantra."
One should offer water with sesame seeds, accompanied by the name of the deceased, preceded by "skanda," followed by "gaṇeśa," or ending with "nāma."
The ritual duties such as these should be performed by one who has not yet attained purity of reality; having bathed again, they should recite the *Śivasamhitā* with a serene countenance.
In that regard, a specific rule has been stated:
at the conclusion of the bath, having drunk either the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) or clarified butter (*ghṛta*), one should recite [the mantra] to Śiva.
In the *Vidveṣaṇasaṃhitā*:
"The Guru, facing the sun, shall perform the penance and recite [the mantras];
for the sapindas and those of his own caste, he shall practice the Vedic and Shaiva rites."
In the Kāmika [Tantra]:
"For celibate students and ascetics who are fit for the sequence of renunciation,
one should recite the Bahurūpa mantra a hundred times over the bathing garment until it is dried."

The carriers of the funeral pyre and those who bear it likewise receive double [the usual fee]; having taken that according to their capacity, [the merit accrues] to both the carrier and the cremator.
In the *Ṣaṭsāhasrikā*:
"Standing on a seat facing north, one should recite the weapon-mantras a hundred times; or a thousand, or a hundred plus eight, if one is joined with meditative concentration."
The kinsmen, however, shall receive half of that, or half of that again, or the carrier [shall receive it].
As stated in the Kāmika:
"Whether he has taken a vow or not, a Brāhmaṇa who has been initiated into Śiva, whomsoever he [finds] in the forest..."
For one who rides [the horse], death shall not occur at an improper time.
In the *Cintya*:
"By performing the funeral rites for a destitute preta, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
In the *Kāmika*:
If, having performed the impurity rites for a corpse in this manner, one returns to one's own home, one should eat neem leaves while remaining restrained at the entrance of the house.
Having sipped water (ācamana), they should enter after obtaining fire, water, cow dung, a banyan leaf, and mustard seeds,
having placed their feet gently upon the ground.
In the *Ṣaṭsahasrikā*:
"When the night has arrived, or at the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), one should especially worship Śiva.
At the conclusion of the recitation and the fire-oblation, the preceptor should then partake of food.
Surrounded by his kinsmen and disciples for the sake of pacifying their grief—

thus ends the ritual for the funeral rites of one who has taken initiation (*samayāntyeṣṭividhi*) in the *Dīkṣādarśa* composed by Vedajñāna, the son of Vāmadeva. Now, the specific ritual for the funeral rites (*viśeṣāntyeṣṭividhi*) is described.

Having prepared the seat in the mind, one should perform the separation of the soul, its extraction, and so forth; and being established therein, one should carry out the entire initiation, including the measurement of the ritual actions.
The sequence here is as follows:
having performed everything previously mentioned, one should invoke and worship Agni, Hṛtpadma, Vāgīśī, and Vāgīśa, and bring them into proximity.
Having offered three oblations for each [deity] and visualized them in union,

one should sprinkle the disciple with the *astra-mantra*, strike the region of his heart with the *sapuṣpanārāca-mudrā* while reciting "Oṃ haḥ huṃ phaṭ," and [expel the impurities] through one's own exhalation (*recaka*) by means of the syllable *huṃ*.

Having entered his body, one should separate [the soul] with the Jyeṣṭhā mantra: *oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ haḥ huṃ phaṭ*; then, having led it to the *dvādaśānta* (the end of the twelve) with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā* while reciting *oṃ hāṃ haṃ hāṃ svāhā*, one should contemplate the *jīva* (life-principle) in the form of a drop on the tip of a blade of grass.

Having gathered [the breath] with the *saṃhāramudrā* by means of the *ātman-mantra*, having established it in one's own heart through the function of inhalation (*pūraka*), and having performed retention (*kuṃbhaka*) while recollecting the root mantra,
one should lead it to one's own *dvādaśānta* by means of the *ātman-mantra* through the process of abandoning the causal deities beginning with Brahmā.
Having extracted [the soul] from the union with the parents and having dissolved it by means of the *vāmā* and *udbhava* mudrās,

one should unite it with Vāgīśī using the *ātma-mantra*. Then, having offered a hundred, a thousand, or half that number of oblations with the root mantra, one should empower that self with the *pūrṇāhuti*, by means of Śiva as the presiding Lord.
Having joined [the mantras], having gratified Vāgīśī and Vāgīśa, and having dismissed them,
one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the Astra-mantra for the sake of atonement; [then] the Lord of the Altar (Sthaṇḍileśa).

Having united [the deceased] with the Vanistha [fire], one should dismiss Śiva. Then, having placed the head of the dog upon the funeral pyre and covered it with an inverted cloth soaked in clarified butter (*ājya*), having performed everything as before and surrounded [the site] with Indra and the other deities, one should kindle it with the fire from the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Standing at the head of the disciple, the Guru, having lifted the *sruc* ladle filled with ghee, honey, and milk along with the *sruva* spoon, should cast it while uttering this "Full" (*pūrṇā*) formula.
As stated in the *Cintyaviśva*:
O Agni, you are the southern time; accept this great oblation, purified by mantras and offered by Śāṇḍilī, presented by Time itself.
Having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with this very mantra in the presence of Bhava, one should place the vardhanī vessel,
consecrated with the weapon-mantra, on the left side.
Having established that [image] there, one should then go to the bank of a river and look back toward the west as far as the unbroken earth.
Having bathed, having spread out the ritual materials, and having arranged them in the *apasavya* (leftward) manner:
*Oṃ hāṃ śuddhātman skando bhava svadhā* | *Oṃ hāṃ śuddhātman caṇḍo bhava svadhā* | *Oṃ hāṃ śuddhātman gaṇādhīśo bhava* ||

Saying "svadhā," one should offer three handfuls of water-libations (añjali) upon the ground; then, having bathed again, one should repeat the Aghora mantra one hundred times for the sake of expiation (prāyaścitta), and having recited the Skandadātāra and Tadāhaka mantras twice, one should go to one's own abode and perform the remaining rites for his sake as previously described.
One should perform [the rite].
In the *Kālottara*:
"At the conclusion of one's own fire-ritual, the Lord should worship as previously described."

p.1556) "The definition of 'you' (tvam) must be performed precisely by means of the beneficial qualification. Thus ends the procedure for the specific funeral rites (*viśeṣāntyeṣṭi*) in the *Dīkṣādarśa*.
Now, the ritual procedure for the funeral rites at the time of Nirvāṇa is described.
The preceptor should perform the ritual actions up to the joining of the channels (nāḍī-sandhāna),
as has been demonstrated in detail in the *Kriyākramadyotikā* and other works;
however, for fear of excessive length, it is described here in brief.
Likewise, in the *Cintyaviśva*:
"The Kalās beginning with Śāntyatītā reside in the body of the Vidyā: in the subtle [levels], in the head, the face, the heart, and in the body below the navel."
Having deposited the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva), as well as the principle of power (śaktitattva) and Śiva,
one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra for the purpose of invoking the presence of consciousness.
Having taken up the *nivṛtti*-kalā and the others, either simultaneously or in succession, one should unite them with the fire,
perform worship, and carry out the invocation of Śiva and the other deities.

Having performed the striking and the separation, as well as the extraction of the individual soul (jīva) and so forth, one should perform everything— residing in the *karmātman* and situated therein— in the same manner as in an initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Birth, qualification, and experience; dissolution, the purification of the stream, atonement, concealment, and the liberation of the fettered soul from its bonds.
The acts of rubbing, rolling into a ball, burning the noose, and so forth;
likewise, the invocation of the causal deity and the transfer of authority.
Having performed the rites for one's own liberation and so forth, one should unite the consciousness within the imperishable Śiva, who is devoid of qualities and transcends all mental cultivation.
In the *Kāmika*:
"In this very manner, one should purify the other feet above; according to the stated manual of ritual action (*karmapaddhati*), those [feet] extend up to Śiva."
Having extracted [the soul] from others, one should unite it with the stainless state, so that once liberated, the individual soul (aṇu) is not born again nor becomes subject to another.

Having thus performed the sacrifice for those whose bonds have been entirely severed, one should dismiss them; and having projected the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) into that [liberated] body, one should place the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) in its own proper station.
Having likewise withdrawn even Sthaṇḍileśāna into his own place,
the Guru places him upon the bed within the corpse, which is covered with kuśa grass.

The *sruc* and *sruva* ladles and other implements made of pearl should have their heads facing south and their bases facing north; the preceptor and the practitioner should face them, while others should look at them from another direction.
Having brought together frankincense, agallochum, camphor, excellent sandalwood, and pine wood, and having covered [the fire],
one should bring it to the sacrificial pit and cast the fire therein.
Having cast honey, sesame oil, and clarified butter into the rising fire,
one should offer worship by lifting up a ladle filled with clarified butter, honey, and milk.
Standing at the head of the fire-pit, facing the eastern direction, he should pour a stream [of water] while uttering this formula:
"O Agni..."
O Agni, you are the southern time;
accept this great oblation of Śāvī, purified by mantras and offered by Time itself.
(Cintyaviśve)
Having cast the *vāṅmukha* [mantras] there, and immediately thereafter the *sruk* and *sruc* ladles,
the Guru, having appointed four experts in the ritual acts of worship, [proceeds].
Having brought her in counterclockwise and seized her by the neck with a sword, he raised her up with her face turned upward; then, covering his head, he turned away with his left shoulder.
Release the earth joined with those established in their own duty, circumambulating it clockwise;
then, proceeding counter-clockwise, go to that *vardhanī* vessel which is turned face-downward.
One should cast the head of the evil-doer there into the river Śastravardhanī;
then, having gone to the bank of the river, one should not look back.

Having bathed, having spread out the ritual arrangements, and having performed the rites with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), [one should recite]: Oṃ hāṃ, O pure self, become beautiful, svadhā! Oṃ hāṃ, O pure self, become Sadāśiva, svadhā!
Oṃ hāṃ, O pure self, become peaceful, svadhā!

With these mantras, one should perform the libation for the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*) with a concentrated mind. Having bathed, the Guru should repeat the recitation (*japa*) of the *Aghora* mantra one hundred times.
Those who provide the shoulder-bearer [for the palanquin] shall receive double [the merit], and the waters shall return to their own source. Therein is the God.
Having worshipped him thoroughly with special intent for that purpose,
[it is said] in the *Kālottara*:
"One should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the teacher (*ācārya*), consisting of garments, gold, rings, and ornaments."
Then, after that, the gift of gold and the gift of cows.
Then, having performed the gift of land, the gift of elephants, and the giving of parasols,
chowries, foot-protectors, and so forth;
One should cause the gift of a bronze trident, as well as rice and a couch, and especially the attendants, to be given according to one's capacity.
O Maheśā, one should first perform the rite for the sons or for the disciple,
and afterwards one should arrange the *sādhana* for the Śivas.
Having thus resolved, one should perform the funeral rite (antyeṣṭi) according to the prescribed rules.
Thus ends the procedure for the funeral rite of the Nirvāṇa-initiation in the *Dīkṣādarśa* composed by Vedajñāna, the son of Vāmadeva.
Now, the procedure for the collection of the bones is described.
In the Kāmika [Tantra]:
"On the second day, a person should cause the cremation of all [the deceased],
provided with funeral cakes (piṇḍas) and combined with ghee and milk."

Or else, one should perform the third [rite] by offering it; when the funeral pile has been built, one should take [the remains] and place them in an earthen vessel containing milk and mixed with water.
Alternatively, one may perform the collection of the bones without piling them up, using a single, three, five,
or seven-day-old earthen vessel.
O Brahmin, having removed the vital organs, one should gradually collect the bones of those who were foremost and cast them in the four directions for the sake of the Piśācas.
Having gathered the limbs with the limbs using that mantra, one should cast them out; having cast them outside the village, one should perform the casting into the Ganges and other such rites.
One should deposit it on that very day, or after five days, at the end of a month, or after three months; or when six months or a year have been completed, or even thereafter.
Having cast [the vessel] into that sacred ford and performed his bath along with sesame seeds,
he should offer the ancestral libation (tarpaṇa) and likewise satisfy the gods and other deities.
One should perform an act of giving according to one's ability, having offered a *piṇḍa* upon the fourfold ground.
Thus ends the procedure for the collection of bones. (p.
1660) Now, the procedure for the installation of the fire and the stone is described.
In the Kāmika:
"Purification for a Brāhmaṇa shall take ten days; for a Kṣatriya, it lasts twelve days;
for a Vaiśya, purification takes fifteen days; and for a Śūdra, it is indeed monthly."
This rule has been proclaimed for ordinary mortals,
as well as for those Śūdras who are devotees of Maheśvara and wear sacred ash and Rudrākṣa beads.
For them, purification occurs after fifteen days even in the case of death;
and those who are known as Māheśvara Śūdras and so forth [are included].
Likewise, for those who know the songs of Śiva and who dwell in the hermitages of Śiva,
purification for a temple servant is proclaimed to occur within twenty days.
Those purified in twenty days, and others in twenty-five; in Raurava,
the ascetic and the temple servant are purified in half a fortnight.
Such analysis has been elaborated in our *Śaivaśaucadīpikā*; let it be understood from there. In the *Kāmika*:
For householders who follow the ways of the world,
it is obligatory to bring the ancestral offerings to the courtyard or to the outer part of the house.
Or on the pedestal according to the method stated for the pedestal;
or else, for the Brahmins and others in their respective order, with *darbha* grasses or *kuśa* grasses measuring from five to ten units [in length],
one should prepare bundles (*kūrca*) with their tips pointing toward the south.
Having offered obeisance with prostration and a seat, one should then invoke the form; one should install oneself, endowed with that lineage and so forth, while uttering the syllable *praṇava*.

The water for the feet and other offerings, as well as the food offering (*naivedya*), should be prepared from one *māḍhaka* or even half of that; whatever is pleasing to him [is what should be offered].
All of this [should be offered] with that [mantra] ending in *svadhā* and joined with the heart-mantra;
or else, one should offer the water for the guest (*arghya-jala*), while elsewhere one should prepare the food.
Having removed that rice-ball (piṇḍa), together with its flowers and either accompanied by the Ādya [mantra], from that place,
one should cast it into the middle of a sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
All of this, however, one should lead to a meritorious place such as a river and so forth; this is common for Brahmins and the other classes, but the specific rule is now stated.
For those whose nature is that of Maheśvara,
the funeral rites (antyeṣṭi) must be performed together with the daily satiation (tarpaṇa), known as the "giving of power" (śaktidāna) and so forth.
On the first day, they should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) separately for each [deceased]; at the conclusion of the libation, one should offer a bali-oblation either by a river or even in the home.
For Brahmins, there are ten piṇḍas; for Kṣatriyas, it is said to be two; for Vaiśyas, fifteen are prescribed; and for Śūdras, thirty are proclaimed.
As long as their period of impurity lasts, so long should the offering of ground rice and water be performed; however, once ten days have passed and the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite has been completed.
At that time, a single funeral ball (piṇḍa) should be offered, and the period of impurity (āśauca) is primary; at the end of the impurity, the twice-born man should then perform the ekoddiṣṭa rite.
In the eleventh [fortnight], in the third fortnight, and likewise every month, whatever rite has been expanded is joined with the annual [observance].
It is said that the "sixteen śrāddhas" are the gifts made on these occasions; indeed, this sixteen-fold śrāddha is remembered as the *ekoddiṣṭa*.
For one for whom these nine and sixteen śrāddhas are not performed, the state of being a piśāca remains fixed,
even though śrāddhas have been offered by others at intervals.
On the second day after the Ekoddiṣṭa, the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite is performed;
for one whose Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa occurs before the completion of a year, [the rites are performed accordingly].

One should also provide food along with a water-pot to the preceptor for one year; previously, the *nava-śrāddha* (recent funeral rite) should be performed together with the *ekoddiṣṭa* (single-offering rite).
One should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite; for that purpose, one should worship Śiva.

The meal should be offered as a single *vardhana*. Having gathered these together, it should be performed specifically for the Self of the Preceptor (*deśikātman*), or else it should be given to Śiva who is the Self of the Preceptor.
In the Kāmika:
"At the conclusion of the Ekoddiṣṭa rite, the Pakṣa-śrāddha is considered essential;
likewise, the Pākṣika and Māsika śrāddhas should be performed for Śūdras as well."
Everything else would be the same for the three castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
In the *Kāmika*:
"For one who has taken lifelong vows (*naiṣṭhika*), the daily libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the bali offering need not be performed; [only] once a day."
And at the end of the burning, with the three beginning with Īśa.
For that purpose one should perform libations, and for that purpose one should worship Śiva;
O best of the twice-born, the *āma-śrāddha* should be performed in the forenoon.

Having reached a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) while naked, or during an eclipse of the moon or sun, one may perform an *āmaśrāddha* (a śrāddha with raw food) in cases of incapacity; the same applies when the moon is in the asterism Ārdrā and so forth.
Having formed such a resolution, one should perform the *śrāddha* rite;
this and more has been demonstrated in detail in the *Ṣoḍaśakriyāprakāśikā*.
Let this be understood therein.
Thus ends the procedure for the installation of the stone.
Now, the procedure for the funeral rites of a Śaiva ascetic is described.
In the *Cintyaviśva*, it is stated that for Śaiva renunciants (*sannyāsins*), there are two types of final rites (*antyeṣṭi*):

cremation and burial. Thus, I shall now describe the procedure for the final rite, which is twofold—cremation and burial—and by which the knowledge of the *dhruva* (the eternal) is attained, arising from the knowledge of one's resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
One should observe that [moment] at that time according to the path taught in the Kālajñāna; however, in the Kālottara, one should abandon the body at the moment of the division of the initiation.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"The cremation of ascetics who have renounced the world and of Paramahaṃsas occurs only after they have previously deposited the fire of the world into the fire of their own bellies."
And because there is no need for external fire-rituals, one should have [the body] laid down with salt;
the depth of the pit for digging should be one-fourth of the height [of the body].
The width should be two cubits, and the excavation below four cubits.
As stated in the Kāmika:
"For ascetics or for those possessed of knowledge, the ritual act should consist of a pit."
The yogi digs with a staff one cubit long, or even half a cubit.
One should reflect thus: having resorted to a secluded place, one should smear it with cow dung; and having performed purification of the body, one should adorn it with perfumes and garlands.
With a white covering and with water-vessels, one should place the *nāstika* (non-believer) at the very end;
then, upon the conclusion of the powder-festival (*cūrṇotsava*), follows the descent of the deceased (*pretāvarohaṇa*).
In the *Kāmika*:
"Having placed [the image] in a palanquin or similar vehicle, one should go to a cremation ground on pure ground, or to the bank of a river or a pond,
where a level pavilion has been well-decorated."
A sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) should be prepared there with rice grains; one should take five jars, including the vardhanī vessel.
One should place the Śiva-kumbha in the center, complete with its thread, its lid, its cloth, and filled with water; and the Vardhanī vessel to its left.
One should especially place four water-pots in the four directions;
then, recollecting the mantra of the deity, one should install [the central vessel] within the midst of the pots.
Having taken recourse to the goddess’s mantra, one should place water in the *vardhanī* vessel;
[the diagrams] are a square, a half-moon, a triangle, and a hexagon.
And the spheres of the earth and the other elements are respectively well-rounded in shape; they are yellow, white, likewise red, blackish, and smoke-colored.
Earth and the other elements are the seeds; *la*, *ra*, *ha*, and *ka* are their causal agents. One should join the elements beginning with earth up to the end of Īśāna with *sa* and the others.
In the Kālottara, however, [it] should be performed... O God, one should indeed install the deity in each respective jar according to the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama).
Alternatively, in another manner, it is provided with a wheel-pivot, joined with ten pegs,
and having twelve pegs at the doors.
One should encircle [the area] with a triple thread made from a milky tree;
one should worship the ten weapons together with the pegs, starting from one peg to the next.
Having invoked Kālāgnirudra into the central pitcher in the northwest,
and having worshipped him with all ritual offerings, [one should recite] the Raudra and Pāśupata [mantras].
Having thus worshipped the King of Weapons according to the ritual procedure, one should then lead it to that spot on the ground along the path from south to north.
Having sprinkled [the site] with Vāmadeva according to the eight-tāla measurement, one should perform the half-measure, well-remembered, in accordance with the path of the scriptures.
Having taken a sacrificial tree, one should cause a stake to be fixed right there;
one should wrap it with a thread using the Astra-mantra, proceeding in a counter-clockwise direction.
It should be joined with six threads for both its width and length; therein, one should leave five spaces in each direction and discard the central five spaces.
Thus, there is one [square] of five parts; the earth is yellow in color, and it is located between Varuṇa and Nairṛta, as well as at the position of the Śrutis.
Thus, in this specific location, the color of the Apāya [hell] is said to be white; in the fire, the scriptural locus is described as having a single smoky color.
The Vedic word *jīve* is declared for the description of Kṛṣṇa; likewise, the Vedic word *īśe* is declared for the description of Mekadhūmra.
In the lotus of Indra and Antaka (the South), it is yellow-black; in that of Soma (the North), it is white-black. This is declared to be the cremation ground;
the wise one should worship [the deities] in their respective locations.
Oṃ hlāṃ, obeisance to Nivṛttikalā and Sadyojāta; thus in the center.
Oṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Pratiṣṭhākalā and Vāmadeva. (p. 1666)
In the southwest (nirṛti):
Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Aghora, the aspect of the Vidyā-kalā. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa, the aspect of the Śānti-kalā.
In the northwest: Oṃ hauṃ, obeisance to Īśāna, the deity of the Śāntyatīta Kalā. In the northeast:
In the eastern, western, southern, and northern directions: Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Indra;
Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Yama; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Varuṇa; Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Soma.
Having thus performed the worship, one should thereafter especially offer the bali; there, facing eastward, one should prepare the seat and other requisites.
Having placed [the vessel] upon the seat, one should worship it in sequence with perfumes and other offerings;
then, for the sake of the disciples and others, one should worship according to the prescribed characteristics for the purpose of the sacrificial oblation.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:

"One should perform all rites as before, except for the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*); since the ascetics (*yatīnām*) are already joined with the fire-ritual of Śiva, they should indeed burn [the offerings] by that means alone."
In digging and burning, one should provide a staff together with a loincloth;
as stated in the Kāmika: "Or else, having filled [the pit] with salt, or especially with ashes."
In the *Cintyaviśva*:
"One should fill the hand with auspicious, unctuous [substances] and strike it against the deity; above that, one should fashion a pedestal (*pīṭha*) and arrange the peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) there."
There, having fashioned and installed either a pedestal joined with a base, or a *liṅga*, or that which has the nature of the form of consciousness itself, one should worship it.
1667) In that regard, even the *piṇḍa* offering, the water libation (*udaka*), and whatever else [is prescribed for] the *śrāddha* is not desired.
As stated in the *Cintyaviśva*:
In that place, one should indeed cause the installation of a *liṅga* and so forth, or else [an image of] its form,
or a pedestal, or even a mural painting on a wall.
Or one should have a gabled temple constructed in that place; one should also perform the rites beginning with the invocation and ending with the offering of oblations and lamps.
Thus, the digging is declared; one should burn [the site] again as previously described.
Incidentally, the method for the installation of images for Brahmins and others has been stated.
In the *Kāmika*:
The Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra, as well as those of mixed or external castes— of these three [upper classes],
the king or [the priest] performs the consecration according to the injunctions of the Vedas.

Whether he be alive or even dead, one who is endowed with devotion to Bhava— having performed the *prakṛti* rite for him and having consecrated [the image], one should bring the ceremony to completion.
In the *Śivadharmottara*:

"For those who have attained the excellence of initiation (*dīkṣā*) yet are still bound by fetters (*pāśa*), who are radiant with self-qualities equal to Śiva himself, but are distressed by the fatigue of bearing the burden of the body and so forth..."
There is no other auspicious cause than the falling away of the body.
By means of this body, some attain supernatural powers (*siddhi*) and worlds, while others attain liberation at the time of dissolution;
having cast off the body at the end of that dissolution, this state of being abides within one's own self.
Likewise, in the Śivadharmottara:
"Having enjoyed extensive pleasures, when the dissolution has arrived, one casts off the sheath of the body and attains absolute liberation through knowledge."
The omniscient one, completely full and established in his own self,
should envelop all the paths, being complete and possessing the nature of the Lord.
In the *Brahmagītās* of the *Sūtasamhitā*, it is said: "The pure-souled one always performs the play of delight within the Self alone.
In the *Cintyaviśva*:

That bull among men who performs the installation of a devotee of Śiva shall attain prosperity, victory, and radiant splendor, and in the end, he shall obtain liberation through union with the Divine.

Thus ends the ritual for the final rites of Śaiva renunciants. At the beautiful peak of Kailāsa, the sage approached and stood before the one dwelling at the foot of the banyan tree, who was in the form of the Southern Image (Dakṣiṇāmūrti).
Agastya, Kāśyapa, Bharadvāja, Gautama,
and Kauśika [came] from the Supreme Lord for the sake of the true meaning of the scriptures.
Having understood this with delighted minds, all those sages,
as well as their infinite disciples headed by Sanaka, waited upon them.
Some, having attained the meaning of the scriptures, remained as heads of monasteries;
the fourth group, however, was established on the side of glorious Kailāsa.
Āmardaka, Puṣpagiri, Golakī, Raṇabhadra, and the venerable Sanatkumāra,
the lord of the Āmardaka monastery.
The Kadamba tree should indeed be for him who possesses the *saṃtānika* [lineage]; Puṣpagiri, Maṭhapati, Sanaka, Vṛkṣa, and Marjana [are likewise].
Some of his descendants were the Golakīnagnāyakas;
the sage Sanātana remains as a tree with Jambū leaves.
The lord of Raṇabhadra is called Sanātana; he is said to be the Nyagrodha tree, and those who belong to his lineage are the Kāśeyas.
On the bank of the Godāvarī river, his auspicious Santānikā groves exist;
in that place, from ancient times, Maṇḍaraka, Kāla, and others dwell, as does Śaṅkara.
Regarding the origin of those Śaiva teachers in particular:
there were the four monasteries (maṭhas) of Maṇḍarābī,
Mahīdā, Āmardakī, Puṣpagiri, Golakī, Raṇabhadraka, and the one known as Rājendra Cola.
The lord of the earth [stayed] on the sugarcane field.
Having come to bathe in the Gaṅgā and having seen those devoted to Śiva,
he then bathed and, while returning, took some of the Śaivas with him from that place.
Then we shall establish excellent Śaiva teachers in our own kingdom, so that they may spread everywhere throughout Kāñcī in the land of the Colas.
The great Guru, the head of the monastery in the lineage of Śrī Puṣpagiri, [is here]; many seekers of liberation belonging to his tradition reside here.
Then he composed the manual known as the *Kramaraktakamālā*; and in the debate on the Vidyā, he [established] the six categories under the name of the teacher Saundara.
In that region of Toṇḍīramaṇḍala, at the great site of Rudrakoṭi, there was one renowned as Ādiśaiva,
who lived according to the practice of the five limbs.
The great ascetic Vāmadeva, a resident of Śrī Vyāghrapura, was his elder brother; his younger brother was the great yogi Vedajñāna, a lord among sages.
Aiming for Bṛhatsabheśa, he reached the illustrious Tillivana together with many disciples and flourished there for a long time.
While King Sadāśiva was capable of protecting the earth, he had many dwellings constructed,
including gate-towers and other structures.
O Keśava, the venerable sage Vedajñāna composed the Drāviḍa and other works, as well as the Śivadharmottara and other scriptures.
In the glorious Tillivana, at the great site of Aruṇādri,
in the place known as Śrī Vṛddhācala, and at the great station of Madhyārjuna;
Where Śveta worshipped [the Lord] in the city of Ghaṭa in the White Forest (Śvetāraṇya), he established the Vedic scriptures in many places among the outcastes.
A certain son of his, named after him, was a learned scholar who composed the great work *Dīkṣādarśa* and an even more extensive *Paddhati*.
Out of compassion for embodied beings, he indeed established this traditional [system].
Thus ends the *Dīkṣādarśa*, composed by Vedajñāna, the son of Vāmadeva, a resident of Śrī Vyāghrapura.
Salutations to the venerable Guru, the crest-jewel of deities. Salutations to the venerable Guru Ṣaṇmukha.
